Florida court reverses felony murder charge for death of baby left in hot car
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
14:00:00 UTC
23:00:00 KST

A state appeals court in Florida reversed the felony murder conviction of a woman who accidentally left a baby in her car, resulting in the child’s death.
In July 2023, while babysitting four children from two different families, 46-year-old Rhonda Jewell forgot 10-month-old Ariya Paige was in the back of her car, and went inside to care for the other kids. Strapped into her carseat in the Florida summer heat, Ariya died of hyperthermia before Jewell realized her mistake. Jewell was convicted the following year of third-degree felony murder, predicated on the underlying felony of leaving a child unattended in a vehicle. She was sentenced to 17 years in prison.
On Wednesday, Florida’s first district court of appeal reversed Jewell’s convictions for third-degree felony murder and leaving a child unattended in a vehicle, finding that both required Jewell to have knowingly left Ariya in the car.
The charges against Jewell represented an attempt to dramatically expand the felony murder doctrine, a sweeping legal theory in which any individual involved in a felony that leads to a death can be held criminally responsible for that death. Nearly every state, as well as the federal government, has some form of a felony murder rule. These statutes have resulted in shocking outcomes: women being convicted of murders committed by their abusers, the friends of a 19-year-old boy who was killed by law enforcement being charged with his death and a man being held responsible for a fatal accident that occurred while he was handcuffed in the back of a police car miles away.
Defenders of the felony murder doctrine argue that even if an individual didn’t intend to kill anyone, because they made the choice to commit a felony that resulted in death, they should be held responsible for the resulting harm. But Jewell’s case represented a stark departure from this logic. At trial, jurors were told they did not need to find evidence that she intended to commit the underlying felony of leaving Ariya in her car – or even knew it was happening – in order to convict her of third-degree felony murder. In fact, jurors acquitted Jewell of aggravated manslaughter, the only charge they were told required a finding that Jewell acted in a way that showed reckless disregard for the baby’s life.
“This really takes tragic accidents and elevates them to murder offenses,” Caitlin Glass, a Boston University School of Law instructor, who co-authored an amicus brief in support of Jewell, told HuffPost.
More than 650 children in the US have died after being accidentally left in hot cars since 1990, when the rise of airbags prompted parents and caregivers to put young children in the back seat, according to Kids and Car Safety. The deaths follow a familiar pattern: the parent or caregiver is usually stressed, exhausted, distracted or navigating a change in routine. The baby is asleep and out of view in a rear-facing carseat in the backseat of the car.
Whether these deaths are treated as tragic accidents or punished as crimes is remarkably arbitrary – but it is exceedingly rare for prosecutors to bring felony murder charges in these cases. Amber Rollins, the executive director of Kids and Car Safety, told HuffPost she was aware of fewer than 10 cases in which the responsible adult was charged with felony murder after accidentally leaving a child in a car.
Jewell, who was close friends with Ariya’s family, struggled with depression, panic attacks and suicidal thoughts after the baby’s death. “I feel guilty if I laugh or smile. I just have so much guilt from that day,” she told HuffPost. “I don’t know how it happened. I just go over and replay it in my head and say, ‘what if’ or ‘why not,’ ‘Why didn’t I just – why? Why?’”
On Wednesday, Florida’s first district court of appeal appeared to reject the use of felony murder charges in accidental hot car deaths. “Third-degree felony murder cannot be based on an unenumerated predicate felony that does not require any proof of intent,” the court wrote in its opinion. “This case highlights how imperfect our criminal justice system is to adjudicate an accidental death. There are no winners here; moral outrage is not assuaged. And beneath the tragedy, the issues are legally important.”
Christine Monta of the MacArthur Justice Center, one of the lawyers representing Jewell on appeal, said in a statement: “Tragic accidents are not the equivalent of murder, and the court rightly recognized that Ms Jewell should not be criminally punished for an act that the State of Florida did not – and cannot – prove was knowingly and consciously done.”
The appellate court called for the case to be remanded to the trial court for a new trial. Brian Kramer, a Baker county state attorney deferred to the attorney general’s office, which did not respond to a request for comment. An attorney representing Ariya’s family in a civil suit did not respond to a request for comment.

The remains of Bulgarian Tsar Samuil were placed in a sarcophagus during a solemn ceremony at the St. Sofia Basilica in the Bulgarian capital. The memorial service was led by Patriarch Daniil.
“With reverence and filial respect, we welcome the sarcophagus containing the remains of one of the greatest and most worthy rulers of the Bulgarian people — Tsar Samuil”, Bulgarian Patriarch and Metropolitan of Sofia Daniil said during the service. At the end of his address, he called for eternal and blessed remembrance of the Bulgarian tsar.
PHOTO BTA
The sarcophagus, weighing around two and a half tons, is made of white marble quarried in the Prilep region of North Macedonia — lands that were part of Tsar Samuil’s state in the late 10th and early 11th centuries. It was crafted by a stoneworking company in Velingrad with the blessing of Bulgarian Patriarch Daniil. The sarcophagus was placed in the southern part of the church’s transept, near the altar.
The area around the Church of St. Sofia is also home to other memorials commemorating the era of Tsar Samuil. In front of the basilica stands a monument to Tsar Samuil by sculptor Aleksandar Haytov, unveiled in 2015, while opposite it is the sculptural composition “Samuil’s Blinded Soldiers” by Lyubomir Dalchev, dating from the 1970s.

Unknown

Controversial American media personality Tucker Carlson has continued his string of increasingly extreme remarks, questioning in an interview with a former British lawmaker published over the weekend why Britain fought Nazi Germany in World War II. 
Carlson argued that Hitler’s invasion of Poland followed a territorial dispute over former German lands, saying “the UK had nothing to do with it at all.”
Watch the interview excerpt starting at 31:53:
The interview was with former Conservative Party lawmaker Jacob Rees-Mogg and focused on his support for sending aid to Ukraine in its war with Russia. The discussion turned to the killing of innocent civilians, with Rees-Mogg saying: “I think it’s very difficult to have fought the Second World War without innocent people being killed.”
Carlson replied: “I've never understood why fight the Second World War in the first place.”
He went on: “Hitler said that 15% [of Poland] was once Germany and it was given to Poland at the Treaty of Versailles. That was German territory with Germans in it. That was his case. And by the way, that was true.”
Carlson continued: “I’m certainly not here defending Hitler. I’m just saying the idea that Hitler just randomly rolled into Poland is a lie and everyone believes it because they know nothing about the actual facts. But the truth is, Germany had big pieces of it carved off, including part of Prussia and it was given to this other country. It infuriated the Germans. Maybe it shouldn’t have, but it did. And that was a justification for it. The UK had nothing to do with it at all.”
Rees-Mogg sought to defend Britain’s decision to enter the war, while Carlson insisted that the British “destroyed their empire and their country fighting this war that they still pretend was a good idea, but it wasn’t.”
The exchange then continued:
Rees-Mogg: “It was fundamental. It was the classic good-versus-evil.”
Carlson: “Has the UK benefited from it?”
Rees-Mogg: “We did the right thing.”
Carlson: “Is it a better country than it was?”
Rees-Mogg: “To have defeated Hitler? Yes.”
Carlson: “So the UK is a better country now? It’s a healthier country now?”
Rees-Mogg: “Otherwise, we’d all be speaking German.”
Carlson: “Who cares? There are a lot of people in Britain who can’t speak English. So it would be nice to have, like, at least a European language spoken in your country.”
Rees-Mogg: “No, I see no advantage of speaking German over any other language. We want to speak English, thank you so much.”
Carlson, formerly a popular Fox News host, has for years been one of the most prominent voices on the populist right in the United States and until a few years ago was considered a staunch supporter of President Donald Trump. Their relationship has deteriorated in recent years, reaching a low point amid Carlson’s opposition to the war in Iran.
At around the same time, against the backdrop of close ties between the United States and the Netanyahu government, Carlson began promoting antisemitic and anti-Israel conspiracy theories about Jewish power and influence in politics, the media and other spheres. In July, he announced that he would establish a new party and declared: “Israel is destroying my country.”

G7 leaders agreed on Friday to release 100 million barrels of diesel and crude after US pressure on Europe, with supplies squeezed by Iran's restrictions on shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.
The International Energy Agency said Saturday that member countries had so far released 325 million barrels of oil and oil-derivative products from strategic reserves, from the 400 million barrels promised in March.
The update came a day after G7 leaders, in a statement issued by French President Emmanuel Macron's office, agreed in coordination with the IEA to immediately release 100 million barrels of diesel and crude oil, following US pressure on Europe to tap its reserves and ease supply concerns caused by the US-Iran war.

Donald Trump's administration has been pressuring allies to release diesel reserves to ease a spike in prices for the fuel, being felt in America and elsewhere.
The war in the Middle East has squeezed diesel supplies, with Iran restricting shipping through the Strait of Hormuz in response to US and Israeli attacks.
The market has also been hit by Ukraine's strikes on Russian refineries, as Kyiv hits back against Moscow's own attacks.

Exiled Russian filmmaker Zvyagintsev takes aim at Putin's war in Oscar bid
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
13:58:30 UTC
22:58:30 KST

Exiled Russian filmmaker Zvyagintsev takes aim at Putin's war in Oscar bid
PARIS, Oct 3 - Exiled Russian filmmaker Andrey Zvyagintsev takes on Vladimir Putin's war in Ukraine in "Minotaur", a drama about conscription and moral compromise released nearly five years after Moscow launched its full-scale invasion.
The film, which won the Grand Prix at the Cannes Film Festival this year and is an entry for the 2027 Oscar for best international film, is released as debate persists over Russia's ability to sustain troop numbers in a conflict that has left hundreds of thousands dead or wounded.
One scene shows Russian conscripts boarding a bus for the front, with a father saying goodbye to his teenage son, while the mother of another screams in anguish. Later, the image of an older recruit appears on a roadside billboard: he is dead and celebrated as a war hero.
The story centres on Gleb, the owner of a logistics company who is coming to grips with his wife having an affair, while being pressured by the local mayor to identify 14 employees for military service.
Unwilling to send his existing workers to the front, he recruits new drivers with promises of high salaries, only to dispatch them straight to the war.
"For a director who has lived there, was born there, and speaks only Russian ... how could he not talk about what has become the main, if not the most important, event of recent years?" Zvyagintsev said of himself in an interview with Reuters.
The 62-year-old director, best known internationally for "Leviathan" and "Loveless", both Oscar nominated, now lives in France, having left Russia in 2021, months before Moscow launched what it calls its special military operation in Ukraine.
PROPAGANDA VERSUS SOFT POWER
"Minotaur", produced in France, is in Russian but its topic means it will never be officially released in Russia. Zvyagintsev is sceptical anyway that it can shift opinion about the war. Support in Russia for the military campaign in Ukraine remained above 70% in 2026 polling by the Levada Center, although 67% of respondents also favoured peace negotiations.
"Propaganda is like a heavy hammer, like pliers, like an anvil. It's a very crude instrument," he said.
"Art, on the other hand, deals with subtleties. This soft power works over the long term."
Moscow has avoided another compulsory mobilisation since its politically damaging 2022 call-up, relying instead on recruitment drives and signing bonuses, though some analysts say a fresh mobilisation cannot be ruled out.
Videos of Russia's mobilisation campaigns posted online helped shape the screenplay, Zvyagintsev said. Unable to shoot in Russia, where he has not returned since suffering a severe bout of COVID-19 in 2021, he used a Latvian town as a stand-in.
"I don't think that after 60 years of life experience a person can suddenly lose touch with reality in just one year," he said.
Critics have described "Minotaur", which opens in French cinemas on October 14, as one of Zvyagintsev's most overt commentaries on Russia's political and moral condition.
"This is all we could do: tell the story as we see it and find the human being in this unbearable state of compromise," he said.
In August, Russia designated Zvyagintsev a "foreign agent", a label applied to public figures accused by authorities of carrying out anti-Russian activities with foreign support.
He declined to comment on what impact the designation might have on him personally or professionally.
FROM CHABROL TO UKRAINE
Zvyagintsev had originally sought to remake French director Claude Chabrol's 1969 thriller "La Femme Infidele" ("The Unfaithful Wife"), about a husband who suspects his wife is having an affair.
But when the rights were finally secured and work on the screenplay began in 2022, Russia's invasion of Ukraine transformed the project.
Chabrol's suburban Paris setting became a bleak Russian town, and the domestic tensions of the original story were recast against the backdrop of war.
"I realise now that we were simply lucky that in 2018-2019 we weren't able to acquire the rights," he said. "If we had made the film in 2018, it would have been completely different." REUTERS

Ukraine receives €50m from Council of Europe bank and Italy for destroyed housing compensation
Ukraine has received €50 million under the Council of Europe Development Bank (CEB) project HOME: Compensation for Destroyed Housing. The funds will be used to finance housing certificates under the state-run eRecovery programme.
Source: Ukraine's Ministry of Finance; European Pravda
Details: CEB provided €25 million, and another €25 million was contributed with financial support from the Italian government.
The framework agreement on the second additional financing for the HOME project was signed on 26 June during the Ukraine Recovery Conference (URC-2026) in Gdańsk.
The total volume of the new financing package is €100 million, half of which – €50 million – is being provided by the Italian government through the CEB mechanism.
Ukraine previously raised €200 million under the earlier stages of the HOME project. These funds financed over 6,000 housing certificates for citizens who lost their homes as a result of the war.
Background:
- At the end of September, the international Register of Damage caused by Russian aggression against Ukraine opened all 43 categories envisaged by its mandate for the submission of claims. This marked the completion of the phased launch of the claims submission system, which began in April 2024.

Elmo Nüganen: Burning Dostoevsky won't burn down the Russian world
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
13:50:00 UTC
22:50:00 KST

Elmo Nüganen: Burning Dostoevsky won't burn down the Russian world
Actor and director Elmo Nüganen, who in recent years has been closely involved with Südalinna Teater (formerly the Russian Theater in Tallinn), says he understands those who do not wish to consume Russian‑language culture — but avoiding Russian‑language culture will not destroy what Russia as a state is.
This autumn is a busy one for Nüganen. A few weeks ago, VAT Theater premiered Merle Karusoo's documentary production "Kui juuri raiutakse…" ("When Roots Are Cut…"), in which Nüganen also appears on stage as an actor. The production brings to the stage the family stories of Estonian theatre makers with Ingrian Finnish roots.
According to Nüganen, being on stage as himself is a different kind of experience. The process of creating the production has also been different, because, he says, the issue is not what is being talked about, but how it is done.
"You have to stay within a certain frame. Merle had quite a hard time with me. She mentioned the metaphor of a trotting race several times: if someone breaks into a gallop during a trotting race, they get disqualified. She hinted to me repeatedly during rehearsals that I should be disqualified here, because there is a certain established form or expectation of how an actor exists on stage in this kind of story," Nüganen said.
How much the actors reveal about themselves to the audience was up to each performer. "Merle has great experience with these kinds of works, and she always asks at a certain stage whether everyone agrees that what has been said so far will remain, or whether someone wants to remove a topic," he explained. In this production, no one removed anything.
Last year, Nüganen staged "Jumalad" ("Gods"), a production about the war in Ukraine, at Südalinna Teater. He said the theatre was a good place for it because he wanted to stage the work in two languages — Estonian and Russian.
"I don't think I've ever had a theatre project where I could think so broadly about which actresses of different generations would fit into the story, regardless of which theatre they come from. Their individuality is such that their combination could be as interesting and unique as possible," he said.
This Friday, Südalinna Teater will premiere Johan Elm's production of Jaan Kruusvall's final play "Kõrberebase elu" ("Life of the Desert Fox"), with Nüganen playing the lead role. As in Kruusvall's other texts, this one also contains many undercurrents, he noted.
"The situation is contemporary in the sense that what runs underneath in this story is very similar to what is running underneath in our society right now," the actor said, lifting the veil slightly.
The production is performed in Russian with simultaneous translation into Estonian. Nüganen says he also understands those who do not wish to attend Russian‑language cultural events.
"My hand doesn't reach for Dostoevsky either — his books stand untouched on my shelf," he said. "If some people think that way and stay away, then in the big picture it doesn't matter — they can burn the books, but burning Dostoevsky won't burn down the Russian world. These are separate things. I understand the person who doesn't want to hear Russian, doesn't want to pick up a Dostoevsky book, but unfortunately that doesn't annul anything."
In addition to his theater work, Nüganen is once again active at the drama school, where he has taken on a new class this year. He says his feelings toward the group are good: "There's no confusion in me, no excessive anxiety — just a calm, steady start."
--

PARIS – France will step up its support for efforts to eradicate Ebola in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot said on Oct 3 during a visit to a region hit by the virus, warning that it could quickly resurge if vigilance waned.
Barrot made a rare trip by a Western leader to the north-eastern Congolese city of Bunia, where a laboratory-confirmed case of mpox was identified in mid-September.
France allocated €13.4 million (S$19.3 million) to the fight against Ebola between January and July.
Barrot said he would propose additional humanitarian funding for Ebola during upcoming French budget discussions.
France’s response came through humanitarian aid, medical research and the PRISM programme launched during President Emmanuel Macron’s 2023 visit.
A national humanitarian conference is to be held in Paris on Oct 6, during which Ebola is to be discussed.

Barrot praised the Congolese authorities, UN agencies, humanitarian organisations and medical workers for containing the epidemic and preventing it from spreading to major urban centres in Congo and beyond.
“There is no need to fear or worry. First and foremost, we must fight the epidemic where it emerges,” Barrot said when asked whether it could spread after a case was reported in France. REUTERS

This protective enzyme could help stop fatty liver disease from getting worse
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
13:46:11 UTC
22:46:11 KST

This protective enzyme could help stop fatty liver disease from getting worse
- Date:
- October 3, 2026
- Source:
- Cedars-Sinai
- Summary:
- Scientists have identified an enzyme that may act as a natural defense against the worsening of fatty liver disease, which affects an estimated 100 million Americans. The enzyme, called UBE2N, helps liver cells clear away damaged mitochondria and break down fat, potentially preventing the inflammation, scarring, and cell damage associated with the more dangerous condition MASH.
- Share:
Researchers co-led by Cedars-Sinai Health Sciences University have identified an enzyme that may help protect the liver from the damage that can occur as the most common form of liver disease becomes more severe. The findings, from a preclinical study published in Nature Metabolism, could eventually support new strategies for preventing serious liver injury and progression toward liver failure.
An estimated 100 million people in the U.S. have metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD), formerly called nonalcoholic fatty liver disease, according to the American Liver Foundation. Roughly 20% to 25% of those affected go on to develop metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH), a more serious form of the condition in which excess liver fat is accompanied by inflammation, cell injury and scarring.
Why MASH Is Difficult to Treat
Current care mainly centers on lifestyle changes and efforts to limit additional liver damage. Although medications are available, treatment options are still limited, and there is currently no cure for MASH.
Earlier research has suggested that damaged mitochondria, the structures that produce energy for cells, may contribute to the development and progression of MASH. In the new multicenter study, Cedars-Sinai researchers found that levels of an enzyme called UBE2N decline in liver cells as the disease becomes more advanced.
"The UBE2N enzyme appears to protect the liver from the inflammation and damage associated with MASH by helping remove damaged mitochondria and supporting the breakdown of fat," said Ekihiro Seki, MD, PhD, professor of Medicine and Biomedical Sciences at Cedars-Sinai and co-corresponding author of the study. "When levels of the enzyme fell, we saw more damaged cells and injury to the liver."
Restoring UBE2N Reduced Liver Damage in Mice
The researchers then restored UBE2N to normal levels in the livers of laboratory mice. After doing so, they observed reductions in fat accumulation, inflammation and scarring.
Those results suggest that UBE2N could become a potential treatment target for preventing MASLD from advancing to MASH.
"The identification of this enzyme's role in regulating mitochondria in the liver is an important advance in understanding steatotic liver disease," said Shelly Lu, MD, the Women's Guild Chair in Gastroenterology and director of the Karsh Division of Gastroenterology and Hepatology at Cedars-Sinai. "Future studies can test whether enhancing this protective pathway can complement existing treatments, identify patients most likely to benefit and lead to new therapeutic approaches for preventing advanced disease."
Additional Cedars-Sinai authors include Michitaka Matsuda, So Yeon Kim, Takashi Tsuchiya and Yoon Seok Roh.
Additional authors include: Feng Wang, Jin Lee, Jeong-Su Park, Meizhou Huang, Hwan Ma, Guoyan Sui, Zixiong Zhou, Xufeng Wu, Haram Lee, Soohwan Oh, Hanseul Park, Key-Hwan Lim, Chun-Woong Park, Sang-Bae Han, Jin Tae Hong and Michael Karin.
Funding: This work was supported by the National Research Foundation of Korea (grant nos. RS-2025-02273102 and RS-2025-02603096), Regional Innovation System & Education (RISE) programme of Chungbuk (grant no. 2025-RISE-11-014-03), the Pinnacle Research Award of American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases (AASLD, to J.L.), the San Diego Digestive Diseases Research Center (SDDRC) Pilot/Feasibility Grant (NIDDK P30 DK120515, to J.L.), the National Institutes of Health (grant nos. R01DK085252, R01DK138591 and R01CA301632) and the National Natural Science Foundation of China (grant no. 82404726).
Story Source:
Materials provided by Cedars-Sinai. Original written by Laura Coverson. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Feng Wang, Jin Lee, Jeong-Su Park, Meizhou Huang, Hwan Ma, Guoyan Sui, Zixiong Zhou, Michitaka Matsuda, So Yeon Kim, Takashi Tsuchiya, Xuefeng Wu, Haram Lee, Soohwan Oh, Hanseul Park, Key-Hwan Lim, Chun-Woong Park, Sang-Bae Han, Jin Tae Hong, Michael Karin, Yoon Seok Roh, Ekihiro Seki. UBE2N deficiency contributes to MASH development via p62-regulated mitophagy and PANoptosis. Nature Metabolism, 2026; 8 (9): 1926 DOI: 10.1038/s42255-026-01590-0

Series of drone attacks disrupt power supply near Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Plant, IAEA says

Series of drone attacks disrupt power supply near Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Plant, IAEA says
The Zaporizhzhia Thermal Power Plant (ZTPP), whose switchyard helps supply electricity to the Russian-occupied Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant (ZNPP), was targeted in a series of drone attacks in recent weeks, the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) said on X on Oct. 3.
The ZTPP and the ZNPP have been occupied by Russia since the start of the full-scale war in 2022.
The IAEA did not specify in its statement who carried out the attacks, only saying that they occurred on Sept. 19, 20, and 27. The strikes damaged transformers considered vital for maintaining the ZNPP's off-site power supply.
To enable repairs at the ZTPP, IAEA Director General Rafael Grossi is negotiating a new localized ceasefire between Ukraine and Russia, hoping to put it into effect soon.
It would be the eighth IAEA-brokered ceasefire aimed at securing the ZNPP's off-site power supply. The facility has faced repeated external power outages since Russia's full-scale invasion began.
An attack on Sept. 22 reportedly disabled an off-site radiation monitoring station, reducing the ZNPP's ability to monitor nearby radiation levels, the IAEA said.
Other attacks hit buildings in the Russian-occupied city of Enerhodar, where many ZNPP staff live, reportedly killing one person.
The Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant is Europe's largest nuclear power plant and among the 10 largest in the world. Ukraine has repeatedly warned that Russia's occupation of the plant poses one of the greatest threats to nuclear safety — not just in Ukraine, but worldwide.
The IAEA warned in May 2026 that increased drone activity near the ZNPP intensified the risk of a nuclear accident at the site.
In August, the agency also reported that a drone exploded at a bus stop used by ZNPP staff, killing one person and injuring 15 others.

US to deploy NMESIS anti-ship system on Japanese island closest to Taiwan for first time
Unprecedented deployment to Yonaguni, 110km from Taiwan, during joint drills this month comes amid high tensions between Beijing and Tokyo
3-MIN READ3-MIN
2
 Listen
The US is set to deploy one of its signature anti-ship missile systems to the Japanese island closest to Taiwan, an unprecedented move that comes as tensions in the region between Beijing and Tokyo continue to simmer.
The ground-based US uncrewed missile platform known as the Navy-Marine Expeditionary Ship Interdiction System (NMESIS) will be deployed on Yonaguni Island in Japan’s Okinawa prefecture during biennial joint exercises this month, according to the regional bureau of the Japanese defence ministry.
It will mark the first NMESIS deployment on Yonaguni, Japan’s westernmost island lying just about 110km (62 miles) from the eastern coast of Taiwan, although the US military operated the system elsewhere on Okinawa last year.
The deployment during the Keen Sword joint exercise moves the system closer to Taiwan than during the Resolute Dragon joint drills in September last year. Then, NMESIS was stationed on Okinawa’s Ishigaki Island – roughly 127km east of Yonaguni and about 240km from Taiwan.

Iran climbs to sixth at Asian Games 2026
TEHRAN - Iran finished in sixth place at the Aichi-Nagoya 2026 Asian Games, collecting 19 gold, 18 silver and 15 bronze medals, taking its total to 52 medals in the overall standings.
Iran's latest gold came in dramatic fashion on Saturday as the men's volleyball team defeated Japan 3–1 in the final. The victory secured Iran's fourth consecutive Asian Games volleyball title and gave the country its 19th gold medal of the competition. Amin Esmaeilnezhad led Iran with 22 points in the final.
Wrestling has been one of the main sources of Iran's gold medals. Yones Emami won the men's freestyle 74kg title after defeating Japan's Yoshinosuke Aoyagi 9–5 in the final. Emami's victory was Iran's 17th gold medal at the time.
Shortly afterward, Amirali Azarpira added another wrestling gold in the men's 97kg freestyle category. Azarpira dominated Uzbekistan's Sherzod Poyonov 10–0 in the final to claim Iran's 18th gold medal.
Freestylers Mohammad Nokhodi in 86kg and Amirhossein Zare in 125kg had previously won two golds. Also, Alireza Abdeval in 77kg and Amin Mirzazadeh in 130kg had also seized two gold medals in Greco-Roman for the Iranian delegation.
Iran's success has not been limited to wrestling. Arian Salimi won the men's +80kg taekwondo gold medal after defeating Uzbekistan's Marat Mavlonov 2–0 in the final. His victory was Iran's 16th gold of the Games. Saghar Moradi had previously won the women's 67kg taekwondo title, giving Iran another gold in the sport.
Other important Iranian gold medalists in weightlifting include Ali Davoudi, who claimed gold in the men’s 110kg and Ali Alipour in the men’s 95kg category.
Kurash athlete Majid Vahid Barimanlou won a gold medal in the men’s -66kg.
Iran has also collected medals in climbing, padel, kabaddi, boxing, fencing, gymnastic,canoe spring, shooting, climbing, and 3x3 basketball.
Kimia Zarei and Zeynab Norouzi seized a gold medal in the women's lightweight double sculls as well as a gold medal in women's lightweight singles sculls won by Fatemeh Mojallal. Mohammadreza Tayebi in men’s shot put, Morteza and Mahmoud Nemati in karate, Iran’s Esports, and Soheil Mousavi in wushu snatched also gold medals in the Games.
With 19 gold, 18 silver and 15 bronze medals, Iran's 52-medal haul places it among the leading teams at Aichi-Nagoya 2026. The final standings may still change as the remaining events are completed, but the performances of athletes including Yones Emami, Amirali Azarpira, Arian Salimi, Saghar Moradi, Alireza Abdevali, Ali Davoudi and the men's volleyball team have already made Iran's campaign one of the country's significant Asian Games performances.
At the top of the Asian Games medal table, China, Japan and South Korea occupy the first three positions, earning 169, 83 and 39 gold medals, respectively . China has built its lead through a large number of gold medals across numerous sports, while host nation Japan has also produced a substantial medal haul. South Korea remains among the leading Asian sporting nations.
Japan's strong performance has made the host country one of the central stories of the Games. Its rivalry with China and South Korea has been visible across several disciplines, while Iran has continued to challenge the leading Asian nations in sports such as wrestling, volleyball and taekwondo.
The Iranian men's volleyball team's victory over Japan was particularly significant because it not only delivered another gold medal but also completed an undefeated campaign. Iran defeated Kyrgyzstan, Thailand, Indonesia, South Korea and Pakistan on its way to the final before beating Japan 3–1.
Iran had finished seventh in the previous edition, gaining 13 gold, 21 silver and 20 bronze medals.

Showers and storms across Spain this weekend, floods kill 102-year-old woman
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
13:40:27 UTC
22:40:27 KST

A 102-year-old woman has died and about 90 people were rescued in Madrigueras, Albacete, after floods dumped 142 l/m². Rain will persist, with a new storm possible in the west on Sunday.
A 102-year-old woman died and 90 people had to be rescued on Friday in Madrigueras, in the province of Albacete, after flash flooding swamped the entire town.
According to a statement from the regional government, the municipality recorded 142 litres of rain per square metre, a level that forced the deployment of a large emergency operation. The regional authorities also activated the Adverse Meteorological Risk Plan (METEOCAM) at operational level 1.
In the house where the victim was found, the water reached a height of one metre. During the afternoon and the early part of the night, emergency services carried out around 90 rescues, mostly of people in homes affected by the build-up of water. The regional government said it had received numerous calls from residents who "were frightened and did not know how to act".
Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez expressed his support on X. "All my love to the relatives of the woman who has died as a result of the flooding, and all our support and solidarity to the affected residents," he wrote. The president of Castilla-La Mancha, Emiliano García-Page, is in Madrigueras on Saturday, where the Civil Guard is working on clean-up operations.
Storms over the weekend
Heavy rain fell during the night and on Friday morning in Tarragona and Castellón, especially in the Lower Ebro area, where most of the problems were concentrated. On Friday afternoon, orange alerts were in place in Tarragona, the Valencia region and the Balearic Islands, and also in the Region of Murcia and in the provinces of Almería, Granada and Albacete, for storms that could be strong and bring hail. The unsettled weather is spreading to more areas of the peninsula and will continue throughout the weekend.
Saturday may start with further heavy rain along the Tarragona coast, where a red alert has already been issued for torrential rain, as well as in Extremadura, Salamanca, the Central System and Aragon. From midday, and especially in the afternoon, showers and thunderstorms could reach virtually any part of the peninsula.
They will again be intense and accompanied by hail in some places, namely the Iberian System, the south-eastern sierras, the Pyrenees, the north-western quadrant, the Balearic Islands and the Mediterranean coast. They will be less likely in western Galicia and in the Canary Islands. Temperatures will rise in Galicia, Aragon, Navarre, the Basque Country and the Canary Islands, fall in Catalonia, the Balearic Islands and inland Spain, and remain unchanged elsewhere.
On Sunday, the unsettled conditions will continue, with widespread rain and thunderstorms and the possible formation of a DANA, a slow-moving high-altitude low that can bring torrential rain over the western half of mainland Spain. This does not mean that the rainfall will be heavier than in recent hours in Tarragona or Castellón, but it does make it more likely that these conditions will be repeated or spread to other areas. Only along the Galician coast are largely clear or slightly cloudy skies expected.
During the early hours, showers and storms could be heavy along the Cantabrian coast, in the Balearic Islands and in Catalonia. Later, locally heavy showers will become widespread across much of central and northern Spain, and will be less likely in the southern third. The Canary Islands will remain largely unaffected. Temperatures will change little compared with Saturday, with the weekend still feeling warm.

Russian Billionaires Fund 1% of State Budget in ‘Voluntary’ War Levy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
13:40:00 UTC
22:40:00 KST

Russia’s wealthiest business executives have financed more than 1 percent of total federal government spending this year through coordinated “voluntary” donations arranged following a closed-door meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin, official state budget documents revealed.
According to Reuters, the financial transfers, registered in Russian treasury dispatches as “voluntary receipts,” have injected 471 billion rubles (approximately $5.63 billion) into the federal budget so far in 2026.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The capital infusions have provided emergency fiscal relief to the Kremlin as swelling military expenditure and ballooning state borrowing expand the federal budget deficit to more than double the government’s baseline targets.
According to budget records, Russia’s federal deficit will reach 3.2 percent of gross domestic product this year, totaling 7.3 trillion rubles ($87.2 billion), compared to an initial statutory projection of 1.6 percent of GDP. Treasury calculations indicate that without the billionaire contributions, the shortfall would have widened to 3.4 percent of GDP.
The informal levies were negotiated during a confidential March assembly between Putin and Russia’s foremost industrial oligarchs, most of whom are subject to Western sanctions. While the Kremlin did not publish an official attendee roster, Putin confirmed in September that “hundreds of billions” of rubles had been transferred to state accounts following the consultation.
Lukashenko Calls Himself, Putin ‘Co-Aggressors’ in Ukraine
According to Kremlin accounts, an unnamed corporate executive proposed the initiative, arguing that because prominent Russian industrialists accumulated their fortunes through state-backed privatization schemes during the 1990s, they bore a civic obligation to subsidize state expenditures during wartime.
The revenues derived from the voluntary assessments exceeded the proceeds collected through Russia’s corporate windfall profit taxes, which were levied primarily on metallurgical and fertilizer conglomerates benefiting from elevated global commodity benchmarks.
Emergency revenue mechanisms
The voluntary billionaire contributions coincide with an aggressive state-directed campaign to seize and liquidate private commercial assets to finance the war effort.
Russian fiscal planners anticipate securing 385 billion rubles ($4.6 billion) in 2026 from the resale of nationalized or confiscated commercial enterprises, representing the most extensive redistribution of corporate property in the Russian Federation since the post-Soviet privatizations of the 1990s.
The Russian Prosecutor General’s Office has justified the seizures by citing historical regulatory infractions, corruption investigations, and prohibited foreign ownership across designated strategic sectors.
To manage the widening fiscal gap, Moscow implemented substantial tax increases and raised domestic sovereign borrowing throughout 2025, prioritizing expenditures dedicated to the armed forces and security services, which are projected to consume 38 percent of total federal outlays this year.
As the full-scale war in Ukraine nears the end of its fifth year, Russian finance authorities have prepared further structural tax increases for 2027 alongside administrative crackdowns on domestic tax evasion schemes.
Among the incoming fiscal measures is a revised levy on personal bank deposit interest designed to generate an estimated 1 trillion rubles ($11.9 billion) in revenue, capturing returns from citizens capitalizing on prolonged double-digit central bank interest rates.
Record 2027 defense allocations
The reliance on ad hoc corporate levies arrives as the Kremlin prepares an unprecedented expansion of military spending for the 2027-2029 budget cycle, compelling severe expenditure reductions across civilian infrastructure, education, and public healthcare.
Under draft federal budget legislation submitted to the State Duma on Sept. 30, Russian military spending will escalate to 17.1 trillion rubles ($204.4 billion) in 2027 – a 27 percent increase over previously enacted multi-year fiscal targets and the highest nominal defense allocation enacted since the February 2022 invasion.
Over the full three-year planning framework, Moscow projects cumulative military appropriations to approach 50 trillion rubles ($597.8 billion).
Defense-related lines are projected to absorb more than a third of all federal outlays in 2027, surpassing the aggregate combined allocations for healthcare, education, and social policy.
Independent fiscal analyses indicate that defense expenditures absorbed 43.8 percent of federal disbursements during the first half of 2026, compared to less than 20 percent prior to the full-scale invasion.
To sustain the military budget, the draft statute imposes structural cutbacks across social sectors relative to prior multi-year projections. Spending on public education is slated to contract by roughly 6 percent, social welfare policy by 7 percent, and healthcare programs by nearly 7 percent.

ESA’s Juice just used Earth as a slingshot to Jupiter
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
13:34:11 UTC
22:34:11 KST

ESA’s Juice just used Earth as a slingshot to Jupiter
- Date:
- October 3, 2026
- Source:
- European Space Agency (ESA)
- Summary:
- ESA’s Juice spacecraft raced past Earth on September 28, using our planet’s gravity to dramatically reshape its path toward Jupiter without burning much fuel. The flyby changed its direction by 20 degrees and increased its speed by 3.5 km/s, while also giving scientists a rare chance to test its instruments on Earth and the Moon.
- Share:
The European Space Agency's Jupiter Icy Moons Explorer (Juice) made a close pass by Earth on September 28, skimming the outer reaches of the atmosphere and using our planet's gravity to reshape its path toward Jupiter while consuming very little fuel.
The carefully planned gravity assist changed Juice's direction by 20° relative to its previous trajectory and increased its speed by 3.5 km/s. During the four weeks leading up to the encounter, mission controllers needed to make only one small course correction (out of six opportunities set aside) to place the spacecraft on the precise approach needed to take full advantage of Earth's gravity.
Controllers began monitoring Juice particularly closely on August 17 and will continue that intensive tracking through October 10.
Juice Makes a Close Pass Over Earth
Juice reached its closest point to Earth at 13:45 CEST (11:45 UTC) on September 28. At that moment, the spacecraft passed just 8640 km above the Indian Ocean while taking a sequence of images with its onboard monitoring cameras.
"The flyby required ultra-precise navigation in real time. Thanks to our very careful planning, we used only a small amount of the propellant reserved for this flyby," says Angela Dietz, Juice's Spacecraft Operations Manager. "This gives us more to use at Jupiter to carry out observations of the planet's icy moons."
Preserving that fuel is especially valuable because Juice will eventually need it while carrying out its ambitious scientific campaign around Jupiter and its moons.
Earth Becomes a Test Site for Juice
Changing the spacecraft's trajectory was the primary purpose of the flyby, but the encounter also gave the mission team a valuable chance to test Juice's science instruments using a real planetary target.
This was the third such opportunity during the mission. The first came during Juice's 2024 lunar-Earth gravity assist, followed by the spacecraft's 2025 observations of Comet 3I/ATLAS.
Teams from ESA's spacecraft operations, science operations and technical centers spent months coordinating with the outside groups responsible for Juice's 10 scientific instruments. Their goal was to carefully schedule when each instrument could operate and extract as much science and calibration time as possible from the spacecraft's limited resources.
"Juice's journey to Jupiter provides only a few opportunities to calibrate and validate the instruments under well-understood environmental conditions," explains Juice project scientist Claire Vallat, who led the effort.
"Given the limited time available and operational constraints, instrument activities sometimes have to be prioritized, for example when Juice was in Earth's shadow this morning, and relying on battery power alone. During this flyby, calibration activities were prioritized based on their relevance to preparing the instruments for their work at Jupiter, while also considering whether an opportunity is unique or can be scheduled later in the journey."
Preparing for Jupiter's Icy Moons
Although the Earth encounter required extensive preparation, it is relatively simple compared with what awaits Juice at Jupiter. The spacecraft is scheduled to carry out 35 flybys of the giant planet's large moons Ganymede, Callisto and Europa.
Planning for those encounters began years in advance. For the Europa flybys, discussions about how the instruments will operate began about 10 years ago and will continue until Juice finally passes the moon in the early 2030s.
Earth therefore serves as an important rehearsal. Scientists can use the flyby to calibrate the instruments, learn how they behave once they are operating in space (where they always work a little differently to on Earth!), and refine the tools that will later be used to analyze the data.
The encounters with Jupiter's icy moons will be much more scientifically demanding. By then, Juice will need to be ready to capture as much high-quality information as possible during each precious flyby.
Juice Explores Earth's Magnetic Tail
The spacecraft also spent several days traveling through Earth's magnetotail, the long extension of Earth's magnetic field that stretches away from the Sun.
That gave Juice an opportunity to measure magnetic fields and electrically charged particles far from Earth. At the same time, the European-Chinese Smile mission has been observing the northern lights while measuring magnetic fields and particles much closer to the planet.
Combining measurements from Juice and Smile could give scientists a rare way to link activity deep in Earth's magnetotail with events occurring around the planet's polar regions.
Scientists expect to release images and spectra from some of Juice's instruments in the coming weeks, once the data have reached Earth and instrument teams have had time to evaluate them. Among the anticipated results are high-resolution images of Earth and the Moon taken by JANUS, Juice's scientific camera.
Juice Will Return to Earth One More Time
Juice is not finished with Earth yet.
In January 2029, the spacecraft will return for a third and final flyby of our planet. That encounter will place Juice on the final trajectory needed to reach Jupiter in 2031.
About Juice
ESA's Jupiter Icy Moons Explorer, 'Juice', is humankind's next bold mission to the outer Solar System. It will make detailed observations of gas giant Jupiter and its three large ocean-bearing moons - Ganymede, Callisto and Europa. This ambitious mission will characterise these moons with a powerful suite of remote sensing, geophysical and in situ instruments to discover more about these compelling destinations as potential habitats for past or present life.
Juice will monitor Jupiter's complex magnetic, radiation and plasma environment in depth and its interplay with the moons, studying the Jupiter system as an archetype for gas giant systems across the Universe.
Juice launched on an Ariane 5 from Europe's Spaceport in Kourou in April 2023. It has an eight-year cruise with flybys of Earth and Venus to slingshot it to Jupiter. It will make 35 flybys of the three large moons while orbiting Jupiter, before changing orbits to Ganymede.
Story Source:
Materials provided by European Space Agency (ESA). Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

Iran stone industry targets $5b exports as 18th intl. stone exhibit opens in Mahallat-Nimvar
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
13:31:35 UTC
22:31:35 KST

Iran stone industry targets $5b exports as 18th intl. stone exhibit opens in Mahallat-Nimvar
TEHRAN- Bahram Shokouhi, Head of the Iran Stone Association, said Iran’s stone industry has the capacity to generate at least $5 billion in foreign currency earnings and exports if its potential is properly guided and supported.
Speaking at a press conference for the 18th Iran International Stone Exhibition in Mahallat and Nimvar, he said this capacity, combined with job creation, could make the stone industry more prominent in the national economy.
The exhibition will be held from October 6 to 9, focusing on block stones and products from Iran’s stone industry. More than 600 domestic and foreign companies are participating. It covers about 120,000 square meters, with more than 45,000 tons of block stone offered. Trade delegations from Russia, Pakistan, Turkey, India, and Egypt have been invited.
Shokouhi said that for the first time a stone service desk will be set up with experts from the Deputy for Mining Affairs, the Trade Promotion Organization, the Mining Engineering Organization, and representatives of the Iran University of Science and Technology. Specialized panels, training workshops, cultural and artistic programs, the campaign “Behind Every Stone Is a Life,” and discussions on risks in the stone industry and family issues of activists are among other programs.
He noted that the Stone Headquarters, previously the Stone Policy Council, has been reactivated with the association’s follow-up and the cooperation of the Ministry of Industry, Mining and Trade. It examines exploration, extraction, processing, and export issues. The 14th meeting of the National Stone Desk and a joint meeting of the Mining Commission of the Iran Chamber with the Arak Chamber will be held on the sidelines.
Shokouhi, who also heads the Mining Commission of the Iran Chamber, pointed to new technologies entering Iran’s stone industry. One is cutting machines using wires as thin as dental floss, currently used for soft stones, which can increase extraction and processing efficiency while reducing waste. He said this technology can create about 35 to 40 percent more recovery from block stone and reduce finished costs.
He stressed the need to reduce the carbon footprint in the stone industry. Programs include training and developing environmental product passports, courses on carbon footprint, and active participation at the COP31 climate summit in Antalya. The goals are lower carbon emissions, lower production costs, and a competitive advantage for Iranian stone exporters.
Shokouhi also mentioned the formation of the World Stone Federation. With cooperation among stone associations from various countries, a global stone alliance and federation has been formed to strengthen natural stone’s position in global markets. One goal is to create a carbon passport or ID for stone, determining carbon emissions from extraction at the mine to destination, so the natural stone industry can strengthen its global position based on this data.
On production and export statistics, Shokouhi said that in 1403, about 10 to 12 million tons of stone were produced in Iran, but export value was only about $230 million. Compared with the approximately $42 billion value of global stone exports, Iran’s share is very limited. About 85 percent of produced stone is processed and consumed domestically, and nearly 15 percent is allocated to exports, of which about 5 percent is exported as block and 10 percent as cut stone. Turkey, by contrast, produced about 15 million tons of stone in 2025 and exported nearly 41 percent of its production.
Shokouhi said the Iran International Stone Exhibition can introduce the diversity of Iranian stones to foreign buyers. Instead of visiting different mines across the country, buyers can see, choose, and order products in one place. Offering stone blocks in global markets can pave the way for recognition and, later, development of processed stone exports.
He called fuel shortage one of the serious problems of mines. A significant part of mining machinery is old and high-consumption, and last year fuel distribution was announced about 25 percent less than stated need. As a result, some mines bought fuel from the free market and in some cases faced smuggling-related cases.
Referring to transportation problems under wartime conditions, Shokouhi said long truck queues at land borders and stopped shipments can cause exports to face penalties and loss of customers. Coordination with neighboring countries is needed to speed up truck passage, and special routes or a “green lane” should be considered for export shipments that have customers. During the exhibition, some stone shipments reached their destination late due to customs and transportation problems, and with coordination between the Iran Stone Association and Customs, part of these shipments were cleared and transferred out of turn.
Shokouhi emphasized that the main demand of economic activists is to reduce barriers and cumbersome regulations so producers and exporters can continue. In the current situation, the issue of the stone industry is no longer merely development; rather, it is maintaining existing production and employment, and removing barriers can help continue activity.
Ziba Yazdani, Secretary of the Iran Stone Association, said that if the goal is synergy, economic growth, and business development in the stone industry, no link in the chain can be ignored, and the Iran International Stone Exhibition can be the connecting link. She noted the difficult conditions of holding the 18th edition, saying that continuing the event when even some more ordinary exhibitions were not held shows its importance for the economy and related businesses. The association participated in planning and execution within its responsibility for coordination and paving the way for business development.
Yazdani said five specialized panels are planned: Iran’s stone industry in the carbon era, a stone block is not raw, multi-wire technology, social issues of miners’ families, and export development solutions. Booth layout began about a month ago, and more than 2,000 executive operations have been considered for preparing and holding the exhibition.
Ali Joudaki, Head of the Industry, Mine and Trade Organization of Markazi Province, pointed to the region’s capacities for hosting the exhibition. He said holding it in Mahallat is an important advantage because a significant part of the country’s stone mines is concentrated there. About 70 percent of Iran’s stone mines whose products are exportable are located within a 300-kilometer radius of Mahallat. The exhibition venue is next to the stone export terminal, allowing trade delegations and foreign buyers to view products and have suitable access to mines and production capacities.
Joudaki continued that the stone economy chain—from exploration and extraction to processing, supply, export, and sales—must be fully formed so the industry has economic justification. Given the region’s mining capacities, access to mines, export terminal, and existing facilities, the Mahallat exhibition can become a platform for introducing Iran’s stone industry and increasing the country’s share of global markets.
Hassan Khazaeipour, Governor of Mahallat, referred to the county’s diverse capacities in tourism, agriculture, and industry. With more than 150 active mines and about 300 stone processing units, Mahallat is one of the important hubs of the country’s stone industry, and the 18th exhibition is an important opportunity to introduce these capacities. With a population of more than 65,000, Mahallat is an important tourism area of Markazi Province and has capacities such as the Abgarm area, production of ornamental flowers and plants, and production and export of ornamental fish. More than 900 hectares of the county’s lands have been allocated to greenhouse cultivation and production of ornamental flowers and plants.
Khazaeipour said more than 14 percent of the world’s travertine stone is located in the Abbasabad area of Mahallat County, and holding the international stone exhibition in Nimvar is a valuable opportunity to introduce this capacity and develop export markets. So far, the presence of activists from about eight countries, including India, Portugal, Bangladesh, China, Turkey, Russia, and Armenia, has been announced. Last year, stone industry activists from 27 provinces attended. This year, the exhibition will also be held in an area of about 120,000 square meters.
Abbas Karbalaei, a private sector activist in the stone field, said the complex has been launched as the country’s first exhibition site with 100 percent private sector investment and the participation of miners and stone industry activists. Alongside the International Stone Exhibition, the country’s first export terminal in the stone field has also been launched in this complex so that necessary infrastructure for export development and a more active presence in international markets is provided.
Mohammad Hallajian, organizer of the 18th Iran International Stone Exhibition, said the brand of the Iran International Stone Exhibition, Mahallat–Nimvar, has been introduced in more than 10 countries over the past 12 years, and it is the only Iranian stone exhibition included in the global calendar of exhibitions in this field. With about 38,000 square meters of net exhibition space and about 45,000 tons of products, it has a notable record among specialized stone exhibitions worldwide in terms of stone brought in. More than 600 entities, including companies and mines from 27 provinces, are present.
Hallajian continued that considering about one thousand active building stone mines in the country, more than 400 mines are present. Service desks with the Deputy for Mining Affairs of the Ministry of Industry, Mine and Trade, the Mining Engineering Organization, the Iran Trade Promotion Organization, and the Iran University of Science and Technology are being held to provide specialized answers on exploration, extraction, export, foreign exchange commitments, and supply of machinery. He also announced the unveiling of Iran’s first quartzite mine at the exhibition, saying Iran has a special position in diversity of building stones, and the discovery and introduction of Iranian quartzite can help complete the chain of mineral diversity.
The Executive Director of the Exhibition referred to cultural and social programs. The campaign “Behind Every Stone Is a Life” will be unveiled to support and educate the families of miners who are away from their families for long periods due to work conditions, and it is planned to be developed nationally with the support of the Iran Stone Association. Artistic programs including music, calligraphy, painting, and sculpture with stone will also be held so that the cultural and artistic capacities of this natural material are introduced alongside its industrial and mining capabilities.

Pentagon’s new religious office faces watchdog challenge
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
13:29:54 UTC
22:29:54 KST

Pentagon’s new religious office faces watchdog challenge
The Freedom From Religion Foundation (FFRF) has announced plans to launch a probe into a new religious affairs office recently unveiled by US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth.
The Wisconsin-based nonprofit said on Thursday that it is seeking transparency into the office’s funding, operations and plans to assess troops’ “spiritual fitness.”
The announcement came shortly after Hegseth said the Pentagon was establishing the Office of Religious Affairs (ORA) to address what he described as a decline in religious community in the military following an era of “political correctness.”
In his State of the Force address on Wednesday at Marine Corps Base Quantico in Virginia, Hegseth said the new office’s head is expected to serve as the secretary and deputy secretary’s chief adviser on religious affairs.
Hegseth argued that the military had previously prioritized “political correctness and secular humanism” over religion, with “secular careerists in cubicles and lawyers running around with red tape” overseeing service members’ spiritual lives instead of military chaplains.
According to the memorandum signed by the secretary earlier this week, the office is tasked with aligning religious-affairs policy, overseeing the Armed Forces Chaplains Board, representing the department to civilian religious endorsing organizations, and sponsoring research and tools to “support and assess spiritual fitness, spiritual readiness, and spiritual resilience.”
The FFRF said it will use the Freedom of Information Act (FOIA), which allows the public to request records from US government agencies, to seek documents on the office’s funding, budget and staffing. The group also wants records on how the Pentagon defines and plans to assess “spiritual fitness,” “spiritual readiness” and “spiritual resilience,” including any technologies or tools being considered. The requests will also cover ties to outside religious groups and records concerning atheist, humanist and other nonreligious service members and potential First Amendment issues.
Americans United for Separation of Church and State President and CEO Rachel Laser said Hegseth’s new office would elevate Christianity’s role in shaping US military policy. She also accused him of using his position to advance what she described as a “Christian Nationalist agenda” in the military.
Hegseth’s personal Christian beliefs have previously drawn media attention, with some analysis arguing that they are increasingly influencing US military policy.
In March, The Washington Post cited former senior military officials and experts on religion and law as saying that Hegseth’s religious policies had challenged longstanding norms limiting the promotion of a particular faith. The war secretary reportedly held monthly evangelical services at the Pentagon at the time, while department employees were reluctant to discuss concerns related to his religious campaign.
Earlier this year, the Pentagon, at Hegseth’s initiative, cut the number of recognized religious denominations and belief systems for service members from 211 to 31. The department’s latest official breakdown from 2019 shows that about 70% of active-duty service members identified as Christian, 2% as atheist or agnostic, and 24% as having no religious affiliation or an unknown religious affiliation.

Grandmother and granddaughter killed by Russia in Kyiv home where three generations grew up
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
16:24:00 EEST
22:24:00 KST

Grandmother and granddaughter killed by Russia in Kyiv home where three generations grew up
Yevheniia, 45, and her 94-year-old grandmother Mariia were killed in a Russian drone strike on a house in Kyiv on 30 September. The evening before the attack, Mariia took medication because she was worried about a possible missile strike.
Source: Yuliia Haharina, a relative of Yevheniia and Mariia, chemist and founder of the Laborantki scientific and creative association, on Facebook
Details: A Russian Shahed drone detonated in the bedrooms of the house where three generations of the family had grown up.
The evening before yet another Russian attack, Yevheniia, an aunt of Yuliia's, turned on the gas boiler and gave Mariia her medication. That evening, Mariia felt anxious after warnings of a possible missile strike.
At about 03:00, the family heard the sounds of an aerial attack. A Russian drone later struck their home, where the three women were staying. Only Yehor, a nephew of Yuliia's, was not at home: he had gone to a friend's house for a sleepover.
Quote from Yuliia: "Businka [Yevheniia's beloved dog – ed.] was hiding on grandma's bed. My aunt texted everyone for the usual roll call: 'How are you?', saw the replies and went to the toilet. She came out and the next thing she saw was a brick wall flying at her.
The Shahed detonated literally in Zhenia's [short for Yevheniia – ed.] and grandma's bedrooms. The bricks were scattered like Lego, you couldn't see the ground under them at all. The beautiful wooden ceilings, which our grandfathers were so proud of, caught fire, and the fire was still being put out the next day."
Details: Yuliia said the family home, damaged by the Russian strike, was built in the 1950s by her two grandfathers, who were brothers.
Quote from Yuliia: "They put it together from bricks, wood and, as they used to say, 'from bottles of vodka', which they gave in exchange for building materials."
Details: She says everyone lived peacefully in the house for the most part, recalling a funny childhood incident with her cousin Zhenia as an example of "discord".
Quote from Yuliia: "I was about seven years old. I ran to my aunt in the kitchen, shouting: 'Zhenia hit me right in the heart with a pig!' The 'pig' was a rubber baby doll that she threw at me. The adults told this story at family dinners for a long time."
Details: Her grandmother was the oldest resident on the street, where she helped locals as a family doctor. The woman left her profession after she turned 70 to take care of her great-granddaughter, and later her grandson Yehor.
On the evening of 29 September, Mariia had everyday worries: she was anxious that she might not have time to plant garlic before the cold weather set in. She did not dare to do it herself, fearing she would get into trouble with her relatives.
The family was worried that Mariia might fall again and break her hip. This had already happened a month before the full-scale war began. After a successful operation, the woman was even able to move around independently, although she needed a walking stick.
In those days, her granddaughter Zhenia, who had only recently celebrated her birthday, was happy because she had bought new curtain magnets, carefully chosen to match the newly redecorated room.
Quote from Yuliia: "She was a Virgo, she loved making the space around her beautiful. She used to tease me: 'How does your husband live with you?' (he is also a Virgo). I would reply that only my childhood with her allowed me to be understanding towards my husband. The secret to a happy life: respect your neighbour's neurosis as your own. She definitely had this match with her husband."
Details: A farewell ceremony for the women will be held on 4 October at 10:00 at the crematorium of the Baikove Cemetery.
Background: A Russian attack on 30 September killed two people and injured five others, two of whom had to be taken to hospital.

====================================================================================================

Ukraine fired its first FP-7 ballistic missile in combat. Its maker says next version will do what Ukraine needed since 2022
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
13:21:56 UTC
22:21:56 KST

- Ukrainian forces have fired a Fire Point FP-7 ballistic missile in combat for the first time
- The launch heralds a new phase of the wider war: the ballistic phase
- Soon both Ukraine and Russia will be able to bombard each other with hard-to-intercept missiles
Ukraine has fired its new Fire Point FP-7 ballistic missile in anger for the first time, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky announced on Thursday, 1 October.
Kyiv hasn't said what the missile targeted or how much damage it caused. The Wall Street Journal, citing an unnamed source, reported that it struck a target in Russian-occupied Ukraine. Zelensky was ecstatic on social media. "Thank you for the result," the Ukrainian president wrote. "Next up: production. Glory to Ukraine!"
The FP-7 can hit back at Russia, but it can't stop the Iskander ballistic missiles Russia fires at Ukrainian cities. Its twin is meant to. Fire Point is building an interceptor version, the FP-7.X, as the core of Freyja, its bid for a cheaper alternative to the American Patriot, and the company aims for a first ballistic missile interception by mid-2027.
Kyiv drone- and missile-maker Fire Point, most famous for its FP-1 and FP-2 one-way attack drones and FP-5 Flamingo cruise missiles, has been hard at work on ballistic missiles for at least a year. Ballistic missiles can cost millions of dollars per round, making them much more expensive than a $50,000 drone or $500,000 cruise missile.
But the extra expense buys a lot more destructive potential. An FP-1 packs a 60-kg warhead; an FP-7's warhead weighs about 200 kg. While an FP-1 might motor as far as 1,000 km, it's slow and fairly easy to shoot down. An FP-7 possesses less range—up to 250 km under the best conditions—but it streaks through the atmosphere at several times the speed of sound, making it extremely difficult to intercept.
The only Russian air defense systems that stand any chance of swatting down an incoming FP-7 are also among the most in-demand in the Russian inventory and thus the most over-stretched: the S-400 surface-to-air missile batteries.
Ukrainians know better than anyone the kind of damage and terror ballistic bombardment can inflict. Since effectively running out of Patriot surface-to-air missiles earlier this year, Ukraine has been unable to defend itself against weekly Russian bombardment that now usually includes several Iskander ballistic missiles.
The Russian bombardment threatens to disrupt commerce, throttle electricity generation, and grind down Ukrainian morale at a critical juncture in Russia's wider war on Ukraine. Ukrainian troops are holding their own along the 1,200-km front line, but behind the front line everyday Ukrainians are suffering under missile and drone impacts.
That suffering will only get worse as winter closes in, temperatures drop, and the Russians resume intensive attacks on the electrical grid, potentially depriving millions of people of household heating. Ukrainian batteries firing FP-7s can't directly prevent Russian attacks. But they can retaliate for the attacks.
Expect the ballistic tit for tat to intensify. It may not be the first Ukrainian ballistic missile fired in anger: in June, Russia said it shot down a Ukrainian ballistic missile over Moscow, and Kyiv never said what it was. But the FP-7 is the first Kyiv has confirmed using in combat, and it has the range and payload to inflict serious damage on targets inside Russia. But an even more powerful Ukrainian missile, the Fire Point FP-9, is coming soon. It reportedly ranges 850 km with an 800-kg warhead.
Trending Now
The ballistic phase
The FP-7 can smash Russian depots, air bases, and factories in oblasts bordering Ukraine. The FP-9 could wreak havoc as far as Moscow. The only major constraint on the Ukrainian bombardment will be Fire Point's production capacity, and Kyiv's ability to finance that production.
The Ukrainians will be incentivized to produce as many FP-7s—and, later, FP-9s—as possible. The same factories that produce surface-to-surface FP-7s will also churn out a surface-to-air variant, the FP-7.X.
That missile, which is overall similar to the standard FP-7 but includes a sophisticated seeker head, is the main munition for Ukraine's new mostly homemade air defense system being developed by Fire Point and various foreign partners under the auspices of the European missile defense program Freyja.
Ukraine has five ways to stop Russia’s Iskanders. Only one arrives before the strikes on the grid begin
If the FP-7.X works as advertised and Fire Point can scale production, it could bolster Ukraine's defenses against Russian ballistic missile strikes while the standard FP-7 and its bigger cousin the FP-9 retaliate for Russian ballistic missile strikes.
A new phase of the wider war is about to begin—the ballistic phase, where both sides can pummel the other with hard-to-intercept missiles.
The side that makes the most and best missiles, for offense and defense, will prevail in the coming ballistic fight.

Feature: "Auntie Basketball" brings Chinese culture to Utah high school
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
21:20:44 CST
22:20:44 KST

by Xinhua Writer Gao Shan
WASHINGTON, Oct. 3 (Xinhua) -- Forget the traveling call, just run with the ball. Forget about winning or losing, just enjoy the game.
Cheers, applause and laughter filled the gym at Crimson Cliffs High School in Washington, Utah, on Friday as a women's basketball team from Guizhou Province in southwestern China took on the school's team in a highly unusual game that brought together two groups of young people - and two cultures - on the same court.
The visiting team, known as "Auntie Basketball," comes from a grassroots sporting tradition that originated in the Miao villages of Leishan County in southeastern Guizhou.
In the Miao community, women who have married and returned to their hometowns are affectionately called "Gu Ma," or "aunties." What began as a recreational activity for women returning home has gradually grown into a showcase for Guizhou's ethnic culture and rural vitality.
Unlike conventional basketball, Auntie Basketball has its own playful rules: Players can carry the ball and run with it rather than having to dribble.
The result is less about the intensity of competition and more about fun, community and participation.
Before the game, the gym came alive with songs from the Miao villages and energetic traditional dances. Dressed in colorful ethnic costumes, the visiting players performed for hundreds of students and teachers, drawing enthusiastic applause from the crowd.
But the biggest excitement came when the players took the court.
The aunties faced Crimson Cliffs' Mustangs, whose mascot is the mustang, in what quickly became a lighthearted cultural exchange through basketball.
The American players initially struggled to adjust to the unusual rules, particularly the idea that they could run while carrying the ball instead of dribbling. But their solid fundamentals and teamwork soon kicked in.
Fast-paced plays, quick passes and accurate shots kept the game lively, with the two teams trading baskets and giving the crowd plenty to cheer about. The chants from the stands grew louder: "Go, Gu Ma!" in Chinese and "Go, Mustangs!" in English.
At one point, a tall Crimson Cliffs student dressed in a shirt and tie joined the aunties on the court. His exaggerated, "wild" and playful style of play sent the crowd into fits of laughter and pushed the atmosphere to another level.
Reagan Haws, a Crimson Cliffs player, said that she found the game "really fun," especially because of the unusual rules.
"It was just like a new experience. It was great to see the other cultures," she added.
Crimson Cliffs Principal Kim Monkres welcomed the Chinese team to the school and said the visit provided an opportunity for cultural exchange between the two countries.
"I'm just so thrilled that we have the opportunity to bring Chinese culture together with ours," she told Xinhua.
"The dual language program in our school has been such a blessing. It's one of my favorite classes to sit in to. I have no idea what they're saying, but the kids do."
Monkres said seeing how much the students have learned over the years and how fluent they have become in Chinese is "truly phenomenal."
Monkres also expressed enthusiasm about China's plan to invite 100,000 young Americans to visit China for exchange and study programs over the next five years, saying she hopes Crimson Cliffs will have an opportunity to participate.
Shen Xin, vice president of the Chinese People's Association for Friendship with Foreign Countries, who led the Auntie Basketball delegation to the United States, said the sport's grassroots and entertaining nature makes it an effective way to bring people from the two countries closer together.
"It can help American people get a closer look at the everyday lives of ordinary people in China and learn more about the country's diverse ethnic cultures and traditions," Shen said, adding that he believes such people-to-people exchanges can help strengthen the foundation of China-U.S. relations.
The Auntie Basketball team's U.S. tour, which began earlier this week, includes stops in California, Nevada, Utah and Washington state. ■
