FTA with Eurasia is a new capacity for expanding trade exchanges: TPO head
TEHRAN- The Head of the Iran Trade Promotion Organization (TPO), referring to the holding of three important economic-trade events in Belarus, described the free trade agreement with the Eurasian Economic Union as an important capacity for expanding trade exchanges between Iran and the member states of the union.
According to the Public Relations Office of the Iran Trade Promotion Organization, Mohammad Ali Dehghan Dehnavi, noting the Islamic Republic of Iran’s observer membership in the Eurasian Economic Union and the signing of the free trade agreement between Iran and the member states of the union, said: “This agreement has provided considerable capacity for expanding economic and trade exchanges.”
Referring to Iran’s presence at the Innoprom 2026 International Industry Exhibition in Belarus, he added: “The national pavilion of the Islamic Republic of Iran in this edition of the exhibition is among the large and notable participants in this event, and after the host country, Iran has been allocated one of the largest pavilions of the exhibition.”
The Head of the Iran Trade Promotion Organization also described the holding of the 19th Joint Commission on Iran-Belarus Economic Cooperation and the presence of an Iranian delegation at the meeting of the prime ministers of the Eurasian Economic Union as an opportunity to pursue and develop bilateral and multilateral cooperation.
It is worth noting that during this trip, the Islamic Republic of Iran, by participating in the meeting of the prime ministers of the Eurasian Economic Union, the Belarus International Industry Exhibition Innoprom 2026, and the 19th Joint Committee on Iran-Belarus Economic Cooperation, pursued the development of trade and economic cooperation with the member states of the Eurasian Economic Union.
Presence of 20 Iranian companies at Belarus International Exhibition
The international exhibition of industrial capabilities and innovations, known as “Innoprom 2026,” has been held in Minsk, the capital of Belarus, while 20 Iranian companies, in addition to displaying their achievements, have also commemorated the memory of the Minab martyrs.
According to IRNA, citing the Iranian Embassy in Belarus, these Iranian companies operate in various fields, including petrochemicals, oil and gas, petroleum refining, steel, mining, and joint investment.
According to this report, Mohsen Omidzamani, Iran’s Ambassador to Belarus, visited this industrial exhibition and the pavilions of Iranian companies.
During this visit, the Ambassador of the Islamic Republic of Iran in Minsk, while visiting the pavilions of Iranian companies, met with the managers and representatives of these companies and was informed about their latest capabilities, products, and export and investment capacities.
At this exhibition, which concluded on October 1, in addition to Iran and Belarus, companies from Russia, Uzbekistan, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, and the Republic of Azerbaijan participated in this industrial and economic event.
Innoprom is the title of an international industrial exhibition in Belarus that annually brings together representatives from various industries, innovative companies, investors, and government organizations.
Iran-Belarus automotive cooperation in testing and inspection
On the sidelines of the Innoprom International Exhibition and with the presence of the Head of the Iran Trade Promotion Organization, a cooperation memorandum of understanding was signed between the automotive testing centers of Iran and Belarus with the aim of improving safety standards and research and development infrastructure in the automotive industry.
According to the Public Relations Office of the Iran Trade Promotion Organization, during the specialized meetings of the Joint Commission of Iran and the member states of the Eurasian Economic Union and on the sidelines of the Belarus Innoprom International Exhibition, a cooperation memorandum of understanding was signed between the automotive testing centers of Iran (ISQI) and Belarus (Centromash) with the aim of improving safety standards and research and development infrastructure in the automotive industry.
It is worth noting that this memorandum was signed at the venue of the Eurasian Joint Commission and in the presence of high-ranking officials of the two countries, including the Minister of Industry of Belarus, Mohammad Ali Dehghan Dehnavi, Head of the Iran Trade Promotion Organization, and Farshad Moghimi, Chairman of the Executive Board of the Industrial Development and Renovation Organization of Iran (IDRO). The conclusion of this document indicates the serious will of Tehran and Minsk to move beyond mere trade cooperation and enter the phase of technological cooperation in the automotive industry value chain.
The main focus of this cooperation is interaction between the main vehicle testing and crash testing centers of the two countries. Centromash is recognized as one of Belarus’s main and reputable arms in the field of standardization, technical inspections, and advanced automotive tests. With the implementation of this memorandum, the two sides committed to closely cooperate in areas such as upgrading crash test equipment, joint research, facilitating the issuance of approvals, the supply chain, and etc.
This memorandum was signed at a time when economic ties between Iran and Belarus are on a path of development within the framework of Eurasian cooperation. The closeness of Iran’s engineering capacities to Belarus’s laboratory and standardization capabilities not only reduces research and development costs for automakers but can also serve as a model for expanding exports to the member states of the Eurasian Economic Union. The signing of this document on the sidelines of the “Innoprom” exhibition—recognized as one of the most reputable industrial exhibitions of Russia and like-minded countries—indicates the two sides’ strategic view toward using international platforms to break monopolies in technological fields and achieve self-sufficiency in supplying automotive safety standards. It is expected that with the implementation of the provisions of this memorandum, the process of quality improvement, safety enhancement, and export opportunities for Iranian automotive products, by using Centromash’s specialized capabilities, will accelerate further and the ground will be paved for a stronger presence of Iran’s automotive industry in target markets.

Pakistan summoned India's chargé d'affaires on Saturday over the killing of two Pakistani civilians by Indian border forces, Pakistan's Foreign Ministry said.

Two Pakistanis were killed and another wounded in the shooting near the international frontier separating the two countries.

Neither India's External Affairs Ministry nor the BSF immediately responded to requests for comment.

The sources said the three were unarmed and had not attempted to cross the border fence.

Pakistan called on India to conduct an "immediate, transparent and credible" investigation into the shooting and take disciplinary and legal action against anyone found responsible.
The ministry also asked New Delhi to formally communicate the findings of the investigation and any action taken to the Pakistani government.
Islamabad urged India to "strictly observe relevant bilateral arrangements and established border procedures" and exercise maximum restraint in dealing with incidents along the frontier. It also called for measures to prevent similar incidents from recurring.
Some Indian media reports described the incident as an attempted "infiltration" that had been foiled by border forces.
Pakistan's Foreign Ministry rejected that account, saying it "categorically" opposed any attempt to describe those killed as "infiltrators."
The incident comes amid longstanding tensions between the nuclear-armed neighbours, whose heavily guarded border has witnessed periodic security incidents and exchanges of accusations.

Thousands of Bulgarians from all parts of the country, along with visitors to Bulgaria, filled Prince Alexander I Square in front of the Royal Palace in Sofia for the state ceremony marking the arrival from Greece of the remains of one of Bulgaria’s most renowned medieval rulers, Tsar Samuil (997–1014).
PHOTO BGNES
The ceremony was attended by Prime Minister Rumen Radev, President Iliana Iotova, and three former Bulgarian presidents — Georgi Parvanov, Petar Stoyanov and Rosen Plevneliev. Former prime ministers, ministers, deputy ministers, GERB leader Boyko Borissov, We Continue the Change leader Assen Vassilev, Patriarch Daniil, Sofia Mayor Vasil Terziev, as well as numerous MPs, politicians and public figures, were also present. The Bulgarian national anthem was performed, followed by a 21-gun artillery salute.
PHOTO BTA
The return of the Bulgarian tsar’s remains was made possible after six decades of negotiations between Bulgaria and Greece. They were transported from Greece to Sofia aboard a Spartan military aircraft, which was escorted through Bulgarian airspace by two pairs of MiG-29 and F-16 fighter jets. The formation flew over Prince Alexander I Square greeted by cheers and applause from the crowd.
At Vasil Levski Airport in Sofia, Tsar Samuil’s remains were received by a guard of honor and carried to the square by the Bulgarian Armed Forces.
To the sound of the Guards Brass Band, the coffin containing Tsar Samuil’s remains was placed on a platform at the center of the square.
PHOTO BTA
“Before us are the remains of Tsar Samuil. He was destined the heavy burden of defending his homeland on the Balkan Peninsula, bordering the mighty Byzantine Empire, enduring attacks from behind by those close to him while also guarding our eastern and southern borders…
The old capital, Preslav, fell, and Samuil and his brothers inherited a weakened Bulgaria. Samuil was destined to wage wars in defense of Bulgarian identity, enduring the pain of his wounds alongside his soldiers. Centuries later, it was precisely his arm, which had healed improperly, that helped archaeologists establish his identity on the island of St. Achillius.
He spent his days on horseback in order to preserve the unity of the Bulgarian state. The final chapter in the life of our great ruler is worthy of a biblical tragedy. In 1014, Samuil was wounded and died upon seeing his blinded soldiers. What greater nobility could there be in the heart of a ruler, torn apart by the sight of his soldiers’ suffering?”, Prime Minister Rumen Radev said during his speech, as quoted by BGNES.
PHOTO BGNES
From Prince Alexander I Square, the remains will proceed in a procession to the Church of St. Sofia.

In an official dispatch, Moscow warned foreign citizens, including accredited representatives of foreign diplomatic missions, against staying in Kyiv or traveling into Ukrainian territory.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The Russian foreign ministry claimed that its armed forces would systematically escalate the aerial bombardment, characterizing the operations as sustained “massive retaliatory strikes.”
The warning from Moscow marks an explicit rhetorical escalation against foreign embassies operating in Kyiv, arriving amid an intensified wave of ballistic missile and jet-powered drone barrages directed against the capital’s central administration districts, river crossings, and municipal utility networks.
Diplomatic threats
The Russian statement directly follows international reporting regarding potential contingency protocols among Western embassies stationed in the capital.
The Guardian reported that senior Western diplomats had drafted contingency blueprints to evacuate personnel from Kyiv to the western city of Lviv or across the border into eastern Poland if the Kremlin commenced deliberate kinetic strikes against foreign diplomatic representations.
Lukashenko Calls Himself, Putin ‘Co-Aggressors’ in Ukraine
Western diplomats cited in the report stated that while missions publicly maintain an unbroken diplomatic presence to prevent handing Moscow a symbolic victory, private assessments warned that the capital’s security posture is deteriorating rapidly ahead of winter.
The Ministry of Foreign Affairs of Ukraine (MFA), however, refuted claims that foreign representations were preparing to withdraw.
Ukrainian MFA spokesperson Heorhii Tykhyi confirmed on Friday that established international diplomatic protocols mandate formal prior notification to host governments before any mission relocates, emphasizing that zero transfer notices or appeals had been submitted by foreign missions in Kyiv.
Despite recurrent air raid alerts and collateral damage to surrounding urban infrastructure, allied diplomatic missions have maintained continuous operations in Kyiv since returning in mid-2022 following the defeat of Russian forces around the capital.
The US Department of State, while maintaining its Level 4: “Do Not Travel” advisory for Ukraine due to active hostilities, reaffirmed that the US Embassy in Kyiv remains open, staffed, and operational.
Infrastructure targeting
Moscow’s threats to the diplomatic corps coincide with a concerted aerial offensive aimed at paralyzing Kyiv’s civilian life-support systems, transit arteries, and transport infrastructure.
On Friday, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko warned that maintaining basic municipal functions under unrelenting missile and drone attacks has become an urgent matter of “safety and survival” for the city’s three million residents. 
Klitschko warned that municipal authorities can no longer operate under peacetime assumptions as strikes batter bridges, energy facilities, and residential districts.
The mayor’s warning was underscored by consecutive drone strikes against strategic river crossings spanning the Dnipro River. 
Municipal authorities were forced to shut down vehicular traffic across the South Bridge on Friday after repeated loitering munition hits damaged the roadway and protective barriers shielding the Green Line metro crossing. 
On Saturday morning, a Russian jet-powered drone struck the North Bridge, severing overhead trolleybus cables and damaging the roadway surface to sever westbound commuter traffic.

Putin claims Russia seized 1,301 square kilometers of Ukrainian territory in September, sharply diverging from ISW data
This is reported by the ISW (Institute for the Study of War), according to Ukrinform.
Infographic: ISW
Analysts drew attention to Putin’s statement on October 1 during a meeting of the Valdai Club. He claimed that in September 2026 alone, Russian troops seized 1,301 km² of Ukrainian territory—2.5 times more than Russia’s claimed territorial gains in previous months.
At the same time, the ISW analyzed the available evidence and concluded that in September 2026, Russian forces suffered net territorial losses of 80.81 km². And if one also takes into account the Russian troops’ advances into areas over which they have not established full control, Russia’s net territorial losses in September amounted to 175.18 km², analysts note.
“Putin’s absurd statements continue to paint a fabricated picture of the fighting, supporting the Kremlin’s cognitive warfare aimed at falsely portraying the Russian offensive as large-scale across the entire battlefield,” the analysts write.
The ISW notes that it cannot assess whether Putin is aware of the inaccuracy of the figures he cites or whether he simply accepts the fabricated data on the course of hostilities provided to him by the Russian military leadership—data that is fed to him through a culture of deception deeply ingrained in the Russian military command structure.
However, the analysts state that Putin’s claims about the successes of Russian troops on the front lines in September 2026 are so far removed from reality that they more closely resemble hallucinations.
As reported by Ukrinform, on August 23, 2026, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky stated that 820 km² of Ukrainian territory had been returned to Ukrainian control since the beginning of the year. He also emphasized that, as of that moment, Russia had occupied 990 km² since the start of the year and that Ukraine expects to reach parity in terms of territory by the end of the year.

Ethiopian gov’t forces advance in Tigray as rebels retreat: What to know
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
13:00:57 UTC
22:00:57 KST

Ethiopian gov’t forces advance in Tigray as rebels retreat: What to know
Military and pro-government forces recapture main airport in Tigray’s capital as fighting also rages in Amhara and Afar regions.
Ethiopia’s military and pro-government forces have recaptured the main airport in Mekelle, the capital of Tigray, as the government forces advanced in the northern region after more than a week of intense fighting.
Fighting erupted last week between the federal government of Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed and the Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) and its allies, shattering the fragile Pretoria Agreement, a peace deal signed in November 2022.
The fighting has stoked fears that it could escalate into a wider regional conflict, potentially drawing in neighbouring countries in the Horn of Africa.
This is what you need to know about the latest developments:
What is the latest on the fighting?
Ethiopian troops regained control of Alula Aba Nega Airport in Mekelle, a source with knowledge of the events in the city and a humanitarian source told the Reuters news agency.
The airport, about 10km (6 miles) east of the centre of Mekelle, was one of three airfields in the region that were seized by rebel forces at the start of the fighting on September 23.
A third source, a Mekelle resident who asked not to be named for security reasons, confirmed government forces had retaken the airport and added that gunfire could be heard outside the city centre.
This source reported seeing some fighters from the TPLF abandoning their posts and heading home and said looting of government facilities was taking place in the city.
This was also confirmed by a local journalist who told the AFP news agency the “TPLF militants and leaders are leaving Mekelle.”
The journalist added that government offices and police stations had also been left without security personnel.
A local resident told AFP that he was concerned “government and public property could be exposed to looting”.
“Lawlessness could spread in the city, and I am also afraid for my life. I want us to quickly return to law and order,” another resident said.
On Friday, Al Jazeera’s bureau chief in Ethiopia, Mohammed Taha Tawakel, reported that forces loyal to the federal government have made significant gains in Tigray, taking control of several towns and closing in on Mekelle.
Where is the fighting taking place?
The fighting has occurred on several fronts across northern Ethiopia that stretch across the Tigray, Amhara and Afar regions.
Last week, the Tigray Peace Force, an armed group composed of Tigrayan fighters aligned with the federal government, said it had captured the town of Alamata.
Alamata is important because it sits near Tigray’s southern border with Amhara and serves as a supply hub for troops, fuel and food. Control of the town could allow federal forces to push north towards Mekelle.
The offensive in Afar could threaten supply routes from Djibouti, through which most Ethiopian imports, including fuel, pass.
The fighting in Afar also comes amid allegations of direct Eritrean involvement.
Ethiopia has accused Eritrea of backing armed groups opposed to its government. Eritrea has rejected the accusations
Fighting has also spread into Amhara, including around North Wollo. The Ethiopian military has said about 270 Tigrayan fighters have been killed and more than 200 wounded there.
Outside northern Ethiopia, the conflict appeared to spill into the capital, Addis Ababa, for the first time early on Thursday as an explosion was reported at the Ministry of Defence.
What is the humanitarian situation like?
The fighting is already taking a devastating humanitarian toll.
At least 52 civilians have been killed due to fighting in northern Ethiopia.
Doctors Without Borders, also known by its French acronym MSF, said last week that there had been a surge in the number of wounded in the north.
Amnesty International said on Friday that since the fighting has restarted, it has received “credible reports of destruction of civilian objects through shelling and air strikes, intensified forced conscription, and other acts that may constitute violations of international humanitarian law and international human rights law”.
“The African Union’s Peace and Security Council cannot wait for mass atrocities to unfold or for a surge in civilian casualties before placing Ethiopia, its host country, on the agenda. The AU, which was one of the guarantors of the ceasefire agreement that has now effectively collapsed, must learn from past mistakes and urgently activate its response mechanisms and mobilize its member states before it is too late,” Tigere Chagutah, Amnesty International’s regional director for East and Southern Africa, said in a statement.
“The starting point is for the Peace and Security Council to urgently convene an emergency session on the situation in Ethiopia. This is especially critical as fears of regionalisation of the conflict are on the rise”.
Could the current conflict spread in the region?
Analysts fear the current conflict could spread beyond Ethiopia’s borders.
On Thursday, Eritrea cut off diplomatic relations with Ethiopia, escalating a long-simmering conflict between the two states.
In a statement, Eritrea’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs said Ethiopia’s actions had left it with “no option but to reciprocate in kind and sever all diplomatic ties with Ethiopia”.
The ministry accused Ethiopia of pursuing a years-long “agenda of incessant hostility”, including by infringing on its coastal areas and arming fighters opposed to Ethiopia’s government.
Eritrea and Ethiopia restored ties in 2018 under Abiy’s leadership after more than 20 years of tensions, but their relations have since soured over Addis Ababa’s accusation that Asmara backs the Tigray rebels.
Ethiopia and Eritrea now also find themselves on opposing sides.
Conflict in their shared neighbour, Sudan, has drawn in both countries, alongside other states in Africa and the Gulf.
Down the coast, Somalia’s security crises are deepening, threatening to fragment the country further as foreign powers eye its self-governing regions for their coastline.
Against this backdrop, the United States-Israel war on Iran and the involvement of Yemen’s Houthis just across the Red Sea from Eritrea have also increased concerns over trade routes through that waterway.
Laura Hammond, professor in development studies at SOAS University of London, told Al Jazeera on Friday that this scenario is already under way.
“The risks that conflict will spread to other countries or that neighbours in the region will be brought into the present conflict are already playing out in terms of Eritrea’s support for the TPLF and the Alliance for Survival,” Hammond said.
“There is a strong possibility that Eritrea will become more involved in the conflict on the ground inside Tigray if it continues much longer,” she continued. “There is also a risk that the conflict could inflame relations with and inside Sudan.”
Eritrea has denied it is involved in the war.

High school students in Paris' deprived suburbs spark national protest movement
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
13:00:42 UTC
22:00:42 KST

Maisa, a 17-year-old in a poor Paris suburb who aspires to be an English teacher, joined tens of thousands of other students and their supporters this week in protests that spread across France over dilapidated schools, classroom overcrowding and teacher shortages.
At Lycee Le Corbusier school in Aubervilliers, a suburb north of Paris in the Seine-Saint-Denis department, protesters said schools in poor neighborhoods like theirs faced the worst conditions.
“Last year I took the high school French exam without a French teacher, and teachers have a huge impact,” Maisa said.
"These are not conditions to study in."
As protests raged at more than 1,200 French high schools this week, police responded with tear gas and rubber bullets in some cases. More than 5,000 people were arrested, and some protesters were seriously hurt with eye injuries, broken teeth and blows to the head. Interior Minister Laurent Nunez called it a "climate of unacceptable violence" and called for order.
Amelia, 15, joined Maisa in the crowd outside the school gates and held a sign reading, "Our address should not decide our future." She said she was demonstrating to demand the same rights as students elsewhere in the country.
"The education authority is not investing enough in the suburbs. It's classist and racist," she said.
Ulysse Rabate, a political scientist at Paris 8 University, said the protests show the way that France's marginalized urban neighborhoods are increasingly influencing national politics.
"When there is a collapse of the public service, of public education, those who feel it the most, and the most violently, are those at bottom," he said.
Protests become political flashpoint over 2027 budget cuts
The nationwide demonstrations and blockades, which began last week, have become a political flashpoint at a sensitive moment for the government, which announced a series of deeply unpopular spending cuts in its 2027 budget on Thursday.
The education budget is set to increase by a below-inflation 1.7% to €65.53 billion, excluding teacher pensions.
The education ministry did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Education Minister Edouard Geffray said that education remained a priority and the below-inflation budget increase was due to population decline.
The protests started in the Parisian suburbs, where poverty levels are high, then spread to Paris itself and other French towns, including Marseille, Strasbourg, Tours and Lille.
At Lycee Le Corbusier, classes including maths, humanities, English and sport have been canceled since the start of the academic year due to a teacher shortage, according to Karima Kara Ali, an elected parent representative.
In Seine-Saint-Denis, two-thirds of high schools took part in protests on Thursday, the CGT labor union said. Youth, teachers and parents in four towns complained of unsanitary school conditions and chronic staff shortages including of nurses and social workers.
Louise Paternoster, a representative for the Seine-Saint-Denis branch of the CGT's education union, said the area does not get adequate resources for its student population and their educational needs.
Two-thirds of schools in the department have unfilled teacher positions, according to a union survey.
Not enough teachers, poor learning conditions
"Our students are losing out on study time. Some schools don't have drinking water. We are not equal to other departments," she said, blaming shortages on government cuts of 3,256 teacher positions nationwide in 2026.
In Pantin, a town on the northeastern edge of Paris, teacher Dilan Roche joined her students as they protested outside their school this week to support their demands and protect them from the police.
"What they wrote on banners, we wrote in a letter to the local education authority: overcrowded classes, no nurses, no social workers - which is problematic for students with learning difficulties, many living in precarity," she said.
While France ranks in the middle of OECD countries for spending on education, the average expenditure per secondary school student has remained little changed over the last decade, standing at €11,660 in 2024 and €11,910 in 2010, according to education ministry data.
France sees largest high school protest movement since 1990s
The last nationwide high school protest movement on this scale demanding more funding came in the 1990s. That followed the government sharply expanding access to the baccalauréat, the school-leaving exam that typically paves the way to university, without providing schools with sufficient additional resources, said Professor Clemence Cardon-Quint at Paul Valery University, who researches education funding.
The movement won an increase in funding, but spending per student later stagnated despite growing demands on schools.
Cardon-Quint said students and teachers have taken on additional responsibilities over the years, including navigating Parcoursup, the university admissions system introduced in 2018 and criticized by some students and teachers as opaque and discriminatory.
"In a period of budgetary restraint, it is more difficult to reduce inequalities," said Cardon-Quint.

As part of the US's economic pressure campaign against Iran, there has been a push to prevent Iranian airlines from flying to various countries. Now Iraq will continue to enable Iranian flights, but it has sought a workaround for the US policy by routing all the flights to the holy city of Najaf. The concept is that the flights can now pose as “pilgrimage” flights for Shi’ites. It appears that the US will accept this for now, as US forces left Iraq on September 30 and Washington has no interest in igniting a crisis with Baghdad over the flights.
According to Rudaw media in Iraq, the country “announced on Friday that it had secured a US sanctions waiver allowing Iranian carriers to operate up to 40 flights daily to and from Najaf International Airport per day, excluding Mahan Air, a week after flights were suspended.”
Iraqi PM praises US cooperation on Najaf flight exemption
The goal is to ease “travel for passengers, particularly for humanitarian, medical, tourism and educational purposes.” Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al Zaidi has supported this. His efforts "resulted in an agreement allowing Iranian airlines to operate 40 daily flights to and from Najaf International Airport, with the exception of Mahan Air," his office noted.
His office added that “as part of the governmental efforts aimed at facilitating the movement of travelers and visitors arriving in Iraq or departing from it, and supporting humanitarian, medical, tourism, and educational aspects, and with persistent follow-up by the Prime Minister, Mr. Ali Falih Al-Zaidi, regarding the file to resume flights for Iranian airlines to and from Najaf International Airport, through a series of communications and follow-ups with the relevant parties.”
Iraq’s leader says he appreciates the US in this context, describing Washington’s response as positive. “This cooperation reflects the importance of dialogue and understanding in addressing files with a humanitarian dimension, and confirms that diplomatic channels and responsible communication are capable of finding practical solutions that take into account people's interests and needs.”
Iranian Mahan Air sanctioned since 2011 over IRGC activity
Meanwhile, Rudaw also noted that “Mahan Air has been under US sanctions since 2011 over what Washington says is its support for Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps-Quds Force (IRGC-QF), including transporting personnel, weapons and military equipment. The Iraqi statement did not specify why the airline was excluded from the waiver. Commercial flights between Iran and Iraq, including the Kurdistan Region, were suspended last week as Iraqi airports moved to comply with tightened US sanctions targeting Tehran’s aviation sector.”
Rudaw also said that “the agreement follows an earlier measure on Tuesday, when the US Treasury Department granted Iraqi Airways a highly restrictive license to operate flights between Najaf and Iran for religious pilgrims, valid until the authorized transactions are completed or October 28, whichever comes first.”
Iraq’s ability to navigate US sanctions is important. It shows how Iraq is trying to hedge, working with the US after the US withdrawal, and also working with Iran. Iraq is very much a center of the chessboard in the region as Iran seeks to expand is influence and threats. Iran is also suffering setbacks at sea. Tehran will want to keep a firm grip on Iraq.

Your Questions About Voting in the 2026 Midterm Elections, Answered
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
13:00:07 UTC
22:00:07 KST

Election Day is Nov. 3, 2026, in the United States. Held midway through each four-year presidential term, midterm elections give voters a chance to choose local representatives, weigh in on state issues, and determine which party controls Congress.
Read More: Congress Is Headed for a Massive Turnover
This year’s midterms will take place among unique challenges to the democratic process itself.
The Trump Administration has attempted to restrict mail-in voting and gather voter data from several states. There have also been concerns raised about the presence of federal agents at polling stations, which President Donald Trump has not categorically ruled out.
The TIME staff has put together answers to some of your most pressing questions about the midterm elections in our 2026 Voting Guide.
Questions:
Answers:
What's on my ballot?
Unlike presidential election years, there is no candidate or issue that appears on every ballot across the U.S. in 2026.
Instead, the ballots in every state will vary—and many will be different from county to county, as well. There are U.S. Senate races in 35 states, and gubernatorial elections in 36 states. All 435 seats in the U.S. House of Representatives are up for election, as they are every two years. There will also be downballot races for positions in the state legislature.
In four states—Idaho, Missouri, Nevada, and Virginia—voters will be deciding on ballot measures concerning abortion rights. Voters in six states, including Alaska and Arizona, will decide on whether to add or strengthen citizenship requirements for voting in state and local elections.
There are multiple ways for voters to request a sample ballot so they can see both what propositions will be on their state ballot and what local, state, and federal positions will appear on their ballot. Vote.org and Ballotpedia both have sample ballot lookup tools.
Many official websites—including those in Minnesota, Wisconsin, and New York City—also have their own “What’s On My Ballot” pages, which allow voters to enter their address and look up a sample ballot. —Rebecca Schneid
Who can register to vote?
People can register to vote in federal elections if they are a U.S. citizen and meet their state’s eligibility and registration requirements. Voters generally must be 18 years old on or before Election Day, although almost every state allows people to register before their birthday if they will be 18 by Election Day. North Dakota does not require voter registration.
Voters must also meet their state’s residency requirements, but people who are experiencing homelessness or who are between homes also are able to vote. Depending on state law, they may need identification. They can generally use a shelter, religious center, or P.O. box as a mailing address and identify the place where they live or sleep as their residential address.
Non-citizens, including permanent legal residents, can vote in some local elections but cannot vote in federal or state elections.
In some states, people who were convicted of a felony or are currently incarcerated are also restricted from voting. Check this federal voter guide for voting after a felony conviction to see what rules exist in your state. —Rebecca Schneid
How can I check my voter registration status?
You can check if you’re registered to vote by going to the National Association of Secretaries of State website. After you choose your state in the dropdown menu, you’ll be sent to the state’s election website. The information required to check if your voter registration is active varies by state, but most will ask for information like your name, date of birth, and address.
If you’re not already registered to vote, you may be able to register online, by mail, or in person, depending on your state. Check your state’s requirements and registration deadline before submitting an application. —Chantelle Lee
When is the deadline to register to vote?
The deadline to register to vote varies by state. Check the U.S. Vote Foundation’s website to find your state’s deadline. —Chantelle Lee
What documents do I need to register to vote?
In most cases, you will need a driver’s license or state identification card—or information from one—to register to vote. If you don’t have either, your state may accept other documentation, such as a utility bill or bank statement. Requirements vary by state, so check with your state election office to find out what information and documents you will need. —Anna Gordon
Can I vote if my voter registration is inactive?
Your registration may be marked inactive if election officials believe you have moved and you do not respond to a notice asking you to confirm your address. Inactive voters generally remain registered and can still vote, although they may have to confirm their address or follow other state-specific procedures at the polls.
Voters can contact their state or local election office to learn how to restore their registration to active status and what identification or documentation may be required. —T. Michelle Murphy
How can I update my registration (change of name, address, party enrollment)?
Voters in states that record party affiliation may change it through their state’s election office. However, party enrollment is not necessary to vote in the midterm elections in November, and party affiliation does not limit you to candidates from that party in a general election. Party affiliation may affect which primary a voter can participate in, depending on state law.
To change a name or address, voters generally follow the same process used to register to vote. They can use the national Election Assistance Commission map, click their state, and see how each state prefers updates to voter registration.
Voters can also submit a National Mail Voter Registration Form, which can be used to re-register to vote in every state except North Dakota, New Hampshire, and Wyoming, and it is available in 21 languages. —Rebecca Schneid
How do I vote early—and what are the benefits of early voting?
People who want to avoid long lines and those who might not have time to go to their polling location on Election Day may wish to take advantage of early voting. Early voting began in four states Sept. 18 and will expand to the rest throughout October.
As of 2026, 47 states and Washington, D.C., allow any voter to vote early in person. Alabama, Mississippi, and New Hampshire require an eligible excuse.
The process for early voting differs depending on your state. You can find the specific times and rules for early voting in your state at USA.gov. —Chantelle Lee
How do I request an absentee ballot?
If you live in the U.S., you can request an absentee ballot by visiting the National Association of Secretaries of State website and selecting your state from the dropdown menu. Because eligibility requirements, deadlines, and application procedures vary by state, be sure to follow the instructions provided by local election officials.
U.S. citizens living outside the country, absent members of the Uniformed Services or Merchant Marine, and their eligible family members can register to vote and request an absentee ballot through the Federal Voting Assistance Program. They can do so by completing a Federal Post Card Application, or FPCA, using the U.S. address that establishes their voting residence. For overseas citizens, this is generally the last place they lived before leaving the country; for military voters, it is generally their address in their state of legal residence. The completed form must be signed and returned to the appropriate election office in accordance with that state’s submission requirements. —Rebecca Schneid
What's the difference between absentee voting and vote-by-mail?
Absentee voting and vote-by-mail both allow voters to cast ballots without visiting a polling site. This can be done by returning a ballot by mail, at a dropbox, or in person, depending on state law. The terms vary by state, but a key difference is often whether voters must request a ballot or receive one automatically.
In states where vote-by-mail exists, all active registered voters are automatically delivered a vote-by-mail ballot to their registered address. Eight states—California, Colorado, Hawaii, Nevada, Oregon, Utah, Vermont, and Washington—conduct elections this way.
In states without universal vote-by-mail programs, individuals must request absentee ballots ahead of time. There are often deadlines and rules that voters must meet in order to participate in the program, and some states may require individuals to have an excuse in order to be eligible for an absentee ballot. —Anna Gordon
How do I know if my mail-in ballot arrived and was counted?
Most states offer some form of online ballot tracking, according to Vote.org. Illinois, Missouri, and Wyoming do not have statewide online mail-ballot trackers, although tracking may be available in some local jurisdictions.
Each state’s tracker is a little different, but they generally allow you to log in with your voter registration information to see if your ballot has been received yet. If your jurisdiction doesn’t offer online tracking, contact your local election office to ask whether your ballot was received and accepted for counting. —Anisha Kohli
What if there’s an issue with my mail-in ballot? Can I fix it?
If election officials identify a problem with your ballot, they may notify you and give you an opportunity to fix—or “cure”—it, depending on your state and the type of problem.
“The election official who is reviewing ballots will tell you what information you need to provide to make that cure, such as signing a new ballot envelope or providing a copy of your ID,” according to Nick Morrow, a communications and design director at Vote.org. Be sure to complete the process by the deadline set by your state.
The criteria for rejection varies by state, but to prevent your ballot from being rejected, do your best to ensure it’s returned in good condition and early. A missing or unverifiable signature can cause your ballot to be rejected. —Simmone Shah
Do I need to bring my ID to vote?
As of 2026, 36 states require you to show some form of identification before you can legally cast your ballot. But the forms of identification that are acceptable vary by state; they may include a driver’s license, passport, voter registration confirmation, utility bill, or bank statement. You can check your local requirements on USA.gov.
If you do not have the requested identification, you may still be able to vote by signing a statement confirming your identity or casting a provisional ballot. In some states, you must provide acceptable identification after Election Day in order for your ballot to be counted. Federal law also requires certain first-time voters who registered by mail to provide identification if their identity was not verified during registration. —T. Michelle Murphy
What’s the best time to vote to avoid long lines?
Long lines can be a strong deterrent to voting, especially for Black and Latino voters, who on average have experienced longer waits than white voters, according to a June 2020 report by the Brennan Center for Justice.
Since polling hours and conditions vary by county, and even within a county, wait times can be unpredictable. But early mornings and after-work hours tend to be the busiest times.
Additionally, lines tend to be longer on Election Day than they are during early voting periods, which do not demonstrate any consistent high-traffic time slots.
However, there is no universally confirmed “least busy” time to vote. —Solcyre Burga
Can I bring my kids or dog to the polls?
Voters generally may bring children with them to the polling place, although rules about their ages, how many children may accompany a voter, and whether they may enter the voting booth vary. To learn about the guidelines at your polling site, contact your local election office.
Dogs, however, are a different story. Voters are allowed to bring certified service animals to voting sites, but accommodations for pets and emotional support animals vary by location. It is best to presume they are not allowed but to look into the specific guidelines for your polling location. —Rebecca Schneid
Read More: Why I Bring My Kids to Vote with Me
What should I do if someone tries to stop me from voting?
Voter intimidation is illegal and relatively rare. If someone tries to stop you from voting, you should alert nearby poll workers and your local election officials, who can determine if law enforcement should be involved, says Sean Morales-Doyle, the senior director of the Brennan Center for Justice’s Voting Rights and Election Program. You should also contact the nonpartisan Election Protection hotline for assistance at 866-OUR-VOTE.
The same service is also available for non-English voters. Spanish speakers can call 888-VE-Y-VOTA. Most Asian language speakers can find assistance in their native language at 888-API-VOTE. Arabic speakers can call 844-YALLA-US.
If you feel like you’re in danger, call 911. —Mariah Espada
What do I do if I see ICE or federal agents at the polls?
The Trump Administration has not said that immigration enforcement officers would be at the polls this November, but it also has not ruled out the possibility. When asked in May whether he would deploy federal agents on Election Day, Trump told reporters that he would do “anything necessary” to make sure the U.S. has “honest” elections.
The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) has said that Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is not planning operations targeting polling locations, while leaving open the possibility of enforcement in the event of a public safety threat. In September, DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin confirmed that agents could serve warrants at polling places.
Gen. Dan Caine, Chair of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, said Aug. 31 that there are no plans to station military personnel or the National Guard at polling sites.
For voters, it’s important to know that federal interference at the polls is against the law. The law prohibits federal officials from stationing troops or armed personnel at polling places, except when necessary to repel armed enemies of the United States.  Voter intimidation is also, separately, prohibited and should be reported.
If you see any federal agents at the polls, the best move is to contact the election protection hotline at 1-866-OUR-VOTE. This hotline has other language options, including 1-888-VE-Y-VOTA for Spanish, 1-888-API-VOTE for several Asian languages, and 1-844-YALLA-US for Arabic.
The American Civil Liberties Union suggests that voters look up the contact information for their local election officials here and report intimidation if it occurs before or on Election Day. —Rebecca Schneid
How late are polls open?
Polling hours vary state by state—sometimes even county by county. For example, poll closing times vary in North Dakota and New Hampshire; in such instances, you can utilize search functions on each state’s respective website.

‘Sadness, cynicism and deep disappointment’: the Cornell gang-rape case and the failure of #MeToo
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
13:00:01 UTC
22:00:01 KST

Student safety advocates in the US call the start of the fall semester at universities “the red zone”. Fraternities, sororities and off-campus bars throw parties welcoming students back to school. It’s supposed to be fun, but it can also be dangerous: more than 50% of sexual assaults that occur at colleges happen during that six- to 10-week period.
It was mid-October of 2024, during the red zone and just before a deluge of Halloween celebrations, when, a former Cornell University student says, she was gang-raped by a group of fraternity brothers. Recent attention on these allegations sparked widespread outrage this week, reviving a contentious national debate about how authorities respond to allegations of sexual assault on US college campuses.
The anonymous young woman at the center of the story – known as Jane Doe in court documents – filed a civil lawsuit last month, accusing seven men of plying her with drugs and alcohol and assaulting her over the course of seven hours at their fraternity house. The woman originally went to the house to visit a friend; she claims she arrived intoxicated and willingly took the party drug ketamine with the men. Later, she says, she became incapacitated by the drug, which is a dissociative anesthetic, while the men “commanded” her to keep snorting it.
Jane Doe also alleges that the Ivy League university’s ensuing internal investigation was too lenient toward the men. None have ever been charged with a crime. Two were expelled for their misconduct, while five were given lighter punishments: writing an essay, attending a workshop or serving a suspension. Some still attend the school. All seven men denied wrongdoing during Cornell’s investigation.
Public outcry over the case reached a breaking point on Thursday, when the New York governor Kathy Hochul stepped in to appoint a new special prosecutor to investigate the incident, which the original district attorney declined to prosecute. Now, state attorney general Leticia James will decide whether or not to take the case to a grand jury, which would decide whether there was enough evidence to charge the men with a crime.
In a statement, Cornell University defended its investigation of the incident. It closed the fraternity chapter involved and barred the group from campus. “We will continue to examine and strengthen our policies to ensure we are doing all we can to foster a culture where sexual misconduct is never tolerated, those who come forward are supported, and individuals found responsible through our processes are held accountable,” the statement read. (Cornell directed the Guardian to this statement when reached for comment.) After intense public pressure, the university agreed to hire external, independent lawyers to investigate whether its handling of the allegations was appropriate.
Matthew Van Houten, the Tompkins county district attorney, has said that he did not pursue the case two years ago because the woman’s first account to police did not say that she was drugged, incapacitated or forced into sex. He later said he did not read her full interview, only a shorter statement written by campus police and signed by Jane Doe. Her full statement included the sentence: “I can say with 100 percent confidence that I was raped,” but this did not make it into the final statement sent to Van Houten.
In the immediate aftermath of the incident, the woman exchanged friendly messages with some of the men, expressing concern about rumors that were spreading on campus about the event. She also maintains that the alleged assault began as a consensual encounter. It is common for sexual assault survivors to downplay their experiences as a coping mechanism. False rape accusations are incredibly rare.
One of the most damning pieces of evidence in the lawsuit involves screenshots of Snapchat messages sent in a fraternity group chat; at one point, an alleged participant named Jonathan Newell referred to Jane Doe as “free pussy”, advertising the alleged assault as it unfolded.
What upsets many women most about this case is how normalized such actions seem. About one in four undergraduate women experience sexual violence during college; 60% of rapes involving university students involve perpetrators who are known to the victims. Last year, a survey of female undergrads at Cornell found that 35% of respondents experienced “nonconsensual sexual contact involving physical force, threats of force or incapacitation”. That figure was up from 23% in 2023.
“There are so many people in America who find this so familiar,” said Lisa Wade, an associate professor at Tulane and author of American Hookup: The New Culture of Sex on Campus. “Not just the incident itself, but also the response by Cornell.”
As the case plays out in the courts, the so-called “Cornell 7” have become the literal faces of the enduring prevalence of sexual assault on campus, and the institutional failure that allows that behavior to flourish. Their names and images are plastered on social media posts calling for accountability. The Cornell Daily Sun, a student newspaper that has doggedly covered the lawsuit, led the way with an op-ed column titled “Cornell Won’t, We Will”. The piece began by listing the alleged assailants’ names. “We know who you are and we refuse to let you benefit from this University’s concealment,” wrote the editorial board.
A former South Park writer named Toby Morton launched a website detailing the specifics of what Jane Doe alleges each man did to her. Morton wrote on Instagram that he plans to sponsor billboards about the case. The actor Florence Pugh weighed in, pleading on social media for men to be “as horrified and as sickened as us [women]”. She added that “college/schools/universities repeatedly fail women around the world [building] men [who] get taught through time and time again that they can do extreme harm and won’t be harmed in return”.
When content creator and commentator Michael Tracey threatened to release the name and personal details of Jane Doe – going against decades of established journalistic norms for reporting on alleged rape victims – women flooded TikTok in her defense. The Spartacus-style rallying cry of “I’m Jane Doe” hit feeds, with users sharing stories of their own experiences with sexual assault. “All of us women are jane doe, and we will all continue to ban [sic] together for her,” reads the caption of one clip liked more than 267,000 times.
College admissions advisers told the New York Post that some of their high school clients pulled their early decision applications to Cornell because they would not feel safe in the community.
This outpouring recalls the early days of #MeToo, a global hashtag campaign against sexual abuse ignited in the wake of initial allegations against convicted rapist and former film producer Harvey Weinstein. But Wade, the Tulane professor, said she sees this case as “metabolizing the failure of #MeToo”, which promised a so-called reckoning in 2017. Ten years later, manosphere influencers teach their followers to see women as sex objects, and Americans re-elected a man who infamously bragged about grabbing women “by the pussy”.
Sexual assault survivors have long faced victim-shaming. Jane Doe’s narrative is complicated, and the New York Times reported that the alleged victim did not realize she had been raped until she read someone else describe the event as such on a social media forum; she had texted one of the accused that: “At the end of the day non of the sexual stuff was illegal and honestly i really liked being w u and matt.” This is not an unusual trauma response: it is common for victims to continue relationships with their abusers, as it provides some semblance of control over the situation.
But the messy timeline emboldens bad actors and conservative commentators who seek to advance an anti-woman agenda. These young men have not been convicted of a crime, and it would be difficult for prosecutors to convict them of rape due to a New York state legal loophole that does not consider a victim to be incapacitated if she willingly contributes to her own intoxication. (Jane Doe stated she arrived at the fraternity house drunk and willingly took substances with the men, though she also says they coerced her into snorting ketamine.)
The Free Press, a vocally “anti-woke” publication run by Bari Weiss, chastised the “court of public opinion” for “already puni[shing]” the Cornell 7. Dasha Nekrasova, one of the edgelord hosts of the Red Scare podcast, spent much of this week trying to shame Jane Doe and calling women who are upset over the lack of accountability in this case “deranged”.
“There’s a sadness, cynicism and deep disappointment that is also driving the response to this,” Wade said. “#MeToo happened, and nobody cared. Here it is again.”
Elizabeth Armstrong, a professor at the University of Michigan who studies gender inequities in universities, says that there have been “big waves of outrage” over sexual assault on campuses since the 1980s, when Mary Koss first coined the term “date rape”. The last national dialogue took place around 2015, when a Columbia University student carried a mattress around campus for a performance art piece based on her sexual assault.
More than a decade later, the issue has only gotten worse. The Trump administration has gutted Title IX protections, which prohibit sex-based discrimination in universities that receive federal funding, and limited the definition of what constitutes sexual harassment under it. Just this week, Trump announced that universities no longer have to investigate assaults on students that take place off-campus. (The Cornell case occurred at a frat house.) “We have an administration that is actively rolling back protections for student survivors,” said Amanda Walsh, deputy director for external affairs at the Victim Rights Law Center.
But Walsh, who works closely with survivors, says that gen Z women have much less internalized shame over their assaults than previous generations, who were often taught that women invite sexual assault through their actions. “It feels like the focus has shifted away from talking about what the woman did, and more appropriately to exploring the behavior of the men involved,” she said. “I always admire how much they focus on the behavior of the person who harmed them, rather than asking: ‘What could I have done differently? Why did this happen to me? I see college students really pushing back against that.”
The Cornell case has revived discussions on abolishing Greek life, the student social club system that is behind fraternities and sororities in the US. This week, a Vogue article called for universities to “ban frats once and for all”. It’s not unprecedented: the Pennsylvania liberal arts college Swarthmore did so in 2019, after campus publications leaked racist, sexist and homophobic documents written by fraternities. “That would be a really real change, but I doubt that will happen,” said Armstrong.
Elizabeth Allan, who leads the Hazing Prevention Research Lab at the University of Maine, added: “It’s important for everyone [in Greek life] to think how these groups might reflect larger societal norms and expectations and the ways in which [bad] behavior is reinforced.”
Most of all, Walsh worries how all the attention on this case will affect Jane Doe, and the countless other anonymous victims who are sure to come after her. “I’ve been in this field long enough to know that however much support she receives is exactly how much negativity she’ll get on the other side,” Walsh said. “At this point, with the political moment and online response, it almost feels like supporting a survivor of sexual violence feels political or partisan, which is wild.”

Badenoch returns to Conservative conference much stronger than a year ago
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
13:00:01 UTC
22:00:01 KST

A year ago, Tory MPs were braced for the prospect of yet another leadership battle to topple Kemi Badenoch as the party sunk to historic lows of 14-16% in the polls.
At the time, the word “November” was uttered in hushed tones – this being the decisive month when rebels would be able to mount a challenge, Badenoch having served 12 months in office.
But times appear to have changed and – against the odds – the Tories have undergone what has been termed a “Keminisation”, with the leader asserting her style and authority on the party, despite its wider poor performance in the polls.
“Right now, Kemi is the only thing that’s holding them up,” says Luke Tryl, the director of the More in Common thinktank, which conducts focus groups and polling. “If they ditched her, I think they’d be certain for electoral oblivion.”
Badenoch is running a party still discounted as toxic and incompetent by much of the electorate, but polling numbers and focus groups suggest some of them have recently begun to give her more of a hearing.
The party has crept up from the teens to the low 20s – occasionally edging ahead of Reform UK for the first time in almost two years.
“It’s not great for them, but it’s a lot better,” says Tryl. “The problem is the party brand. She is now in our approval ratings net neutral and has been net 1 or net 2. She was in the minus 30s and now only her and Burnham have positive approval.
“Progressives don’t like her, but when you come to those who might conceivably be Tory voters there’s a lot of ‘like her, don’t like the party, she tells it like it is, wish she was in another party’. I do think the Kemi bounce is real. People talk about her having improved and they have seen her PMQs clips.”
Data from the other pollsters backs up the idea that the public is more open to Badenoch than before. James Crouch, the head of policy and public affairs at Opinium, said Badenoch’s approval rating had been rising since May 2025, when she was at -27, to -3 in its latest poll. He said that among 2024 Conservative voters she had the approval of 64%, compared with just 8% who did not approve, while of those who voted Conservative in 2019, 56% approved of her, while 16% did not.
Further research from YouGov this week found four in 10 people used at least one negative term to describe the Tory leader, one of the most common themes being a perceived unpleasantness. But three in 10 included one or more positive terms in their description, strong and intelligent being the main compliments.
Some Tory MPs attribute Badenoch’s improvement over the last year to a willingness to learn and take advice on her performance. This is in spite of her having the preternatural public self-confidence to claim to the FT this weekend that she couldn’t think of any mistakes she had made, saying everyone makes them but “nothing comes to mind”.
But insiders say she has listened to people warning she needs to focus more on the economy and less on culture war talking points, with the party’s conference slogan set as “Stronger economy, stronger country”.
She has also improved her prime minister’s questions appearances, partly with help on preparation from Conservative grandees such as David Cameron.
Tory MPs believe a turning point for Badenoch was the defection of Robert Jenrick and Suella Braverman to Reform – because their departure removed a source of destabilisation on the right, and it gave her an opportunity to show decisiveness in pushing Jenrick before he jumped. She has also been aided by the increasing questions over Nigel Farage and Reform UK’s finances, with the party’s dominance in the polls slipping.
However, the arrival of Andy Burnham on the scene for Labour has changed things.
Giles Kenningham, the former Conservative director of communications who now leads the Trafalgar Strategy advisory firm, says Burnham “raises the bar … he’s a great communicator and comfortable in his own skin”.
“It’s a harder ask now. Starmer was not a great orator or someone who electrified voters … Burnham has had a great conference but all eyes are now on the budget, so her conference needs to be on the economy and welfare. John Healey’s speech didn’t say anything, and there is an opportunity for Badenoch to put pressure on them and drive the agenda.”
Badenoch’s star has also risen further with the membership of the party, the most recent ConservativeHome poll showing she has a 87% net satisfaction rating with the party faithful.
Despite this, a number of Conservative aides and insiders believe that Badenoch’s future is still not totally secure if the party does not start to creep above Reform UK on a sustained basis. One pointed to the Tory selection races – excluding some high-profile former MPs from standing – as a sign of perceived weakness that those around Badenoch are worried about her being challenged. “She is not alone among politicians in not liking tall poppies,” said one Conservative strategist.
“Ultimately, she is not immune from a challenge,” said another. “The shelf life of politicians is getting shorter and shorter. Leaders are much more exposed and the job is precarious. The thing most in her favour is that there are currently no other obvious contenders.”

QinetiQ sets out its role in Scottish warship sinking
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
14:00:01 BST
22:00:01 KST

The decommissioned American frigate sunk during Atlantic Thunder 2026 went down in deep water around 150 miles off the Western Isles, and the company that runs the range from which the exercise was controlled has now set out what it contributed, according to QinetiQ.
The firm operates MOD Hebrides under the Long-Term Partnering Agreement, the arrangement through which it runs most of the Ministry of Defence’s test and evaluation estate. Its staff safeguarded the exercise area from the Range Control and Range Head buildings on South Uist, managing the safety of a large volume of sea and airspace while live weapons were fired into it.
Will Blamey, Chief Executive of QinetiQ UK Defence, said: “Atlantic Thunder is a complex exercise, delivered in partnership with the US Sixth Fleet and Royal Navy to ensure they are warfighting ready.
“Our experts coordinate a range of activity to ensure the exercise is successful for our partners, from managing the safety of a vast area of sea and air space, to planning and overseeing the realistic live-fire scenarios.”
The company also put its own hardware into the air over the range. Banshee Whirlwind uncrewed aerial targets, flown by the Combined Aerial Targets Service, ran sorties over the exercise area to provide realistic threats, and were tracked by an RAF P-8 Poseidon maritime patrol aircraft.
The range at MOD Hebrides, on South Uist and the surrounding islands, is the only place in the United Kingdom where an exercise of this kind can be run, which is the practical reason an American hull was towed across the Atlantic to be sunk off Scotland rather than disposed of closer to home.

Unexploded ordnances left by Israel in Gaza pose a constant danger to Palestinians
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
13:00:00 UTC
22:00:00 KST

On November 23, 2025, Adham al-Firy, 28, from Gaza City’s al-Nasr Neighborhood, found a small object weighing about 1.5 kilograms while working to clear rubble from buildings destroyed during Israel’s genocide in Gaza.
After searching online, it appeared to be a scooter battery, so he decided to take it home and use it for electricity and internet access amid the city’s ongoing electricity blackouts.
At about 7:00 p.m., he brought the object into his family’s second-floor apartment in their four-story building. He placed it on a table in the living room, where nine family members were gathered. Shortly afterward, his 18-month-old son, Yahya, carried the object and walked towards his father, who watched in fear that the child might drop it on himself.
“My son took one step, a second step, and then suddenly the object exploded,” he recalled. My son was thrown into the air before my eyes, and then everything went dark.”
The battery-like trap that killed his son
Adham initially thought that the rubble dust was preventing his vision. The blast threw him into the street and buried him beneath the rubble. He could move his arms and right leg but not his left leg, realizing it had been severely injured.
“I cried out for help until my 30-year-old brother, Muhammad, with the help of some relatives, pulled me out after tying a rope around my sound leg. At that moment, I realized I had lost sight in one eye, as I could not see anything or anyone around me,” he said.
While Adham was being transported by an ambulance to al-Shifa Medical Complex, rescuers found an amputated hand near the area. Medical staff confirmed that none of the injured had a missing limb. It was in that moment that Adham realized the hand belonged to his missing son.
“My family hid the truth of my son’s death from me for three days until my condition improved after my left leg was amputated below the knee,” Adham said. “Then they told me part of the truth — that he had been killed.”
“Two weeks later, I learned the rest from neighbors,” he added. “My son had been torn into pieces scattered around the house, including his hand and rib cage.”
Adham said that everyone inside the apartment was either injured or suffered burns. He lost his left leg and sight in one eye, and doctors warned that his second eye is also at risk.
Lacking experts and proper equipment
Since October 7, 2023, over 200,000 tonnes of explosive ordnance were dropped on the Strip by Israel, with about 70,000 tonnes remaining unexploded, according to Mahmoud Basal, spokesperson for Gaza’s Civil Defence.
Last April, the United Nations Mine Action Service (UNMAS) reported that 1,000 people had been killed due to “indirect conflict from the remnants of war since the start of the attack,” which Basal attributed to the loss of explosive ordnance engineers and the lack of equipment needed to identify and safely dispose of unexploded ordnance (UXO) contaminated in debris.
About 90 percent of those engineers have been killed, he said, either at home or while carrying out what he describes as “humanitarian work”, leaving the city without experts capable of conducting full UXO operations from detection and surveying to safe disposal.
“There are now no experts who know where the explosives are and how to remove them,” he said. “The remaining engineers can handle a small missile or a grenade if people report a UXO remnant, but they can’t handle a high-explosive remnant such as the MK-4 missile because it requires heavy equipment unavailable in Gaza.”
He added that even if experts were available, Gaza lacks the equipment needed to clear UXOs, making the task difficult amid widespread destruction and a high population density in a limited area, with residents living in only about 36 percent of the territory, following the expansion of Israeli military control to around 64 percent of Gaza last March.
As a result, the exact locations of UXO remain largely unknown and are mainly identified only when civilians report suspected objects, according to Basal. They were likely to be concentrated in heavily affected areas, including Gaza City and northern Gaza, where repeated military operations caused massive destruction.
He warned that it poses risks to residents living in or near damaged homes and neighborhoods, as well as to civil defense crews clearing the rubble, with an estimated 50 to 60 million tonnes of rubble that are reportedly contaminated with UXOs.
Basal described these remnants as air-dropped bombs, missiles, and drone munitions, as well as abandoned grenades and explosive devices found in streets, homes, and neighborhoods.
Many of them could be disguised as everyday objects such as cans, juice containers, and children’s toys, which could explode if handled and kill more civilians.
The Humanity and Inclusion organization estimated that clearing UXO in Gaza could take between 20 and 30 years. Basal said that the Israeli authorities should, under international laws, provide detailed information on the UXO locations to support disposal efforts and reduce the risks faced by civilians.
The toy that was not a toy
Yayha and Nabeela al-Shurbasi were among the several victims of another unexploded ordnance incident after finding a suspected object near their home on Gaza’s al-Jalaa Street at about 10:00 a.m., October 24, 2025. They were both six years old.
Yahya, who survived the explosion, told his family that they had found what they thought was a toy in the street while returning from a nearby supermarket after buying some snacks. They took it and played with it near their house.
The object exploded while they were playing with it. Their parents, Muhammad and Nadia, were inside and initially thought a nearby building or passing vehicle had been hit.
When a passerby told them two children had been injured, the family rushed into the street and found Yahya and Nabeela lying on the ground, soaked in blood.
“They were in a terrible condition,” Tawfiq al-Shurbasi, the twins’ grandfather, recounted. “They were bleeding continuously, with torn flesh and missing limbs.”
The twins were taken by car to al-Shifa Hospital, where they underwent multiple surgeries over several weeks.
Yahya lost his right hand, left leg, and a finger on his left hand. His appendix had been removed after shrapnel penetrated his abdomen. His right leg was badly burned, leaving bones exposed. Doctors warned it might need amputation unless he urgently traveled for treatment abroad.
Nabeela had severe fractures to her left leg, lost three fingers, and suffered internal bowel damage, requiring part of her intestine to be surgically removed due to shrapnel injuries.
She died 20 days after the explosion while waiting to be evacuated for treatment abroad.
“Her twin brother Yayha was lucky to be evacuated for treatment in Italy with his parents via Karam Abu Salem on December 7, 2025,” al-Shurbasi said.
“He was hospitalized and underwent several surgeries to save his remaining leg from amputation,” his grandfather added. “He is now receiving rehabilitation before being fitted with prosthetic limbs.”
Losing his legs and his future
Most UXO-related cases arriving at Gaza’s hospitals are children with critical wounds requiring surgical treatment and prolonged stays in intensive care units amid the city’s collapsing health system, according to Dr. Issam Abu Ajwa, a consultant surgeon at the Gaza Baptist Hospital.
“Patients arrive drenched in blood, with limbs missing, severe burns, and at times, partial or complete loss of vision,” Abu Ajwa described.
He said that, despite working with limited resources, medical staff are trying to avoid amputation whenever possible, but it can sometimes become unavoidable, particularly when patients cannot be urgently evacuated to receive treatment outside Gaza.
Nineteen-year-old Daoud Eid lost both legs after a suspected UXO object exploded on November 28, 2025, as he and his cousin returned from Jabalia Refugee Camp.
They had gone to check on their family home after hearing on social media that Israeli forces had withdrawn from the camp. When they arrived, they found the camp completely devastated and their home reduced to rubble.
On their way back to the displacement tent where their families were sheltering in central Gaza, one of them accidentally came into contact with a suspected object that exploded, severely injuring them.
They lay bleeding for nearly three hours before people could safely reach them. During that time, Daoud’s cousin had died, succumbing to his injuries.
Daoud was taken to al-Shifa Hospital with precipitously low hemoglobin levels, and spent two months undergoing multiple surgeries before both of his legs were amputated.
“I missed my Tawjihi exams that year while undergoing several surgeries to save my legs,” Daoud said. “I missed the exams the following year, too, despite scoring above 90 percent during school years.”
Although referred for treatment abroad, Daoud remains unable to leave Gaza, where the destruction of rehabilitation and prosthetics facilities has left artificial limbs unavailable amid restrictions on the entry of medical supplies.
“I dreamed of finishing high school and studying engineering at university,” he said. “Today, my dream is simply to travel outside Gaza and receive artificial limbs.”

US and Russia are negotiating multibillion-dollar deal on Lukoil assets, says NYT
The US presidential administration's negotiations with Russia to end the war in Ukraine have expanded to include a multibillion-dollar oil deal that could benefit Middle Eastern business executives linked to President Donald Trump's two main negotiators, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner.
Source: The New York Times, as reported by European Pravda
Details: The deal, which requires approval from the US government and the Kremlin, covers Lukoil's vast global portfolio of oil fields, refineries and petrol stations. Lukoil is one of Russia's largest energy companies.
The leading group seeking to finalise this agreement includes US investor Todd Boehly, who has donated US$2 million to President Trump's political causes; two Middle Eastern groups that have done business with Kushner or Witkoff's family; and a branch of the US government itself.
The negotiations, which have been ongoing for several months, were described to the newspaper by eight people familiar with the matter.
The NYT notes that there is no evidence that Kushner or Witkoff stand to profit personally from the agreement. Still, the proposed deal highlights the close links between personal business interests and geopolitics – even under an administration that routinely dismisses concerns about potential conflicts of interest.
Russian leader Vladimir Putin brought up this deal during a meeting with Witkoff and Kushner at the Kremlin on 5 September, according to three people familiar with the meeting. One of the sources said Putin proposed the agreement to show Russians they can do business with the US.
The Americans replied that they would work on the deal, the source noted. They viewed it as an opportunity to build good relations with the Kremlin while bringing down global energy prices.
This deal is also highly lucrative for the buyers: US approval for the sale would lift American sanctions from the assets, instantly boosting their value.
In Moscow, the decision on the deal is widely considered to be up to Putin, even though Lukoil is officially a private company. Ultimately, the massive transaction, which encompasses assets as diverse as oil fields in Cameroon, refineries in Europe and petrol stations in New Jersey, boils down to decisions made by Putin and Trump.
Trump has been promoting the idea of sealing business deals with Russia since early last year, describing the country as a "tremendous opportunity". This deal once again draws attention to Trump's cryptocurrency company, World Liberty Financial, co-founded by Witkoff. One of the investors in the Lukoil asset deal is also a co-owner of World Liberty.
Background:
- In October 2025, Trump imposed new sanctions on Russia for the first time in his second term, targeting two major oil companies, Rosneft and Lukoil, among others.
- Meanwhile, the US has repeatedly extended the deadline for the sale of assets belonging to sanctioned Russian energy company Lukoil. The latest extension, announced in August, gave potential buyers until 19 September to complete the sale, subject to additional approval from the US Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC).
