Saudi Arabia weighs possible offensive to retake Bab el-Mandeb
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
08:46:00 UTC
17:46:00 KST

Saudi Arabia is preparing for a possible military offensive against Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen, with Riyadh considering a limited operation to retake territory around the strategic Bab el-Mandeb strait or a broader assault on several fronts, regional and Western officials told Reuters.
The operation could begin as soon as the coming weeks and would be led by Saudi-backed Yemeni forces on the ground, supported by Saudi airstrikes, according to six people familiar with the preparations.
The officials, who include Gulf and Yemeni officials and Western diplomats, spoke on condition of anonymity because they were discussing sensitive security matters.
The United States is providing intelligence, including targeting information, to support Saudi operations, while several regional and European countries are supplying mainly defensive military assistance. Saudi allies are not expected to take a direct combat role, the people said.
The planned offensive, which has not previously been reported, would seek to reverse recent Houthi advances along Yemen's western coast and restore access to the Bab el-Mandeb, a vital maritime chokepoint at the southern entrance to the Red Sea.
The Houthis seized control of the strait after advancing down the coast last month, giving the group greater leverage over one of the world's most important shipping corridors. The Bab el-Mandeb connects the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden and is a major route for commercial traffic between Europe and Asia.
The officials said Riyadh is considering two main options. The first would be a focused assault around Bab el-Mandeb aimed at restoring control of the coastal areas. The second would involve a much larger, coordinated campaign across several parts of Yemen, including Al-Bayda, Marib, Taiz and Al-Jawf.
More than 100,000 Yemeni troops could be mobilized depending on the scale of the operation, the officials said.
Saudi Arabia has concluded that it cannot return to peace negotiations with the Houthis while the group controls Bab el-Mandeb, according to Western diplomats and a Gulf official.
The timing remains uncertain. The six people familiar with the preparations gave estimates ranging from within a week to a launch after the U.S. midterm elections in early November.
Michael Ratney, a former U.S. ambassador to Saudi Arabia, said he expected any operation to be relatively limited compared with the Saudi-led campaign launched in 2015.
He said Riyadh would have an interest in reversing the Houthis' territorial gains around Bab el-Mandeb without becoming trapped in another large-scale war.
"it would be a fairly limited operation to retake coastal areas and get back to normal maritime traffic," Ratney said.
Saudi Arabia intervened in Yemen's civil war in 2015 at the head of an Arab coalition supporting the internationally recognized government after the Houthis seized Sanaa and large parts of the country.
A truce reached in 2022 largely held until this year, when the Houthis resumed attacks involving missiles and drones against Saudi-linked shipping and oil infrastructure amid the wider regional conflict involving Iran.
The Houthis have emerged as one of Iran's most powerful regional allies, particularly as Hezbollah's military capabilities in Lebanon have been weakened over the past three years.
A new Saudi offensive would open another major front in a region already engulfed in conflict since the Hamas-led attacks on Israel on Oct. 7, 2023, and the subsequent U.S.-Israeli war on Iran.
Washington remains Saudi Arabia's most powerful ally and is providing military advisers and intelligence to support Saudi air operations in Yemen, according to a Western diplomat.
But the extent of U.S. involvement could remain limited. Reuters has previously reported that President Donald Trump rejected requests from Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman for direct U.S. military support, including airstrikes.
Türkiye and Pakistan have also provided military equipment to Saudi Arabia under a broader defense relationship between Riyadh and its allies.
Pakistan sent four cargo aircraft carrying equipment including air defense systems, light artillery, drones and counter-drone systems to Aden last month, according to a Pakistani government official.
Pakistani military advisers are also in Saudi Arabia working with Saudi counterparts to support Yemeni forces, according to Pakistani, Gulf and Western officials.
Riyadh's concerns extend beyond the battlefield. Regional officials said Saudi Arabia is particularly focused on protecting its oil facilities and other critical infrastructure from Houthi missile and drone attacks and has asked allies for additional defensive systems.
Pakistan has deployed between 30,000 and 40,000 troops to Saudi Arabia to help protect its borders and assist with missile and drone interceptions, according to a Pakistani official. The troops arrived in waves beginning last year and following the latest escalation, the official said.
Pakistan has not decided to send troops into Yemen in a combat role, the official added.
The Pakistani and Turkish defense ministries did not respond to requests for comment.
France has also announced plans to send defensive systems and troops to Saudi Arabia to help protect the Red Sea port city of Yanbu.
Any Saudi-backed ground offensive would depend heavily on Yemen's fragmented anti-Houthi forces, many of which were armed and trained by Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates during earlier stages of the civil war.
The groups have struggled to maintain unity, raising questions about their ability to sustain a large-scale offensive against the Houthis.
"Many anti-Houthi forces are still not organised or prepared for the kind of sustained offensive required to push back a disciplined Houthi military force," said Yemen analyst Mohammed Albasha.
The anti-Houthi camp became more divided last winter after UAE-backed southern fighters attempted to seize territory in eastern Yemen and announced plans for secession. Saudi-backed forces eventually defeated them after a series of clashes.
Ali Shihabi, a Saudi political analyst close to government thinking, said the success of any offensive would ultimately depend on the performance of the Yemeni forces leading the ground campaign.
"The priority so far has been to defend the positions on the ground and stabilize the front, but certainly they will be going on the offensive," he said. "Success greatly depends on the quality of the performance of the local forces."
The prospect of a new offensive comes as fighting and cross-border attacks have intensified.
The Houthis said Friday that Saudi forces had carried out 94 strikes against areas under their control during the previous 24 hours. The group claimed Saudi Arabia had conducted 1,350 strikes since the latest fighting began.
Saudi Arabia's coalition supporting Yemen's internationally recognized government said Friday that it intercepted and destroyed three ballistic missiles launched toward the southern Saudi city of Khamis Mushait.
The coalition said the missiles were intercepted without providing details on casualties or damage.
A day earlier, the coalition said it had intercepted two ballistic missiles over Khamis Mushait and Jazan, as well as four drones over Khamis Mushait.
Saudi Civil Defense said debris from an intercepted Houthi ballistic missile targeting residential areas fell in Khamis Mushait on Thursday, damaging several buildings and vehicles. No casualties were reported.
Khamis Mushait has been repeatedly targeted during the latest escalation. On Sept. 14, the Houthis claimed a large-scale attack involving dozens of ballistic missiles and drones against King Khalid Air Base in the city.
On Saturday, Saudi Civil Defense said shrapnel from another intercepted ballistic missile injured one person in Ahad Rafidah governorate in the Asir region, according to Saudi state media. The missile was fired Friday by the Iran-aligned Houthis, it said.

US-Ukraine Fund Seals First $30M Minerals Deal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
08:43:00 UTC
17:43:00 KST

The joint US-Ukraine Reconstruction Investment Fund has finalized its inaugural critical minerals transaction alongside four additional economic initiatives, directing roughly $70 million toward strategic sectors as Ukraine prepares for winter, a senior US official told Reuters.
Established under a bilateral agreement signed in April 2025 following an initiative by US President Donald Trump, the fund targets capital deployment across five strategic fields: critical mineral resources, defense manufacturing, energy resilience, transport, and municipal infrastructure.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Conor Coleman, head of investments at the US International Development Finance Corporation (DFC), stated that the transaction demonstrates Washington’s tangible commitment to sustaining Ukraine’s wartime economy and long-term reconstruction.
“It’s absolutely imperative for the Ukrainian people that we’re investing now,” Coleman said, pointing to the urgency of capital injections amid recurring Russian aerial assaults on infrastructure ahead of the winter heating season.
Rare earths, uranium, and mining platform
The primary transaction injects approximately $30 million into a dedicated joint investment platform alongside BGV Group, an investment firm founded by Ukrainian billionaire Hennadii Butkevych, co-owner of the ATB retail supermarket chain.
Coleman explained that the platform will initially focus on financing early-stage extraction and processing operations across Ukraine, prioritizing deposits of rare earth elements, uranium, beryllium, and zirconium.
Russian Ballistic Missiles and Drones Hit Kyiv, Killing 1
“They are all on the US critical minerals list, so it ties in very well with what we’re looking to do from a [US] administration priority [standpoint],” Coleman noted.
Securing access to critical and non-fuel raw materials has emerged as a central pillar of Western industrial policy, designed to diversify supply chains away from geopolitical rivals while anchoring Ukraine’s resource wealth within Euro-Atlantic supply ecosystems.
Winter energy resilience
Alongside the mining platform, the fund unveiled two energy projects engineered to stabilize Ukraine’s battered power and heating networks following escalated Russian missile and drone bombardments.
One initiative supplements nearly $100 million in debt financing recently approved by the DFC for DTEK, Ukraine’s largest private energy enterprise, to construct an industrial-scale battery energy storage system.
The battery complex is designed to provide immediate backup electricity for roughly 600,000 households for up to two hours during grid disruptions, with provisions ensuring access to emergency capital if facilities sustain physical combat damage.
Concurrently, the fund acquired an equity stake in a combined heat and power (CHP) co-generation platform. The platform is designed to build and operate a network of decentralized “energy hubs” across municipal centers, restoring localized heat and power distribution lines to residential buildings severed from damaged central generation plants.
Coleman added that fund managers are actively seeking to raise additional public and private capital to expand financing capacity.
Bilateral framework
The US-Ukraine Reconstruction Investment Fund was established under an intergovernmental pact signed on April 30, 2025, structuring the vehicle as an equal 50/50 partnership between Washington and Kyiv.
Ukraine’s statutory participation is managed by the Agency for Public-Private Partnership Support under the Ministry of Economy, while the US is represented by the DFC.
The fund operationalized its sourcing portal in early 2026, receiving 138 investment applications within its opening 60 days. An interagency project committee selected 22 initiatives for prioritized development, identifying eight projects valued at approximately $1.2 billion that had achieved advanced operational readiness.
Energy and grid security dominated early applications, accounting for 62 percent of submitted bids, followed by transport logistics at 16 percent, critical mineral extraction at 12 percent, and telecommunications and advanced defense technologies at 8 percent.
Global advisory consultancy Alvarez & Marsal serves as the fund’s primary investment adviser, directing early-phase capital primarily through equity stakes and quasi-equity instruments to finance Ukrainian industrial recovery without generating unsustainable sovereign debt obligations.

Poland Drafts New “Prewar” Defense Law to Speed Up Allied Troop Deployments
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
08:37:23 UTC
17:37:23 KST

- Category
- World
Poland Drafts New “Prewar” Defense Law to Speed Up Allied Troop Deployments
Poland’s Defense Ministry is drafting a new law to prepare the state for a possible prewar period, including earlier troop deployments and stronger coordination between civilian authorities and the military, Rzeczpospolita reported on October 2.
The proposed legislation would create a clearer legal framework for moving from peacetime readiness toward full defense readiness before martial law is formally introduced. It would also allow earlier deployment of Polish and allied forces to strategically important areas, Rzeczpospolita wrote.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Poland’s efforts to strengthen defense readiness come amid repeated Russian aerial threats near its eastern border. Days earlier, a Russian jet-powered drone crashed near the Yahodyn checkpoint on Ukraine’s border with Poland, prompting Warsaw to scramble fighter jets and place air defense and radar units on heightened readiness.
Poland’s Defense Ministry confirmed to Rzeczpospolita that the draft is intended to strengthen national defense capabilities and improve cooperation between the armed forces and agencies responsible for internal security.
The ministry stated that the legislation is designed to adapt Poland’s legal framework to “modern threats, in particular those of a hybrid, cyber, and disinformation nature.”
According to Rzeczpospolita, the law would also link Poland’s Defense Response Plan more closely with NATO’s Response System and expand preparations for military infrastructure and logistics. It would broaden the number of institutions involved in permanent duty systems and clarify responsibilities across public administration.
The legislation is also intended to improve planning outside the military sphere, change rules governing defense training and exercises, and prepare civilian institutions to carry out defense tasks under both permanent and full defense readiness.
Poland currently operates under two levels of defense readiness introduced in March 2025, Rzeczpospolita noted. Permanent readiness applies during peacetime, while full defense readiness can be introduced in the event of an external security threat or war and allows mobilization and the full deployment of the state’s defense system.
“Due to the complex legislative process, it is currently unknown when the bill will be submitted to the Sejm for consideration,” the Defense Ministry told Rzeczpospolita.
A similar proposal was prepared in 2023 under then-President Andrzej Duda, but it did not enter into force. Rzeczpospolita reported that some of its provisions were later incorporated into government regulations.
Poland had previously simplified its military procedures for identifying and shooting down foreign objects entering national airspace. The new rules allow Polish forces to act on radar, surveillance, and Ukrainian data without first requiring visual confirmation, giving air defenses more time to respond during Russian drone and missile attacks near the border.

Yemen’s army claims over 1,500 Houthi casualties, attacks Sanaa
Government forces close a key crossing connecting Houthi-held al-Houban to government-held Taiz city.
Loud explosions have been reported in Yemen’s Houthi-held capital, Sanaa, while missile, drone and artillery attacks targeted Houthi positions across the country, according to the military.
Colonel Majed Abdullah al-Nazili, Yemen’s military spokesman, wrote on X on Saturday that the armed forces are carrying out a military operation “on legitimate vital military targets in Sanaa”, adding that they are “capable of executing strategic attacks against the Houthis”.
Earlier, al-Nazili said Yemen’s internationally recognised government forces carried out nearly 500 military operations, killing or wounding 1,540 Houthi rebels in the past 24 hours.
Most of the casualties were in the governorate of Taiz, where the operations halted the Houthi advance, al-Nazili said. The government-held city of Taiz has become a focal point of the renewed fighting.
The army spokesman did not mention any casualties among government forces.
Al Jazeera’s Maha Ali, reporting from Yemen’s Taiz, said the region is seeing continued escalation and intense fighting across several fronts around the city, with some of the fiercest fighting happening on its western outskirts.
The Houthis have used an exceptionally heavy volume of fire during the assault, she noted, adding that the sound of continuing artillery fire, particularly from the Houthi side, targeting western areas, could still be heard.
Residents are appealing for evacuation as the shelling continues, Ali reported, adding that there have been civilian casualties in the fighting, including from a shell that hit a residential area in Dhubab, killing a baby who died from shrapnel injuries.
On the Samea front, she said, the Houthis made advances on Friday in the mountainous area and fierce clashes are continuing there today between government forces and the Houthis.

Key border crossing closed
On Saturday, the army’s media official Ammar al-Sami’i told Al Jazeera that the government had closed the al-Houban crossing in Taiz.
The crossing had previously been closed for nine years and was later reopened to civilians in 2024 for “humanitarian reasons”, Sami’i said, as the road is one of Yemen’s most important connections between territory held by the opposing sides. It connects Houthi-held al-Houban to government-held Taiz city.
Sami’i said security reasons are behind the closure, following an attempt by the Houthis to infiltrate Taiz via the road, attacks in the vicinity and a general military build-up.
A fragile truce struck between the government and the Houthis in 2022 collapsed in July this year, and fighting in Yemen has escalated significantly since then.
In mid-September, the Houthis swept across parts of western Yemen, seizing the port city of Mocha and key strategic islands in the Bab al-Mandeb strait.
Since then, anti-Houthi forces have largely stabilised the front lines.
Hundreds of thousands of people have been displaced since the fighting restarted.
Yemen has been embroiled in civil war since the Houthis seized the capital of Sanaa in 2014, forcing the internationally recognised government to retreat to Aden.

Can Britain really afford to diverge from EU tariffs on Chinese EVs?
Unless London can turn its independent tariff policy into real bargaining power with Beijing, it will lose more by being shut out of an integrated European industrial framework
3-MIN READ3-MIN
2
 Listen
Adriel Kasonta is a London-based political risk consultant and lawyer, and a graduate of London School of Economics and Political Science (LSE). 
The European Union’s demand that Britain raise tariffs on Chinese cars exposes an awkward truth about post-Brexit trade. Britain might have left the EU, but it cannot easily escape the bloc’s industrial policy.
According to the Financial Times, EU officials have told Prime Minister Andy Burnham that Britain needs to align more closely with EU trade policy towards China if it wants British manufacturers to avoid discriminatory treatment under the bloc’s proposed “Made in Europe” rules. The proposal is tied to a larger European effort to favour locally produced goods in public procurement and state-supported schemes, including the automotive sector.
The timing is not accidental. China’s car export machine is accelerating. Its electric vehicle (EV) exports in August rose 33 per cent year on year to more than 284,000, while year-to-date exports as of the end of August were more than 2.1 million, up 53 per cent year on year. Almost 95,000 of those exports went to Europe in August.
Following its anti-subsidy investigation in 2024, the EU has imposed countervailing duties ranging from 7.8 to 35.3 per cent on Chinese battery EVs. In contrast, Britain has retained a standard tariff regime that is less punitive towards Chinese cars. That has helped turn the UK into an important market for Chinese manufacturers. Chinese-made cars accounted for 14 per cent of British new-car sales in 2025, according to the European Automobile Manufacturers’ Association.

Inglourious subtitlers and the art of cinematic transcreators
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
08:30:00 UTC
17:30:00 KST

Inglourious subtitlers and the art of cinematic transcreators
Often criticised but rarely appreciated, subtitles have been essential to global cinema for nearly a century. The head of the Swiss Film Archives, Vinzenz Hediger, explains why, in multilingual Switzerland, they are also a vital part of film history.
When Sony Pictures distributed Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon in theatres in the United States in 2000, they came up with a clever trick in order to get people into cinemas to watch a foreign film in a foreign language. The trailer External linkportrayed no scenes with Mandarin dialogue, relying instead on an English voice-over to narrate the synopsis.
Subtitled films represent between 1.1% and 2% of the box office in the US; in the European Union, roughly 53% of theatrical releases are shown exclusively dubbed, 29% in both dubbed and subtitled formats, and a smaller minority rely strictly on original-language subtitles. Yet Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon remains the highest-grossing non-English film in the US.
The film’s success proves that translation can redefine a movie’s global reach, making subtitles essential – if often overlooked – components of the cinematic experience. Today, in this extremely globalised era in which we can access films from every corner of the world thanks to subtitling, subtitles become increasingly crucial yet remain largely invisible.
But the translator is “also doing a creative act”, Vinzenz Hediger, head of the Swiss Film Archives (Cinémathèque Suisse) tells Swissinfo. He discusses how translation plays a role in the archival world, specifically in the Swiss context. For him, “the concept of transcreation” demands a lot of creativity from the translator to make possible for a film “to live in a different linguistic environment”.
Subtitles or dubbing, that is the question
Up until the talkies – from the late 19th century until the late 1920s – films provided our world with the promise of a universal language. In the silent film era, intertitles (a piece of printed or hand-lettered text edited into the middle of a silent film to show dialogue, narration or story details) were easily swapped for other versions and the moving image allowed for common ground across languages.
However, when sound appeared at the end of the 1920s, so came the subtitles: although it still used intertitles for dialogue, The Jazz Singer (1929) was the first film to be subtitled. Meanwhile, Hollywood poured funds into what they called multiple-language versions of the same film. This involved using the same set and crew, but different actors in order to film simultaneously various versions. During the 1930s, both subtitling and dubbing were developed simultaneously.
Meanwhile in Europe, countries generally split into two camps: subtitling foreign films or dubbing them into the local language. Switzerland, considering its linguistic diversity, opted for subtitling, both for “historical reasons that date back to the 1930s, but also for simply economic reasons”, Hediger says.
According to him, subtitled versions remain the preferred choice for moviegoers in Zurich and Lausanne, even for commercial releases, reflecting a continuity with the policies adopted nearly a century ago when talkies first emerged. Interestingly, research shows External linkthat prioritising subtitled content has contributed to higher English proficiency in countries like Switzerland, Portugal, and Norway.
More
Schiff ahoy! Why dubbed films are making waves
The figure of the translator has always been rendered invisible. This plight is now being accelerated by the rise of streaming platforms and artificial intelligence (AI). Yet these ghosts still haunt our film prints and digital streams as much as they do our books.
Since the early days of cinema, credit has rarely gone to those who enabled international audiences to understand one another; studios simply bought translations outright without granting copyright or screen credits. To this day, many countries still refuse copyright protections to subtitlers. Streaming giants and VOD platforms External linkhave pushed this dynamic even further by bringing subtitling entirely in-house and leaning heavily into machine translation and AI automation, the human author is being erased faster than ever.
Compare that to dubbing, where recognition is built into the craft: specific voice actors become tied to Hollywood legends. Rosa Guiñón became the definitive voice of Meryl Streep in Spain and Philippe Peythieu plays the iconic French Homer Simpson. Subtitlers, meanwhile, remain cinema’s ghostwriters.
As Hediger puts it, “translation work is the most thankless intellectual endeavour that you can think of”. There are no notorious subtitlers. While some actors know the names of their foreign dubbers, most filmmakers don’t bother to know the names of those who subtitle their films.
Swiss Babel on the screen
Navigating film distribution in Switzerland means tackling a uniquely complex, multilingual terrain. Here, every film must cater to distinct French- and German-speaking audiences, while carefully balancing separate strategies for the smaller Italian-speaking market: translation isn’t just an afterthought; it’s a non-negotiable commercial necessity.
This intricate balancing act is preserved in the archives of the Cinémathèque Suisse, home to one of the richest film collections in the world. As Hediger explains, “that has everything to do with the fact that the people who ran the Cinémathèque early on struck a deal with distributor in Switzerland: once a film had run its commercial course, the distributors would deposit all prints in the Cinémathèque, which would keep the best five or eight”.
As a result, virtually everything screened in Switzerland since 1952 has been safeguarded alongside its corresponding French and German subtitles. For the Italian-speaking market, distributors often imported Italian prints that were already either dubbed or subtitled.
Yet localising cinema across Switzerland goes far beyond standard language barriers. Hediger emphasises that language is deeply situated: “dialects are always regionally specific, but in Switzerland, if you grow up as a Swiss German native speaker, you will be able to place people by about 30 kilometres if you hear them speak”. Capturing these accents and social nuances on screen is a delicate task for any translator, and virtually impossible to fully convey within the constraints of a subtitle line.
What actually gets found in translation?
When people talk about subtitles, the feedback is usually limited to whether they are “bad”. The audience tends to dwell on what’s lost in translation rather than seeing subtitling as a key part of the creative process, even if that connection seems obvious once we think about it.
Digging deeper into the conversation surrounding translation, Hediger refers to transcreation, which is when translation doesn’t choose the literal path but, rather, a more tonal and emotional approach. As such, we can acknowledge not what is “lost” in the meaning through the process of translation, but actually what is transformed.
Perhaps what does fall short in subtitling films are the nuances found in each language or dialect that is spoken. Films are situated, so are the languages we speak. Hediger shares a recent experience where they screened a Nigerian film in the Hausa language which will soon be restored by the Cinémathèque Suisse “in the presence of a room full of Hausa native speakers”. He describes the experience as “totally unfair because they were laughing through half of the film while I sat there, wondering what the hell was going on? What are we missing?”
In this way, subtitles can oftentimes feel like a “crutch” simply allowing us to follow along the best we can. On the other hand, we’re unable to grasp the nuances of the spoken dialogue when we are reading a text on the screen, especially if we are completely foreign to that culture.
When visiting Cairo and watching local films without translation, Hediger and his wife found themselves piecing together the plot like solving a riddle, an experience he found deeply “intellectually stimulating”. This exercise echoes Henri Langlois’ provocative belief that it’s best to watch foreign films without any subtitles at all.
Subtitles are often treated as invisible bridges, but theoretically, they also function as unique historical markers. Looking at archived prints, a subtitle track offers tangible proof of how a work crossed borders at a particular time. It reflects the linguistic nuances, ideological choices and technical standards of its era, making the translation inseparable from the film’s archival identity.
This theoretical dimension comes into sharp relief when looking at specialised collections like the Arsenal Filminstitut in Berlin. Originally founded to spotlight alternative and emerging cinema, the institute has maintained a practice since the 1970s of retaining every film screened in its Forum programme as a subtitled print.
In discussion with Hediger about international archival practices, he points out a striking reality: for many of these works, the Arsenal’s subtitled copy is the only surviving print in existence. The act of translation, initially meant just for a local screening, ultimately doubled as an act of absolute preservation.
More
‘Maybe films should be subtitled in SMS language!’

Tallinn's crumbling Linnahall has one employee left — and he's been there 43 years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
08:28:00 UTC
17:28:00 KST

Tallinn's crumbling Linnahall has one employee left — and he's been there 43 years
When the rain pours through the roof of Tallinn's long-shuttered Linnahall, Leo Lõoke starts his morning emptying buckets.
After 43 years in the building, he is now its only employee and has to safeguard it even in its dilapidated state, with challenges ranging from trespassers to leaky roofs.
While hundreds of people once bustled around Linnahall at its peak, today Lõoke, the facility manager, is responsible for maintaining the entire complex, alone. "If something has broken down, some things have to be repaired. That's how it goes. You have to do it yourself. We get nighttime visitors again, and then you also have to make sure the hole they made from outside gets closed up. Fortunately, that hasn't happened so often lately, but it still does happen. Usually when you least expect it. It has even happened during the day, with someone smashing a window," Lõoke told "Ringvaade."
Linnahall, the monumental concrete complex beside Tallinn Bay, opened in 1980 but its interior has been mostly closed to the public since 2010, with various proposals about its ultimate fate coming and going during that time.
When the building was closed in 2010, Leo was asked whether he would stay on. "I said all right, and I've stayed up to now. There's no one else left who knows this building as well. Now, in a way, it would be sad to leave without a decision on what will become of the building.
The difficulty of Leo's lonely working day can depend even on the weather. If it rains heavily all night, with the roof leaking, his morning starts out wet. Emptying the buckets takes time and energy. More buckets would be useful, but the problem is that with only one person, the net result would be Leo would not get time to empty them all out anyway.
"Sometimes, when you're carrying away water that has dripped from the ceiling, you wonder what it's all for. I get it done, the next day there's less water, and my spirits lift again," he added.
He has worked at the Linnahall for 43 years – just three years less than the building has been standing.
That early period represented the Linnahall's halcyon days, he recalled, with Soviet and other acts approved for appearance by the regime all taking the limelight, often to packed schedules "I still remember my first concert. It was the comedy show 'Eide selge on valge.' Later there were Vanessa-Mae, Bonnie Tyler and Uriah Heep," Lõoke recalled. "Plus all the leading performers in the Soviet Union at the time. The most we ever had was 27 concerts in 10 days."
Although Linnahall may appear to be standing idle, quite a lot has taken place there. The most famous example from recent years was the scenes filmed there, along with those in other locations in the capital, for the Christopher Nolan-directed thriller "Tenet." More modest-scale filming including for TV has also been carried out there, and architecture tours are regularly held.
Again, with only the one employee, demand greatly outstrips supply, when it comes to potential tours. "There could be even more, but I can't accommodate everyone. The architecture biennale currently taking place inside lasts a long time and is also being held with their support," Leo explained.
This interim "temporary" stage has remained in place for years now, and it does not allow the venue to reach its full, multifarious potential.
The largest stage was intended to be 42 meters wide, with the first 10 rows moving from the floor to the stands. This would also have made room for one competition volleyball court and two practice courts. The stage has in the past also hosted boxing matches and circus performances.
"When there was a circus with animals, an elephant walked on the stage, as did other larger animals. There has been a tiger cage on the stage," Lõoke recalled.
Famously the Linnahall also hosted an ice rink. Nowadays, this is one of the most dilapidated, not to mention hazardous, parts of the complex. It is pitch dark, and the pours through the roof.
"The ice arena is a textbook example of what happens when you turn off the heating in a building and leave it standing," said Leo, who has himself discussed with the city government what to do with the space. "My first suggestion was that it would be good to turn it into a studio for film shoots. For some reason, they were wary of that."
Back in the day, "you could watch ice hockey, you could watch figure skating, and there was also a circus on ice," Leo went on.
"The Prodigy have played here, and Whitesnake have performed here," he added.
Built for the 1980 Moscow Olympics, when Tallinn hosted the sailing events, the Linnahall was originally known with the rather more grandiose name of the "V. I. Lenin Palace of Culture and Sport" ("V. I. Lenini nimeline Tallinna Kultuuri- ja Spordipalee"). The sprawling waterfront complex has been protected as an architectural monument since 1997, but this is a double edged sword – it preserves the site but makes more difficult planning and efforts to renovate or redevelop it. A fast catamaran link to Helsinki used to depart from the site, as did a helicopter line plying the same route, but these both ended a decade or more ago, leaving the Linnahall mostly the name of a public transport stop, and a site from which to get a nice view of summer sunsets.
Meanwhile, the surrounding area has been transformed, including with the redeveloped Old City Harbor area, a tram extension, the Porto Franco waterside development, and new builds in the Kalamaja and Noblessner areas.
The City of Tallinn has considered various plans for the Linnahall's future over the years, but the only thing that has remained constant up to now is Leo keeping watch over the edifice.

Launch of the FP-7 returns Ukraine to the small group of countries that produce ballistic missiles - NYT
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
11:26:14 EEST
17:26:14 KST

Launch of the FP-7 returns Ukraine to the small group of countries that produce ballistic missiles - NYT
Kyiv • UNN
The FP-7 was developed and is manufactured by the Ukrainian defense company Fire Point.
The first combat use of Ukraine’s FP-7 ballistic missile brings Ukraine back into the small group of countries capable of producing ballistic missiles. This is reported by The New York Times, writes UNN.
Details
On October 1, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy published a video of the launch and reported the first combat use of the FP-7 ballistic missile.
As The New York Times notes, before the collapse of the Soviet Union, Ukraine had a powerful military and aerospace industry and enterprises that produced, among other things, intercontinental ballistic missiles. After 1991, the relevant production lines were shut down, and the missile industry largely declined.
The FP-7 was developed and is manufactured by the Ukrainian defense company Fire Point. According to the company’s data, the missile has a range of approximately 250 km and a warhead weighing about 200 kg.
Military analysts, commenting to the NYT, suggest that the FP-7’s primary mission will be strikes against Russian launchers and other military targets in border areas. At the same time, Fire Point is developing the longer-range FP-9, which will be capable of striking targets in the Moscow area and strategic facilities of Russia’s defense industry.
Thus, the first combat use of the FP-7 demonstrates not only the emergence of a new type of Ukrainian weapon on the battlefield, but also the revival of domestic ballistic missile production in Ukraine.
Fire Point said that it is restoring ballistic missile production in Ukraine virtually from scratch and is using new technologies.

Polls open in Latvia against backdrop of perceived Russia threat
Latvia is not expected to shift its pro-Europe and pro-Ukraine trajectory, but coalition negotiations could be complex.
Polls have opened in Latvia for an election taking place against the backdrop of perceived security threats from Russia and a nationwide cost-of-living squeeze.
Saturday’s vote is the first electoral test for Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs after coming to power in May this year when his predecessor resigned due to a backlash from stray drone incursions from Ukraine.
Kulbergs, whose right-wing United List party is currently polling at about 20 percent, is expected to hold onto his position, but the decline of two allies in his current coalition means he is set for a complicated negotiation over the makeup of any future government.
Polls opened at 05:00 GMT and will close at 17:00 GMT. The results are not expected to change Latvia’s pro-European and pro-Ukrainian course.
About 1.5 million people are eligible to vote in the country’s 11th parliamentary election since independence from the Soviet Union in 1991.
Latvian politics are highly fragmented, with parties rarely seeing above 20 percent vote share and coalitions being the norm.
This year, 14 electoral lists are contesting the election, but polls indicate only seven are likely to enter parliament, with the rest expected to fail to meet the minimum 5 percent vote threshold.
Rising living costs, low wages, strains on the healthcare system and long-term population decline have all featured prominently in campaign debates.
Fragmented political parties
Most parties in Latvia are pro-Ukraine; however, the populist Sovereign Power party – which says it wants Ukraine to win but argues money spent supporting Kyiv would be better spent at home – looks likely to become the country’s second-biggest party, with more than 9 percent of the vote. Most other parties have ruled out forming a coalition with Sovereign Power.
Latvia First, a pro-Ukraine and populist nationalist party currently polling at about 9 percent, could be a potential coalition partner for PM Kulbergs.
The Progressives, a pro-European social democratic party, are polling at 6 percent.
Ethnic Russians make up roughly one in four Latvian citizens, but their vote, which has traditionally been cast along identity-based lines, looks set to be made according to economic and social issues.
Latvia is the poorest of the Baltic states, and it has sharply increased its defence spending since Russia invaded Ukraine, now allocating nearly 5 percent of its gross domestic product (GDP) to defence.

Archaeologists excavating the ancient city of Blaundos in western Türkiye have uncovered the remains of a 250-meter-long wall surrounding the North Temple, revealing new evidence about the religious and urban life of the settlement during the Hellenistic period.
The wall formed the temenos, a sacred enclosure reserved for religious use and separated from the city’s public and social spaces. Archaeologists also uncovered water channels inside the enclosure that supplied water to the temple.
Ilhan Çavuş, director of the Uşak Museum and head of excavations at Blaundos, said the team had fully exposed the wall during this year’s work.
“We uncovered the 250-meter-long temenos wall, built approximately 2,500 years ago. At the same time, we exposed the water channels inside the temenos wall that supplied water to the temple,” Çavuş said.
The North Temple itself is believed to be around 1,900 years old, meaning the surrounding wall predates the existing temple by several centuries. Excavations at the temple, which began last year and continued this year, have revealed much of its foundations.
Researchers also excavated parts of the temenos floor and continued toward the naos, the inner section of the temple. Çavuş explained that the temenos wall served to distinguish the sacred area from the city’s social spaces. Everything within the enclosure was regarded as sacred and associated with the deity or deities worshipped at the temple.
Blaundos, located in Uşak’s Ulubey district, is believed to have been established by Macedonian soldiers who came to Anatolia during Alexander the Great’s campaigns. The settlement is therefore also known as a “garrison city.” Over time, civilian settlement expanded and religious structures such as the North Temple emerged.
The ancient city has a naturally fortified appearance, with deep valleys formed by the Ulubey Canyon surrounding it on three sides and a single entrance providing access.
Excavations at Blaundos have been ongoing since 2018 under the direction of the Uşak Museum as part of Türkiye’s Heritage for the Future project, which supports archaeological research and conservation at heritage sites.
The site contains remains from different periods of occupation. Among the latest discoveries were Roman-era coins found in the North Temple. Çavuş said the coins may have been offerings left by worshippers along with their prayers and wishes.
The North Temple is located about 200 meters from the city’s main entrance, while restored ancient aqueducts can be seen roughly 500 meters from the entrance.
Yavuz Çakar, Uşak’s provincial culture and tourism director, said Blaundos attracts around 350,000 domestic and international visitors each year, adding that ongoing archaeological work contributes to the site’s tourism potential.

Against this backdrop, FSSAI on September 29 directed food safety authorities across the country to step up surveillance and enforcement against adulterated, counterfeit and unsafe food products during the festive season.
The regulator has specifically identified milk and milk products, sweets, snacks and savouries, edible oil, beverages and ghee for heightened scrutiny.States have been asked to conduct inspections and sampling at identified hotspots and sensitive locations. The directive also asks authorities to record inspection, sampling and outcome data on the Food Safety Compliance System (FoSCoS) and Food Safety Compliance through Regular Inspection and Sampling of Food (FoSCoRIS) on a real-time basis.The national directive also allows states to focus on products specific to local consumption patterns, including kuttu atta and singhada atta in northern and western regions.

Latvia heads to the polls on Saturday in a parliamentary election focused on security, Russia, and the cost of living. With the war in Ukraine next door, the vote is being watched well beyond the Baltics.

Opinion polls put Kulbergs’ centrist United List ahead, with about 14% of votes, but followed closely by the overtly pro-Russian Sovereign Power.
A businessman and amateur rally driver, Kulbergs, 47, came to power in May after the previous coalition crumbled over its handling of incidents in which stray military drones flew undetected into Latvia. Though the drones were Ukrainian, officials have blamed Russia for causing them to divert from their flight paths.
“We have to give Ukraine everything necessary right now [so] that they can have the upper hand and win”, Kulbergs told Reuters in an interview last month.
Throughout his campaign, he has also promised more anti-drone capabilities for Latvia and to maintain defense spending at 5% of gross domestic product, one of the highest levels in NATO.

Divided nation

Kulbergs’ ability to forge a working coalition will depend largely on how many votes they receive and how many other parties cross the 5% threshold to enter parliament.
He might also need to cobble together a deal with Latvia First leader, businessman Ainars Slesers, who appears to have shifted towards a more anti-Ukraine stance in recent months, courting votes on both sides.
“His message is that [the party] condemns Russia’s invasion and stands with Ukraine, but that supporting Ukraine comes at the expense of Latvia’s economy,” said Roberts Kits, researcher for the Latvian Strategy and Economic Research Institute, in a note.
Latvia, with a population of 1.9 million, is sandwiched between the Baltic Sea, with EU and NATO allies Estonia and Lithuania to the north and south, and Russia and Belarus to the east.

Israeli man used AI, ChatGPT in covert tasks while spying for Iran, prosecution indictment reveals
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
08:13:53 UTC
17:13:53 KST

A 25-year-old Israeli man allegedly carried out assignments for an Iranian handler and used AI, including consulting ChatGPT, while performing the tasks, Haifa District prosecutors said in an indictment filed on Friday.
Mohammad Khalaf, a resident of Baka al-Gharbiya who works as a security guard at a youth boarding school, was charged with the serious espionage offense of contact with a foreign agent.
By agreement between Haifa District Prosecutor's Office attorney Amir Eliel and defense attorney Morsi Abu Mokh, who has represented Khalaf since his arrest and is reviewing the investigation file, Judge Ibrahim Boulos extended his detention until further notice.
According to the indictment, filed on behalf of the prosecution by attorney Yossi Gimpel, the case began with a Telegram group intended for people seeking temporary work. Khalaf noticed an offer for courier work and contacted a person on Telegram who initially identified himself as "Thomas" and later as "Martin."
Khalaf allegedly carried out a series of tasks for the contact and received payments through a cryptocurrency wallet. Court documents indicate that he used AI to carry out some of the assignments and consulted ChatGPT.
Crypto payments and covert assignments
By September 6, around three weeks after his contact with the Iranians began, the Shin Bet (Israel Security Agency) had arrested him. He has remained in custody since then.
During questioning by police and the Shin Bet, Khalaf admitted to the allegations against him, including his contact with the handler, the assignments he carried out, and the money he received, according to the indictment.
The investigation, conducted jointly by the Shin Bet, the Israel Police Cyber Unit in Lahav 433, and the Asher District Central Unit, found that Khalaf had joined a Telegram group for temporary jobs and, on August 17, contacted "Martin," who had advertised courier work. He was subsequently moved to a dedicated account.
According to the allegations, the two used the OKX application to transfer payments in cryptocurrency. The handler purchased a Telegram Premium subscription for Khalaf and transferred $50 in Bitcoin to him in an effort to gain his trust.
During the investigation, cyber investigators found the full correspondence between the two on Khalaf's cellphone, along with photographs and videos documenting the completion of assignments that had been sent to the handler. Investigators also obtained communications and location data that matched Khalaf's account, security camera footage, and records showing funds entering and being withdrawn from the cryptocurrency wallet.
The indictment states that during his contact with the Iranian handler, Khalaf traveled on his instructions to an area near a tool store in Kiryat Haim, where he located a Samsung Galaxy phone that had been concealed beneath branches and leaves near a tree. He photographed and filmed the location in accordance with the handler's instructions.
He allegedly received NIS 1,050 for the assignment.
Three days later, according to the indictment, Khalaf withdrew money from his cryptocurrency wallet at a currency exchange in Pardes Hanna, placed NIS 300 in an envelope, and concealed it inside a light fixture in a restroom at a Dor Alon gas station near the Sha'ar Menashe psychiatric hospital.
On the same day, he allegedly documented additional possible hiding places, including beneath a sink in a disabled restroom at a gas station near Metzer and above ceiling tiles in a restroom at a cafe in Baka al-Gharbiya.
Security details and planned meeting abroad
Prosecutors further alleged that Khalaf returned to the gas station the following day to retrieve the envelope. He later printed an English-language letter at a print shop in Baka al-Gharbiya that purported to be an invitation to a secret meeting in Paris.
According to the indictment, he concealed the letter in an envelope beneath a rock near a jujube tree marked with a numbered yellow tag in a grove near Kibbutz Lahavot Haviva, then sent the handler documentation of the location together with its precise coordinates.
He later took the phone he had retrieved in Kiryat Haim for repair after being instructed to do so.
The indictment also alleges that Khalaf provided the handler with details about his work as a security guard employed by G1 at the boarding school, including security procedures, night shifts, and the positioning of security cameras. He also allegedly promised to photograph the site.
Several days before his arrest, according to the indictment, Khalaf agreed to a request to renew his passport ahead of a planned meeting with the handler abroad.
Alongside the indictment, prosecutors filed a request to keep Khalaf in custody until the end of legal proceedings.
In the detention request, the state argued that Khalaf admitted he had continued carrying out the assignments even after developing a substantial suspicion that the handler was working on behalf of entities hostile to Israel and that the tasks he was performing could harm state security.
According to the allegations, Khalaf and the handler also agreed on a concealment mechanism. They would discuss assignments on one account, while on Khalaf's personal account they would exchange texts for translation in a way designed to portray the payments as compensation for editing and translation work.
The prosecution argued that the allegations describe an ongoing and systematic series of actions demonstrating a high level of danger to state security and the public, which could not be adequately addressed through an alternative to detention.
Judge Dr. Zaid Falach was assigned to hear the prosecution's detention request.

How local can a global restaurant really be?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
08:13:35 UTC
17:13:35 KST

In hospitality, standardisation creates a sense of trust; in gastronomy, it can sometimes disconnect a restaurant from the place it inhabits. While speaking with Mark Vaessen, Global Culinary Chef of OKU Hotels, in Bodrum, we found ourselves returning to one question: What truly makes a restaurant local — the ingredients it uses, or how deeply it understands the place to which those ingredients belong?
Consistency is one of the fundamental principles of hospitality. When you stay with the same brand in Istanbul, Paris or Tokyo, you expect certain standards, from the room to the service. In gastronomy, however, that same logic can work in reverse. What is an advantage in a hotel room can easily become a disadvantage in the kitchen. If the dish you eat in Ibiza is replicated in Bodrum and the one in Bodrum appears again in Kos, eventually the destination becomes little more than the view outside the restaurant window.
This was precisely what Vaessen and I discussed in Bodrum. OKU’s hotels in Ibiza, Kos, Andalusia and Bodrum share certain codes: The sea, olive oil, vegetables, fire and a culture of sharing. But for Vaessen, that is where the similarities between their kitchens should end. Consistency, in his view, should lie not in serving the same dishes but in a shared philosophy: Good ingredients, clean flavours, simplicity and generosity. Everything else should respond to the place. One sentence captures his entire approach: “Bodrum should taste like Bodrum.”
“Local” has become one of the restaurant world’s favourite words. Menus are filled with terms such as local, seasonal and farm-to-table. Buying vegetables from a nearby grower and serving locally caught fish are, of course, valuable choices. But as Vaessen points out, buying a local tomato does not automatically make a restaurant local.
First, you have to understand where you are. That means visiting markets, eating in local restaurants, talking to fishermen, farmers and producers; listening to chefs who grew up there and learning what people eat at home — and why. Buying an ingredient and understanding the culture to which it belongs are two very different things. Locality is not simply a matter of distance; it is also about how well you can read the knowledge accumulated around an ingredient.
That is exactly what Vaessen did after arriving in Bodrum, eating his way through local restaurants and discovering the region’s food. What struck him most was not a new ingredient or technique, but how much flavour could be achieved with so little intervention. Vegetables, wild herbs, olive oil, fish… When the ingredient is good enough, there is often very little you need to do to it.
He was also struck by a way of eating that we ourselves may barely notice: Small plates arriving one after another, dishes placed in the middle of the table to be shared, food and conversation flowing into one another. This social rhythm of eating also resonates with the culture of sharing that OKU seeks to create. But Bodrum reminded him of something more fundamental: Travelling as a chef does not always mean adding a new technique to your repertoire. Sometimes it teaches you to do less.
Perhaps this is one of the significant shifts taking place in contemporary gastronomy. There was a time when we measured a chef’s skill by how much technique could be brought to a plate; transformation, surprise and the creation of new textures were highly prized. Today, another form of mastery is coming to the fore: Rather than demonstrating everything you are capable of doing, knowing when to stop.
Vaessen takes a similar view when it comes to intervening in traditional dishes. He believes that a chef’s desire to leave a signature on every plate can sometimes have more to do with ego than with making the food better. Before reinterpreting a dish, he argues, you first need to understand why it exists, how people remember it and what makes it special.
Techniques can then change and an element can be reinterpreted. But if everything is altered simply to make the chef’s signature visible, the memory of the dish can disappear with it. Vaessen’s position is disarmingly simple: Sometimes the smartest thing a chef can do is taste something and say, “This is already good. Don’t touch it.”
This idea becomes even more interesting at Teyo, OKU Bodrum’s restaurant centred around Japanese influences and techniques. The kitchen in Bodrum is led by Executive Chef Muhammed Karaaslan. Ultimately, it is in the hands of Karaaslan and his team that the relationship between a global culinary philosophy and local ingredients is tested every day.
At first glance, Japan and Bodrum may seem like two distant culinary cultures. Vaessen, however, sees their common ground not in recipes but in their attitude towards ingredients. He draws a parallel between the Japanese respect for seasonality and produce and the Aegean instinct for simplicity when faced with excellent fish, olive oil and wild herbs. In both, the point is not to obscure the ingredient but to preserve its character.
Fire is another language they share. Cooking over fire may look simple, but it demands an understanding of when to intervene and when to leave the ingredient alone. This is where Vaessen sees Teyo’s potential in Bodrum: Not in allowing Japanese technique to overpower Bodrum’s ingredients, but in letting the two speak to one another. The distinction matters. In restaurants that bring different cuisines together, local produce can easily become little more than a stage on which to showcase a foreign technique. The real challenge is to create an encounter in which neither side loses its identity. Vaessen also believes the menu should continue to evolve as the team eats in local restaurants, meets producers, listens to those around them and gains a deeper understanding of the ingredients.
Seen from this perspective, OKU’s kitchens in Bodrum, Kos, Ibiza and Andalusia offer an interesting case study. All four share the sea, olive oil, vegetables, fire, seasonality and a culture of sharing, yet each expresses them differently. Vaessen’s aim is not to turn them into versions of the same restaurant, but to allow knowledge to circulate between them.
An ingredient or technique discovered in Bodrum might inspire the team in Ibiza, but it should not simply be reproduced there; it needs to be reinterpreted through Ibiza’s own ingredients and culinary culture. The wild herbs, local olive oil and clean, saline character of the Aegean that Vaessen would like to take from Bodrum are therefore not recipes to be exported, but starting points for new culinary ideas.
Perhaps this is the most interesting possibility globalisation offers gastronomy: Not replicating the same plates in different parts of the world, but allowing places to learn from one another. The global restaurant of the future may not be defined by how perfectly it can reproduce itself around the world. The real skill may lie in understanding how much it needs to change each time it arrives somewhere new.
And the starting point is remarkably simple: Sit down at the table, taste the food of that place and truly listen.

Choosing life, building hope: Former hostage turns to disability advocacy to honor wife, daughters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
08:13:30 UTC
17:13:30 KST

"I cannot change what was taken from me, but I can choose what I build,” says Eli Sharabi, a former resident of Kibbutz Be’eri who was taken hostage by Hamas terrorists on Oct. 7, 2023, and freed after enduring 491 days of brutal imprisonment in the tunnels of Gaza.
The image of an emaciated Sharabi freed from Hamas captivity, walking slowly through a jeering throng of Gazans into the hands of the International Red Cross on February 8, 2025, is permanently imprinted on the Israeli psyche. Sharabi, who lost 30 kilos during his imprisonment, weighed just 44 kilos upon his release. It was only after he returned to Israel that he learned that his wife Lianne, 48, and daughters Noiya, 16, and Yahel, 13, were murdered by Hamas terrorists in their Kibbutz Be’eri home on Oct. 7.
After his release, Sharabi became a prominent voice for the remaining hostages, met with world leaders, addressed the United Nations Security Council, and recounted his ordeal in interviews and his memoir, Hostage, which became an international bestseller.
Outwardly, at least, Sharabi, now 54, looks much as he did before his captivity, returning to a healthy weight. We sit at Shalva, the Israel Association for the Care and Inclusion of Persons with Disabilities, at the organization’s Jerusalem headquarters, with Kalman Samuels, Shalva’s founder and president, and his son Nachman, the group’s CEO.
Shalva provides therapy, education, rehabilitation, and family support for people with disabilities, from infancy through adulthood. Founded by Samuels and his wife Malki in 1990, it promotes inclusion while helping families navigate the challenges of caring for a loved one with disabilities.
What is Sharabi’s connection to Shalva?
“When my wife was younger and lived in England, she volunteered with children who had special needs,” he explains. Sharabi’s oldest daughter Noiya followed in her mother’s footsteps.
Noiya and Yahel often played with a girl with special needs who lived on the kibbutz, and they valued their relationship with her.
When Sharabi was working as the business manager for Kibbutz Be’eri, he came to the Shalva campus for a convention in 2017. “I was fascinated with the place, and after I came home to Be’eri, I told my wife and daughters, ‘I have to take you there.’ Sharabi never had the chance to bring them, but he says he always knew the work being done there would resonate with them.
Then came the horrors of Oct. 7. Sharabi, along with hundreds of other hostages, was held captive by the terrorists in Hamas’s underground tunnels in Gaza, under inhuman conditions. At that time, he did not know that his wife and daughters had been murdered.
“I remember sitting 50 meters underground, thinking about all the possible scenarios that could have happened to my family. I told my fellow hostages that if my wife and my daughters hadn’t survived, I would have no doubt where I would memorialize them – it would be through Shalva.”
After Sharabi was freed, he spent 10 days in the hospital, and then traveled throughout the world, met with world leaders, and lobbied for the remaining hostages’ freedom. Several months later, he visited Shalva, to ask the organization to name a room in memory of his wife and daughters.
Samuels recalls that Sharabi had told him, “I speak around the world, but there’s only one place that I want to actually be part of and create something and work together with. This is at Shalva.”
He explains the genesis of Sharabi’s interest in Shalva. “Eli called my wife Malki two weeks after he got out of Gaza. He told her he had visited Shalva once as the CFO of a company at a conference, and he went back and told his wife and children how amazing this magical place is.
“They were all involved in special education, and they begged him to take them to show them this magical place. That never happened.
“Two weeks after he came out [of Hamas captivity], he said, ‘Malki, Shalva is the only place I want a memorial for my wife and two daughters who were murdered.’
“Malki cried and said, ‘Eli, please come down in person, and we’ll do it together.’” Several months later, Sharabi came to Shalva, and Malki shared the idea she had. She went up one flight of stairs in the lobby and pointed out the area she wanted to dedicate to Sharabi’s wife and children.
“Malki asked him for a picture of him with his wife and daughters, and he sent a photograph. From that photo, the artist painted the image, and Eli provided the wording on the wall. That was his wording, and the butterflies, of course, we added. The wall was completed several months ago.”
Honoring the departed: Diagnostic services, family support, and trauma treatment
Samuels and the Shalva team wanted to do more with Sharabi to help him fulfill his mission of memorializing his wife and daughters. Before their meeting, the government had turned to Shalva and asked them to create a center in Ashkelon to help residents of the South. The proposed center would provide diagnostic services, family support, and trauma treatment.
Samuels’s son Yochanan, along with the Shalva team, began investigating possible sites for the new Shalva center, and decided to build a new facility. They asked Sharabi for permission to call the center the Shalva Sharabi Family Center. “Eli said ‘yes,’ and that’s how we began,” he says.
Since then, Sharabi has traveled worldwide, raising funds for the new center, which is still under construction. The facility will serve 28 Gaza border communities as well as the southern region, operating from a permanent facility in the Marina View complex opposite the Ashkelon marina.
The Shalva Sharabi Center will address two pressing needs in southern Israel: accessible services for people with disabilities, and support for those affected by trauma. Families across the South often contend with long journeys, lengthy waiting lists, and fragmented care when seeking specialist assessments and treatment.
Building on Shalva’s existing model, the Family Center will bring diagnosis, therapy, rehabilitation, and family support together under one roof. Multidisciplinary teams will provide assessments and individualized care for infants, children, and adults. Services will include occupational therapy, physiotherapy, speech therapy, and Shalva’s “Me and My Mommy” early intervention program, alongside parental guidance and peer support.
The Horizons Pavilion will focus on trauma recovery and resilience for children and adults, soldiers, first responders, civilians, and families affected by the Oct. 7 Hamas-led massacres and the war. The initiative draws on Shalva’s experience providing therapeutic care, respite, and emotional support to evacuees, particularly people with disabilities and their families.
The center’s location near the Ashkelon Marina makes it an ideal site to combine individual and group therapies with outdoor and sea-based activities, designed to support recovery. Its programs will seek to strengthen coping skills, restore independence, and help individuals and families rebuild their connections to community life.
For Sharabi, the Shalva Sharabi Center in Ashkelon will remind him of his wife Lianne’s smile, Noiya’s passion for working with children with special needs, and how Yahel used to play with the child with special needs, in Kibbutz Be’eri. “This project gives me a great deal of strength, and is a meaningful way to honor the memory of Lianne, Noiya, and Yahel,” he says.
Having his name associated with the Shalva Center in Ashkelon epitomizes Sharabi’s philosophy of refusing to give up hope. “It just shows that life goes on. We cannot stop time. We can shape our future,” he adds.
“I can choose to stay in bed and cry all day. I chose differently from the moment I decided to act. Initially, it was for the remaining hostages who were held in Gaza; after that, for Jewish communities all around the world fighting antisemitism. For me, doing things means choosing life and helping to change the lives of others for good.
“The community of Be’eri lost more than 100 people in one day. So for me, it’s a big victory – after spending 491 days in captivity, most of them spent in Hamas tunnels – to believe that one day, I could come back to life and have a second chance to do things and impact others and influence Israeli society. It’s more than a dream.”
Sharabi says it will be deeply moving to walk into the Shalva Sharabi Center one day and see children and families receiving care. “It will be amazing. I can’t think of anything else that will provide the same amount of emotional happiness.”
Samuels and Sharabi: Different but intersecting worlds
Both Sharabi and Samuels say that although they come from different worlds, they have learned a great deal from each other. Sharabi says the partnership has introduced him to a world he barely knew. “I learned that, first of all, I know nothing about this world of kids with special needs and education. I always had my businesses and my career.
“The philanthropic world wasn’t part of my world, and it’s become very meaningful to me. It’s much more satisfying than another business. I learned a lot from Kalman about his passion. He is relentless about caring for all these kids, getting them and their families the services they need. It’s amazing to be with the Samuels family and to understand and learn.”
Samuels shares that he has learned how to rise above despair from Sharabi. “There’s every reason in the world that Eli should not have been able to get back on his feet. Yet he made a decision, early on, to ensure that his wife and daughter’s names would be in the public sphere and always remembered. Thank God, it is happening.
“But the idea that a person can get out of that and be a source of inspiration and hope for generations of people… Eli is spreading hope, which is probably the most important, most powerful element of mankind. When a person loses hope, he’s finished. And if a person has hope, it doesn’t matter what his situation is; life still has power. Eli has become this symbol of hope for the world.”
Like Sharabi, Shalva is also associated with that word. Its motto, “Inspiring Hope. Changing Lives,” suggests that the partnership between Sharabi and Shalva will bring hope and provide much-needed services for Israelis living in the South.
The Family Center, the first phase of the Shalva Sharabi Family Center in Ashkelon, is scheduled to open in January 2027, and the trauma center is planned to open in spring 2027. Samuels says they have raised $5 million toward the $10.5 million budget to complete the project. With nearly half the funding secured, the support of additional partners will help turn Sharabi’s vision of a living memorial into a place of healing for families across the South.
The drawing on the inside wall of the Shalva lobby features Eli, his wife, and his two daughters, with the words “Memory and hope light the way” in English and Hebrew, accompanied by three-dimensional images of three butterflies, to symbolize his family.
Samuels relates that when the artist began to paint the butterflies, a large butterfly flew inside the building and perched on the ledge. The artist, who was standing on a ladder some six meters above the building’s entrance, was a bit unnerved by the incident, he says.
On the second day, a different butterfly flew in, and on the third day, when she painted the third image, yet another butterfly arrived. “We have been in that building for over 10 years, and I have never seen a butterfly inside the lobby,” Samuels says. “The artist saw three large butterflies that sat and perched themselves near her.”
Samuels, who considers himself a realistic person with his feet on the ground, found the butterflies’ appearance inexplicable.
“For me, I feel very clearly that it’s just a good sign of the acceptance of his prayer – that his wife and daughters wanted to be there,” he says. “They didn’t get there in life, and somehow [Eli] wanted to give them a sense of peace.”■

Side by Side: Helping people with disabilities connect socially
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
08:13:06 UTC
17:13:06 KST

"The goal is not inclusion. What I’m looking for is belonging. There’s a huge difference between being included and belonging,” said Jacki Edry. A Netanya-based author, educator, and advocate for those with special needs, she is now creating a new program – Side by Side: Building Community, Together – to help fulfill the social needs of young adults with disabilities.
“Belonging means that you’re part of the community. Everybody looks after you, and you look out for everybody else, because communities take care of each other,” she added.
Edry is a mother of five, one of whom, a 29-year-old son, is on the autism spectrum. Through her son’s experiences, she realized that there was a desperate need in Israel for a program to help those with disabilities find a true sense of belonging.
People are generally familiar with autistic savants who serve in the army’s elite 8200 unit, as well as those on the other extreme of the spectrum, who can barely communicate and require 24/7 supervision. However, many of those with autism generally do not fall into these extremes, she said, something that is true of people with all kinds of disabilities.
“There are lots of people in the middle. Most people are not at one end or the other. Most people are somewhere in between,” she said.
Edry's son has few opportunities to interact with his peers
While the Welfare and Social Affairs Ministry does not release detailed statistics on the functioning levels of people with disabilities, Edry said there are clearly thousands who are not served by any existing programs or frameworks.
After years in an educational system that provides them with a daily schedule, activities, social contact, and professional support, disabled people “age out” of the school system at age 21. They can suddenly find themselves with far fewer opportunities to meet people, participate in their communities, and build meaningful adult lives.
Edry has seen this happen with her son, who works part-time at a local branch of the Aroma café chain, thanks to Edry’s persistence and a kind manager who was willing to invest time showing her son the ropes. But outside of his working hours, her son spends most of his time at home and has few opportunities to interact with his peers. She searched hard, but didn’t find any programs that could help him.
She noted that Temple Grandin, a well-known autistic professor and activist in the US, wrote that she made friends when she was younger because she had opportunities to do interesting things with others.
“You build relationships by doing interesting things together – through a common interest. So, this program developed along those lines. One goal is to have people with disabilities become much more integrated into the community. But I didn’t want it to be a traditional ‘mentoring’ situation,” she noted.
“I therefore created a model where all participants would have the opportunity to do something meaningful together, through volunteering in the community and doing good for others.”
'They have fun together...they do wonderful things'
SHE IS DEVELOPING the Side by Side program in partnership with Et La’asot (A time to Act), an Israeli nonprofit organization that works with children and young people with disabilities and their families. Founded in 2006, Et La’asot runs programs across the country, including recreational activities, camps and vacations, weekend getaways, play centers, mentoring, family assistance, and volunteer training.
“Et La’asot’s existing model works with high school students,” said Edry. “High school students have volunteer requirements, and they work with children with disabilities. They have fun together. They travel around the country; they have play centers, one-on-one activities, and all kinds of programs. They do wonderful things.
“When I approached Et La’asot and proposed creating a similar model for older people, they were happy to partner with me to bring this project to fruition.”
Plans include volunteering with elderly people, assisting with food distribution, working in agriculture and animal care, and taking part in other community projects. The groups will also participate in trips, social activities, and special events.
But there was a problem. “People in their 20s and 30s often don’t have time simply to volunteer. The people I’m looking for are students who need to work to support themselves and pay tuition. So, I thought we could combine those things.
“The students will receive a grant for participating, and we can bring disabled and non-disabled young adults together to do enjoyable and meaningful things. If they go out and volunteer together in the community, they will be helping somebody else. They will be doing something useful together, something meaningful.”
Side by Side does not receive government funding. “A few very generous people have given us grants to get started. One donor has given $10,000 and is willing to match another $10,000, so donations made now, up to that amount, will be matched.”
The pilot program would start in Netanya, but Edry emphasized that it should become national.
Edry devoted herself to finding treatment and education after son's autism diagnosis
THE MORE you know about Edry, the more inspiring it is that she has taken on this ambitious project with the potential to help so many. Born and raised in a secular family in Great Neck, Long Island, she moved to Israel in her 20s, married a man from a more religiously observant background, and became interested in Judaism, gradually becoming observant herself. After one of her sons was diagnosed with autism, she devoted herself to finding treatment and education that would be most helpful to him, and he flourished.
About 13 years ago, when her son was a teen, she was diagnosed with a large tumor on her brainstem. Fortunately, it was benign, but she required complicated surgery that left her with numerous disabilities, including difficulties with sensory processing, similar to the types of neurodivergence typical of autistic individuals. These disabilities present her with many daily challenges. But her commitment to helping her son realize his potential has never wavered, and she is focused on reaching others in his situation.
In addition to taking the program national, she envisions Side by Side eventually adding a professional component.
“If my son had an apprenticeship – if professionals were willing to teach him one-on-one – he could learn many different types of jobs very well. I think most people with skills similar to his, if given that opportunity, could learn.
“There is a school in Colorado called TACT, which prepares people for apprenticeships and properly paying jobs – electricians, auto mechanics, plumbers, all different kinds of trades. The program has a waiting list for graduates. If we had something like that in Israel, it would be incredible.”
But in its initial phase, Side by Side will concentrate on creating social bonds.
“It is an opportunity for students to meet somebody different from themselves and realize that somebody who may need support can contribute to the community as well.”
The most important part of the program, she said, is that “by doing something meaningful together, hopefully real friendships will develop.”■
For more information, visit the Et La’asot website at www.etlaasot.org.il/BuildingCommunity
