OpenAI says its review into hacks, including on Australian government sites, is costing $500,000 a day
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
05:39:22 UTC
14:39:22 KST

OpenAI says its review in response to the Medicare and Hugging Face agent attacks is costing the company more than US$500,000 per day, as it deploys AI to examine data that would take a human 66m years to read.
The company has warned the review is ongoing, and more organisations may be informed they’ve been targeted in the near future.
On Friday evening, OpenAI revealed agents had hacked into a New South Wales government website in June and accessed historical non-public data on bushfires without authorisation.
It is the sixth government website in Australia to be notified by the AI giant since last month of agent activity on their services, after the prime minister, Anthony Albanese, announced OpenAI’s agents had hacked into Services Australia’s Medicare statistics portal.
The reason for the delay compared to the revelation of the Medicare attack is due to the sheer volume of data OpenAI needs to review.
In a blog post this week the company revealed the large amount of work involved in reviewing its agents’ activity.
OpenAI said it has to review 50 petabytes of data – roughly 50m gigabytes.
“We’re working back through the records month by month, looking for potential unintended activity beyond the cases we’ve already found,” the company said.
“To put that in perspective, if that were all plain English text, it would take one person about 66 million years to read it at 240 words a minute, reading nonstop without ever sleeping or taking a break.”
The company is searching records for where models accessed and changed websites, or took actions involving passwords, application programming interface (API) access or other sensitive credentials.
AI is being used to help sift through the records, and it was costing the company more than half a million US dollars per day to go through. OpenAI said it also plans to increase its computing power as the process is refined.
As of late last month, more than 100 organisations had been notified of having being targeted by OpenAI’s agents, but the company said notifying an organisation does not mean private information was accessed or that their system was compromised.
OpenAI said it expects to find more cases and notify more organisations about events that may have occurred months ago.
Organisations will be informed privately if they need to investigate and address potential security issues, and OpenAI has said it will publicly report findings about agent behaviour and identified weaknesses in safeguards for the broader AI sector.
“We err on the side of notification when our models’ activity exposes a potential security vulnerability, even in cases where it is unclear if the information accessed was intended to be public, so the organization can investigate and take appropriate action,” OpenAI said.
OpenAI discovered the latest NSW government website breach on Tuesday, and informed the state government and the Australian Signals Directorate after a 48-hour review.
The Medicare breach has prompted the Australian government to require departments and agencies to undertake a stocktake of legacy technology to reduce the number of ageing systems within government and reduce the cybersecurity risk they may present in the event of an AI agent attack.
Executives from OpenAI, Anthropic, Microsoft and Google will front a joint parliamentary committee on artificial intelligence in Sydney on Tuesday.

Authorities redirected buses Nos. 21, 73, and 101 to detour across the Podilskyi Bridge crossing, routing commuter traffic toward the Poshtova Ploshcha metro station and European Square to preserve transit links between the city’s eastern and western sectors.
The Ukrainian Air Force had issued an aerial warning at approximately 6:37 a.m. local time tracking a jet-powered unmanned aerial vehicle flying on a direct vector toward the Northern Bridge, minutes before heavy detonations echoed across the capital.
Drones Strike Russian Tsymbulovo Jet-UAV Base in Oryol
Local monitoring channels and eyewitnesses reported smoke and an active blaze near one of the primary bridge piers immediately following the blast.
Later, Klitschko stated that two people were injured as a result of a Russian strike on the North Bridge.
“Two people were injured this morning as a result of an enemy strike on the North Bridge in the capital. Medical personnel treated one of the injured on the spot. The other was hospitalized and is currently receiving outpatient treatment,” the mayor said.
Compounding pressure on capital transit crossings
The morning strike on the North Bridge follows days of systematic aerial targeting directed against Kyiv’s strategic river crossings, severely constraining vehicular and rail mobility across the Dnipro River.
On Friday, persistent Russian drone bombardments forced municipal authorities to completely close the South Bridge and impose severe traffic restrictions on both the Paton and Metro bridges, triggering gridlock across the capital.
Russian unmanned systems had repeatedly struck the South Bridge over the preceding 48 hours, damaging roadway sections, bridge piers, and structural barrier systems engineered to protect municipal metro infrastructure.
The recurring hits have placed immense strain on Kyiv’s surviving transport arteries, forcing hundreds of thousands of daily commuters to funnel through limited bypass corridors as municipal authorities work to reinforce critical transit nodes against standoff strikes.
Deadly overnight barrage
The strike on the river crossing occurred hours after a coordinated Russian ballistic missile and drone assault targeted the Ukrainian capital ealry Saturday morning, killing one person and injuring two others.
Mayor Klitschko reported that falling missile debris triggered structural fires across non-residential areas in the Sviatoshynskyi and Obolonskyi districts, while another fire ignited within a commercial garage cooperative in Sviatoshynskyi.

North Korea fired a ballistic missile towards the sea on Saturday, South Korea and Japan said, a day after it rejected Seoul’s accusation of its mines wounding soldiers.
The missile was launched from the Wonsan area at about 6.30am towards the East Sea – also known as the Sea of Japan – and flew more than 700km (434 miles), the South Korean military said. Seoul and Washington were analysing the test for details, it added.
Japan’s coast guard, citing the defence ministry, said the object may have been a ballistic missile and appeared to have come down, warning ships to take precautions.
South Korea’s military said it heightened its monitoring of any further missile tests and would share intelligence with the US and Japan. The South Korean presidential office’s national security council convened an emergency meeting on Saturday to assess the situation.
Pyongyang’s Kim Yo-jong, the powerful sister of ruler Kim Jong-un, issued a statement on Friday that dismissed Seoul’s demand for an apology for what it said were North Korean mines that seriously wounded South Korean soldiers in the demilitarised zone – the heavily guarded buffer between the two Koreas.
South Korea’s president, Lee Jae Myung, had urged Pyongyang on Thursday to return to dialogue, despite his military demanding an apology a day earlier. Kim Yo-jong responded by calling Seoul “really despicable” and ridiculing Lee’s latest overture, calling it “the climax of the farce that everyone should watch”.
Kim also warned that Pyongyang was “ready for anything” Seoul might do over the mine blast – remarks followed the next morning by North Korea’s ballistic missile launch.
South Korea said this week that North Korean mines caused the blast that injured three South Korean soldiers on a reconnaissance mission inside the 4km-wide buffer zone that stretches across the Korean peninsula.
The missile test might be an attempt by Pyongyang to draw a response from South Korea to the sister’s statement, said Cheong Seong-chang, vice-president at the Sejong Institute in Seoul, a research centre on North Korean affairs. North Korea might also have tested a new type of missile, he added.
North Korea has launched missile tests on more than 10 occasions so far this year. Some came after North Korea protested against joint military drills between Seoul and Washington.
North Korea has ramped up hostility against the South in recent years, disavowing unification as a national goal and calling South Korea its “primary foe”.

Latvia elects its 15th Saeima today
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
05:24:19 UTC
14:24:19 KST

Latvia’s 15th Saeima election takes place today, with 1,428 candidates from 14 political party lists competing for 100 seats in parliament.
There are five electoral districts in the Saeima election – Riga with 38 seats, Vidzeme with 26, Latgale with 12, Kurzeme with 11 and Zemgale with 13. Voters abroad cast their ballots for candidate lists in the Riga electoral district. As before, voters will be able to cast their ballots at any polling station in Latvia.
Data from the Central Election Commission (CVK) show that an average of 14.3 candidates are competing for each Saeima seat in this election. Competition has decreased compared with the 14th Saeima election, when an average of 18.3 candidates competed for each seat in 2022.
This time, 14 candidate lists with a total of 1,428 candidates have been submitted for the election – five fewer lists and 398 fewer candidates than in the previous parliamentary election.
The Sovereign Power/Young Latvians alliance will appear under number one on the ballot in the 15th Saeima election, while the Progressives drew the final number, 14.
We Are Changing the Rules will run under number two, Harmony Centre under number three, the Union of Greens and Farmers (ZZS) under number four, the National Alliance (NA) under number five, Gobzems’ List under number six and the United List (AS) under number seven.
Latvia First (LPV) will have number eight, New Unity (JV) number nine and the New Conservative Party (JKP) number ten. Latvia’s Development will run under number 11, Rising Sun for Latvia under number 12 and Stability! under number 13.
Seven political forces have fielded the maximum possible number of candidates across all five electoral districts – 125 each. They are the National Alliance, Latvia First, the Progressives, New Unity, the United List, the Union of Greens and Farmers and Sovereign Power/Young Latvians.
The remaining lists have fewer candidates: Harmony Centre has 105, JKP 85, Latvia’s Development 84, We Are Changing the Rules 77, Rising Sun for Latvia 75, Gobzems’ List 73 and Stability! 60.
The largest number of candidates is running in the Riga electoral district, where 527 people are competing for 38 seats. In Vidzeme, 347 candidates are competing for 26 seats; in Zemgale, 207 for 13 seats; in Latgale, 180 for 12 seats; and in Kurzeme, 173 for 11 seats.
At the same time, competition relative to the number of seats is highest in Zemgale and Kurzeme, while Riga has lower competition despite having the largest number of candidates.
LETA’s analysis of CVK data shows that candidates in the 15th Saeima election are older and more highly educated than in the previous election. The average age of candidates is 48.5 years, compared with 46.6 years in the previous election.
A total of 78.7% of candidates have reported having higher education, compared with 74.6% in 2022.
Of all candidates, 34% are women and 66% are men. The highest proportion of female candidates is in the Latgale electoral district, where women account for almost 40% of candidates. Meanwhile, 74.3% of candidates have identified themselves as Latvian and 7.6% as Russian.
Of all 1,434 candidates, 475, or one-third, also ran in the previous Saeima election, while around two-thirds are new candidates or at least did not stand in the 2022 parliamentary election.
A total of 933 in-person polling stations will operate in Latvia for this Saeima election, 15 fewer than in the previous election. At the same time, several municipalities plan to expand the network of mobile polling stations.
This year, voters can also cast their ballots at unconventional locations not previously used for voting, including Riga Airport, Riga Zoo, hospitals and shopping centres. Mobile polling stations will also operate at various locations across Latvia.
More than 83% of all polling stations will be accessible to people with reduced mobility.
Polling stations across Latvia will be open on Saturday from 08:00 to 20:00. Voters can cast their ballots at any polling station in Latvia regardless of their declared place of residence. Latvian citizens living abroad will vote for candidate lists in the Riga electoral district.
Preliminary election results will become available after polling stations close and the votes are counted.
At the polling station, each voter will receive a set of ballot papers and a stamped ballot envelope. Alone in a voting booth or screened-off area, the voter must select one candidate list.
The ballot can be left unchanged, or the voter can mark individual candidates by filling in the oval in the “for” column if they particularly support the candidate’s election, or in the “against” column if they do not support the candidate. Candidates’ names and surnames do not need to be crossed out.
The selected ballot paper must then be placed in the election envelope, which must be sealed and deposited in the ballot box.
Voters who are unable to visit a polling station due to their health, as well as people caring for someone who is ill, can apply to vote at their current location.
The CVK encourages voters to submit a written application in good time, preferably by 12:00 on 3 October. Applications received later will be fulfilled by the polling station commission if it is possible to reach the voter before voting ends.
If a voter previously deposited a ballot for safekeeping but chooses to vote again on election day, only the most recently cast ballot will be counted.
After voting ends, polling station commissions will begin counting the ballots. Votes will be counted manually during open commission meetings, which may be observed by authorised observers and media representatives.
Preliminary results will be published gradually as vote-counting data are received from polling stations.

The Disney generation: What unites Baby Boomers, millennials and Gen Z
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
05:20:48 UTC
14:20:48 KST

Disney stories may be aimed at children, but their lessons can last a lifetime. A study by SWPS University in Poland found that values such as friendship, loyalty, family, courage, resilience and being yourself can stay with us well into adulthood.
Some stories stay with us long after childhood is over. With time, details of the plot, the order of the songs and even the characters’ names may fade. What remains are the emotions and the ideas these stories gave us about the world.
For decades, Disney has been part of childhood for generations of Poles. Research by SWPS University found that 84% of adult Poles regularly watched Disney films and animations as children, while 82% still have a soft spot for them.
But it is not just about nostalgia. Our attachment to these stories is also linked to values that can stay with us well into adulthood.
The values mentioned most often were friendship and loyalty, cited by 46% of respondents. They were followed by the triumph of good over evil (43%), overcoming difficulties (32%) and family (31%).
Money, fame and prestige did not feature among the most frequently mentioned values, nor did the drive to be the best. For adult Poles, Disney is associated above all with relationships, kindness, personal growth, loyalty and responsibility.
In other words, it seems to be less about what we achieve and more about who we share our lives with and the kind of people we want to be.
Friendship before success
In Disney stories, heroes rarely make it on their own. Friends, family and sometimes unexpected allies are there to support them, helping them through their toughest moments.
It is therefore no surprise that friendship and loyalty rank among the values most strongly associated with Disney.
The message remains relevant at any age. Some 89% of Poles say kindness towards others matters, while the same proportion believe in the value of being yourself. Courage is valued by 87%, family by 86%, and 84% agree that love can help us overcome difficulties.
The differences between generations are relatively small.
This could help explain why Disney continues to resonate with people who grew up at different times. The characters may change, but the need for connection, friendship and the sense that we are not alone remains the same.
Each generation sees these stories differently
Sharing the same core values does not mean that every generation sees these stories in quite the same way.
For Baby Boomers (born between 1945 and 1965), the idea that the world should have clear rules seems particularly strong. Some 54% say the triumph of good over evil is one of the values reflected in Disney stories. Their responses also highlight honesty, hope, perseverance and a belief in justice.
Generation X (born between 1965 and 1980) are more likely to associate Disney stories with responsibility, growing up and dealing with adversity. For 74% of respondents in this group, Disney also offered a glimpse of the Western world.
Millennials (born between 1980 and 1995) place more emphasis on authenticity, acceptance and the freedom to live life on their own terms. Characters such as Mulan, Elsa and Vaiana do not simply try to meet other people’s expectations. Their stories are about discovering who they are and finding their place in the world.
“I have the right to be myself”
This shift is most apparent among the youngest participants.
Self-acceptance is mentioned by 12% of the oldest respondents, compared with 29% of Gen Z (born between 1995 and 2010). Independence and diversity show a similar pattern, rising from around 10% among the oldest respondents to 18% among Gen Z.
The difference is even more striking when it comes to pursuing dreams: 14% of Baby Boomers mention this, compared with 38% of Gen Z.
The pattern is reversed when it comes to the belief that good triumphs over evil. This is cited by 54% of the oldest respondents, compared with 24% of the youngest.
This does not mean that younger people have stopped believing in good. Rather, what they expect from a hero appears to have changed.
Simply defeating evil and restoring order is no longer enough. What also matters is whether a hero can choose who they want to be and the path they want to take.
For Gen Z, self-realisation, identity, belonging and acceptance of diversity are particularly important. The key message can be summed up simply: find your own path.
The classics still matter
It might seem that a generation with almost unlimited choice of content would be ready to leave classic Disney behind. Yet Gen Z are not rejecting its core values. Instead, they want to see them combined with a more contemporary approach to storytelling.
Almost half of Gen Z respondents (46%) favour combining Disney classics with modern ideas.
The picture is similar across all respondents. A large majority (87%) want Disney’s classic values to be preserved. Of these, 45% would like them to remain unchanged, while 42% would prefer to see them combined with modern values. Only 4% would like Disney to fully adapt its values to current social trends.
Contemporary stories are also well received, particularly when they focus on overcoming difficulties (75%), working together (74%) and perseverance (72%).
So the choice is not really between classic Disney and modern storytelling. It is about holding on to values that still resonate while telling stories in a way that reflects the world we live in today.
Lessons from childhood stay with us
This may be why Disney has become a shared experience for so many generations. Not because everyone remembers the same films and characters, but because each generation has found something of its own in these stories.
Baby Boomers remember justice, honesty and hope. Generation X associate Disney with responsibility, perseverance and the strength to overcome adversity. Millennials value authenticity and the freedom to live life on their own terms. Gen Z place more emphasis on self-realisation, identity and the courage to find their own path.
Yet beneath these differences, the same values come through: friendship, loyalty, family, courage, kindness and perseverance.
They are not new or particularly fashionable. But perhaps that is why they have lasted.
Disney has never been only about castles, crowns and happy endings. Its stories have also taught generations the value of having people they can trust, the strength to get through difficult times and the freedom to choose their own path.
Growing up does not necessarily mean leaving these stories behind. We may forget some of the details, but the lessons can stay with us long after childhood is over.

Government extends reduced indexation for top officials' pay, saving €32 million
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
05:11:00 UTC
14:11:00 KST

Government extends reduced indexation for top officials' pay, saving €32 million
The government's decision to slow salary growth for some higher‑ranking state officials over the next three years will save €32.3 million, but judges argue the move may violate the constitution.
In the state budget strategy approved by the government, the reduced indexation of certain top officials' salaries — introduced in 2024 — was extended until the end of 2030.
Under current law, full indexation of all top state officials' salaries should resume on 1 April 2028.
"The government has now approved continuing the reduced indexation in the state budget strategy for 2028–2030. Over three years, this means €32.3 million in savings," said Ministry of Finance spokesperson Elo Ellermaa.
She explained that the indexation exception was introduced in 2023 as a temporary measure, intended to apply from 1 April 2024 to 31 March 2028 for certain top officials. These include members of the government, judges, the prosecutor general, the secretary of state, the national conciliator, and the gender equality and equal treatment commissioner. Their salaries also determine the pay of other officials, such as chancellors and prosecutors.
As of 1 April 2026, the highest salary rate for top state officials is €10,240 (rounded), determined automatically by law.
The highest salaries are paid to the president, the speaker of parliament, and the chief justice of the Supreme Court.
Under the law on top state officials' salaries, the highest salary rate is 4.8 times the average Estonian wage, and this ratio has remained stable over the years.
Judges say the decision may violate the constitution
Judges argue that the government's earlier decision to slow salary growth may be unconstitutional.
"We constantly face the problem that too few good lawyers apply to become judges, and we have no real choice. We're lucky if we find even one suitable candidate, and sometimes competitions fail entirely because there are no candidates," said Ivo Pilving, chair of the Supreme Court's administrative chamber.
Pilving noted that judges leave the profession because of salary issues.
"Not everyone says directly that it's because of low pay; they usually point to high stress and workload, which is indeed a fact. These things are connected: if the salary doesn't compensate for the workload and stress, people find jobs with less pressure or places that pay more," Pilving said.
Judges have challenged the earlier decision to slow salary growth in court.
"The dispute over the initial cut, which dozens of judges contested, reached the Supreme Court just this week. The Supreme Court accepted two of those complaints, and more are on their way," Pilving said.
He emphasized that he personally cannot take a position on whether the complaints are justified.
"According to the constitution, the parliament, government, and courts should be — not 100 percent equal — but reasonably comparable. The longer this reduced indexation continues, the wider the gap becomes," he said.
Recently, rescue workers earning €1,600 gross have publicly raised concerns about their pay. A journalist asked whether judges, out of solidarity, might send a message that they are willing to accept somewhat lower pay during difficult times.
"This balance of powers concerns comparisons between the government, parliament, and courts. They are the constitutional institutions that should be on roughly the same level," Pilving replied.
He stressed that this comparison does not concern rescue workers, teachers, or nurses.
"I do not want to diminish any of those professions in the slightest. I — and I believe all judges — hold them in the highest respect. But judges have a special constitutional status that no other profession, including rescue workers or police officers, has," Pilving said.
He emphasized that the constitution requires judges' social guarantees to be set not by ordinary law but by a constitutional law, which requires at least 51 votes in parliament.
Pilving explained that judges have this special status to ensure there is no doubt about whether they dare intervene in government actions or conduct constitutional review of parliamentary laws when necessary.
"All of this harms the rule of law if judges' guarantees are now eroded," Pilving said.
Judges' salaries are also tied to the lifetime nature of the position.
"If we keep undermining judges' motivation and social pressure builds for them to leave the profession, then we can no longer speak of lifetime appointments," Pilving said.
According to him, this is a clear constitutional infringement.
"These serious discussions still lie ahead, and they are extremely uncomfortable, because it does not look good for the courts to have to assess judges' own salaries. Fortunately, none of the complainants are members of the Supreme Court," Pilving said.

Flydubai pilot who tried to crash plane in Israel identified, had ‘extremist materials’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
05:08:22 UTC
14:08:22 KST

U.S. media outlets early Saturday revealed the identity of the Omani pilot who stabbed the captain of a flydubai flight to Israel on Wednesday and tried to crash the plane with its Israeli passengers on board.
Hammam al-Hamami, whose previous employment with Oman Air ended amid suspicions that he had become radicalized, admitted during questioning that he intended to crash the plane in Israeli territory, ABC News reported, citing sources familiar with the investigation. The sources told the network that he was “cooperating” with investigators in the United Arab Emirates in an investigation that Israel is also expected to take an active part in, according to reports.
The Wall Street Journal, which first reported that he had been suspended from flying for Oman Air, said it remains unclear whether those suspicions were later passed on to flydubai before the airline hired him.
According to a LinkedIn account bearing his name, he worked for Oman Air for seven years before leaving Oman’s national carrier in February 2025. He joined Moroccan carrier Royal Air Maroc in June 2025 but left six months later, in January 2026. His LinkedIn profile did not list his subsequent employment with flydubai, which began this year.
According to ABC News, in 2024, while he was still a co-pilot with Oman Air, “extremist materials” were found in his possession. As a result, the airline decided to remove him from flying duties, though he continued working for the company in an administrative role. Reports said it remains unclear whether that information was later passed on to the other airlines he worked for, Royal Air Maroc and flydubai.
Saudi network Al Arabiya reported Friday that al-Hamami became radicalized while staying in Syria. “He spent most of his time outside Oman, particularly in Syria,” the network reported. A source cited in the report said Omani authorities realized that he held extremist views and that he had spent time in Syria because his mother is Syrian, adding that he may have been influenced there by the ideas of radical groups.
CNN reported that only two posts appeared on the pilot’s LinkedIn profile, both published Wednesday, nine hours after the attack. The network said it was unclear who uploaded the posts but raised the possibility that they had been scheduled in advance.
According to the report, the first post contained a series of videos filmed in the cockpits of Boeing 737 MAX aircraft. The flydubai plane that al-Hamami allegedly tried to crash was also a 737 MAX.
CNN said one of the videos was filmed at Dubai International Airport, with the person recording it zooming in on an El Al aircraft. A cockpit display visible in the video showed the flight number of the Oman Air flight he was operating at the time, from Dubai to Muscat on October 11, 2023, several days after the Hamas-led October 7 massacre in Israel.
The post included additional videos showing El Al aircraft, as well as one Arkia plane. It ended with an image of al-Qaeda leader Ayman al-Zawahiri, Osama bin Laden’s successor, who was also killed by the United States.
The second post published on the now-deleted LinkedIn account included an AI-generated image depicting the three cities considered holy in Islam — Mecca, Medina and Jerusalem — connected by a continuous glowing path, according to CNN. A song playing in the background included declarations against “humiliation,” with the speaker saying he was not afraid of death and would defend his honor.
According to the profile, al-Hamami studied at Buckinghamshire New University in England. A university official confirmed to CNN that a person by that name completed a three-year distance-learning program, graduating in 2023 with a degree in aviation management.
CNN also reported that an account on X, formerly Twitter, belonging to a person with the suspect’s name and since deleted contained expressions of extremist religious views.
In several posts, for example, he described his mother’s difficulty finding him a prospective wife who would agree to his requirement that she wear a niqab, the Muslim face covering that leaves only a narrow opening for the eyes.
“They all refused. Then my mother told them, ‘My son is a pilot,’ and suddenly they all agreed,” read a February 2022 post.
In another post, he expressed opposition to men and women working together.
“How many respectable, religious young women have been ruined in mixed-gender workplaces and manipulated?” read the January 2022 post.
The investigation into al-Hamami is being conducted in the United Arab Emirates. A source familiar with the matter said the pilot will be questioned by the State Security Department, which reports directly to President Mohammed bin Zayed. Israel hopes the co-pilot’s transfer from Saudi Arabia to the UAE will allow for cooperation as the investigation continues. Israel’s exact role remains unclear, but whether it participates directly in the questioning or serves as an observer, officials in Jerusalem are expected to receive regular updates from Abu Dhabi. Despite the close ties between the two countries, however, the Emiratis are expected to keep Israel’s involvement low-profile.
After U.S. President Donald Trump said he had “heard Iran” was connected to the Omani pilot who tried to crash the flydubai flight, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu suggested in a video Friday that someone may have been behind the attempted crash. It is unclear what his remarks were based on, however, and Israeli security officials say that while all possibilities are being investigated, there is currently no indication that the co-pilot was acting on behalf of or under the direction of any outside party. The current assessment is that he acted alone and on his own initiative. The Associated Press reported overnight, citing a source familiar with the investigation, that there is currently no evidence linking the attacker to Iran.
The UAE attorney general provided an update on the investigation Saturday morning, saying the co-pilot is suspected of attempting to carry out a terrorist attack, after Abu Dhabi on Friday formally described the incident aboard the plane as an attempted terrorist attack for the first time.
“He attacked the captain with an emergency ax and attempted to take control of the flight systems. The investigation is continuing with the aim of uncovering all the circumstances and motives behind the incident on the flight,” the attorney general said.
Meanwhile, amid reports pointing to a potentially serious security failure, flydubai said Saturday morning that the circumstances of the incident remain under investigation and that it therefore could not comment further. Netanyahu has already acknowledged that allowing the Omani pilot to operate a flight to Israel, which has no diplomatic relations with Oman, was a “loophole” the attacker was able to exploit.

====================================================================================================

‘It’s given my mental health a massive boost’: Why everyone should hone their bushcraft skills
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
05:02:26 UTC
14:02:26 KST

The Bushcraft Bus is reconnecting Europeans with nature.
If you’re not a military green-clad survivalist or a forest-bathing wellness enthusiast, you might feel “a little bit lost” in the great outdoors, says bushcraft instructor and conservationist Jim Todd.
It’s a problem the brightly coloured Bushcraft Bus – the mobile home of wilderness and nature education – aims to solve.
“We’re trying to fill that gap in the middle, where you don't have to identify with anything. You just need to have a little bit of kit, and just be up for it,” says Jim.
Jim, 39, and Bushcraft Bus co-founder Tom Young, 37, met in Dorset five years ago while qualifying to be bushcraft instructors. Now they host foraging walks, wilderness skills workshops and fire-roasted woodland dinners in the south of England and beyond. In the UK – which ranked 55th out of 61 nations in a global study on “nature connectedness” – some of the people who join them have never even set foot in the woods.
It doesn’t take long for them to realise what they’ve been missing.
“The excitement builds through the day,” Tom tells Euronews Earth from their camp in the Cotswolds’ Voltaires Wood. “Some people are quite timid at the start but they’re often the ones who get the most out of it,” adds Jim.
King Alfred’s Cakes or ‘cramp balls’ are a particular crowdpleaser. Resembling round lumps of coal, this fungus is commonly found on fallen ash and beech trees, and can be used as a fire lighter – a discovery that left a recent participant of their woodland cookout “just ecstatic”, recalls Tom.
What’s the most essential wilderness skill?
Being ‘apocalypse-ready’ isn’t a focus of the Bushcraft Bus – but the skills it teaches feel increasingly important. The UK government recently advised citizens to prepare for threats from the climate crisis and hostile states, including by stocking up on tinned food.
It came after a record-hot summer placed swathes of Europe under heat and water stress – compounded by soaring household bills resulting from tensions in the Middle East, not to mention the looming threat of water- and energy-hungry AI.
Jim says these factors are a motivating force for some participants who join their courses, and many leave less fearful, more confident and better connected.
“When you start thinking through that lens, you realise how little you actually know to defend yourself or survive in that situation,” he says. “We’re so reliant on all of these big systems working. And if any of them collapse, we’re back to basics really quickly… Like, what if there was no heating and it was the middle of winter? Or how do I find water and purify it?”
Fire-making is “instrumental” – not only for survival but also for “how much you can enjoy the time that you have in the woods,” says Jim. “Fire ties everything together”, agrees Tom – from “learning about tree identification, so you can burn the right woods, to learning about what to forage and how to cook it”.
For this reason, Tom always carries a ferro rod (a metallic fire starter stick) – a tool that was indispensable on his 66-day solo hike through the European Arctic in 2018.
But bushcraft skills only go so far – and the biggest lifeline often gets overlooked: community. That could mean curating your friendship group: “Making sure you’ve got a friend who’s a nurse and who would know how to treat an injury, and someone else who’s got a mechanical mind who could help turn a dead car into something useful,” says Tom.
‘When you pour energy and curiosity into nature, you get it back’
This collaborative spirit is something off-grid living seems to nurture – not only between fellow humans, but with the land itself.
“A lot of people don’t learn about the woods anymore. So from a very young age, you’re already disconnected,” says Tom.
There are signs that this is slowly starting to change: the UK government recently approved a new Natural History GCSE (an exam subject that can be chosen at 14-years-old) for secondary school students, which it hopes will “grow the next generation of green careers”.
“I think if you can teach people and give people some of that knowledge and awareness, they’ll naturally start caring and appreciating more about those spaces,” says Tom.
This can look like conserving precious resources: “We’ve wheelbarrowed all of our water up a 15-minute steep, bumpy track,” says Jim, sitting in their woodland camp. “So we’re not splashing it around when we’re up here… Instinctively it does reset your brain to be way more conservative with your usage.”
Or being mindful of what you take from the land: “You need to leave some of whatever you’re foraging for the animals,” says Jim – and in the case of mushrooms, for the fungus itself: “The reason they fruit is to spread the spores,” adds Tom.
Connecting with nature is “like a relationship”, muses Jim. “You have to build it – you can’t just expect it to give you everything. You have to pour energy and curiosity into it, and then you get it back. That’s when it starts providing real value to you.”
‘Exploring the outdoors has given my mental health a massive boost’
Both Jim and Tom admit that in their younger years, they were more interested in going to the pub than on long country walks. These days, it’s more often screens that are keeping teenagers indoors.
Both also think Europe has a lot to learn from other cultures about connecting with nature. During time spent in New Zealand and Canada, they found outdoor skills are embedded more deeply into everyday life. Vast landscapes make the outdoors harder to ignore, while activities such as kayaking, hiking and camping are familiar from a young age.
“The outdoors is all around you all the time,” says Jim, contrasting that with the UK’s denser landscape, where farmland and privately owned woodland can make natural spaces feel surprisingly inaccessible.
As a result, “we almost see ourselves as separate from the natural world,” reflects Jim. “But I think if you do get out into it, most people very quickly feel this connection to it. And when you add in skills that you can use outside, you are just building that self-reliance and confidence.”
Tom’s experience stands as testament to this: “Exploring the outdoors has given me what feels like a purpose,” he says. “It’s given my mental health that massive boost. In life as well, just talking to people with more confidence, and that’s developed through the years.”

House prices keep rising across Europe: Which countries saw the biggest increases and why?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
05:00:54 UTC
14:00:54 KST

House prices in Europe continue to rise, outpacing inflation in many countries. Annual increases ranged from 0.6% in Germany to 16.5% in Portugal in the second quarter of 2026.
House prices continue to rise across much of Europe, but the pace varies widely. Portugal, Bulgaria and Spain recorded double-digit annual increases in the second quarter of 2026, while prices fell in Finland, Luxembourg and France.
Across the EU, prices rose by 4.7% compared with a year earlier, outpacing inflation of 3.2%.
So where are prices rising fastest, and how much of that growth remains once inflation is taken into account?
Over 15% rise in Portugal and Bulgaria
Among 29 European countries, nine recorded double-digit year-on-year rises in house prices, according to Eurostat. Portugal saw the highest year-on-year increase in the second quarter of 2026, at 16.5%, closely followed by Bulgaria (15.5%).
Mikk Kalmet, areal estate expert at Global Property Guide, noted that strong housing demand continues to outstrip supply in Portugal, particularly in Lisbon, Porto and popular coastal areas. “Limited new construction, foreign investment, tourism-related demand and persistent housing shortages have all contributed to rising prices,” he told Euronews Business.
Kalmet explained that in Bulgaria, rising household incomes, wage growth, relatively affordable mortgage financing and strong demand for property as an investment have supported price increases.
Lithuania (14.3%), Slovakia (13.6%), Croatia (12.7%), Spain (12.1%), Romania (12.1%), Latvia (11.4%) and Hungary (10.2%) also recorded increases of more than 10%.
Denmark (9.4%), Slovenia (9.1%) and Czechia (8.6%) were also close to the 10% level.
House prices also rose by more than the EU average in Cyprus (7.9%), Malta (6.9%), Poland (6.3%), Ireland (6%), Estonia (5.8%), Austria (5.1%) and Sweden (4.8%).
Three countries saw declines
Finland (-2.7%), Luxembourg (-2.2%) and France (-0.8%) were the only countries where house prices declined year on year over this period.
Mikk Kalmet pointed to weak economic growth in Finland, along with subdued consumer confidence and the lingering effects of higher interest rates.
“In France, affordability constraints, relatively weak housing demand and the effects of previously elevated mortgage rates have put downward pressure on prices,” Kalmet said, adding that economic uncertainty has also encouraged some prospective buyers to postpone purchases.
Among the EU’s ‘Big Four’ economies, Spain stands out with a 12.1% rise, while Italy (4%) is below the EU average. Germany recorded only a slight increase of 0.6%, just above France, where house prices fell by 0.8%.
“[In Germany] higher mortgage rates are back. Housing affordability is deteriorating. Demand for mortgage loans is weakening,” Carsten Brzeski and Franziska Biehl from ING wrote in their analysis.
Local fundamentals drive Europe’s housing divide
Kalmet pointed out that the different rates of house price growth largely reflect national housing shortages, income growth, mortgage conditions and demographic trends. “Housing markets are fundamentally local, even though European countries share many of the same economic and monetary conditions,” he said.
Countries experiencing strong demand and limited construction tend to see faster price increases. In contrast, countries with weaker economic growth, subdued household demand or greater sensitivity to borrowing costs have experienced slower growth or declining prices.
Growth is still strong in real terms
When inflation is taken into account, real house price growth is still strong in many countries.
In the EU, with inflation at 3.2%, house prices rose by 1.5% in real terms.
However, growth remained much stronger in several countries. In Portugal, for example, inflation was 3.6% over this period, resulting in real house price growth of 12.1%.
Real growth was also above 7% in Slovakia (9.4%), Bulgaria (9.1%), Lithuania (8.8%), Spain (8.3%), Latvia (7.9%), Denmark (7.7%), Hungary (7.7%) and Croatia (7.5%).
Six countries recorded declines in real terms, led by Luxembourg with a fall of 6.4%. Real house prices also fell by 3.2% in France and 2% in Germany.
Explaining what has driven house prices over this one year, Kalmet said: “Three factors stand out: persistent housing shortages, household income growth and changing mortgage conditions. In many European countries, residential construction has failed to keep pace with housing demand.
What’s next for house prices?
Kalmet expects that persistent housing shortages and continued demand could support further price increases in many European markets. However, growth is likely to remain uneven, and another year of double-digit increases should not be taken for granted.
“The biggest uncertainty is interest rates. The ECB raised rates in September 2026 in response to renewed inflationary pressures. Higher mortgage costs, combined with weaker purchasing power caused by rising energy prices, could slow housing demand,” he said.
Brzeski and Biehl noted that prospective buyers in Germany now face a challenging combination of higher property prices, higher financing costs and the lingering effects of weaker real purchasing power, driven by the adverse economic effects of the war in the Middle East.

Half of UK wants to rejoin EU and backing it could drive up Labour vote, megapoll finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
05:00:52 UTC
14:00:52 KST

Andy Burnham’s personal preference to rejoin the European Union after the next election is supported by almost half of all voters, a new megapoll has found, although cabinet ministers concerned about reopening Brexit divides are privately urging him to proceed with caution.
The poll by the Messina Group (TMG) found that renegotiating the UK’s relationship with the EU could boost Labour’s vote share by as much as seven points, if the prime minister offered a fresh referendum in which he campaigned to re-enter the bloc.
Almost a third of voters said an in-out referendum would be needed first, while more than one in six felt that a general election mandate would be sufficient, and the same proportion thought parliament could make the decision.
The overall findings will bolster the case of those inside Downing Street who want to promise at the next election that Labour would at least negotiate over re-entry, which the prime minister has said he wants to see “in his lifetime”.
Burnham used his first Labour conference speech as leader on Tuesday to announce a review of the options for Britain’s future relationship with Europe, and subsequently added that these should include rejoining entirely.
However, there are nerves among some Labour MPs, especially those with constituencies that voted for Brexit, that even testing out public support for the move would be fraught with political risk and a potential boost to Reform.
Two-thirds of cabinet ministers, including Burnham himself, his first secretary, Louise Haigh, chancellor, John Healey, and foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, represent seats that backed Brexit, and previously said they would respect the 2016 vote. However, public opinion has shifted.
Before Burnham’s speech, several ministers had publicly cautioned against the move. Lucy Powell, Labour’s deputy leader, said while the defence and security relationship could be better, going beyond EU reset plans inherited from Keir Starmer was “not possible nor desirable”.
The trade secretary, Jonathan Reynolds, said “constitutional questions” around Britain’s EU relationship were causing uncertainty for business. The home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, said rejoining was “not a simple, straightforward thing” and the costs might be unacceptable.
Downing Street’s strategy appears to be to put the focus on those who made big promises on Brexit but then failed to deliver, rather than accusing those who voted to leave the EU of making the wrong decision. But the government’s shift in position has caused some anxiety among Burnham’s team.
One cabinet minister told the Guardian: “Brexit clearly hasn’t worked and the promises made haven’t been kept so Andy is right to open up the question of what the future relationship looks like. But he definitely needs to proceed with caution because we don’t want to restoke division”.
A second said: “Andy is right to say we need some clarity around our long-term relationship. Security and trade cooperation are higher up the agenda than they were 10 years ago. But whether that adds up to a real desire for big change in the population I don’t know. My constituents will be cautious.”
A third added: “There are obviously different views across cabinet about it, but the Made in Europe agenda means we do need to talk to the EU about what relationship they want with us long term, as what they are currently proposing is very challenging.”
Another cabinet source said: “There’s an awareness among a number of cabinet ministers with leave voting seats that opinions are going to differ and the arguments about the future will have to be carefully made about the national interest.”
A fifth said there were genuine questions about the best option on the table. “I’m sceptical if we go back in, about the terms we’d be going back in on, and whether that can really resolve the problems in people’s lives. But if you look at the global context you cannot start to solve things for people without having a closer relationship with the EU.”
TMG polled 11,461 people, weighted by referendum result, from 12-24 September on seven different options for relationships with the EU. The most popular was rejoin, with 49% in favour and 28.5% against.
The second was to keep the existing relationship but cut as many trade barriers as possible – as the government is attempting to do with its reset – and which was supported by 48.2%, with 20.9% against. A customs union came next, on 47.1% versus 20.7%.
Joining the single market and associate membership were virtually neck and neck – 45.1% and 45.5% of respondents respectively support them – while sticking with the existing relationship was backed by 42%. The seventh option – the UK moving further away from the EU – was supported by only 27.9%, with 41.2% against.
A plurality of voters – 25.9% – said they wanted the UK to rejoin the EU immediately, while a slightly lower proportion – 22.9% – said it should happen in the next three years, and 8.4% over the next decade, while 23% said they did not want a closer relationship at all.
TMG also tested political messaging for each of the options to see how they could affect Labour’s vote share in an election, and found that it went up – by between 4.3 and 7.4 percentage points – for all the scenarios that resulted in closer ties, with most votes coming from the Greens and Lib Dems.
The polling showed that more than two-thirds of voters thought that trading with the EU was more important than the US or China, in the event the UK had to choose; four in five people want to keep the pound; and a majority want to stay in the ECHR – 53.4% versus 24.2% against.
However, it also found that Brexit arguments over immigration control and sovereignty still resonated.
Senior Downing Street officials have been in contact with thinktanks and pollsters as they look to test public support for the UK rejoining the EU. The TMG research is expected to be shared with the current operation.
Some inside No 10 are nervous, however, that promising to renegotiate entry into the bloc could revive the flagging political fortunes of Nigel Farage, who said on Thursday Burnham had given him “the biggest boost in my career” by reviving the Brexit debate.
The TMG research found that 29.7% people thought the UK had been right to leave the EU, while 52.4% said it had been wrong, and 17.9% didn’t know. On whether it had been a success or failure, 12.2% said a success, 54.9% a failure, 23.2% said neither and 9.7% did not know.
Ben Judah, a visiting fellow at Chatham House who was an adviser to David Lammy as foreign secretary, told the Guardian: “These polls are a massive validation of Andy Burnham’s boldness on Europe. There is close to a national consensus that Brexit was not a success.
“Against this background these results show that Europe as an issue has a unique ability to unite the left and grow the Labour vote share among swing voters. The bolder the stance towards rejoin, the bigger Labour’s reward.”

====================================================================================================

I’m not buying into the ‘Keminaissance’. If the Tories lowered the bar any further, they’d be Reform UK | Frances Ryan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
05:00:52 UTC
14:00:52 KST

Kemi Badenoch is considering doing her job. With her second Conservative party conference as leader looming on Sunday, and her rival Nigel Farage finally losing some ground, the provocateur with a reputation for dodging media rounds and being ill-prepared for briefs has seemingly cured her camera shyness.
In recent days, Badenoch has touted a policy to give the unemployed a “subsistence allowance” that would prevent them from buying booze or cigarettes, sought to bar benefits from young people who are straight out of school, accused Andy Burnham of wanting to take Britain “back to the 1970s” with public control of utilities, and enjoyed some mixed polling.
That the rightwing press has greeted this with a relief bordering on delusion (the Telegraph went as far to suggest the Conservatives could win a snap election) gives a hint of how dismally low the bar is in parts of the Tory camp.
More than two years since the Conservative’s crushing general election defeat, it is not simply that the most successful electoral force in the democratic world has collapsed into irrelevance – but that it has happened with barely a whimper. The juggernaut success of Reform UK, mixed with Badenoch’s unwillingness to fully engage, has given large sections of the media licence to treat Farage as unofficial leader of the opposition, with the Conservatives getting most column inches when another one of them defects to Reform.
The so-called natural party of government is essentially now an afterthought in the national conversation, throwing out an anti-migrant comment here and an ableist speech there in the hope of just getting some attention.
Meanwhile, the country quietly gets on with the day-to-day consequences of the last time it let the Tories govern: fundraising to patch up the roof at their children’s school, waiting a year to get a hospital scan, or walking past their now closed local library.
There has been an audible sigh of relief from Badenoch’s team as her personal poll ratings markedly improved over the past year, even as the Conservative’s image has tanked (as of last month, only 19% of Britons feel the party is ready for a return to government). But talk of a “Keminaissance” misses the point: it means little that the electorate are slightly less put off by the captain if they still wouldn’t get on the ship for fear of drowning.
That, as of last week, Badenoch – nostalgic for the days the Tories were a main player in a two-party system – is still ruling out an electoral pact with Reform is only further weakening her chances of ever seeing No 10.
It’s not as if the Conservatives have made any substantive efforts for reputation rehabilitation. Are they regretful of Brexit? What about Partygate? If re-elected, would they repeat Liz Truss’s deep tax cuts or George Osborne’s austerity? As the public faces mounting crises, from gutted living standards to long NHS waiting lists, Badenoch has largely kept stumm rather than offer any meaningful solutions. Indeed, on a rare occasion she has spoken out on a pressing issue – namely social care – it was to refuse to engage with Burnham’s reforms if paying for it involved tax rises.
You could argue that it would have made sense to regroup after such a large-scale loss – not least when Keir Starmer was expected to fulfil a five-year term – or that it is rather difficult to propose solutions for problems that your party has largely caused. There is truth in both. And yet it is telling what Badenoch chooses to spend her energy on. While the former minister has told her MPs not to expect big policy plans until 2027, she has found time to wade into culture wars including, but not limited to: why she hates critical race theory; a U-turn on the Conservative commitment to meet net zero by 2050; and why she wants the UK to withdraw from the European convention on human rights.
It’s not a coincidence that Badenoch’s main policy intervention ahead of gathering in Birmingham for conference is a universal credit cut that would shame unemployed people not trusted to spend cash to have to use a special debit card while saving a paltry £538m a year for the taxpayer (As context, the state pension bill is now £154bn annually.) It is less a substantive socioeconomic policy and more a wink to the audience, a casual cruelty that would make already hard lives even harder for the vague promise of a point in the polls. That Badenoch presumably genuinely believes in this stuff is a grim added bonus.
The Conservatives will clearly be hoping that Reform’s downward spiral continues and in the meantime, the benefits bill – much like immigration – seems easy pickings. The proposed universal credit cut is the latest in their package of welfare cuts worth £23bn. But that Reform recently announced a plan to slice a staggering £50bn from the social security budget shows that as extreme as Badenoch continues to go in the coming months, Reform will go further. That Farage is now being clipped by Rupert Lowe’s Restore shows neatly enough that no matter what depths you are willing to sink to, someone out there will dig their way lower still. Britain’s hard right in 2026 is effectively a Russian doll: each party pushes the previous one inside, only to reveal an even worse version underneath.
In another timeline, Badenoch would be pivoting to the centre, or at least the centre right, picking up traditional Conservative voters who fear Burnham’s threat of higher taxes and squirm at Reform’s race-baiting. But Badenoch is not the candidate for that fight. For all her inaction, she has been clear about her direction: centrist ideas are no longer wanted in the Conservative party, she has said, and if one-nation Tories have qualms about her rightward push, they “need to get out of the way”.
This is not the opposition era of David Cameron with huskies, or William Hague on a log flume wearing a baseball cap. Badenoch has no interest in ridding the Conservatives of their “nasty party” image. She is rejuvenating it. This is the party of the Windrush scandal, mass disability benefit cuts, and “go home” vans repackaged for an even more toxic climate. The only question is: will it actually work? It is hard to say what’s worse: selling your soul for power or selling it and still losing.

‘A beacon of peace’: London’s oldest mosque celebrates centenary
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
05:00:51 UTC
14:00:51 KST

Exactly 100 years ago the Guardian wrote about the opening of London’s first mosque, an impressive white building surrounded by immaculate flower gardens in the heart of south London suburbia.
A report described the mosque, in its incongruous surroundings, as “a thing of beauty”. The journalists who attended the opening ceremony witnessed the mosque’s large black doors being opened with a silver key. About 600 eminent guests attended the grand opening.
Ahead of centenary celebrations at the Fazl Mosque in Wandsworth, also known as London Mosque, there is lots of activity taking place. Putney Labour MP Fleur Anderson pops in and speaks about how well loved the mosque, which is home to members of the UK’s Ahmadiyya Muslim community, is in the area.
“No street party is complete without the wonderful food provided by this mosque,” she says.
According to Mahmood Rafiq of the Ahmadiyya Muslim Community UK, being part of the wider community is a key part of the mosque’s ethos. They give out sweets to local children at Eid, extend Christmas greetings to neighbours, help to keep the local environment clean and show support for other faiths if they are subjected to attacks.
The mosque has been used for all sorts of other purposes alongside prayer, acting as an air raid shelter during the second world war, and more recently as a centre for blood donation and Covid 19 vaccinations.
Its core message is “love for all, hatred for none”, a message particularly pertinent in times of hostile political and religious divisions.
“Thankfully we haven’t experienced a lot of Islamophobia at this mosque,” says Rafiq. “But there has been an increase in incidents of low level harassment such as cars driving by and hooting their horns aggressively.”
The building, which is in the Southfields area, was granted listed status by Historic England in 2018. It appears little changed since it first opened a century ago, with its slim vertical windows, green dome and pristine white exterior. Splashes of colour from English roses still feature prominently in the gardens surrounding the mosque.
The purchase of land to build the mosque on was largely financed by a group of Ahmadi Muslims from Qadian in India, many of them women who sold their jewellery so that London’s first mosque could be established, even though they knew they would be unlikely to ever be able to visit the finished building.
Mosque leaders are billing the message of this significant birthday as “a century of connection”. To mark the anniversary, 10,000 free meals will be provided for homeless people.
Munir Dean, 65, a stalwart of the mosque, can trace its history through his own family, with his grandfather and father playing key roles in the mosque’s development. He said the founders of the mosque had a particular vision in the aftermath of the first world war of faith, peace and uniting humanity.
In its early days the mosque entertained visitors from high society such as Viscount and Viscountess Allenby, and had some very English traditions such as serving tea out of the finest china cups. “Visitors to the mosque were much more likely to be served scones with clotted cream than samosas,” he says.
In its early days when the UK’s Muslim population was much smaller than it is now there were no halal butchers around and instead people would pile into a car for the weekly treat of going to Blooms, the famous kosher salt beef restaurant in Aldgate East in London to tuck into meat sandwiches – kosher meat is accepted as halal because the methods of slaughtering animals are the same.
Bilal Nuttall, who grew up in the same street as Lancashire actor, singer and comedian Gracie Fields, converted to Islam after serving in the Middle East during the first world war and became the mosque’s muezzin calling the faithful to prayer. According to the mosque’s historical records, the imam of the mosque in the 1930s, Abdur Rahim Dard, played a pivotal role in developments leading to the establishment of Pakistan as a separate country from India.
Muhammad Ali Jinnah, an Indian politician and a barrister who trained at London’s Lincoln Inn Fields, was living in Hampstead at the time. According to Dean, he was “a very English gentleman” and a sharp dresser wearing the best Savile Row suits.
He had been advocating for the rights of Muslims in India but had become disillusioned and was considering remaining in the UK and continuing his career in law. Dard convinced him otherwise and he made a keynote speech in the Fazl Mosque gardens, which proved to be a turning point in India’s future and partition of then British India into independent India and Pakistan. He returned to India the following year and became governor general of Pakistan when it became an independent state in August 1947.
Mirza Masroor Ahmad, the current and fifth leader of the Ahmadiyya Muslim Community, says the mosque’s history reflects the principles of serving neighbours, showing loyalty to the UK and making peace with all people regardless of faith or background. “As we mark this centenary, I pray that the mosque may continue to be a beacon of peace and a means of bringing people together for generations to come.”
As the community reflects on the mosque’s last hundred years, Dean is looking ahead. “Our message is quite timeless. It has no expiry date. Bring on the next hundred years,” he says.

Manchester City’s guilty verdict brings football’s great sell-off crashing to earth
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
05:00:51 UTC
14:00:51 KST

It was somehow fitting that Tuesday’s damning ruling against Manchester City landed in the heart of the Labour party conference, in the afterglow of Andy Burnham’s rapturously received prime minister’s speech.
I was there, and read the astonishing 40 pages of findings – that City created “sham” contracts to boost income artificially by £900m – on my phone during a long meeting of the Socialist Campaign Group, where people were celebrating Keir Starmer’s ousting and Burnham’s more leftwing direction.
At the core of Burnham’s speech was the wrong turn he says Britain took under Margaret Thatcher in the 1980s, selling off and privatising council housing, water, energy, transport and care. “We built the common good,” he said, but “the common wealth … created for the many was seen as an opportunity for the few.”
He could have been talking about football, too. Where Manchester City have ended up, having been bought by Sheikh Mansour of the Abu Dhabi ruling family in 2008, is a culmination of decades in which “the people’s game” has been carved up for profits. Clubs like City, formed in the Victorian smog of industry by churches, schools and workplaces, then built by generations of supporters into powerful homes of belonging, were sold off just when football finally had enough wealth to go round.
I investigated and reported on that financial carve up in my early years of journalism, and Burnham worked on it too, at the start of his political career, as the administrator of New Labour’s football taskforce.
My 1997 book, The Football Business, in which I likened football’s commercialisation to Thatcher’s privatisations, chimed with many supporters’ groups campaigning against rocketing ticket prices, exclusive pay-TV deals, and the drawbridge the newly mega-rich Premier League had pulled up behind it.
My moment of clarity had come at Manchester City, reporting on an earlier takeover, in 1994 by a beloved former player, Francis “Franny” Lee. I grew up in Manchester and from as early as I could answer the challenge – “which club do you support?” – it was always City for me. My dad took me, fast-walking, hand-in-hand, to big matches in the 1970s, floodlit glory nights of my boyhood. I have always loved the colour blue, especially sky blue, and have never really worn anything red in my life.
For supporters of my generation, the only trophy City won was the 1976 League Cup, claimed with a wondrous overhead “bicycle” kick goal by our winger, Dennis Tueart. I like art as much as the next ignoramus, but the photograph of Tueart’s goal must be the picture I have gazed at more than any other: the perfection of it, Tueart’s straight back in mid-air, arcing the ball behind him into the Wembley net, Newcastle’s opposition defenders frozen in time for ever.
But unlike Manchester United, Liverpool and Arsenal, City never had a period of sustained success. They compressed a golden age into two years, 1968-70, and soon after that League Cup triumph, they were relegated, in 1983. For years, while City fans became celebrated for their loyalty and sod-it humour – taking bananas and other inflatables to matches – there always remained a mournful yearning for success to return.
When Lee finally took City over, acclaimed by all supporters, it seemed like deliverance. As a fan in the old Maine Road stadium, I cheered him on Saturday, then as a journalist on Monday I pestered for an interview. They agreed, and I was escorted behind the scenes, along some threadbare corridors into the chairman’s office, where Franny sat glowing behind the desk.
Everybody involved was so delighted to have pulled it off that they shared details quite gleefully. And that was when I first understood that Manchester City wasn’t a club at all. It was a company, with “owners”, and this had been a corporate acquisition. Franny was one of many other business people, a consortium, who had bought the shares.
Later, one of the lawyers proudly showed me some corporate engineering they had done. They had formed a holding company, Manchester City plc, that would own the old football club company.
The new millions from Rupert Murdoch’s Sky TV had poured into the Premier League, a breakaway in 1992 by the top clubs from sharing TV money with the clubs in the other three divisions of the Football League. This boosted the value of the top club-companies, and the new consortium planned to float City on the stock exchange, like Manchester United and others, where ultimately their shares could then be sold at a profit.
I learned that holding companies were formed to bypass the longstanding rules of the Football Association – the game’s governing body – that restricted shareholders being paid dividends, and directors a salary. The FA imposed those at the dawn of professional football in 1892, allowing clubs to form limited liability companies, but limiting the personal money shareholders could make.
This was to retain the collective, service ethos of a club. A century on, the rules were still in the FA’s handbook, at No 34. To the relatively small but formidable core of people who really care about these principles, “rule 34” became totemic of football’s sell-off, surrendered to enable vast personal gains by investors. That was now deemed antiquated, blazers’ bureaucracy that must not restrain football’s new business dynamism. To me, it was all a gut punch.
This critique was put forcefully to Labour’s football taskforce, with calls by the Football Supporters’ Association for strong regulation to harness the benefits of the new era. Fans understood that German football’s response to the pay TV transformation was to permit corporate reorganisations, but require clubs to be controlled “50% plus one” by mutual supporters associations.
New Labour was never going to introduce a football regulator or major reforms, but Burnham worked hard for concrete improvements.
The Premier League agreed to distribute 5% of its TV deal to improving desolate grassroots playing facilities via a new grant-giving body, the Football Foundation, which has been transformative. Burnham also championed mutual fan ownership of clubs, helping to establish an organisation, Supporters Direct, to promote it.
But the impossible cost for fans of buying and sustaining their clubs has meant over the years that few are mutually owned. The Premier League roared on, and the sell-offs became more corporate. Some original shareholders made fortunes selling, mostly to US investors: about £90m by Martin Edwards at Manchester United; £90m by the Littlewoods pools heir David Moores for selling his Liverpool shares.
Lee and his consortium never managed it, though, and City were relegated to football’s third tier in 1998. Famously he said City would have won a room full of trophies “if cups were awarded for cock-ups”.
Mansour’s acquisition of Manchester City 10 years later can be seen as the pure essence of “Manchesterism” – spending public money on cultural assets and infrastructure to attract business investors – long before Burnham became mayor of Greater Manchester in 2017 and coined that word this year. The splendid new stadium was built for the 2002 Commonwealth Games with £127m from Manchester city council and the national lottery, the council spending £22m on removing the athletics track and conversion for City to move in. The plan was part of the regeneration of east Manchester, where industry had cranked and smoked, then died in the 1980s.
The council leaders could hardly have imagined that cups-for-cock-ups Manchester City would then attract one of the world’s richest buyers, and the oil wealth of the Gulf. But the Premier League’s global ubiquity, the new stadium and the loyal City crowd all added up for Abu Dhabi.
If you set aside the glaring concerns about the ruler of a country taking over a local heritage football club, the human rights and geopolitical complications that introduces, and the central dissonance of clubs being owned by investors at all, Mansour has been a dream for Manchester. He has poured billions into the club, to attract, buy and pay the world’s best players and the best manager, Pep Guardiola.
His new corporate regime expanded the stadium – named Etihad under a sponsorship deal with the Abu Dhabi state airline, which has now complained that the Premier League’s communication of the commission’s findings has created “damaging implications” for it.
As Burnham acknowledged this week when he described the Abu Dhabi ownership as “a huge partner in the building of modern Manchester”, and gave thanks for the money put in, they have also invested in property development, converting long-derelict mills into apartments for young professionals Manchester was seeking to attract.
The dizzying findings of financial cheating were finally delivered this week from a Premier League investigation process that took eight years, which City repeatedly tried to block. City will appeal, and claim, as they have throughout, that they have “irrefutable evidence” disproving the findings of the three-person commission, which took almost two years.
At the core of Mansour’s ownership has been a ruthless determination not just to make his Premier League acquisition competitive, but to attain total domination. Before 2008, in 116 years of professional football, City only won the old First Division championship twice.
Mansour’s regime has secured the Premier League eight times so far, four FA Cup victories, and the pinnacle, the Champions League, in 2023. The League Cup, so rare and special to my generation, has been brought back from Wembley seven times.
Burnham has boldly broken with accepting Thatcher’s great sell-offs, saying they produced today’s fractures.
As he left the stage to applause and acclaim, football’s great sell-off was crashing to earth.
