‘Elon is my prophet’: how Musk’s Doge team took a wrecking ball to Washington
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
05:00:50 UTC
14:00:50 KST

In the early hours of Saturday 22 February 2025 the following email landed in the inboxes of the entire US federal workforce:
From: HR hr@opm.gov
Sent: Saturday, February 22, 2025
Subject: What did you do last week?
Importance: High
Please reply to this email with approx. 5 bullets of what you accomplished last week and cc your manager.
Please do not send any classified information, links, or attachments.
Deadline is this Monday at 11:59 p.m. EST.
When she noticed the email that Saturday night, Kathleen Walters already had far too much going on in her life. Number one was figuring out if the lump in her breast that her doctor had just detected was a tumour. Half of her known blood relatives had died of cancer, and she was now 52: the lump needed understanding.
Her work life was harder to dramatise with a list. For a start, the specifics of her job at any given moment, as she would have been the first to point out, couldn’t legally be described to others. She was the chief privacy officer at the Internal Revenue Service. She ran a staff of 650 people tasked with preventing any of the 100,000 IRS employees from losing or leaking or even so much as peeking at, unless they had the authority to peek, any of the 266m tax returns they were just then processing from the previous year. “One hundred thousand people is a big-sized town,” said Kathleen. “In any big-sized town, you have some crazy people. I could easily see someone writing, ‘This weekend I audited Beyoncé.’”
Whoever had sent this email asking her to list five things she’d done at work was now demanding that all these people inside the IRS share information that, in many cases, should never be shared. She thought it was nuts.
She responded quickly, and vaguely, with five things she had done the previous week, all the while feeling sure no one would ever read what she wrote. Her phone was already exploding with questions from her subordinates – a few of whom were saying that their replies were bouncing back with a “mailbox is full” notice. Now she had to sit and think about how to minimise the damage that might be caused by 100,000 IRS employees thinking that they’d lose their jobs if they didn’t supply some detailed answer about what they’d done during their work week. A meaningful percentage risked being tossed in jail if they described what they did in an email. It was a crime for an IRS employee even to acknowledge that some specific person had or had not filed a tax return. “People don’t understand what the IRS does,” said Kathleen.
The email came as a surprise, but then the IRS was suddenly full of surprises. Nine days earlier, on 13 February, a Thursday, the first Doge person turned up in the lobby, unannounced, and security called Traci DiMartini, who ran the IRS’s human capital department. There’s a kid down here who said he needs to get into the building, he said. The kid’s name was Gavin Kliger.
Traci called her counterpart at the Treasury department, as the IRS sits inside Treasury, and Treasury always cleared any new political appointees; Treasury had no record of anyone named Gavin Kliger. Traci then called Tim Curry at the Office of Personnel Management – but he had no idea what was going on. Finally, she called security and asked them to escort the young man to her office.
Gavin Kliger came with a chip on his shoulder, it seemed to Traci. He offered not even the faintest smile or the most glancing eye contact. Dressed in black from hoodie to sneaker, he was brusque to the point of rudeness. He looked, and was, just a few years out of college. Eyes on the floor, he explained to Traci that he’d come to sort out the problems inside the IRS and to root out the fraud. “That’s a big job!” she said.
Anyone who worked at the IRS knew that it had its problems; fraud wasn’t likely one of them. Its technology infrastructure was a case study in government dysfunction, but its ethical infrastructure was sound. Like all federal employees, its staff wasn’t allowed to accept more than a free cup of coffee from anyone who might want something from their agency.
Gavin Kliger, in contrast, struck Traci as problematic. He’d somehow laid his hands on badges granting him access to some crazy number of government buildings. His backpack was stuffed with government-issue phones and at least four laptops – and he was now insisting that Traci supply him with an IRS phone and laptop. He also demanded his own IRS email address, access to computer systems with all the taxpayer information, and a meeting with the acting IRS commissioner, Doug O’Donnell. As Gavin sat there, Traci called Treasury again. That guy you said didn’t exist is now here sitting in my office. What do y’all want me to do with him?
The Treasury guy went away, then came back and said that Gavin Kliger had been hired three weeks earlier by the Office of Personnel Management and was attached to Doge – whatever that meant.
In her nine years running human capital departments at various federal agencies, Traci had never seen a new political appointee just turn up in the lobby and demand access to the computer systems. “None of this is normal,” she said, “but we’re still trying to be nice.” She explained to Gavin the IRS rules: before anyone was allowed to work inside the building, he needed to pass a tax audit.
I don’t need to do that, he said.
Yes, you do, she replied.
No, I don’t, he said.
Yes, you do, she replied.
They went back and forth like that a bit until finally Gavin relented. Traci then explained that after he passed the audit, he’d need to be given the mandatory presentations about ethics and taxpayer information. Gavin thought that the IRS should just let him in. “He wanted access to our systems immediately,” said Traci.
Traci’s next call, at 6.30pm that Thursday evening, was to Kathleen, to arrange for her to brief Gavin on data privacy laws and to warn her that the experience might not be entirely pleasant. If I had a kid who behaved the way he does, I’d slap the shit out of him, Traci said – but then Traci was from Philadelphia. Traci was always telling Kathleen that she should try a bit less hard to see the best in others.
By then word of Doge’s arrival at the IRS had spread, and Kathleen had read about them. Anyone who Googled Gavin’s name found a bit more than usually popped up about any given young Doge person. He’d grown up in southern California, where he was into Asian martial arts and the high-school marching band, then had gone on to the University of California at Berkeley. Graduating in 2020 with a degree in electrical engineering and computer science, he’d taken a job as a programmer at Databricks. He’d also been active on X, where he’d retweeted with apparent approval posts from the white nationalists Steve Laws and Nick Fuentes. “One of Musk’s few Doge lieutenants who has embraced the spotlight,” Forbes wrote of him. Most of the other Muskrats scrubbed the internet of their presence. Gavin had written Substack pieces defending two Trump nominees, Matt Gaetz and Pete Hegseth. He’d deleted his X posts, but the Forbes writer John Hyatt had found a research tool, Web.archive, to revive and analyse them. “What emerges is a portrait of an internet edgelord and Musk and Trump superfan who has disdain for government spending, illegal immigrants, and who enjoys the odd racist and ableist joke,” he wrote.
By the time Traci called her, Kathleen was gone for the weekend and 50 miles away from the IRS building: she needed to find someone else to do Gavin’s briefing. Kathleen was white; the two women immediately below her were Black. “They’d both already read about him and were both already uncomfortable,” said Kathleen. Phyllis Grimes, her deputy, agreed to fall on the hand grenade.
Phyllis, who loved working for Kathleen and saw falling on hand grenades as part of her job, never told her how this one had felt. She knew Gavin had expressed enthusiasm for white nationalists, and he likely knew that she knew. She tried to break the ice by walking in with her hand extended; Gavin stared at it and declined to shake it, though he had shaken the hands of the white men who had offered them. “He was kind of cool towards me,” said Phyllis. Before she could even start the briefing, he said, You know, I’ve heard these rules before at other agencies. Yes, she said, but these rules are different, because no other agency is governed by this privacy law, and this law can get you thrown in jail very quickly. As she walked him through the basics – how you can’t use your personal phone for business, how if you happen to so much as glimpse a form 1040 with someone’s name on it you must avert your eyes – Gavin played on his phone. “He’s multitasking right in front of me, typing and texting,” said Phyllis. “It was, here’s a routine that I must endure.”
It fell to Kathleen to draft the five-page agreement required by law for Gavin Kliger to be let inside the IRS building on Monday morning, 17 February. The memo that she wrote over the weekend, and that he signed, gave him access to some of the systems but, explicitly, none that contained taxpayer information.
Traci set him up in a conference room with an assistant at the beginning of the week. “People started getting these calls,” said Kathleen. “It was like getting the call from the principal’s office. ‘Gavin wants to see you.’ ”
Doge had its own private structure in addition to its official one. Officially, President Trump created Doge with an executive order on his first day in office. The president doesn’t have the authority to create or to fund an executive agency, however. Congress does. The Trump administration dodged that problem by taking an office inside the White House created during the second Obama term, the US Digital Service, kicking out the people inside and renaming it the Department of Government Efficiency. The US Digital Service had been given the power to hire talent from the tech sector without going through the usual slow federal hiring process. This now ensured that Doge could hire whomever it wanted without any questions being asked, and make it sound official. In effect, all that Doge had done was create a corpse for itself to occupy.
The zombie killed off the spirit of the original life form. Real Doge had nothing to do with Official Doge or the former US Digital Service or any other government body. Real Doge was more like Elon Musk’s pop-up restaurant. “None of us ever signed a piece of paper saying that we were in Doge,” said one Doge insider. The people who joined either worked for one of Musk’s companies, or knew someone who did, or knew someone who knew someone who did. To be truly a member of Doge was to be included in the group Signal chat and granted access to the sleeping quarters on the sixth floor of the General Services Administration (GSA).
Official Doge employed maybe 10 guys in their 40s and 50s who wore suits and could sort of pass as ordinary political appointees, but none had access to the sixth floor at GSA. “The older guys in the suits were not there to take risks or blow things up,” said one Doge insider. It was hard to say what any of the older Doge suits did except to make way for the young guys when they showed up with explosives.
Most of Doge’s inner circle just wanted to exist in the presence of Elon Musk. “It was, Elon is my prophet, and I worship the ground he walks on,” said one of the older Doge insiders.
As a Doge member, you could get away with saying – or having said – almost anything. What you couldn’t say is that the government actually sort of worked. Or, if it didn’t work, why it didn’t work. This new game rewarded not understanding but speed. The plan was the same plan Musk had executed two years earlier at Twitter: Make sweeping statements about the incompetence and dishonesty of the people working inside the place before you know much about them. Once you’ve terrified the employees, fire them in huge numbers. If it turns out you screwed up and fired the wrong people, hire some of them back.
The people who rallied to the cause and felt qualified to execute Elon Musk’s vision for the federal government shared certain qualities. They were mostly young white males. They were mostly from upper-middle-class or rich families. Most knew or pretended to know how to program a computer. Not all of them, but enough of them for there to be a pattern, had been rejected from the most selective colleges and universities and ended up feeling they’d been screwed by the admissions process. They landed at Penn instead of Princeton, or the University of Nebraska instead of Harvard, with a grievance that added to the foundation of their politics. They thought of themselves as the smartest people in the room and couldn’t understand why the rest of the room didn’t simply stand up and cheer. In Washington they borrowed from Elon Musk their status and sense of superiority. They also seemed to share his pleasure in the idea of people being afraid of them.
Even among the young men sleeping inside the GSA, Gavin was regarded as a force. “Wherever he went, entropy went through the roof,” said one. Just weeks into their new jobs as destroyers of government institutions, the Muskrats had given Gavin Kliger a nickname: the Chaos Agent.
Another surprising email landed in Kathleen’s inbox on 28 February. It was Friday night. “I don’t know why everything always happened on a Friday night,” she said. She’d taken her daughter for pizza and wasn’t meant to be checking her phone when she spotted the emails. The first one that she read had been sent at 6.34pm by a colleague in the IRS legal department. “Melanie requested a data pull,” it read. “It feels not quite kosher.”
Exactly 64 minutes earlier, at 5.30pm, Doug O’Donnell, the acting IRS commissioner, had left his post. O’Donnell’s successor was to be Melanie Krause, until then chief operating officer, who had been installed as acting IRS commissioner by Treasury secretary Scott Bessent. Like Kathleen, Melanie was a career civil servant, though 13 years younger. Kathleen had considered her a friend. “She was really smart, and I thought she meant well,” said Kathleen. “She wasn’t a mean person.” They were both working moms, and Melanie liked to share, and share in, the details of the difficulties. Now she’d apparently told the IRS research department to share taxpayer data. With whom, and for what purpose, became clear in the second email, which came from the IRS director of data management:
Kathleen,
DHS [the Department of Homeland Security] has requested if we could find addresses for 700,000 names of likely undocumented immigrants.
1. Do we have legal authority to use the tax return filing data for this purpose?
2. If the answer to Question 1 is yes, then my second question is related to a file we receive from the Social Security Administration (SSA) that contains Date of Birth (DOB), Date of Death (DOD), Gender, Citizenship, and Name Control Information for all issued Social Security Numbers (SSN). Would our MOU allow us to use this perhaps in conjunction to tax return data for this purpose?
While it is likely that use of SSA data is also needed. The technical feasibility of being able to produce reliable outcome is unknown but likely very low.
Thanks
Kathleen read the first numbered paragraph and stopped reading. The request was plainly illegal. The IRS couldn’t just hand over great gobs of taxpayer information to the Department of Homeland Security or any other agency without a change in federal privacy law. Changing the law was not trivial. She knew that because she’d just done it – to allow the IRS to share taxpayer data with state child support enforcement agencies. The states wanted to know if former spouses who were failing to pay child support in fact did not have the income to do so – and the IRS alone could answer the question. What Kathleen had asked for in that case could not have been less controversial. Basically no one in American politics was willing to come out against child support enforcement, and the change to the federal law had passed Congress in December 2024 with almost no dissent. Yet it had taken 18 months to get it done, with endless meetings on Capitol Hill and the close involvement of the IRS commissioner and the secretary of health and human services. “Doge couldn’t imagine 18 months,” she said. “Doge didn’t have 18 months. Their whole thing was, If you can’t do it legally, we’ll find some way to do it illegally.”
This, Kathleen realised, is how they could grab taxpayer data illegally. By doing it on a Friday night. Using a woman, Melanie Krause, about to take over as acting commissioner, after a 10-minute meeting between her and Scott Bessent. Without informing the executive charged with protecting the information. “She went around me because she knew what my answer is,” said Kathleen.
The violation ran deeper than the law. The specific dataset sought by DHS was in a silo reserved for the tax returns filed by people without social security numbers. The IRS had created the so-called Individual Taxpayer Identification Number (Itin) back in 1996 as a mechanism for undocumented workers and other non-citizens who lacked social security numbers to file a return and pay taxes.
The programme had been a huge success. The IRS had collected hundreds of billions of dollars in taxes through it. Undocumented workers had been able to demonstrate their commitment to the country, and ease their path to citizenship, by paying more than their fair share. (They were still excluded from most federal benefits.) Now DHS wanted their private data, and it wasn’t hard for Kathleen or anyone else at the IRS to see why. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (Ice) had gone hunting undocumented workers but lacked reliable home addresses for many of them. The tax returns told you where roughly 7 million of them might be found.
The second Trump administration had a gift for creating such moments. It was as if all at once all these characters in a grand masked ball were forced to remove their disguises and reveal their identities. In the Great Unmasking, the nation’s leading law firms, led by Paul, Weiss, would cave to what amounted to Trump’s blackmail demands to avoid being shut out of federal business. The nation’s research universities, led by Columbia, would change their internal policies and even pay fines to avoid losing federal dollars.
The revealing moments in the civil service were lonelier. They occurred inside people’s hearts and minds, and seldom leaked to the press. After his arrival at the IRS, one of Gavin Kliger’s first acts had been to demand that the agency fire its 6,700 probationary workers, who had yet to be granted civil service protection. By law they could be fired only for poor performance. Gavin had asked Traci DiMartini, in her capacity as head of human resources, to agree to put her name on an email to the mostly young employees telling them that they had failed at their jobs. The Doge people played this trick often. They’d use or try to use civil servants as a kind of ventriloquist dummy so that they, the Doge workers, could keep their names off official documents. But Traci took one look at the email, saw it was plainly a lie, and refused to have anything to do with it. The price of that single act of resistance was her job. Gavin didn’t have the authority to fire Traci, but his new acting commissioner did. “He asked Melanie to fire Traci, and Melanie did it,” said Kathleen.
Melanie Krause’s predecessor, Doug O’Donnell, had been pushed out by Doge after he, too, refused to send the dishonest email to the IRS’s 6,700 probationary workers. When a Doge guy at Treasury called with the order, O’Donnell, who had worked for the agency for 38 years, said he wanted to sleep on it – then had trouble sleeping. “He was struggling with this notion of sending the termination emails with this false justification for the termination,” said a person in whom O’Donnell confided. The next day, he refused to send the email, and the Doge guy said something like, “Well, let me be the first to congratulate you on your retirement.” Melanie had been installed precisely because she was proving to Doge that she was more pliable.
Standing outside the pizza place with her daughter in late February, Kathleen called Melanie. Ever since Melanie had arrived, in the fall of 2021, she had sought Kathleen’s advice. There had been stretches when they met daily. Kathleen just sort of assumed that, faced with a difficult choice, Melanie would do what Kathleen herself would do. “I don’t really get outraged,” said Kathleen. “But I think people need to be confronted when they have done something inappropriate.”
Melanie, what are you doing? she asked. We already have legal opinions about this, and it is obviously against the law.
I didn’t tell them to do it, said Melanie. I told them to think about how to do it – if it was legal.
But she hadn’t asked anyone to find out if it was legal to send Ice the home addresses of 700,000 undocumented workers – culled, somehow, from the 7 million who had paid taxes. She’d told them to send the data over, on a Friday night. In such a way that Kathleen might never have heard about it – or heard too late.
It’s not going to be any more legal on Saturday, said Kathleen.
Let’s meet on Monday to clear things up, said Melanie.
They didn’t meet. Instead, on Monday – 3 March – Kathleen and several other top IRS leaders were called into a meeting with Gavin Kliger.
I’ve figured out something important about the IRS, Gavin said. He paused for effect.
Oh no, thought Kathleen.
Every agency has a superpower, said Gavin. The IRS’s superpower is data.
Everyone in the agency knew that its data was valuable. That was the reason for the strict laws that prevented it from being exploited for profit or political gain. “He said this in a way that he expected everyone to clap when he was done,” said Kathleen.
“No one said a word.” The people around the table – a group that included a woman who had worked at the IRS for 54 years, or 53 years and 50 weeks longer than Gavin Kliger – looked down, or away. Kathleen felt embarrassed for Gavin Kliger. But now it was clear what the meeting was about. Gavin wanted, in his words, “to explore how we can share our data with other agencies”.
Interestingly, he never once mentioned Ice or DHS. Instead, that week, he sought to share data with himself, by trying to access files detailing IRS contracts with outside consultants that also contained taxpayer information. Kathleen denied him access.
The following Monday, she received a cryptic text from a senior IRS official. I’m going to call your cell, but don’t answer, it read. Her phone rang and she dutifully stared at it. Then came the second text: Gavin is asking where your office is and is now trying to find you to fire you because he says you’re the blocker.
The Blocker! It was one of Elon’s favourite terms. The blocker was the person who didn’t understand progress. The person without vision. The person who could not see beyond the way things were to the way they ought to be. The person who didn’t want to live on Mars or possibly even care if anyone ever got there. The inferior person. Traci had been a blocker. Find the blockers between us and what we want, Elon told his young followers. Find the blockers and eliminate them. Maybe more than anything else, Doge wanted the data. Kathleen was the person blocking them from getting it.
She wasn’t sure what she’d done to anger Gavin. It could have been limiting his access to the procurement contracts. It could also have been pushing back on his request to grant Palantir, Doge’s favourite federal contractor, the right to work with taxpayer data. What Gavin’s issue likely was not was her resistance to handing over to the Department of Homeland Security the addresses of taxpayers who lacked social security numbers. Gavin had never brought that up; this particular attempt to break the law wasn’t his idea. It was coming from somewhere else. As she thought she had stopped it, she ceased to worry about it.
And so, roughly two weeks later, on Thursday, 27 March, she was caught completely off guard by an email chain that popped up on her screen. At the bottom was its origin: a note from Melanie, forwarding some document from the IRS legal department, along with what sounded like an innocuous request. “Kathleen, could you help facilitate I won’t be able to join today?” it read, without explaining what she was meant to facilitate or why Melanie wouldn’t be able to join. Scrolling through, Kathleen couldn’t find the document but did see lots of bewildered replies from others who had been included – What is this about? Happy to help but can you tell us what this is? She called the two young lawyers in the IRS legal office who had authored the document referred to in the chain that had somehow gone missing. They explained that the thing Melanie wanted Kathleen to facilitate was a memorandum of understanding for the IRS to share taxpayer data with DHS. Kathleen was knocked sideways. “I thought that it had been stopped,” she said. “I thought Melanie had been caught with her pants down.” The young lawyers now told her that not only had it not been stopped: they’d been working on it since the end of February. “They told me that they were sorry but Melanie had told them to do it and not to tell me or their boss,” said Kathleen.
The situation was obviously bizarre. Kathleen had never heard of an IRS director asking young IRS lawyers to work on something on the side without telling their boss. And if Melanie didn’t want Kathleen to know that she was handing IRS data to DHS, why had she suddenly included her in the conversation? “I think she got scared and dumped it on me to sign off on,” said Kathleen. Melanie was doing to Kathleen what Gavin Kliger had done to Traci DiMartini. She was presenting her with her own unmasking moment and forcing her to make a choice.
Instead of signing off, Kathleen arranged a Zoom call that day, with the people at the Department of Homeland Security who were requesting the data. The “ICE Innovation Lab”, they called themselves. She’d never heard of it. When she Googled it, nothing came up.
A few others joined the call – lawyers from DHS and a privacy lawyer at the IRS named Julie Schwartz. On the call, Kathleen explained that there were some very narrow circumstances that would allow the IRS to lend a hand. If, for example, an undocumented worker had murdered someone and the police had issued a warrant for his arrest. The Ice Innovators explained that they were looking for more than wanted criminals. “Just how many people do you want information on?” asked Kathleen. The Ice Innovators went back and forth between themselves before agreeing that the number was 7 million. They wanted the current addresses of 7 million undocumented workers who had paid their taxes. The most law-abiding, it turned out, might be the easiest to catch.
After the call, Julie, the IRS privacy lawyer, came straight to her office. Julie was usually ice-calm – someone who kept her wits about her. She hadn’t a trace of drama in her. But now Julie was not calm. Kathleen, after that call I’m not working on this thing, she said. I’m not coming in tomorrow. I might not come in Monday. I might not come in ever again.
“I don’t usually deal with life or death stuff,” said Kathleen. “But this was life or death stuff. At that moment I knew I had to quit. Either that or I’m going to get fired, because I can’t facilitate something that will break the law and is going to hurt people. We all have boundaries. That was my boundary.”
That weekend, Kathleen sent Melanie a note saying she’d be resigning. “I didn’t need to tell her why,” said Kathleen. “She knew why.” She’d be leaving just weeks before her 20th anniversary with the agency. If she’d waited until mid-May, she would have been able to retire and receive benefits for the rest of her life. But she didn’t want to retire. Federal law made it hard for a retired civil servant to return, and if the day ever came when the IRS was rebuilt, she wanted to be able to return. She’d just learned that the lump in her breast was benign.
Days later, Melanie beat Kathleen to it and resigned. Kathleen never figured out how much her note to Melanie – and with it the increased likelihood that the attempted data heist would wind up in the press – led Melanie to quit. On her way out the door, Melanie asked the IRS’s head of communications to plant a story in the Washington Post that she was leaving as a matter of principle. The story cast Melanie as a martyr who had quit rather than divulge IRS data to DHS, when Kathleen knew that she had been caught red-handed trying to do precisely that. “I completely misjudged her character,” said Kathleen.
The Ice agents came for the “illegals” long after the property managers had gone home. The only evidence left behind were grainy videos on security cameras and accounts of terrified residents. “They’re coming in the nights, unannounced,” said Antonio Marquez, who ran a company that owned and managed apartment buildings scattered across the south and south-western United States occupied mostly by lower-middle-income Latinos. “We don’t know how they are targeting the units. It’s wreaking complete havoc.”
Antonio’s apartment complex outside Austin houses a thousand people, mostly young families, at least half of whom are undocumented. It had been visited in the spring late at night by teams of Ice agents. They came in unmarked cars, reported the tenants who remained after the raid. They had no warrants and read no rights. They knew, or thought they knew, exactly which doors to jimmy and which locks to pick and which people to take. The next morning a bunch of tenants were simply gone. All that remained was a pile of discarded possessions.
After the first Austin raid, Antonio had erected a tall metal fence around the property. Occasionally, the Ice agents had taken fully documented tenants – including an older woman who always paid on time, and who returned from Ice custody in an ankle bracelet. The great mystery to Antonio was how Ice knew where people lived. “These are fully targeted,” he said. “They already had these people in mind. They have their addresses. And we don’t know how they’re getting them.”
He was too busy doing his job to notice when, on 11 February 2026, the Washington Post reported that the IRS had shared with the Department of Homeland Security the tax data of 47,000 undocumented workers. On the heels of the Post’s scoop, a federal judge hearing a case on the subject summoned the IRS lawyers who had previously sworn that the agency had rebuffed the DHS demands. Under questioning, the lawyers confessed that the agency had lied to the court and that it had in fact shared the data. “The IRS violated the [Internal Revenue Code] approximately 42,695 times by disclosing last known taxpayer addresses to Ice,” the judge wrote in her opinion.
On a hot, sunny afternoon in early March in north-east Austin, it is a lot quieter than it was a year ago, back when Kathleen Walters was still a blocker. Two small children play in a pool, and a worn middle-aged man squats warily in a corner, smoking a cigarette. The wall of the office where the remaining residents come for their mail is decorated with posters advertising the services that Antonio’s company offers. One is more official-looking than the others. Free File del IRS, it reads across the top – and just below, in finer print, it explains how easy and painless it is for a non-citizen to file their taxes.
This is an edited extract from Blockers: Rebels in the Deep State by Michael Lewis, published by Allen Lane (£25). To support the Guardian, order your copy at guardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.

Henry Harris’s recipe for vegetarian endive au gratin
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
05:00:50 UTC
14:00:50 KST

This is the best comfort dish on planet Earth. Cauliflower cheese held that title when I was a child, but I still remember the first time I ate this gratin, made by Simon Hopkinson at his restaurant Hilaire in London, and wanting to take it away and eat it in a quiet corner. Endive when braised well retains a gentle bitterness that contrasts beautifully with a cheese-heavy bechamel. This dish is traditionally made with comté and with each endive wrapped in a slice of cooked ham, but some dark, crisp-fried mushrooms and emmental serve very well as good, savoury vegetarian alternatives.
Endive au gratin
A chilled beaujolais and a salad are good friends to serve alongside.
Prep 10 min
Infuse 1 hr
Cook 1 hr, plus cooling
Serves 4
600ml milk
1 bay leaf
6 black peppercorns
1 small onion, peeled and sliced
2 parsley stalks (if you have them)
2 large flat mushrooms
120g unsalted butter
Salt and black pepper
4 heads endive
Nutmeg
50g plain flour
1 pinch cayenne pepper, to taste
200g emmental (suitable for vegetarians), grated
Heat the oven to 180C (160C fan)/350F/gas 4. Put the milk in a saucepan with the bay, peppercorns, sliced onion and parsley stalks, if using. Bring to a boil, then take off the heat and leave to infuse for an hour.
Finely slice the mushrooms. Melt a third of the butter in a shallow pan on a gentle heat, then add the mushrooms, season and cook until they release their juices. Turn up the heat just enough so the liquid simmers and evaporates, leaving you with just the mushrooms and melted butter. (Don’t be tempted to tip out those juices, because they are full of flavour and need returning to the mushrooms.) Keep cooking the mushrooms, stirring from time to time, until they brown and turn a little leathery, then transfer to a plate lined with kitchen towel to absorb the excess butter.
Melt another third of the butter in a heavy, ovenproof pan and, when it’s just starting to foam, add the endives and season with salt, pepper and a good rasping of freshly grated nutmeg. Turn down the heat and cook gently, turning frequently, until nicely coloured all over. Cover loosely with foil and transfer to the oven for 40 minutes to an hour, until completely tender. Remove from the oven and leave to cool a little. (The outer leaves will probably need pulling off, because they’ll be quite brown and crisp by now.)
While the endive is roasting, make the bechamel. Reheat the infused milk. Melt the remaining third of the butter in a saucepan, add the flour and cook, stirring, for two minutes. Strain the hot milk into a jug, then whisk it into the flour mixture and keep whisking over a gentle heat for a good five minutes, until you have a thick, glossy sauce. Season with a pinch of cayenne, then stir in two-thirds of the cheese, until it melts. Taste and adjust the seasoning as needed.
Heat the grill. Scatter the fried mushrooms over the base of four individual gratin dishes (or one large one), and top with the braised endives. Spoon over the hot bechamel, scatter over the remaining grated cheese and grill until bubbling and golden. Serve immediately.
- Henry Harris is chef/co-owner of Bouchon Racine, London EC1. His book, The Racine Effect, is published by Quadrille at £40. To order a copy for £36, go to guardianbookshop.com

From food-led escapes to trip of a lifetime hotels: How luxury travel has evolved and ‘doesn’t look one way’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
05:00:16 UTC
14:00:16 KST

The fusion of food and hospitality is a major driving force in the world of luxury travel. We spoke to Michelin Guide's Marie-France Perrel about how the sector is changing.
In years gone by, the luxury travel sector was all about opulent hotels and extravagant surroundings. But for today's travellers, the experience is becoming much harder to define.
Speaking at the Euronews Travel & Tourism Summit 2026 in Brussels last week, Marie-France Perrel, Head of Business Development, Hotels at Michelin Guide, said luxury hospitality has evolved to bring together a fusion of food, wellness, service, as well as connection to the destination.
“Luxury today is completely different than what it was,” she said. “It’s no longer the sort of standards of opulence that we had in mind. It’s no longer about the amount of marble you have in a bathroom or the number of rooms in one property.”
Instead, Perrel said travellers are looking for “properties who are giving you a sense of place” and hotels with a special connection to their surroundings. “It really is a whole ecosystem, and I think that’s what luxury is today,” she added.
Part of the same travel experience
Food is increasingly central to this changing definition of hospitality. While there’s always been a correlation between eating and travelling, Michelin is seeing evidence that visitors increasingly consider the two as part of the same experience.
“Before, they were lived as two separate experiences, whereas now we’re seeing that as one experience,” Perrel said.
Michelin's own data shows that users looking to book hotels in Northern Europe were also searching for nearby restaurants during the same session.
Perrel also pointed to the rise of “intentional travel around food”, with holidaymakers booking trips specifically to experience a particular dish or cuisine.
“They want to go on walking food tours, or they will want to go to a destination because they saw on television this great meal that was being consumed,” she said.
“They want to have that same authentic pizza or whatever that may be. So absolutely, food is a huge component of travel these days.”
What are Michelin Keys?
Michelin's connection with travel stretches back more than a century. The first Michelin Guide was published in France in 1900 to encourage motorists to travel, listing practical information including places to eat and stay. Michelin began awarding stars to restaurants in 1926.
Hotels have also featured in the guides for decades, but the company introduced its “Michelin Key” distinction in 2024, applying a dedicated methodology to identifying outstanding hotel experiences.
Its 2026 global selection includes 2,832 Michelin Key hotels across 79 destinations: 2,020 with one key, 657 with two keys, and 155 with three keys. Some 470 hotels joined the selection this year, while 18 received three keys for the first time.
One key represents a “very special stay”, while two keys signify an “exceptional stay”. Three keys are reserved for the highest level – an extraordinary stay providing the ultimate experience. “This is like the trip of a lifetime type of situation,” Perrel said.
But Michelin's selections illustrate how luxury no longer has to fit a single mould. Its hotel portfolio ranges from grand hotels to independent boutiques and retreats. “What I love about it is that it’s not cookie-cutter,” Perrel said. “Luxury doesn’t look one way. It’s a broad spectrum.”
At the end of her session at the Euronews summit, Perrel was asked to share one piece of advice to travellers when choosing a hotel for their next holiday. Her response was to look at the trip “backwards”.
“Try to think of your next trip in a different way and instead of choosing a destination, choose a hotel first,” she said. “You don't look at the destination, but look at a hotel that speaks to you and then go to that place.”

Russia leads world in cat ownership — yet has 2.8 million strays
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
05:00:03 UTC
14:00:03 KST

Nearly 59% of Russian households own at least one cat, the highest rate globally, but the 2022 mobilisation order left hundreds of thousands of animals abandoned when owners fled the country or were sent to the front in Ukraine. Up to 98% of Russia's stray cats and dogs were once domestic pets.
Russia has the highest rate of cat ownership in the world, with nearly 59% of households keeping at least one cat — and an estimated 2.8 million stray cats living on its streets, a number that rose sharply after the 2022 mobilisation order sent thousands of pet owners fleeing the country or to the front amid Russia's ongoing all-out war in Ukraine.
According to a 2024-2026 study by analytics platform Seasia Stats, Russia ranks first globally for cats as pets. Romania ranks second in Europe at 48%, followed by Poland at 41%, Latvia at 37% and Hungary at 35%.
Outside Europe, Indonesia, the Philippines, Thailand, New Zealand and the US also make the top 10. The Seasia Stats findings are consistent with a 2023 study by insurer Ingosstrakh and the Financial University, in which 58.8% of Russian respondents described themselves as cat owners.
The stray figures come from a separate study by the Centre for Animal Nutrition and Well-being Studies, the Nika animal charity and research firm Ipsos.
They put the total stray animal population in Russia in 2025 at nearly 3.6 million, of which 2.8 million are cats and 800,000 are dogs.
Of those, around 170,000 were in shelters at the time of the study, while the rest were living on the streets. Researchers say up to 98% of stray cats and dogs were once domestic pets abandoned by their owners.
Animal welfare organisations recorded a sharp increase in abandonments after Russia announced partial mobilisation in September 2022.
Men who received call-up papers were either leaving the country or preparing for deployment and in many cases could not arrange care for their animals or find shelter places.
On classified advertising websites, owners threatened to have pets put down if no one took them. Shelter volunteers reported similar ultimatums from people surrendering animals in person.
Russia has 819 shelters, the overwhelming majority privately run, alongside hundreds of charities and tens of thousands of volunteers. Together they care for between 170,000 and 250,000 animals — no more than 5–7% of the estimated stray population.
The popularity of cats in Eastern Europe has historical roots: before industrialised agriculture, cats served a practical function on farms, where their presence and scent deterred rodents.
In Southeast Asia, researchers link rising ownership to urbanisation and the growth of a middle class.
Cats have lived alongside humans for around 10,000 years. Today, they are human companions of choice, alongside dogs.

The long road home: how EU protection policy is affecting Ukrainian refugees
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
05:00:00 UTC
14:00:00 KST

On the one hand, living from one day to the next and worrying about their homeland; on the other, looking for ways to obtain permanent residence in the EU after March 2028. This is precisely how women who fled Ukraine for EU countries at the start of the war described their experiences of living under temporary protection to Suspilne.
This summer, the European Union and Switzerland extended temporary protection for Ukrainians already living there until 4 March 2028. For new arrivals, however, the rules have changed: applicants must now prove that they have been exempted from military service in Ukraine and left the country legally.
Meanwhile, for many Ukrainians who have been living in the EU for several years, temporary protection means ever-deeper integration into the lives of the countries that have taken them in.
According to Eurostat, there are currently over 4.4 million Ukrainians living in the EU who were previously granted temporary protection. With every month of the war, the number of those returning to Ukraine is decreasing, believes Ella Libanova, director of the Institute of Demography and Social Studies at the National Academy of Sciences of Ukraine. At the same time, in her view, it is most likely that women aged over 25 with a higher education will return. After all, back home they have significantly better prospects for professional development.
Suspilne spoke to Ukrainian women who were granted temporary protection in Poland, Germany and Ireland during the early years of Russia’s full-scale invasion. It also sought to find out the views of men who have moved to the EU and hold this status.
Poland: Ukrainians are needed, but attitudes are deteriorating
Inna Bezroda has been living in Poland since 2022: she moved there from Kyiv with her two children after the full-scale war began. Inna has cancer, so her husband joined her a year later after leaving Ukraine legally. Because of her illness, Inna is unable to work, so her husband provides for the family.
The family rents a flat in Warsaw. Apart from child benefit, to which working parents are entitled in Poland, the family receives no other social benefits. Thanks to her husband’s job, Inna is entitled to health insurance and free cancer treatment.
If she were living in Poland on her own, she would have lost her right to access healthcare from March 2026 onwards – due to new changes to the law. These changes have deprived those who are not in work of free access to medical care. Vulnerable groups – pensioners and people with disabilities – are the hardest hit by this.
The Temporary Protection Mechanism in the EU was introduced specifically for Ukrainian refugees on 4 March 2022 in response to Russian aggression. It grants the right to reside and work legally in the EU. Ukrainians are granted this status without lengthy bureaucratic procedures. As part of this scheme, in addition to the legalisation of their status, they were granted access to state healthcare and assistance with renting accommodation.
However, year after year, individual countries review various aspects of the temporary protection arrangements for Ukrainians within the framework set by the European Union. This applies both to access to healthcare and to the provision of accommodation. Furthermore, such protection will come to an end once the EU recognises that it is safe to return to Ukraine.
At the same time, Ukrainians are sometimes helped by charitable organisations or individuals outside this formal framework.
“I lived in Warsaw for three years in a flat with my children for free; it was given to us by a Polish man, a complete stranger,” says Inna. “I recently went on a rehabilitation programme for cancer patients, where I was the only Ukrainian. I was worried about how people would treat me. But everything went brilliantly; I made friends with the Polish women. We talked about politics, and I admitted to them that I’d been afraid to come v and I felt a lot of support. They said: "If you ever hear that we Poles have a negative attitude towards Ukrainians, just think of our faces.”
However, Inna acknowledges that attitudes towards Ukrainians in Polish society as a whole have deteriorated compared with 2022.
Although her command of Polish is limited, Inna avoids speaking Ukrainian on public transport so as not to cause offence. "We used to joke about it in the family: if Poland comes up with anything else [regarding Ukrainians], we’ll get in the car, pack our bags and head further west."
Poland is home to over 970,000 Ukrainians under the temporary protection scheme, the second-highest figure in the EU after Germany. Most of them (68 per cent, according to the UN Refugee Agency) are in work, as the country provides virtually no social support. Many Ukrainians are in jobs below their qualifications, whilst a significant number are still working remotely for Ukrainian employers or running their own businesses.
Ukrainians’ contribution to Poland’s budget exceeds the cost of supporting them: in 2024, the country’s GDP grew by 2.7 per cent thanks to refugees. Warsaw therefore has a financial interest in keeping Ukrainians in the country – despite the anti-Ukrainian rhetoric of politicians.
According to Inna, her family isn’t particularly concerned about how long the EU’s temporary protection programme will last. After all, Poland has already introduced a scheme allowing Ukrainians to switch to a different, more permanent status known as CUKR. This new status is not dependent on having a job or a certain level of income, which is particularly important to Inna.
Ukrainians who held temporary protection status in Poland as of June 4, 2025, and whose status remains valid at the time of application may apply for the Temporary Residence Permit (TRP). TPR status will be temporary (three years – Ed.), but the time spent under this status will count toward the period required to obtain long-term EU resident status.
Inna and her family are planning to apply for the new status in the autumn, once it becomes clear how the new system works in practice. “We meet the criteria, so we’re planning to apply for this status,” she says. “We’ll see what happens next: we’re taking each day as it comes and aren’t making too many plans for the future.”
The family has no plans to return to Ukraine: despite missing home, Inna fears she will not be able to receive the treatment she needs there. She has not yet personally noticed any deterioration in attitudes towards Ukrainians in Poland.
Germany: an uncertain future for the unemployed and men
Further west, in Germany, the situation for Ukrainians is significantly different. As of May 2026, 1.3 million Ukrainian refugees there had been granted temporary protection status – the so-called Paragraph 24.
Recently, there has been an increase in the number of men among them. According to the Federal Office for Migration and Refugees, 60 per cent of Ukrainians who have entered Germany since March 2025 are men of conscription age.
Overall, in the EU, one in four Ukrainians with temporary protection is a man aged between 18 and 64.
Maksym, a Ukrainian (name changed at his request), is living in Berlin under temporary protection from the EU. When Russia’s full-scale invasion began, he was abroad, so he decided not to return to Ukraine. In Germany, Maksym continues to develop his own tourism business, which is linked to Ukraine and caters to Ukrainian clients.
“For four years, I’ve been living as someone who is waiting for the war to end – so that we can live a normal life, because my business depends on it,” he says. “The fate of my 17 or 18 employees and our company depends very much on Ukraine. And we haven’t changed this strategy, because we believe the war will end and we’ll return to some sort of normal life.”
Maksym is critical of the restrictions imposed on Ukrainian men – both those introduced by Ukraine and those approved by the European Union in July 2026. "It was thought that if we didn’t close the borders, everyone would leave Ukraine. But I, for one, would rather come here than leave," he says. "My main problem is that I can’t move about freely. I can’t come to Ukraine and go about my business."
However, Maksym doubts that the European Union’s decision not to accept newly arrived men from Ukraine will deter those who wish to leave. “It will more likely mean that those fleeing Ukraine will find protection outside the EU – in Albania or Turkey,” he believes.
Suspilne also tried to obtain comments from other Ukrainian men who had left for the EU during the war. We asked at least 13 men and sought comments in refugee groups on social media – all of them refused to speak to us.
The proportion of Ukrainians with temporary protection in Germany who are in work is relatively low – 39 per cent. This is one of the lowest figures in the EU. The reasons for this are not limited to access to social benefits, which are generous in Germany. They also include the specific nature of the local labour market, which is rather closed, and the country’s approach to the integration of foreigners, who must first learn the language and either validate their qualifications or acquire new ones.
Oksana Mediana, from Kyiv, used to work as a manager at a fitness club in Ukraine. She has been living in Hamburg with her two children and her mother since 2022, but has not yet managed to find a job there. “All these years I’ve been learning the language and attending integration courses. I’ve reached B2 level in German and am trying to get my qualifications recognised. I’m trying to find a job as an assistant and am willing to do any office work – but it’s proving difficult,” she says. Oksana lives in a small rented flat, the rent for which is partly subsidised by the state, and receives social security benefits.
Once the temporary protection programme comes to an end, Ukrainians like Oksana will have few options for remaining abroad legally. Germany allows Ukrainians who have a permanent employment contract, are studying at university or are married to a local citizen to switch to other types of residence permits. “As long as I don’t have a job, I have no options. You can’t switch to a different status if you’re not self-sufficient,” says Mediana.
Oksana Mediana’s husband has been serving in the Ukrainian Armed Forces since 2022 and occasionally comes to Germany to visit his family. Oksana wants to return to Ukraine, but admits that for her children, aged 9 and 13, Germany has become a second home. She says that over time, her ties with her homeland have weakened: her father has died, and many of her relatives have also moved abroad.
“I’m still in limbo. I hope the war will be over tomorrow, that my husband will ring and tell me to come home,” says Oksana. “The children don’t really want to go back anymore. We’ve been to Ukraine a few times, but we don’t have a large family there anymore.”
Ireland: permission to stay depends on employment and accommodation
Nataliia Minailo arrived in Ireland with her one-year-old daughter in the spring of 2022. At first, she had hoped to return home within a few months, but when a Russian missile struck her house in Vyshhorod, near Kyiv, killing a neighbour, she decided to stay in Dublin for longer. When her daughter started nursery, Natalia began studying at college to become a tour guide, as she had a degree in history from Ukraine.
“I knew right from the start that temporary protection wouldn’t last forever. So, when I finished college, I started looking for a job. Even though people told me: Just stay on benefits, then you can come back to Ukraine. I’ve been working since October 2024,” says Nataliia. She currently works part-time at a museum and also runs her own private guided tours of Dublin.
120,000 Ukrainians have been granted temporary protection in Ireland – this is the eighth highest figure in the EU, although in reality around 84,000 still live there. The rest have returned home or moved to other countries.
In May this year, the country introduced the option for Ukrainians to switch to a different type of residence permit, which ultimately leads to permanent resident status. To qualify, you must have lived in Ireland under temporary protection status for one year and meet strict criteria regarding employment and accommodation: you must have been in employment or self-employed for the past six months, earn at least €29,432 per year, and live in private accommodation without receiving any housing benefit from the state. Applications for this new status will be accepted from September 2026.
However, the housing crisis in Ireland makes the transition to a new status a difficult task for Ukrainians. As of the end of 2025, 68,400 Ukrainian refugees in Ireland (82 per cent) were living in state-provided accommodation or accommodation paid for by the state.
There is a severe shortage of commercial housing in the country: to rent a property, you need to have a job and an income several times higher than the rent, as well as beat dozens of other applicants. For most Ukrainians, this is practically impossible. Dublin is one of the most expensive European capitals, where renting a two-bedroom flat costs an average of 2,241 euros a month.
Nataliia, like many Ukrainian refugees, is still living with an Irish family: many Irish people opened their homes to Ukrainians in 2022. However, the government has announced that it is phasing out payments to those who take in Ukrainian refugees. Moreover, the number of people willing to host Ukrainians in their homes has fallen significantly over the years.
Nataliia, who is planning to switch to a new status, does not yet meet the housing requirements for it. So, for her, a likely extension of the EU’s temporary protection could give her extra time to find suitable accommodation. “If temporary protection is extended, people will have more time to switch to a different visa,” she says. “That will give me time to prepare all the documents and meet the requirements.”
The woman has mixed feelings about returning to Ukraine. “My life is now tied to Ireland. This is where my job is, where my friends are, and where my daughter is growing up and going to school. But Ukraine remains my home, so I don’t want to say "never". For now, I’m living in the present and seeing how things pan out.”

Ukraine approves 1,530 new models of military equipment for service this year
According to Ukrinform, the Ministry of Defense reported this.
Of the 1,678 codified models of weapons and military equipment, 1,530 units—or 91.2%—were manufactured at Ukrainian enterprises.
As noted by the Ministry of Defense, the new weapons models provide the military with potentially additional capabilities for carrying out combat missions: engaging the enemy, conducting reconnaissance, and protecting personnel and logistics.
The pace of codification of domestic weapons models has increased significantly since the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
For comparison, 60 Ukrainian models were approved for service in 2022, while in 2026, that number reached 1,530—a 25.5-fold increase.
Number of certified military equipment models by year:
- 2022 – 110 models in total, of which 60 (54.5%) were manufactured in Ukraine;
- 2023 – 480 in total, of which 295 (61.5%) were manufactured in Ukraine;
- 2024 – 1,409 in total, of which 1,051 (74.6%) were manufactured in Ukraine;
- 2025 – 2,050 in total, of which 1,427 (69.6%) were manufactured in Ukraine;
- 2026, as of September 25 – 1,678 in total, of which 1,530 (91.2%) were manufactured in Ukraine.
The Ministry of Defense also noted a significant increase in the share of domestically produced military equipment for the armed forces’ needs. Since the start of the full-scale Russian invasion, this figure has risen by 67.3%.
“It is important that, in wartime, military equipment manufacturers are working to adapt their products to changes on the battlefield and can receive feedback from the military. This is necessary to more quickly implement solutions within the military that meet the current needs of the Defense Forces,” the Ministry of Defense stated.
As reported by Ukrinform, since the beginning of 2026, the Ukrainian Ministry of Defense has codified and approved for use by the Defense Forces 650 unmanned aerial systems, most of which are Ukrainian-made.

WHO warns of ‘devastating consequences’ due to delayed aid entry into Gaza
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
04:54:20 UTC
13:54:20 KST

WHO warns of ‘devastating consequences’ due to delayed aid entry into Gaza
The WHO’s representative in Palestine calls on Israeli authorities to “release the pressure on medical supplies”.
Repeated delays in bringing life-saving medicines, prosthetics and other supplies from Israel into Gaza risk having “devastating consequences” for Palestinians who urgently need them, the World Health Organization (WHO) has said.
Approved aid can enter Gaza only through Kerem Shalom, at the southern tip of the territory, while Rafah, also in the south, is open only for limited movement of people, including patients needing medical treatment abroad, the WHO said on Friday.
“A truck full of non-priority supplies or the right supplies arriving too late, doesn’t save lives. That’s the question that actually matters,” Reinhilde Van De Weerdt, the WHO’s representative in Palestine, said.
Van De Weerdt called on Israeli authorities to “release the pressure on medical supplies”, saying essential medicines “should not be considered as dual use, as they are globally accepted standards on medical items anybody needs anywhere to run a hospital or a clinic”.
She added that one shipment of prosthetics and assistive devices had been rejected four times over the past six months.
“Every rejection means another delay for someone who has already lost a limb and is simply waiting for the chance to walk again,” she said, noting that medicines “by contrast, move relatively well”, with almost 87 percent approved and just over 1 percent rejected.
“Our ask is simple and has not changed: we need the unimpeded and predictable entry of humanitarian and health supplies into Gaza at scale. We also need a multi-crossing model so that aid isn’t forced to trickle down through a limited number of crossings,” Van De Weerdt said.
Four other main entry points into Gaza – Kissufim, Gate 96, Erez and Erez West – remain closed and under total Israeli control.
She praised the “extraordinary health workers” still risking their lives in Gaza, who she said were not receiving enough supplies to give patients the care they needed.
Winter and disease risk
“As winter begins, this urgency to get supplies into Gaza only deepens,” Van De Weerdt said. “Almost two million people are in need of shelter to protect against the cold and the risk of flooding, exposing people to serious health and safety risks, let alone their dignity.”
She said residents faced a heightened risk of preventable disease outbreaks linked to the lack of safe shelter and clean water, and a high number of rats whose bites transmit infection, a threat made harder to track by the destruction of public health laboratories.
The UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) warned on Thursday of serious public health risks from the accumulation of solid waste in Gaza City, where sanitation gains remain fragile because of a lack of reliable access to heavy machinery, engine oil, spare parts and fuel funding.
Almost 12 months into a fragile “ceasefire” between Hamas and Israel, marked by continuing Israeli air attacks and other military activity, Gaza’s humanitarian situation remains “overwhelming”, according to OCHA.

German reunification: How inequality is shaping a new East German identity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
04:54:00 UTC
13:54:00 KST

German reunification: Why being East German matters again
October 3, 2026
German reunification may be 36 years in the past, but when it comes to wealth, the divide between East and West Germany is far from history. East Germans still earn less on average, receive smaller pensions and own less property, according to Elisabeth Kaiser, the Federal Government Commissioner for Eastern Germany.
Kaiser, born in the state of Thuringia in the socialist German Democratic Republic (GDR) in 1987, has put the enduring wealth gap at the center of the debate. A study she presented in Berlin points to decades in which private entrepreneurship and opportunities to invest in one's financial future were restricted in the East. That meant, Kaiser said, that "families have not been able to acquire or pass on as much wealth." The consequences, she argues, have had a profound impact upward mobility.
How important are personal connections and social background?
But it is not only East Germans who see fewer chances of upward mobility these days. Kaiser pointed to the latest "Deutschland-Monitor," an annual survey she commissioned to make her point. Although this year's survey is still being analyzed, early findings reveal that about two-thirds of respondents across the country believe that financial and social mobility depend crucially on wealth, personal connections and social background.
This perception is reflected in the numbers. Even though the percentage of East German executives in the highest federal agencies has risen from 13.9% in 2022 to 16.3% today, Kaiser says, "The further up the management ladder you go, the lower the percentage of East Germans you find."
East German leaders remain scarce across the board
Based on these findings, the Commissioner for Eastern Germany calls for greater equality in decision-making. "And that is why I would like to see East Germans sitting at the table wherever decisions are made in the country," she said, "in the ministries, in government agencies, in business, academia, the judiciary, culture and the media."
With just under 20%, East Germans are significantly underrepresented in all sectors relative to their share of the population. To back this up, Kaiser cited the "Elitenmonitor," another study commissioned by her office. With over 3,000 top positions examined across twelve sectors over a long period of time, the Elitenmonitor study, conducted by the universities of Jena (Thuringia), Leipzig (Saxony), and Zittau/Görlitz (Saxony), can offer more than just a snapshot.
According to the report, the percentage of East Germans in leadership positions in both the public and private sectors only increased from 10.9% to 12.1% from 2018 to 2024. And in the business and cultural sectors, the percentage of East Germans has actually declined.
Most striking of all is that among the 100 largest German companies, all executives are from West Germany — and the same holds true for the military. East Germans are also severely underrepresented in top positions in the judiciary and the media.
New stereotypes about East Germany
The insufficient representation of East German perspectives in nearly all areas of society also appears to have consequences for how East Germans are viewed. Kaiser says that her generation, born around the fall of the Berlin Wall and German reunification, did not feel East German for a long time. It was only in school and during vocational training that she realized there were differences between East and West that would sometimes put her at a disadvantage.
This has also shaped stereotypes about East Germany, both past and present. "An East German identity is also being created politically to some extent because people are looking for some way to orient themselves, because they're looking for a common bond," Kaiser knows from her many experiences and conversations.
As an example, she cited the symbolic power of the Simson moped, produced in the millions during the GDR era — a symbol of mobility and freedom for many young people at that time.
Leading representatives of the Alternative for Germany (AfD), a party classified in part as far-right extremist by the domestic intelligence agency, frequently make public appearances riding on Simson mopeds. One of them is Ulrich Siegmund, the AfD candidate who recently won state elections in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt.
Without specifically mentioning the AfD by name, Kaiser lamented the exploitation of cultural symbols for political purposes."It creates a very powerful emotional connection," said Kaiser regarding the use of the Simson brand.
As for the AfD and its recent electoral successes in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and Berlin, Kaiser said that these elections send a dangerous signal. She believes that international investors and skilled workers will ask themselves: Should I go there or not?
Kaiser specifically mentioned sectors that have played an important role as drivers of economic growth and innovation in eastern Germany, such as the semiconductor industry, battery cell research, healthcare, biotechnology and renewable energy. Her concern is that the economic upswing in these sectors could suffer as a result.
This article was originally written in German.

Russia strikes key Kyiv bridge for 3rd straight day as attacks intensify
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
04:53:10 UTC
13:53:10 KST

Editor's note: This is a developing story and is being updated.
Russian forces launched a strike on the Northern Bridge over the Dnipro River in Kyiv in the morning hours of Oct. 3 as Russia again takes aim at key bridges in the capital for the third straight day.
Explosions were reported in the city shortly after 6:30 a.m. amid reports of drones approaching the capital. Videos posted to social media of the purported attack appear to show a large explosion on the bridge that connects the right bank of the city with the left bank as vehicles pass by.
Mayor Vitali Klitschko said that the bridge's surface as well as trolleybus overhead power lines have been damaged in the attack. Movement over the bridge was halted following the strike.
The Russian strike on the Northern Bridge injured two people, Klitschko said.
The full extent of the damage caused was not immediately clear.
The Kyiv City Military Administration (KMDA) announced new restrictions on movements over Kyiv's bridges during air raid alerts.
Traffic on the Southern Bridge is restricted from the right to the left bank for the first fifteen minutes of an alert. On the Podilsko-Voskresenskyi Bridge, traffic is completely stopped in both directions for the first fifeteen minutes of an alert.
Traffic on the Northern Bridge, Metro Bridge, Darnytskyi Bridge, and Paton Bridge may resume without restrictions.
The latest strike marks follows days Russian attacks on key bridges within the capital. A day prior on Oct. 2, a Russian drone struck the Southern Bridge over the Dnipro River — marking the fourth such drone strike in two days.
Kostiantyn Kryvolap, an aviation expert and former Antonov test engineer, told the Kyiv Independent that destruction of the bridge is most likely not the intent behind Russia's strikes.
"Destroying a bridge with a 50-kilogram explosive charge, even with a highly effective warhead designed to destroy steel bridge structures, is a major exaggeration. It is practically impossible. For a bridge like this, these strikes are more like mosquito bites," he said.
Instead, the idea behind the Russian strikes may rather be to halt traffic, interrupt logistics, and exert psychological pressure on Kyiv's population, according to him.
Both the Northern and Southern bridges serve as some of the capital's main traffic arteries, with tens of thousands of the city's residents passing over the bridges daily.

It is currently unknown what specific facility may have been the target of the attack. Kaluga is located approximately 180 km from Moscow; the city is home to a number of enterprises, some of which may be connected to Russia's military-industrial complex.

Country diary: The breathtaking sight of a tuna taking flight in British waters | Anita Roy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
04:30:49 UTC
13:30:49 KST

It is a perfect autumn day for a clifftop walk: sea and sky blend into a veil of baby blue, and the water is calm and dazzling. A motorboat unzips the ocean as we squint out over the bay.
My companion points to a dark line snaking along in the water. It seems to intensify for a moment, then erupts in a silver commotion. Through binoculars I can make out the frantic leaping of a shoal of eel-like fish. “Garfish,” he says. “Now just watch.”
Suddenly, the water erupts as a monster bursts into the air, scattering the garfish like sequins. Dark on top, with fins like daggers, its silver underside is lit up by the sun, massive as a billboard caught in headlights. It crashes down, swallowed up by its own whirlpool. Another leaps, and another. Tuna!
By the time I’ve remembered to breathe again, the surface of the water is still and twinkling once more, as if I’d hallucinated the whole thing. Atlantic bluefin tuna (Thunnus thynnus) have, as I’ve just found, made an astonishing return to British waters. And what astonishing animals they are – they can live up to 50 years, grow to 3 metres and reach speeds of more than 40mph. This apex predator hunts in packs, herding its prey to the surface. I’m glad I’m not a garfish.
A common sight off England’s south coast until the 1950s, overfishing then pushed them almost to extinction here. In the early 2000s, strict regulations were introduced – and the results are clear to see. This shows “the power of effective management”, as Chris Graham of the Marine Conservation Society puts it.
But Chris also identifies the “background issue” of global warming, which is changing the migration patterns of tuna and their prey. Bluefin tuna need warm water and, after this year’s heatwaves, the Devon coast must be like heaven.
The multiple catastrophic effects of the climate crisis on ecosystems are … well, too horrific to look at head-on. So let’s focus, if only for today, on this astonishing good news story. In 2021, Atlantic bluefin tuna were reclassified on the IUCN red list from “critically endangered” to “least concern”. It’s a giant leap.

Taiwan's Sinbon revenue reaches new highs on green energy, industrial growth
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
04:29:56 UTC
13:29:56 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Sinbon Electronics Co. continued its strong sales momentum in September, setting multiple revenue records, CTEE reported Saturday.
The cable assembly maker reported September revenue of NT$3.35 billion (US$105.2 million), up 25.51% from the same month a year earlier. The figure marked its sixth consecutive monthly high.
Third-quarter revenue reached NT$9.8 billion, up 28.9% from a year earlier, the company's highest quarterly level. Revenue for the first nine months totaled NT$27.2 billion, up 15.24% year-over-year, also setting a new high for the period.
Growth in September was mainly driven by continued expansion in the green energy sector, which grew 23.41% from the previous month. Sales of industrial applications and electronic peripherals also posted moderate growth.
Sinbon supplies major global green energy companies with cable assemblies for wind turbines, including torsion-resistant cables used in towers, as well as connection components for solar inverters. Long-term demand in the sector is expected to remain strong as countries around the world work toward net-zero emissions, according to 913.
Rather than focusing on high-volume, low-margin orders as a conventional cable harness manufacturer, Sinbon has shifted toward customized connection solutions. The company works with customers from the early stages of product development, providing customized solutions from design through manufacturing.
Its products serve five major sectors: medical, automotive, green energy, industrial applications, and communications. In the medical field, Sinbon supplies precision cable assemblies used in advanced imaging equipment, including magnetic resonance imaging and ultrasound systems. For electric vehicles, it produces charging connectors, high-voltage cable assemblies, and wiring for battery management systems.
The company said its three new business areas — advanced semiconductor equipment, humanoid robots, and commercial drones — are beginning to see stronger demand. It expects industrial applications to become a key source of growth next year.
To meet rising orders, Sinbon is also expanding production capacity. It acquired Everlight Electronics Co.’s Zhongxing plant, which is expected to begin operations between late first quarter and early second quarter of 2027. Additional capacity at its Taichung facility is scheduled to come online in the third quarter of next year.

Taiwan universities improve 2D semiconductor photon conductivity
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
04:29:34 UTC
13:29:34 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) – The National Council of Science and Technology announced on Friday that National Taiwan Normal University and National Cheng Kung University have made photons compatible with next-gen semiconductor manufacturing, according to a press release.
AI is driving demand for more compact power-saving chips. The council sponsored a joint project headed by NTNU Professor Lan Yann-wen (藍彥文), Lu Ting-hua (陸亭樺), Yang Hung-wei (楊弘偉) and NCKU Micro and Nano Center CTO Lin Kuang-i (林光儀).
The council said National Taiwan University, National Yang Ming Chiao Tung University, and the National Synchrotron Radiation Research Center joined to provide additional support. It noted that the team used a two-step chemical vapor deposition to create a specialized MoS2 bilayer, as published in the leading scientific journal Nature.
MoS2 is an ultra-thin 2D semiconductor material known for its high photon conductivity but performs poorly because of structural gaps. Chemical vapor deposition delivers precursor chemicals onto a wafer and converts them into MoS2 at controlled temperatures.
Photons carry electricity more quickly and reliably than copper conduits. Copper wiring is obsolete as AI computing generates too much heat and friction for it to handle.
The method is inspired by atomic layer deposition and has successfully stacked matching structures to improve photon passage without altering source materials. Stacking is the arrangement of material layers to correct crystal structures and conductivity.
Lan said that precise stacking can restructure materials for better conductivity, CNA reported. He suggested more studies on material growth during atom-layering, as it is reliable for making next-gen 2D semiconductors and quantum computing materials.
Lu said the aim is to create a repeatable deposition method to replace automated or manual stacking. She added that controlled, precise stacking is an important reference for similar processes.
