Russia rehearses invasion and occupation of Central Asian country during military exercises – videos
Russian forces have practised seizing territory and "creating a security zone" in a neighbouring Central Asian country during the Centre-2026 military exercises in Chelyabinsk Oblast.
Source: Russian propaganda media outlets; the Kremlin press service
Details: The exercises are taking place from 28 September to 3 October. They involve 47,000 military personnel, 2,000 pieces of military equipment, 90 aircraft and 77 warships and other vessels. Military contingents from Belarus, China, Kyrgyzstan, Mongolia, Pakistan and Tajikistan are taking part in the exercises.
Russian ruler Vladimir Putin arrived at the Chebarkul training ground accompanied by a military helicopter. Several sections of roads in the area were closed to traffic for three days because of his visit, completely isolating the city of Chebarkul.
According to the official scenario announced by Russia's Defence Ministry, the exercises are designed to practise repelling aggression on the Central Asian front and ensuring security in the Caspian region.
Meanwhile, Deputy Defence Minister Yunus-bek Yevkurov, reporting to Russian ruler Vladimir Putin on the progress of the exercises, said that the troops were practising not only repelling an attack but also "creating a security zone in adjacent territories".
"The coalition force is repelling the main attack on the South Urals front, has restored its positions and, since 2 October, has been conducting offensive operations to liberate the captured territory and create a security zone in the adjacent territory," he said.
The Kremlin noted that the exercises involved units that are not taking part in the war against Ukraine. However, Putin stressed that all tasks were being conducted taking into account the experience of warfare in Ukraine.
Of the countries that could fit the description of the "aggressor country" in the scenario, Kazakhstan is the most plausible, as it has access to the Caspian Sea and borders Russia's Chelyabinsk Oblast. During the exercises, four long-range aircraft carried out strikes on critical facilities belonging to the simulated enemy.
Background:
- Russia has previously held similar large-scale military exercises. In particular, around 128,000 military personnel officially took part in the Centre-2019 exercises, while around 95,000 people participated in the Centre-2015 exercises.
- During the 2019 exercises, Russian troops practised neutralising a simulated state in southwestern Russia that had allegedly started a war and was spreading terrorism.

Latvians vote in election in shadow of drone incursions and war in Ukraine

Latvians vote in election in shadow of drone incursions and war in Ukraine
RIGA, Oct 3 - Latvians are voting in a parliamentary election on Saturday that is likely to keep power in the hands of pro-Ukrainian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs, although deep political fragmentation may complicate the formation of a government.
Across the Baltics, including in NATO and European Union member Latvia, many voters are on edge after official warnings of potential Russian aggression and a growing number of airspace incursions related to Moscow's war in Ukraine.
Russia says accusations that it is planning to attack NATO are baseless and Western officials say it is not capable of launching a direct assault, but security concerns have weighed heavily in the election campaign.
"The priority, in my view, is, of course, security – security in Latvia. And then... as a student, I’d say support for students, the economy, and also support for pensioners," said Megija Nordena, 21, from Riga.
Opinion polls put Kulbergs' centrist United List ahead, with about 14% of votes, but followed closely by the overtly pro-Russian Sovereign Power.
A businessman and amateur rally driver, Kulbergs, 47, came to power in May after the previous coalition crumbled over its handling of incidents in which stray military drones flew undetected into Latvia. Though the drones were Ukrainian, officials have blamed Russia for causing them to divert from their flight paths.
"We have to give Ukraine everything necessary right now (so) that they can have the upper hand and win", Kulbergs told Reuters in an interview.
Throughout his campaign, he has also promised more anti-drone capabilities for Latvia and to maintain defence spending at 5% of gross domestic product, one of the highest levels in NATO.
But his pro-Kremlin rivals say Latvia should stop any aid to Ukraine and should instead focus more on cost-of-living issues, particularly among the country's Russian-speaking minority.
"Our voters want peace, to stop looking for shelters, to no longer experience the air alerts", party leader Julia Stepanenko told Reuters. "The war must not be encouraged in any way, including by financing it... Ukraine must win, but through peace talks".
Polls opened at 8 a.m. (0500 GMT) and are due to close at 8 p.m., with the first results expected within hours and the final result likely to be clear after midnight. The 100 members of the Saeima, or parliament, are being elected for a four-year term.
DIVIDED NATION
Surveys show at least two other parties may make it into parliament - the populist, MAGA-style Latvia First grouping and the Progressives, a left-leaning party that attracts younger voters.
Kulbergs' ability to forge a working coalition will depend largely on how many votes they receive and how many other parties cross the 5% threshold to enter parliament.
He might also need to cobble together a deal with Latvia First leader, businessman Ainars Slesers, who appears to have shifted towards a more anti-Ukraine stance in recent months, courting votes on both sides.
"His message is that (the party) condemns Russia's invasion and stands with Ukraine, but that supporting Ukraine comes at the expense of Latvia's economy," said Roberts Kits, researcher for the Latvian Strategy and Economic Research Institute, in a note.
The ethnic Russian minority in Latvia is split between those who feel embarrassed or angry about Kremlin's war in Ukraine, and those frustrated with policies at home aimed at limiting their influence on public life which many see as discriminatory.
Latvia, with a population of 1.9 million, is sandwiched between the Baltic Sea, with EU and NATO allies Estonia and Lithuania to the north and south, and Russia and Belarus to the east. REUTERS

Ukrainian regional head pays tribute to Nazi SS veteran
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
00:02:42 UTC
09:02:42 KST

Ukrainian regional head pays tribute to Nazi SS veteran
The governor of Ukraine’s western Lviv Region has paid tribute to a recently deceased veteran of the Waffen-SS Galicia Division, whose soldiers were implicated in massacres of civilians in Poland and Soviet Ukraine during World War II.
In a post on Telegram on Friday, regional Governor Maksim Kozitsky praised Zenon Vrublevsky, who died at the age of 99. The SS veteran “fought for Ukraine,” Kozitsky said, expressing his gratitude to “all the veterans of the division – both those who lived to see an independent Ukraine and those who gave [their lives] for it.” His death was widely covered by Ukrainian media.
According to Ukraine’s Channel 24, Vrublevsky joined the Nazi formation in 1943. Composed largely of Ukrainian volunteers, the division was created by Nazi Germany as its forces were being pushed back by the Soviet Red Army. Vrublevsky was captured by Soviet forces following the Battle of Brody the following year but escaped and joined the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA), the armed wing of the Organization of Ukrainian Nationalists (OUN).
Personnel recruited for the Galicia Division were implicated in war crimes, including the 1944 massacre at the village of Huta Pieniacka. Poland’s Institute of National Remembrance attributes the massacre to the 4th Galician SS Police Regiment, formed from volunteers recruited for the Galicia Division, together with UPA and other Ukrainian nationalist forces. Around 850 Polish civilians were killed.
The OUN sought to establish an ethnically homogeneous Ukrainian state and described Poles, Russians, Jews, Hungarians, and other minorities as enemies in its documents. The organization initially collaborated with Nazi Germany during its 1941 invasion of the Soviet Union, but its relationship with Berlin deteriorated after Germany rejected the declaration of an independent Ukrainian state and arrested leading OUN members. According to Polish estimates, the UPA and other Ukrainian nationalist formations killed up to 100,000 Polish civilians in 1943-1944 in what is now western Ukraine. Poland recognizes the massacres as genocide.
Ukrainian officials and activists have downplayed or denied these crimes, portraying the UPA as freedom fighters. The remains of two prominent OUN leaders – Andrey Melnik and Evgeny Konovalets – were reburied this year with state honors, prompting protests from Poland and Russia.
In June, Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky approved the addition of the honorary title ‘Heroes of the UPA’ to the name of an active-duty special forces unit, sparking outrage in Poland. Polish President Karol Nawrocki subsequently stripped Zelensky of the Order of the White Eagle, the country’s highest state honor.
Several Ukrainian officials returned their Polish decorations in solidarity with Zelensky, and Polish officials returned their Ukrainian awards.
Moscow has accused the Ukrainian leadership of embracing neo-Nazism. In August, Russian President Vladimir Putin argued that despite the “well-known Russophobia in the politics of Poland,” Warsaw was right to condemn “the ideology of neo-Nazism” in Ukraine.

North Korea fires ballistic missile towards the sea, South Korea says
A ballistic missile fired from the North Korean port city of Wonsan flies more than 700km, South Korea’s military says.
South Korea’s military says North Korea has fired at least one ballistic missile towards the sea off its east coast.
South Korea’s Joint Chiefs of Staff said on Saturday morning that its northern neighbour fired a ballistic missile from the port city of Wonsan on the eastern shore of the Korean Peninsula and that it flew more than 700 kilometres (435 miles).
Seoul’s presidential national security office convened an emergency meeting to assess the situation after the launch, the president’s office said in a statement.
The South Korean military raised an alert for further launches and said it would share intelligence with the US and Japan.
Japan issued an emergency alert on Saturday, saying: “North Korea has launched a suspected ballistic missile.”
The US Pacific Command said it was aware of the launch, adding that it was consulting closely with US allies and partners.
“Based on current assessments, this event does not pose an immediate threat to US personnel or territory, or to our allies,” it said in a social media post.
The launch came a day after Kim Yo Jong, the powerful sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, ridiculed South Korean demands for the North to apologise over landmine blasts that South Korea and the US-led United Nations Command said were caused by North Korean mines planted south of the Military Demarcation Line.
The blasts seriously injured three South Korean soldiers on a reconnaissance mission inside the 4km-wide (2.5-mile) border zone that stretches across the Korean Peninsula.
South Korea has also called on the North to halt recent efforts to fortify its border, including the installation of mines and anti-tank barriers.
Kim Yo Jong dismissed Seoul’s demands as “utterly pathetic”, saying the North intends to permanently cut ties with the South.
Saturday’s launch was the latest in a series of North Korean military displays in recent weeks, including tests of a purported hypersonic missile system, live-fire exercises and the commissioning of a new warship.

Dutch royal house helped slave trade to survive, study finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
23:43:50 UTC
08:43:50 KST

Dutch royal house helped slave trade to survive, study finds
In-depth study also says the royal house made huge profits from the Dutch colonial policies in past centuries.
A historical study has found that the Dutch royal house benefited from the country’s colonial policies in past centuries and helped the slave trade to survive.
The in-depth study, commissioned by King Willem-Alexander and conducted by Leiden University, showed the House of Orange-Nassau “actively supported Dutch colonialism for centuries, but only rarely determined colonial policy”, according to the university’s statement, published on Friday.
“The involvement of the House of Orange-Nassau was wholehearted and without any real reservations,” Dutch historians and human rights experts concluded after a three-year study looking at the period from 1600 to the present.
“The research leaves us in no doubt that the House of Orange shares responsibility for the survival over the centuries of the Dutch slave trade and slavery,” the study said, noting that most of the rulers showed no objections to slavery.
King Willem-Alexander said on Friday he was personally affected by the “explicit” conclusions of the study.
“It is a painful and confronting conclusion. A conclusion that affects me, even though I am three generations removed,” Willem-Alexander said in a speech at the presentation of the research.
“We know the effects of colonialism and slavery are still being felt today. Discrimination and economic exploitation unfortunately happen every day,” he added.
The study also showed that the royal family at times profited substantially from the colonial system, mostly from trade in the Dutch East Indies, modern-day Indonesia.
In the 19th century, for instance, profits accumulated to about $650m in modern terms, the researchers said.
On the other hand, the royal family earned “almost nothing” from the slave trade, the research showed.
Apologies without reparations
The Dutch monarch, who in 2023 apologised for his ancestors’ lack of action against slavery, highlighted their lack of “counter-current leadership” in the face of colonialism.
The House of Orange has ruled the Netherlands since the late 16th century, first as “stadtholders” who presided over the republic, and later as the royal house when the Netherlands became a monarchy.
For most of this time, the Dutch ruled over vast colonies in Southeast Asia and the Caribbean, including what is now Indonesia and Suriname.
The findings could stir up the debate around reparations in the Netherlands. The Dutch government apologised in 2022 after acknowledging the Dutch state bore responsibility for transatlantic slavery. King Willem-Alexander apologised the following year.
The government at the time ruled out reparations, instead creating a 200 million euro ($238m) fund for social initiatives, which anti-racism campaigners have dismissed as insufficient.
The National Institute for the Dutch Slavery Past and Heritage (NiNsee) lauded the king for commissioning the study but said it should lead to a next phase.
“Research impacts society when the new insights into the past contribute to awareness, dialogue, corrections and additions to our national history in the school curriculum and the conversation about responsibility and reparatory justice,” NiNsee director Bianca Groen Gallant said.
The Dutch played a major role in the global slave trade from the 17th century until the Netherlands abolished slavery in the second half of the 19th century.

SBU exposes GRU agents who collected data on military personnel and guided strikes on Kharkiv
That is according to the SBU, Ukrinform reports.
As a result of a special operation personally coordinated by SBU chief Major General Oleksandr Poklad, all four members of the group were detained.
At the Russians' request, the suspects were hiding in a safe apartment in Kharkiv a man who had been convicted of justifying Russia's armed aggression.
The investigation established that the hostile cell included the head of the security department of a mobile communications company and one of his subordinates.
On instructions from the Russian intelligence service, they collected personal data on Ukrainian Armed Forces personnel, law enforcement officers and members of Ukraine's judiciary.
The investigation documented how the Russians instructed them to gather information on a prosecutor and judges involved in criminal proceedings against a propagandist who was being sheltered by the agent network.
To do this, the suspects used their access to the mobile operator's software, which allows them to obtain information about subscribers' phone connections and geolocation.
The third member of the agent network was an employee of a local defense enterprise who, at the enemy's request, rented out an apartment to Ukrainian servicemen and, without revealing her true intentions, elicited information from them about the locations of military units and their movements. She also guided strikes against the defense enterprise where she worked.
Another agent was a Kharkiv resident who, together with two employees of the mobile operator's security department, traveled around the city and surrounding areas in their company vehicle. During these trips, he used a smartwatch to film defense facilities, including reserve command posts, fortifications and checkpoints manned by Ukrainian defenders.
SBU counterintelligence officers acted proactively and exposed the entire agent group before it could carry out further assignments. After documenting the cell's crimes step by step, they detained each of its members.
According to the investigation, the suspects were recruited by the Russian intelligence service through a Kharkiv resident who had left for Russia before the start of the full-scale war and began working for Russia's GRU as a handler.
SBU investigators notified all the detainees that they were suspected of violating Part 2 of Article 111 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine – high treason committed under martial law.
The detainees are in custody. They face life imprisonment with confiscation of property.

In brief
- Daylight saving returns this weekend, renewing calls for southeast Queensland to adopt the time change.
- Border businesses near Tweed Heads and Coolangatta are preparing for booking mix-ups and confusion.
Same headache, new year.
In the wee hours of Sunday morning, daylight saving kicks in for the long Australian summer, when clocks skip forward by an hour from 2am to 3am.
But while the citizens of NSW, Victoria, Tasmania, South Australia and the ACT will enjoy an extra hour of sunshine after clocking off, Queensland remains the eastern seaboard outlier.
Daylight saving is an annual talking point on the Gold Coast, with Mayor Tom Tate on Wednesday reiterating calls for daylight saving to be introduced in Queensland's southeast corner.
Tate suggested drawing a new time zone boundary north of Noosa — cheekily acknowledging the lack of support elsewhere from cows and the wider dairy industry.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
But for businesses in the NSW border town of Tweed Heads, as well as Coolangatta on the Queensland side, the issue is no joke.
Ellen Clark, a cosmetic nurse, recently opened a business in Tweed Heads and is bracing herself for late arrivals from her clientele, most of whom are in Queensland.
"It's going to be interesting trying to navigate that," she told the Australian Associated Press (AAP).
Previously, Ms Clark commuted to Brisbane for work from Tweed Heads, where her partner is based, but decided to set up shop locally after the birth of her first child.
"I used to have to stay on Queensland time while my partner would operate on NSW time," she said.
"It kind of came to my attention yesterday, and I was like, 'Oh my God, we're back here again'."
Sean McMillan is also new to Tweed Heads, having just set up a barber shop on Bay Street.
"All my systems go off bookings, so I'm trying to do some research, and I'm changing my hours a little bit to catch people on both sides of the border," he told the AAP.
"I'm sure there'll be people coming in an hour early or an hour late for bookings ... It's just one of those puzzles to work out."
Queensland Premier David Crisafulli was not keen to buy into Tate's suggestion when asked about the issue by reporters in Mackay on Thursday.
"I've lived at both ends of the state, and I'm here for uniting Queensland, not dividing it," he said.
Queensland trialled daylight saving between 1989 and 1992 before being comprehensively rejected in a state referendum.

Russia Plans Record $200B Defense Budget as Healthcare, Education, Face Cuts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
23:36:35 UTC
08:36:35 KST

Russia plans to sharply increase military spending in 2027 while cutting planned funding for healthcare, education and social programs, as the mounting cost of its war against Ukraine puts growing pressure on the Kremlin’s finances.
The draft federal budget submitted to Russia’s State Duma would raise defense spending to 17.1 trillion rubles (approximately $204.4 billion) in 2027, about 27% above what Moscow had previously planned for that year. It would mark Russia’s highest military spending since the full-scale invasion began in 2022.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Defense spending would account for more than a third of federal expenditures and exceed planned spending on healthcare, education and social policy combined, according to budget documents reviewed by Reuters.
The figures underline how deeply the war has reshaped Russia’s economy as Moscow prepares for another year of high-intensity fighting while simultaneously confronting weaker revenues, growing borrowing needs and rising debt-servicing costs.
The Russian government formally submitted its 2027–2029 budget to parliament on Sept. 30, describing defense and security needs as one of its principal priorities.
Defense spending jumps again
Russia had previously budgeted about 13.5 trillion rubles ($161.4 billion) for defense in 2027. The new proposal raises that figure to 17.1 trillion rubles.
Over the full 2027–2029 period, Moscow is expected to spend roughly 50 trillion rubles ($597.8 billion) on defense, according to budget documents.
Putin Ally Schröder Takes Russian Business Post After Kremlin Floated Him as Ukraine Mediator
Although the government currently forecasts some reduction in military spending after 2027, Russia has repeatedly exceeded its own longer-term defense projections since launching the full-scale invasion.
That makes the headline figures potentially only a starting point.
Alexander Kolyandr, a senior fellow at the Center for European Policy Analysis, has argued that published defense totals should be viewed as an opening position in negotiations between Russia’s Finance Ministry and the country’s security establishment rather than a firm ceiling.
Actual military spending is also partly classified, making the full cost of the war difficult to calculate independently.
Russia’s military burden has already expanded dramatically. Important Stories reported that defense-related expenditures accounted for 43.8% of federal spending in the first half of 2026, compared with less than 20% before the full-scale war.
Healthcare and education squeezed
The surge in defense expenditure comes with cuts elsewhere.
Compared with earlier government plans for 2027, spending on education is set to fall by about 6%, healthcare by nearly 7% and social policy by roughly 7%, according to Reuters’ review of the draft budget.
Healthcare programs face particularly steep reductions.
Important Stories found that funding for the construction and renovation of regional outpatient clinics would be cut by more than half, while spending on cancer medicines and oncology equipment would fall from almost 148.5 billion rubles ($1.8 billion) to about 44.9 billion rubles ($536.8 million). Funding for ambulance development would also be reduced by nearly a third.
Eight of 11 national medical projects face reductions, according to the outlet’s analysis of the budget documents.
The shift continues a trend already visible at the regional level.
Earlier this year, Important Stories found that 19 Russian regions had significantly reduced healthcare spending in their 2026 budgets – the highest number since the full-scale invasion began. Combined planned reductions totaled about 107 billion rubles ($1.3 billion).
Infrastructure and other civilian projects are also being squeezed.
Spending on infrastructure, agriculture and other economic sectors is expected to fall by more than 7% compared with previous plans, AFP reported.
Moscow turns to taxes and borrowing
Russia has run a federal budget deficit every year since launching its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
For 2027, the deficit is projected at around 5.4 trillion rubles ($64.5 billion), while state debt is expected to rise to about 21.7% of GDP – above the 20% level Russia’s Finance Ministry had previously described as a safe threshold.
Borrowing is also rising sharply.
Russia is expected to rely increasingly on domestic debt markets while introducing additional tax increases, including higher levies on some investment income and new windfall taxation on metals and mining businesses.
The Kremlin has also sought unconventional sources of revenue.
Reuters reported Friday that wealthy Russians contributed 471 billion rubles ($5.6 billion) to the federal budget in 2026 through what authorities described as voluntary payments, while the government expects another 385 billion rubles ($4.6 billion) from the sale of seized private assets.
War spending increasingly dominates Russia’s economy
The new figures illustrate the growing trade-offs facing the Kremlin as the war enters another year.
Russia has continued to expand weapons production and military expenditure even as civilian programs are trimmed and higher borrowing pushes up debt-servicing costs.
Those costs are expected to absorb about 9.4% of federal expenditures in 2027 and rise further by 2029, according to Reuters.
Boris Grozovsky, a columnist for Important Stories, described the budget as evidence that the Russian government is running out of fiscal room.
“There’s not enough money,” he wrote, arguing that the government is increasingly signaling that scarce funds will be directed first toward its most politically important priorities.
For Moscow, the draft makes clear what remains at the top of that list: sustaining Russia’s war machine.

Cuba expands foreign companies' access to wholesale market
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
07:25:22 CST
08:25:22 KST

HAVANA, Oct. 2 (Xinhua) -- The Cuban government on Friday expanded foreign companies' access to its wholesale market and allowed their local commercial offices to hire workers directly, outlining new rules aimed at boosting foreign investment and trade.
The rules, published Friday in the Official Gazette of the Republic of Cuba, are part of government reforms intended to increase supplies of materials and other inputs for domestic production.
Under the new provisions, branches of foreign companies established in Cuba can import and export goods and distribute them wholesale within the country.
Deputy Minister of Foreign Trade and Investment Deborah Rivas said the changes would give foreign suppliers more direct access to the Cuban market and reduce the number of intermediaries.
"One of the main effects this measure could have is the elimination of intermediaries in the distribution chain," Rivas told a news conference, adding that fewer intermediaries should lead to lower prices.
Previously, foreign companies supplied goods while Cuban importers handled customs clearance, transportation and distribution, she said. The new rules allow foreign suppliers to handle wholesale distribution themselves.
The hiring changes build on Decree-Law 128, published in September, which amended Foreign Investment Law 118 to allow businesses with foreign capital to choose whether to hire workers directly or through employment agencies.
Rivas said the latest provisions extend that option to foreign commercial representative offices, which operate under separate regulations.
Cuban legal entities can also apply directly for authorization to import and export, without going through intermediaries, using the Foreign Trade Single Window, an online platform accessible nationwide.
A separate Foreign Investment Single Window remains available and has received inquiries from prospective investors in several countries, Rivas said.
Cubans living abroad can also participate in foreign investment projects and contribute capital from inside or outside Cuba on equal terms with other economic actors, she added.
The measures build on initiatives announced by the Ministry of Foreign Trade and Investment since November 2025 to stimulate the sector and support Cuba's economic recovery.
"Cuba is an open door to the world when it comes to foreign investment," Rivas said. ■

Oil prices fell after the Group of Seven nations and the European Union (EU) agreed to release 100 million barrels of crude and diesel from emergency reserves, under a French proposal pairing 50 million barrels of diesel from the EU with 50 million barrels of crude from the International Energy Agency. "Today's soft payroll report demonstrates that the labor market is simmering, not boiling, which should bolster the case for the Fed to remain on hold at the October meeting," said Jeff Schulze, head investment strategist at the Franklin Templeton Institute.
After the nonfarm payrolls report, traders now see about a 22-percent chance of a rate hike at the Fed's Oct. 27-28 meeting, down from about 64 percent a week ago, according to CME FedWatch.
On the corporate front, Nike tumbled about 3.6 percent after fiscal first-quarter revenue of 11.21 billion dollars missed estimates, down 4 percent from a year earlier, and the company forecasted full-year revenue to fall by high single digits while announcing job cuts. Teradyne jumped 8 percent amid strong chip-testing demand and upbeat semiconductor sector outlook.
Tesla shares gained 4.65 percent despite a 2 percent drop in third-quarter deliveries. Nvidia, AMD, CrowdStrike and Palo Alto Networks all closed at all-time highs, while Seagate and Western Digital tumbled on a report of increased hard-disk-drive supply from Toshiba. ■

Former German Chancellor Gerhard Schröder, a longtime associate of Russian President Vladimir Putin whom Moscow has repeatedly promoted as a potential interlocutor with Europe over Ukraine, has joined the supervisory board of a Russian supermarket operator as the Kremlin tightens pressure on European businesses still operating in Russia.
Schröder, 82, has been appointed to the supervisory board of Hyperglobus, which operates the Russian Globus supermarket chain, and will help guide the company’s strategic development, according to Russian business outlet RBC. Hyperglobus confirmed the appointment to German media on Friday.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The appointment gives Schröder a new corporate role in Russia months after Putin publicly singled him out as his preferred European interlocutor for negotiations over Ukraine and a future European security order – a suggestion European officials firmly rejected.
In May, Putin said that of European political figures, he would personally prefer to deal with Schröder. EU foreign ministers responded that Moscow would not decide who speaks for Europe, while EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas stressed that the bloc stood with Ukraine and would choose its own representatives.
Kyiv Post reported at the time that Berlin was also skeptical of Putin’s proposal, citing Schröder’s longstanding Kremlin ties and his refusal to break decisively with Moscow following Russia’s full-scale invasion.
41 Ukrainians Return From Russian Occupation via Volyn, Including 9 children
The Kremlin’s interest did not end there. Schröder traveled to Moscow again in June, where he was spotted at a central Moscow hotel, and the Kremlin subsequently confirmed that Putin had met with him privately without disclosing what was discussed.
The repeated elevation of Schröder as a potential channel to Europe fits a broader Russian effort to cultivate Western politicians and public figures who favor continued dialogue with Moscow.
Schröder’s new Russian role lands at a politically charged moment: Moscow is simultaneously arguing for renewed economic engagement through figures close to the Kremlin while taking control of assets belonging to major European companies.
‘Economic ties’ with Russia
According to RBC, Schröder said maintaining economic relations with Russia was particularly important during periods of crisis.
“It is exactly in these crisis times that these ties are especially important: they allow [us] to hear each other and look for ways forward,” the former chancellor was quoted as saying.
He reportedly singled out the food sector as a fundamental field of economic cooperation.
Hyperglobus owner Thomas Bruch said Schröder was brought onto the supervisory board because of his extensive experience in Russian political and economic affairs and could help the company maintain what Bruch described as a “dialogue-oriented approach.”
The Russian business was separated from Germany’s Globus Holding in 2025 and is now owned by Bruch, the former head of Globus, although its 22 stores across eight Russian regions continue operating under the Globus name. The German parent company says the Russian operation is now legally and operationally independent.
Moscow seizes European businesses while Schröder calls for ties
Schröder’s appeal for continued economic engagement comes amid an intensifying Kremlin campaign against European corporate assets.
Just four days before news of his appointment emerged, Moscow placed the Russian assets of German retailer Metro under temporary state administration. Russia has also moved against assets linked to Auchan and Nestlé as relations with the EU deteriorate further.
Reuters reported this week that 135 foreign-affiliated companies, primarily European, have been subjected to similar Russian measures since the full-scale war began. A Russian government source, discussing the widening corporate crackdown, summed up Moscow’s message to European firms with the words: “Let them be scared.”
That contrast is striking: while Moscow is confiscating or placing European-owned businesses under state control, one of Putin’s best-connected former Western political allies is urging companies to preserve commercial links with Russia.
Schröder’s relationship with Moscow stretches back decades. He served as Germany’s chancellor from 1998 to 2005 and developed a close personal relationship with Putin while in office.
After leaving government, he took senior positions connected to Russian state-controlled energy interests and became closely associated with the Nord Stream pipeline project, which deepened Germany’s dependence on Russian gas.
His Russian ties became particularly controversial after Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Schröder stepped down from the board of Russian oil giant Rosneft that year and declined a proposed Gazprom position, but he did not sever his relationship with Putin.
The former chancellor has continued to visit Russia and advocate maintaining channels with Moscow even as Germany and other European states have sought to reduce the economic leverage Russia accumulated during the years when Schröder championed closer energy ties.

watch carsten höller turn art-world encounters into surreal games for a giant polaroid
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
23:15:22 UTC
08:15:22 KST

watch carsten höller turn art-world encounters into surreal games for a giant polaroid
the world's largest instant camera travels across europe as artists and friends submit themselves to carsten höller’s games.
games as a way of seeing
‘I would prefer not to be in this film,‘ Carsten Höller says. Too late. Over the course of a year and a half, the artist is followed from Venice to London, Arles and the Fondation Beyeler near Basel, joined along the way by Hans Ulrich Obrist, Jürgen Teller, Maja Hoffmann, India Mahdavi, Bas Smets and an unusually cumbersome traveling companion: the Polaroid 20×24, the world’s largest instant camera.
The resulting 20-minute documentary, released by the Polaroid Foundation as The Carsten Höller Episode of The 20×24 Project. The film offers a loose and funny glimpse into the artist’s world through the games collected in his Book of Games. People pull hair, walk, pose and submit themselves to small experiments whose rules are often simple enough to sound almost inconsequential. What Höller is interested in is what happens once somebody agrees to play.
the world’s largest instant camera joins the trip
The camera travels with him through a circuit familiar to those in the art world. Games take place at Palazzo Diedo in Venice, London’s Institute of Contemporary Arts, Rencontres d’Arles and Fondation Beyeler in Riehen. Obrist, Teller, Hoffmann, artist and musician Casey Spooner, Mahdavi and Smets drift in and out. Rather than conventional interviews, the games become a way of approaching them. People have something to do, a rule to follow or another person to respond to, and the camera watches what changes.
At the center of all this is the enormous Polaroid 20×24. Its photographs measure roughly 20 by 24 inches, turning the familiar immediacy of an instant photograph into something closer to an event. The project leaves behind a growing collection of portraits alongside the moving image footage, and fixes individual moments from Höller’s experiments at a scale that feels almost absurd for something normally associated with a photograph developing in your hand.
inside höller’s world of birds, food and experiments
The journey eventually becomes more personal. In Stockholm, Carsten Höller brings the crew home, where around seventy birds live in his aviary, before heading to the roof of Moderna Museet and to Brutalisten, the concept restaurant he founded around food prepared from a single principal ingredient. Elsewhere, the group heads into the Camargue, France, on what the film describes as a ‘sad bird’-watching expedition.
Games have occupied Höller for decades, often as a way of disturbing familiar patterns of behavior and perception. Book of Games, published in 2024, gathers those experiments into instructions that anyone can follow. Some are social, some psychological and some intentionally ridiculous. Höller speaks in the film about removing the middle ground between opposing states, especially joy and fear, to leave players somewhere closer to either end.
what happens when people agree to play
There isn’t much separation between portrait, interview, experiment and joke. A photograph becomes evidence that something happened, while the game creates the conditions for it to happen in the first place. And despite Höller’s stated reluctance to appear, the accumulating footage gradually becomes a portrait of him too: his friends, his birds, his recurring questions and the elaborate situations he keeps inventing to see what people might do next.

project: The Carsten Höller Episode of The 20×24 Project
artist: Carsten Höller | @carsten.holler
presented by: The Polaroid Foundation | @polaroid_foundation
date: October 2nd, 2026

Scientists &quot;edited&quot; a gene and halved &quot;bad&quot; cholesterol – the effect has lasted for a year already
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
02:14:13 EEST
08:14:13 KST

Scientists "edited" a gene and halved "bad" cholesterol – the effect has lasted for a year already
Kyiv • UNN
A single treatment with CTX310 reduced LDL cholesterol by 52.5% in 15 patients. The experimental effect persisted for at least a year.
A single administration of the experimental gene therapy CTX310 reduced levels of “bad” cholesterol by approximately half, with the effect lasting for at least a year. The results of the technology’s first trial in humans were published in the New England Journal of Medicine, UNN writes.
Details
The therapy uses CRISPR-Cas9 gene-editing technology. Following a single intravenous administration, it reaches liver cells and switches off the ANGPTL3 gene, which is involved in regulating blood fat levels.
The study involved 15 patients with lipid metabolism disorders who had responded insufficiently to drug treatment. After 12 months, patients who received the highest dose of CTX310 had, on average, LDL cholesterol levels that remained 52.5% lower and triglyceride levels that were 47.8% lower.
One administration — an effect lasting at least a year
According to Cleveland Clinic cardiologist and one of the study’s authors, Luke Laffin, the duration of the effect proved impressive. During the year of observation, the researchers also recorded no serious adverse events associated with CTX310.
If the effectiveness and safety of this approach are confirmed by larger studies, gene editing could potentially become a fundamentally new way to combat high cholesterol — instead of taking medication continuously, the gene that affects lipid levels is altered after a single administration of the therapy.
At the same time, CTX310 remains an experimental treatment. This is an early-phase clinical trial involving only 15 people, so researchers still need to confirm its long-term safety and effectiveness in a much larger number of patients. The trial participants are planned to be monitored for another 15 years.

Archaeologists found traces of a railroad workers’ camp who built a major terminal in the United States more than 100 years ago
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher

Archaeologists found traces of a railroad workers’ camp who built a major terminal in the United States more than 100 years ago
Kyiv • UNN
In Iowa, archaeologists discovered a camp for workers who built the Milwaukee Railroad terminal in 1916–1918. A museum now operates on the site.
Archaeologists in the U.S. state of Iowa have uncovered traces of a workers’ camp where, more than 100 years ago, people who built a large railway complex lived. The discovery was made on the grounds of the present-day Sioux City Railroad Museum, Siouxland Public Media reports, writes UNN.
Details
The excavation is being conducted by a team led by Michael Batzinger of the University of Iowa’s State Archaeology Office. According to preliminary data, the camp was used by workers who built the Milwaukee railroad workshop terminal in 1916–1918.
After construction was completed, the complex became an important center for repairing and servicing railway transport. It handled trains operated by the Chicago, Milwaukee, St. Paul and Pacific Railroad.
Hundreds of people worked here during the war years
The complex gained particular importance during World War II. At that time, more than 500 people worked in the repair shops and the depot, which had capacity for 30 locomotives.
In the 1950s, railways began switching en masse from steam locomotives to diesel locomotives, causing the old repair facilities to gradually lose their importance.
In 1995, the site was acquired by the Sioux City Railroad Historical Association. The former industrial complex was later turned into a museum, and archaeologists are now studying traces of the people who took part in its construction more than a century ago.

Historic interception – a Ukrainian Mirage shot down a Russian &quot;Banderol&quot; for the first time with cannon fire
Ukraine

2026-10-03
02:00:02 EEST
08:00:02 KST

Historic interception – a Ukrainian Mirage shot down a Russian "Banderol" for the first time with cannon fire
Kyiv • UNN
A Ukrainian Mirage 2000-5F destroyed an S8000 "Banderol" missile using fire from a 30 mm DEFA 554 cannon. This made it possible to conserve a scarce air-to-air missile.
A Ukrainian Mirage 2000-5F has destroyed a Russian S8000 “Banderol” small cruise missile for the first time, using its onboard aircraft cannon. The first known instance of such an interception was reported by the French Aid to Europe project, UNN writes.
Details
To destroy the target, the fighter used not an air-to-air missile, but one of its 30 mm DEFA 554 automatic cannons. The circumstances of the interception, its location, and the name of the Ukrainian pilot have not been disclosed.
The distinctive feature of such an interception is the need to approach the target at close range. The “Banderol” is a jet-powered cruise missile with a maximum speed of 620–650 km/h.
The Mirage saved a scarce missile
The Mirage 2000-5F is equipped with 2 built-in 30 mm DEFA 554 cannons. Each has an ammunition capacity of 125 rounds, and its rate of fire can reach 1,800 rounds per minute.
Using the cannon also makes it possible to preserve the significantly more expensive and scarce air-to-air missiles that Ukrainian aviation uses to intercept airborne targets.
France transferred Mirage 2000-5F fighter jets to Ukraine in 2025 from its own Air and Space Force. The Russian S8000 “Banderol” can travel up to 500 km and carries a warhead weighing more than 100 kg.

How do I know my child is ready to leave the house on their own?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
23:00:00 UTC
08:00:00 KST

How do I know my child is ready to leave the house on their own?
By the time children are around 12 years old, many will begin to ask if they can go out to the local park, playground or shops to spend time with their friends without adult supervision.
This may happen more often during the school holiday period. They might say:
All of my friends are going. Can I hang out with them?
When a child first asks this question, it can be difficult for parents to judge whether their child is ready. Parents might want experts to give them a specific age recommendation, but children develop at their own pace and readiness varies.
This means there is no single right age when children are ready to spend time with friends, out of the house, unsupervised.
As the parent of three children, I've faced this situation myself.
So how do you know when it's okay to let your child go out on their own?
The importance of independence
Children need opportunities for independent activities to build wellbeing.
The freedom to go out with friends without adult supervision gives children the chance to explore, make choices and navigate unexpected challenges. It allows them to develop their autonomy, confidence and resilience.
It can also help kids get more active. Adventurous outdoor activities with friends, such as bike riding, allow children to learn how to cope with potentially risky situations and uncertainty, which may reduce their chances of developing anxiety.
Research on children whose parents allowed them to travel and play in their neighbourhoods also found it may help them cultivate friendships and create a sense of community.
What are the main concerns?
While many parents and carers acknowledge the benefits of letting their child have more independence, they may still feel nervous about the potential risks that come with it.
A 2019 New Zealand survey asked more than 2,000 parents about their attitudes towards risky play and children being out on their own, and the barriers that prevented them from allowing their children to be more independent.
The two biggest concerns were road safety (increased risks of traffic accidents) and "stranger danger" (children potentially having encounters with harmful adults).
So, with these concerns in mind, what are some things you can do to see if your child is ready?
Have a conversation
If your child asks to be out alone, you might start by asking them:
What makes you feel ready to be out on your own?
Your child's answer may give you a clearer idea of whether they're ready or not.
I've stayed at home alone before. I'm responsible. I think you should trust me enough to be able to do this on my own.
Evaluate their readiness
There are a number of things to consider when deciding if your child is capable.
Loading...
First, is your child aware of their surroundings? Do they notice potential hazards? For instance, would they notice if a storm was approaching and they needed to seek shelter?
Second, does your child have good judgement? Would they think clearly if they were faced with an unexpected problem, such as getting a flat bike tyre?
Third, is your child reliable? Do they follow instructions? Can they be trusted to return home at an agreed-upon time?
Agree on some rules
If you think your child is ready, it's important to set ground rules for when they're out. This might include your child agreeing to stay within a particular area, being home by a certain time, and communicating if they are going to be late. You might also ask them to stay with their friends the entire time they're out.
Start closer to home
For many families, it helps to begin with an activity closer to home, such as walking to the park and back. As trust and confidence build for both of you, your child can then be allowed out longer and further away.
It's also good to have a plan with your child about what to do if something goes wrong, they want your help or they need to contact you.
While it can feel daunting initially, independent time with friends without parent supervision helps your child to grow, develop and thrive.
This piece first appeared on The Conversation.

How one Australian state's corruption inquiry shook a major political party
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
22:59:00 UTC
07:59:00 KST

In brief
- NSW ICAC’s Operation Rosny examined alleged links between Liberal Party figures and developer Jean Nassif over donations and influence.
- The high-profile inquiry exposed damaging allegations ahead of the state election and renewed scrutiny of party fundraising.
Phone calls packed with colourful language, meetings at Nobu, Fijian hideouts, all-day drinks at London pubs, promises of millions of dollars.
It was enough to fill out 38 sitting days as the NSW Independent Commission Against Corruption (ICAC) sliced and diced a Liberal Party corruption scandal.
At the heart of the probe, the ICAC examined alleged collusion between fugitive property developer Jean Nassif and party powerbrokers including two brothers of former NSW premier Dominic Perrottet.
Jean-Claude Perrottet, Charles Perrottet and his wife Anita Perrottet endured days of grilling in the witness box.
In an inquiry dubbed Operation Rosny, the watchdog investigated alleged kickbacks involving Nassif and his company, Toplace, between 2020 and 2023.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
Political donations from developers have been banned in NSW since 2009, yet the ICAC's widening net led to mentions of other powerful Liberals, including federal Opposition Leader Angus Taylor.
Former ICAC assistant commissioner and retired Supreme Court judge Anthony Whealy rates Rosny one of the most impactful investigations in the body's almost 40-year history.
"You can already rank it as a very consequential inquiry," he told the Australian Associated Press (AAP) news agency.
"That is because it's taking quite a broad swipe into the machinations of party politics, the relationships between developers and politicians and where those intersections can go seriously wrong."
The inquiry began with a bang in July when counsel assisting Peggy Dwyer launched her opening statement with the adage, "Money in politics, as in other spheres of life, has the potential to corrupt."
It ushered in weeks of forensic accounting and questions over embarrassing text exchanges about surveillance of mayors, sham contracts and fake arrangements spanning Beirut, London and Cessnock.
Twenty witnesses were called, including the bombastic Nassif, who dialled in virtually from his bedroom in Beirut, wrapping up on Tuesday.
Their memories — from a demure Jean-Claude Perrottet and emotional senior Liberal MP Damien Tudehope to brash lobbyist Jeremy Greenwood and a befuddled Anita Perrottet — were put to the test on the stand.
In their responses, revelations were unearthed, and admissions recorded that have damaged the Liberal Party as it heads to a state election in March.
"In terms of the Academy Awards, some would be given out for splendid attempts to shy away from the truth without very much success," Whealy says.
"Overall, the spectacle we saw was rather amusing, but then it wasn't amusing at all; it was really quite serious."
He says a number of witnesses have tarnished their reputations by not being open and honest with the commission.
Central to the probe was how the Reformers, a conservative Christian sub-faction within the Liberal Party, allegedly circumvented donation caps by setting up schemes to hide the money trail.
Taylor, who is not under investigation by the corruption watchdog, has denied making pledges to the ultra-conservative faction.
"I want to shake down Angus for 10K," the now sacked head of Catholic Schools NSW, Dallas McInerney, wrote in a message aired at the inquiry on Tuesday.
The opposition leader said "no payment was made" when questioned about a $15,000 "injection" and monthly $3000 donations to the Reformers.
Former NSW premier Nick Greiner doesn't want to wade into how Operation Rosny will affect the party whose federal executive he served until March this year.
But he credits the creation of ICAC in 1989, during his tenure as premier, as one of his most important contributions to keeping politics accountable.
"ICAC is now close to 40 years old, so in a broad sense it's been successful — and the fact that it's been copied everywhere is a fair indication of that," he says.
Its public airing of dirty laundry, which played a role in Greiner's own political demise, later brought down popular Liberal premier Gladys Berejiklian and Labor heavyweight Eddie Obeid.
Yet it has not been immune from criticism.
Greiner says the commission's sometimes spectacular binge-watching sessions were not all necessary.
"There's room for more common sense and discretion," he insists.
But he reserves sterner ire for how long it often takes the ICAC to establish a probe and make corruption findings, and then whether it recommends prosecutions.
The watchdog aims to have a report tabled in parliament within 180 days of receiving final submissions but in practice it takes much longer.
"Clearly the time frames are absolutely absurd," Greiner says.
"It cannot take years and years when you've got all the powers that ICAC has ... My general impression is it's way too slow."
Rosny was sparked when state Liberal MP Ray Williams used parliamentary privilege in 2022 to claim powerbrokers in his party were engaged in branch-stacking and improper local council dealings.
Whealy says the watchdog's invaluable oversight role should reassure the public that no matter how corrupt political parties might appear, there is always a comeuppance.
"There are some rotten apples around and (the ICAC) reinforces that notion but it doesn't destroy trust altogether in the political system," he says.
"It's a comfort to the community ... that there's a vigilant oversight body doing its job properly."

Christa Pike unconscious after failed execution — attorneys
October 3, 2026
Christa Pike was unconscious and on a ventilator in a Nashville hospital in the hours after her bungled execution attempt in Tennessee, her attorneys said in a court filing on Friday.
Pike, who was sentenced to death for the 1995 murder of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, was audibly snoring after she was injected with two doses of lethal injection on Wednesday.
The court filing is the first account of what Pike went through in the hours after the botched execution attempt.
Pike's attorneys said they believed problems with the IV lines caused the lethal drug, called pentobarbital, to flow into her body instead of her bloodstream.
"Apparently at no point did any member of the execution team realize that the IV lines were not correctly placed or that the veins had blown and that the pentobarbital was, in whole or in part, entering Ms. Pike's body," they wrote in the court filing.
Instead of "remedying this failure," they prepared and administered a second dose of pentobarbital, her lawyers said.
Pike believed to be first person to survive administration of lethal drugs
There are now questions about what happens next and whether the state can attempt to execute Pike again given her medical state.
Tennessee Governor Bill Lee, a Republican, temporarily paused the state execution on Thursday, saying there would be a "comprehensive, third-party review" of the case.
Pike, who is 50 years old, was set to become the first woman executed in Tennessee in 200 years.
She is believed to be the first person to survive after being injected with lethal doses of execution drugs in the modern era of the death penalty, according to the Death Penalty Information Center.

Alamein Africa Forum opens in Egypt with 1,500 participants
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
22:50:52 UTC
07:50:52 KST

Hussien Elkabany, Mohammad Sio
03 October 2026•Update: 03 October 2026
The Alamein Africa Forum opened on Friday in the northern Egyptian city of New Alamein, bringing together 1,500 officials, business leaders, investors and representatives of financial institutions from Africa.
The three-day forum includes three high-level conferences focused on economic development and continental integration, according to a statement.
Egyptian Prime Minister Mostafa Madbouly said at the welcoming session of the inaugural forum that Africa is at an “important moment” that offers significant opportunities for economic transformation and overcoming development challenges.  
He said the continent has vast natural resources, a large market, one of the world’s youngest populations and major opportunities in manufacturing, energy, agriculture, technology, services and the digital economy.
Africa, however, faces challenges related to securing financing, developing infrastructure, high cost of capital, strengthening links between markets and removing barriers that continue to restrict intra-African trade and investment, he said.
Madbouly said the forum is taking place at a time of rapidly accelerating economic and technological changes globally, with supply chains and centers of production, trade and investment being reshaped.
“These transformations require everyone to look at Africa not only as a continent facing development challenges, but also as one that offers real opportunities and has the ability to become an active part of the new global economy,” he said.
The forum's agenda includes trade, food security, energy, infrastructure, financing, digital transformation, artificial intelligence and critical minerals.
Discussions are also aimed at turning development priorities into implementable projects and investments, while boosting intra-African trade.
Egyptian Planning Minister Ahmed Rostom said Africa’s economy is estimated at around $3.6 trillion.
Despite accounting for about one-fifth of the world’s population, he said, Africa’s share of global trade stands at only around 1.5%, while foreign direct investment flows remain limited compared with the continent’s potential.
New Alamein will host a summit on Saturday of the founding states of the African Union Development Agency, or AUDA-NEPAD, the official technical development body of the AU.
Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi will chair the meet, with broad participation by African leaders and officials, his office said.
The 8th Mid-Year Coordination Meeting of the African Union, meanwhile, is scheduled for Sunday.
The events are part of Egypt’s efforts to strengthen African economic integration, attract investment and mobilize financing for development projects across the continent.
The African Union approved holding the Alamein-Africa Forum every two years in New Alamein at its February 2026 summit.
The forum is co-organized by Egypt, the African Export-Import Bank, or Afreximbank and AUDA-NEPAD.

Speaking on Friday from a hospital bed in Abu Dhabi via video call with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Machchhar said that he knew the aircraft was going down as he lay bleeding on the floor.
“I had suffered so many injuries that I had collapsed. At that time, I could feel that the aircraft was going down. I knew this was the last push, that the door was right there,” he said in a nearly 10-minute video released on the prime minister’s social media channels.
He added: “I was being hit even then, but I just opened the door and everyone came in.”
Machchhar, who has 17 years of aviation experience, including 11 as a captain, said that experience helped him grasp what was happening even while wounded.
He told Modi he had recited a Hindu devotional prayer during the ordeal.
“I know God himself saved me,” he said, in an emotional exchange with Modi, who is from the same home state of Gujarat.
Modi praised Machchhar’s bravery, saying his presence of mind had saved lives and the reputation of Indian pilots.
Machchhar said he allowed passengers and crew to overpower the co-pilot and let a second pair of Flydubai pilots take control and land the plane in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia.
The Flydubai flight was carrying 174 people as it briefly plunged around 17,000 feet (5,180 metres) before it was brought back under control.
UAE presidential adviser Anwar Gargash has called the incident a “terrorist act”, while Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said the co-pilot had undergone “Islamist radical indoctrination” and appeared “suicidal”.
US President Donald Trump has warned that Iran would be “hit very hard” if found to be linked to the attack.
The United Arab Emirates has said it will launch an investigation into the incident.

Zelensky: Putin’s Goal Is Not Donbas but All of Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
22:49:09 UTC
07:49:09 KST

President Volodymyr Zelensky warned that Russian President Vladimir Putin’s latest rhetoric shows the Kremlin’s ambitions extend far beyond Donbas, as Moscow seeks control over all of Ukraine and the restoration of Soviet-era influence across Russia’s neighborhood.
Speaking remotely at the fifth annual Helsinki Security Forum on Friday, Zelensky cited Putin’s own rhetoric to challenge European skeptics and the idea of neutral mediation.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“So his goal is not the east of Ukraine. It is not Donbas. His aim is to occupy our entire state,” Zelensky said.
Pointing to remarks Putin made at Russia’s Valdai Forum a day earlier, the president argued that the Kremlin’s objectives extend far beyond eastern Ukraine.
“An independent Ukraine, a strong Ukraine, is a big problem for Putin,” Zelensky said.
He highlighted Putin’s assertion that Ukraine cannot exist independently and that other states are supposedly using Ukrainians to wage war against Russia.
“There were important signals yesterday,” he said. “I don’t think he said it accidentally: ‘Ukraine is not a state, and it is not an independent state.’”
Zelensky linked Putin’s latest rhetoric directly to the Russian leader’s long-running fixation on the collapse of the Soviet Union.
He recalled Putin’s infamous 2005 declaration that the fall of the Soviet Union was the greatest geopolitical catastrophe of the 20th century, contrasting that political grievance with the actual human tragedies of the era.
Sandu: Russia Will Remain Major Threat to Europe Even After Ukraine War Ends
“He did not speak about the First World War as a tragedy. He did not recognize the Second World War as [the greatest tragedy]. He did not mention other wars,” Zelensky said.
“He could have mentioned Afghanistan and other things, or the Chornobyl disaster – a horrible disaster. He mentioned none of the things that were connected to human lives.”
Instead, Zelensky argued, Putin focused entirely on the loss of Soviet power.
“Therefore, his goal is obvious: to bring it all back, to bring the USSR back.”
“The fact that he was saying this again yesterday serves as yet another indication of what he wants – of his attitude toward peace, whether he wants the war to end and, even if he does, at what price.”
Zelensky argued that Moscow seeks to recreate not necessarily the Soviet Union in its former institutional form, but the sphere of influence the Kremlin once exercised across neighboring states.
“Undoubtedly, this is about bringing back the influence of the USSR – or Russia’s influence – but making it comparable with the influence the former USSR once had,” he said.
“He has total influence over Belarus. But I am sure that he wants all of that back.”
Warning for the Baltic states and Russia’s neighbors
Zelensky warned that the implications extend beyond Ukraine.
If Putin’s ambition is to restore Moscow’s former regional dominance, he argued, the Baltic states and other countries sharing borders with Russia would also face pressure.
“Therefore, these challenges would also concern the Baltic states and countries with which Russia shares borders,” Zelensky said.
He urged those in Europe who remain skeptical about the scale of Russia’s ambitions to look directly at Putin’s own words.
“And nobody stops him in these messages,” Zelensky said. “And that is weakness of the world.”
Asked about Ukraine’s biggest EU obstacle, Zelensky answers: ‘Putin’
Zelensky was also asked what he considers the greatest obstacle facing Ukraine as it pursues European Union membership while simultaneously fighting Russia’s full-scale war.
His answer was one word:
“Putin.”
“He really doesn’t want that to happen,” Zelensky said.
“And it’s not about his opinion, but what he’s doing for this not to happen – against the development of our state, against the geopolitical choice of the people.”
“When we are talking about what the EU means for Ukraine, it is a victory over Russia – even a victory over Putin,” he said.
“Because the EU is the choice of our people.”
Security guarantees, he added, are critical because they protect Ukraine’s ability to follow the geopolitical course chosen by its citizens.
“And therefore it is important to have security guarantees, because these guarantees protect the path that the people of Ukraine have chosen.”
The Helsinki Security Forum is being held in the Finnish capital from Oct. 2–4 under the theme “Layers of Security.” The fifth annual gathering brings together policymakers and experts to discuss European defense, technological sovereignty, transatlantic relations, energy security, nuclear deterrence and Russia’s role in European security.
‘You cannot build total defense’ by buying weapons
Zelensky also used the forum to lay out lessons Ukraine has learned after years of defending itself against Russia.
A country seeking genuine security must first develop strength from within, he said, beginning with its military.
“The main guarantee for Ukraine is the army of our state.”
But an experienced army alone is not sufficient, Zelensky argued.
He emphasized the importance of a technologically advanced force, a domestic military-technology sector and defense production capable of rapidly adapting to battlefield requirements.
Energy resilience is another critical component, he said, particularly decentralization of infrastructure vulnerable to attack.
Ukraine shifts from weapons recipient to security partner
The second layer of security, Zelensky said, is international cooperation.
He thanked the EU, European countries and the US for financial, technological and military assistance since the outbreak of the war.
Ukraine received weapons it previously lacked, including NATO-standard systems, he noted, but its relationship with partners is increasingly becoming a two-way exchange.
Ukraine is now sharing knowledge gained through years of high-intensity warfare.
Zelensky highlighted a recent drone cooperation agreement with Finland as an example.
“It’s not about just selling or buying drones or missiles,” he said.
“It’s about sharing your security experience throughout the duration of this agreement.”
Ukraine is willing to share that knowledge with countries that supported it, Zelensky said, pointing to the trust built between Kyiv and Helsinki.
The third layer is collective security, particularly NATO.
Zelensky congratulated Finland on securing guarantees through membership in both the European Union and NATO.
“These are allies in economy, allies in technology, and allies in security,” he said.
“This is of utmost importance, and this is what Ukraine is counting on.”

Up to 80 punctures and mobility after triggering a mine — how the Ukrainian military quad bike was further reinforced

The ATC NORD 1000 was reinforced with steel protection, 10-ply tires, and a run-flat system. The version costs UAH 415,000.
The Ukrainian military all-terrain vehicle ATC NORD 1000 has received an updated special configuration developed with consideration for experience gained from its use at the front. The vehicle has been reinforced to remain operational after sustaining damage, protected from below, and adapted for evacuation and logistical tasks, Defense Express reports, according to UNN.
Details
One of the main features is the wheel survivability system. The ATC NORD 1000 is equipped with steel rims, 10-ply tires, and a system that allows it to continue moving even after losing tire pressure.
According to tests conducted by the manufacturer GROUND FORCE, the wheel can withstand up to 70–80 punctures by metal objects and an impact equivalent to the detonation of an antipersonnel mine containing 50 g of TNT equivalent.
Protected against mines and fiber-optic cables
Steel protection made of Hardox 500 has been installed under the floor, engine, variator, and in the crew footwell area. According to the manufacturer, it was tested with charges of up to 200 g of TNT equivalent.
The all-terrain vehicle has also received a protective bar with a mesh screen against fiber-optic cables, branches, and stones; a reinforced system for transporting cargo and evacuating the wounded; as well as a “Night” mode that switches off the exterior lighting, brake lights, and instrument illumination with a single button.
The ATC NORD 1000 is equipped with a 976 cm³ engine producing 92 hp, has 310 mm of ground clearance, and a winch with a pulling capacity of 1,500 kg. The stated cost of the version with 10-ply tires and their special filler is UAH 415,000.

'Every fallen hero will be found' — Kyiv to speed up identification of fallen Ukrainians, Budanov says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
22:37:44 UTC
07:37:44 KST

'Every fallen hero will be found' — Kyiv to speed up identification of fallen Ukrainians, Budanov says
Ukraine is developing a plan to accelerate the process of identifying the bodies and remains of deceased Ukrainians repatriated from Russia, Presidential Office Head Kyrylo Budanov said on Oct. 2.
Repatriation operations are one of the few areas of continued humanitarian cooperation between Kyiv and Moscow. Ukraine regularly repatriates fallen soldiers and civilians from Russian territory, with return efforts increasing after peace talks resumed in early 2025.
Over 26,000 bodies and remains of Ukrainians have now been returned, according to Budanov. But of those tens of thousands, "a significant portion" remain unidentified.
"Why is the identification process so slow, and why are families forced to live in a state of uncertainty for months and years?" Budanov said.
The problem was discussed at an Oct. 2 meeting, chaired by Budanov, between the Families of Fallen Defenders of Ukraine and the Coordinating Council on the Protection of the Rights of War Veterans and Family Members. Participants developed an action plan to accelerate the process of identifying repatriated bodies.
An interagency organization will be established to review the work of forensic departments in various regions of Ukraine and facilitate additional international resources for DNA analysis, Budanov said. The government, in turn, will "adopt all necessary legal and regulatory decisions" in order to speed up identification procedures.
"I am convinced that bureaucratic delays and violations of regulations in the forensic examination system are unacceptable," Budanov said.
Budanov did not specify how many bodies remain unidentified.
read also
Bodies repatriated from Russia can present serious challenges to the forensic examiners and medical personnel tasked with identifying the deceased. These remains are often returned months or years after death, complicating autopsies. Sometimes, only a bone or a finger is returned.
The vast number of Ukrainian war dead has also put a strain on staff and facilities. Following a repatriation event, which occurs roughly once a month, already overwhelmed morgues may be flooded with hundreds of bodies.
The most recent repatriation operation was recorded on Sept. 17, with Ukraine returning the bodies of 252 Ukrainians from Russia.
While Ukraine regularly reports the number of repatriated bodies it receives from Russia, it does not publish data on the remains of Russian soldiers returned to Moscow.
Budanov said that accelerating the identification process was "a matter of state responsibility" for Ukraine.
"Families must receive information about the fate of their loved ones as soon as possible," he said. "Every fallen hero will be found and properly honored."

LOS ANGELES, Oct. 2 (Xinhua) -- Google launched a prototype satellite into orbit on Thursday to evaluate how its Tensor Processing Units (TPUs) operate in space.
The prototype satellite, carrying four Google TPUs, was launched aboard SpaceX's Transporter-18 rideshare mission.
Google said its team has confirmed contact with the satellite and it is operating as expected.
Google said the launch is the first step of its Project Suncatcher, a long-term research project conducted in partnership with Planet Labs PBC to explore whether scalable machine learning infrastructure could eventually be hosted in space.
Over the coming weeks, Google will collect in-orbit data on how its TPUs handle the physical stress, radiation and thermal extremes of space. The company will use it to refine its future designs.
In low Earth orbit, satellites can access near-constant sunlight, generating up to eight times more solar power than on Earth, according to Google.
In the future, multiple satellite constellations could potentially be linked together, enabling them to handle larger AI workloads in orbit, the company said. ■

Details

Ukraine is also facing export problems. Due to Russian strikes on port infrastructure and difficulties shipping oil to India, sunflower processing in Ukraine could decline by approximately half from October to March — from the usual level of around 600,000 tonnes per month.

Unknown Publisher

Glaciers are disappearing before our very eyes – scientists warn of “catastrophic decades” ahead for the Alps
Kyiv • UNN
In the first 8 months of 2026, Swiss glaciers lost 6.5% of their mass. By the end of the century, they could almost disappear without emissions reductions.
Swiss glaciers have lost almost a fifth of their mass over the past five years and could practically disappear by the end of the century. LRT reports on the rapid changes in the Alps, citing a new report, writes UNN.
Details
In just the first eight months of 2026, Swiss glaciers lost 6.5% of their mass. Scientists estimate that more than 2 trillion liters of water melted away—more than four times the amount of fresh water consumed by Swiss households in a year.
Ice thickness decreased by 2.5–4 meters in some areas in this year alone. Researchers emphasize that the scale of the changes, which just a few years ago seemed like a future climate scenario, has become a reality.
"We are living in a new world"
This year, I would say, was catastrophic. There are no other words for it. But 2022 was already catastrophic, and I am convinced that even more catastrophic years await us in the coming decades
Scientists are recording not only the melting of glaciers but also their destruction from within. Cavities are forming in the ice mass, causing glaciers to break down faster and potentially collapse, posing a danger to surrounding areas.
At the current rate of developments, Switzerland's glaciers could almost completely disappear by the end of the 21st century. At the same time, according to researchers' estimates, stringent measures to reduce emissions and combat climate change could still preserve around 30–40% of the glaciers.
