Pope calls on artists to unite against AI
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
22:21:41 UTC
07:21:41 KST

Pope calls on artists to unite against AI
Pope Leo XIV has called on artists to join forces to protect human creativity in the age of AI.
Speaking to cultural figures at the Vatican on Friday, the Pope said the Catholic Church hopes to renew its alliance with them to safeguard “what is human.”
“We live in the age of search engines that offer us thousands of instantaneous answers,” he said, contrasting them with art, which he described as a different kind of “search engine” that “does not proceed by indexing but by inquiry.”
He warned that one of the dangers facing modern culture is “homogenization,” arguing that art can provide a counterweight by challenging people rather than simply giving them what they expect.
”Your art… when it draws our gaze, when it compels us to pause before that which cannot be consumed, is a form of cultural and spiritual regeneration,” he said.
Turning directly to AI, the Pope said it is becoming increasingly important to distinguish human art from machine-generated works.
“The Church needs you,” he said. “Algorithms lack the spark of the human, whereas authentic culture and art preserve this spark.”
The American-born Pope has repeatedly raised concerns about AI since his election in May 2025, warning of its implications for human dignity, justice, and labor, and calling for clear ethical limits on its use. His first encyclical, published earlier this year, focused on safeguarding humanity in the age of AI and argued that human judgment and responsibility must remain paramount.
He told reporters this week that he is not in “panic mode” over AI and can still “sleep at night,” but said warnings from experts about the potential dangers should be taken seriously.
Artists and other creative professionals have increasingly pushed back against generative AI, arguing that developers have trained models on copyrighted works without permission or compensation. They have also raised concerns that AI-generated images, music, and writing could displace human creators, drive down the value of their work, and make it increasingly difficult to distinguish original art from machine-generated imitations.
Concerns over AI have intensified following a series of incidents in which self-improving models circumvented safeguards and accessed external networks without authorization. In July, OpenAI models bypassed controls designed to isolate them from the internet and compromised parts of the company’s internal infrastructure and Hugging Face’s systems. OpenAI later described the incident as a “warning shot” over the risks posed by increasingly capable systems.
Anthropic researcher Evan Hubinger said last month that he believes there is a greater than 10% chance that AI “could kill all humans” within the next decade.
Others have expressed optimism, with US President Donald Trump dismissing concerns over an AI takeover as a “hoax.” On Tuesday, he signed a deal with executives from Google, Anthropic, Meta, OpenAI, xAI, and Nvidia aimed at introducing safeguards to ensure that “their technology behaves as intended.”

Airlines are required to provide Israeli authorities with advance information about passengers and crew through Israel’s national passenger-data system. Why Carney’s economic overhaul is clashing with Canada’s unions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
22:14:34 UTC
07:14:34 KST

Why Carney’s economic overhaul is clashing with Canada’s unions
Unions say proposed changes to Canada’s labour laws could weaken workers’ right to strike.
Toronto, Canada: As Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney races to make the country less dependent on the United States, attract billions in new investment and get major projects built faster, his economic overhaul is running into resistance from a group that says it wants many of the same things: organised labour.
The latest clash, over the right to strike, comes after months of mounting pressure on Ottawa from Washington, DC.
US President Donald Trump, since taking up a second term in office last year, has imposed steep tariffs on Canadian goods and weakened trade agreements – perilous moves as Canada has historically sent close to 80 percent of its exports to its southern neighbour. He has repeatedly piled on with the tariff threats to make Canada the 51st US state.
Canada has responded with retaliatory tariffs, while a broader movement to “Buy Canadian” has taken hold. The hockey-inspired “elbows up” — meaning a readiness to defend against an opponent — has become a national rallying cry.
With trade talks stalled since August, Carney has moved with urgency to shore up the economy and invite new investments. Last month, he announced Bill C-39, known as the Building Canada Strong Act, promising to bring “speed, certainty and predictability” to investors.
Along with measures to speed up approvals for major projects, the bill would also give Ottawa clearer powers to intervene in legal strikes and lockouts in federally regulated workplaces — a provision that has put Carney on a collision course with unions.
Canada’s largest unions have come together against the changes. The largest, the Canadian Union of Public Employees (CUPE), had its national executive go as far as voting to defy the bill’s proposed limits on the right to strike if it passes Parliament without amendments.
CUPE National President Mark Hancock credited Carney’s handling of Trump and said the union’s 800,000 members, who work everywhere from hospitals to schools to municipal services, want to be part of “Team Canada”.
“But at what cost?” he said in an interview with Al Jazeera.
A fight over the right to strike
The controversy centres on Section 107 of the Canada Labour Code, which already gives the Labour Minister broad powers to step into disputes if needed to maintain “industrial peace”, end work stoppages and force the two sides into a binding arbitration.
Beginning in 2024, Ottawa used the provision eight times to intervene in disputes involving airlines, Canada’s two largest railways, three major ports and Canada Post and again during the Air Canada dispute in 2025 when flight attendants went on strike.
Unions have challenged the use of that law in court and had hoped the proposed C-39 would restrict, if not repeal, that clause while businesses wanted it strengthened.
The bill does neither. Instead, it introduces two conditions that the government would have to fulfil first before turning to Section 107.
Before stepping in, the government would have to appoint a special mediator, wait for a public report and consider whether a work stoppage is hurting the “national interest”.
Once a strike or lockout is underway, the minister could direct the Canada Industrial Relations Board to get operations running again and impose a binding process, such as arbitration.
The government says those steps put clearer guardrails around a power that already exists, and Carney has said the bill “absolutely reinforces the right to strike”, according to the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation.
Unions have rejected this defence, pointing out that the meaning of “national interest” would ultimately be decided by the minister. They also argue that the prospect of government intervention is bound to change what happens at the bargaining table.
“The political lesson that employers will draw from it is simple,” Larry Savage, a professor of labour studies at Brock University, told Al Jazeera. “Hold out long enough, emphasise the economic damage, and then Ottawa will remove the union’s leverage for you.”
Disruption, Savage said, is precisely what gives a strike its power. “Every effective strike is disruptive,” he said.
Unions say they have already seen employers expect Ottawa to intervene.
Teamsters Canada alleges the Canadian National Railway (CN) and the Canadian Pacific Kansas City (CPKC) railroad companies were counting on Ottawa to step in when they locked out thousands of workers in 2024. Section 107 was invoked within hours.
“Companies have gotten used to the idea that if there is a labour dispute, they can just wait for the government to intervene,” Christopher Monette, Teamsters Canada’s director of public affairs, told Al Jazeera.
CUPE said it saw a similar dynamic at Air Canada in August 2025. Hancock said bargaining stalled after more than 10,000 Air Canada flight attendants voted overwhelmingly to strike because the airline was “expecting the government of Canada to step in and end the strike” — an account Air Canada disputed.
Less than 12 hours after workers walked out, Ottawa invoked Section 107. Air Canada CEO Michael Rousseau later told BNN Bloomberg the airline had expected the provision to be enforced and did not expect a strike.
“That was why they didn’t have a strategy on how to deal with the strike,” Hancock said.
Building Canada faster
The fight over the right to strike is also part of a much bigger argument taking shape around Carney’s economic agenda: Who gets a say in how Canada should change, and how quickly, in the name of making itself less vulnerable to the US?
Critics accuse Carney of using the economic threat from the US to push through changes that go well beyond responding to Trump’s trade war.
New Democratic Party leader Avi Lewis has accused him of using the “fear and disorientation around the trade war to push through a series of unpopular measures that he did not run on, has no mandate for and would never get away with under normal circumstances”.
That tension was on display in Toronto just a week before C-39 was introduced. Inside Canada’s first national investment summit, hundreds of global investors met with government officials and executives as Carney pitched a country ready to build.
Outside, hundreds of protesters marched through downtown towards the summit’s opening gala under the banner “The Many vs The Money”. The rally brought together labour, Indigenous, environmental and migrant-rights groups, with signs and speeches taking aim at everything from fossil fuel and military projects to AI and the use of public money to attract private investment.
For unions, C-39 has sharpened that debate, pitting the government’s promise of greater certainty for investors against workers’ ability to exert pressure through strikes.
But Jim Stanford, an economist and director of the Vancouver-based Centre for Future Work, questions how much of an economic threat strikes actually pose.
While work stoppages can be costly for individual companies, Stanford said, “It is very, very rare that you would see a noticeable and sustained impact on GDP, employment or incomes.”
Production and transportation are often delayed rather than permanently lost, he added, with businesses catching up once work resumes.
Stanford also questioned the idea that strikes are driving away investment, noting that more than 95 percent of collective bargaining ends without a work stoppage and saying there is “no empirical evidence whatsoever” that strikes have reduced investment.
“This is more of the government giving some icing on the cake for business. It’s not that this has to happen or else our investment won’t work,” he said.
There is also an economic cost to weakening the right to strike, Stanford argued. Workers need bargaining power to win higher wages, which can support consumer spending, productivity and worker retention.
“It may seem like labour peace is a good thing, but if it means that a worker’s share of the pie shrinks, then this actually hurts the economy.”
For labour leaders, that’s where Carney’s economic push goes too far.
“Canada’s unions are part of Team Canada. We have our elbows up,” Canadian Labour Congress President Bea Bruske said in a statement. “But we can’t have our elbows up against Trump with our hands tied at the bargaining table.”
Savage said the government’s “Team Canada” rhetoric risks treating workers’ bargaining power as a national liability.
“I don’t think Canada becomes stronger by telling workers in ports or railways or airlines that their rights have to be surrendered whenever employers invoke competitiveness or the national interest,” he said.

Ukraine lost another MiG-29 and its pilot on Thursday. It needs the jets to guard its cities, and almost none are left to replace them
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
22:09:59 UTC
07:09:59 KST

- Ukraine has lost another Mikoyan MiG-29 fighter as well as its pilot
- The Ukrainian MiG fleet is slowly dwindling owing to combat losses and wear and tear
- The Ukrainian air force is acquiring new Western types to replace the MiGs and other ex-Soviet jets
Ukraine has lost another Mikoyan MiG-29 fighter and its pilot. The Thursday shoot-down extends the steady attrition of the Ukrainian air force MiG fleet, potentially drawing down the fleet to its pre-war strength.
That means Ukraine may have lost as many of the twin-engine, supersonic MiG-29s as it has received from its allies or restored from surplus stocks since February 2022.
It's an ominous milestone. The Soviet-vintage MiG-29 is no longer the Ukrainian air force's most important fighter. That honorific belongs to the air force's ex-European Lockheed Martin F-16s.
But the MiG-29 is still the air force's second most important fighter—and will remain so through 2027 as Ukraine awaits its first ex-Swedish Saab Gripens, due early next year, and French-made Dassault Rafales, due from 2028. Ukraine sorties MiG-29s for ground attack missions targeting Russian troop concentrations, strikes on Russian air defense systems, and air defense sorties over Ukrainian cities and ports.
The air force announced the loss of the MiG-29 and its pilot, Capt. Marat Mambetov, shortly after it occurred on Thursday. Mambetov, 25, was a flight commander in the 40th Tactical Aviation Brigade, known as the "Ghost of Kyiv" brigade. "Flying a MiG-29 fighter jet, [Mambetov] carried out missile and bomb strikes against Russian occupiers along one of the front-line directions," the air force stated. "During the mission, his aircraft was hit by an enemy missile. The pilot ejected, but tragically did not survive."
It's the 37th confirmed combat loss of a Ukrainian MiG-29 since Russia widened its war on Ukraine in February 2022, according to a tally by the Oryx open-source intelligence collective. Oryx has also registered damage to an additional three Ukrainian MiG-29s.
Thirty-seven write-offs, plus the likely grounding of several previously flyable MiG-29s owing to intensive wear and tear since 2022, may have reduced the Ukrainian air force's MiG-29 fleet to around three dozen active jets.
Fighter subtraction
The math is simple. The air force probably had between 30 and 35 MiG-29s in service when Russia attacked in February 2022. As losses cut into the fleet, Poland donated 14 surplus MiGs, Slovakia donated 10, and Azerbaijan reportedly donated three. Meanwhile, Ukrainian engineers tapped a global pipeline of spare parts to reactivate an estimated 20 grounded MiG-29s moldering in hangars at various Ukrainian airfields.
That's as many as 82 MiGs in and, as of Thursday, 37 out owing to Russian action—plus additional jets grounded due to airframe fatigue. The resulting active fleet should number around three dozen planes, around as many as Ukraine had on the eve of the wider war.
There aren't many more old MiGs that Ukraine could obtain to bolster the fleet. Poland still has as many as nine very tired airframes, but Kyiv and Warsaw have consistently failed to negotiate a transfer. There may yet be a few ex-Soviet MiG-29s, grounded for years or even decades, that Ukrainian engineers can restore to flightworthy status. Other than that, options are scarce.
Ukraine’s Swedish radar planes have flown inside Russian missile range for six months. None has been shot down.
Trending Now
The three dozen MiGs still in the inventory may have to last a little while alongside the few survivors of Ukraine's other Soviet-vintage warplanes, including Sukhoi Su-27s, Sukhoi Su-24s, and Sukhoi Su-25s.
Older Western types—the 80 or so F-16s European allies have pledged, about half delivered, as well as potentially a dozen or so ex-French Dassault Mirage 2000s—are steadily replacing the ex-Soviet jets. (So far, Ukraine has lost five F-16s and one Mirage.) Next year, the transformation of the Ukrainian air force from a largely Soviet-equipped force to a largely Western-equipped force will accelerate when the first of 32 Gripens arrive. Sixteen Rafales are to follow from 2028.
Barring catastrophic combat losses among Western types and assuming Ukraine can maintain and arm these new warplanes, by the end of 2027, the air force may not need its remaining MiGs and Sukhois, which by then could be very tired.
Russian missiles are steadily reducing the MiG and Sukhoi fleets, effectively forcing Ukraine to switch to new types.

- Ukraine is now sending its tanks into battle with drone escorts: they can drive into a Russian kill zone and come back alive
- Ukraine retook 240 square km north of Lyman and nobody reported it for three months

Five Great Reads: ICE 2.0, millennial motherhood, and skinny-dipping with Christine Baranski
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
22:08:31 UTC
07:08:31 KST

Hello and welcome to the weekend.
The Guardian’s range was on display this week across these five very different stories. Grab a coffee and dig in, digest, and reflect on harrowing accounts of Trump’s immigration crackdown, investigations into modern motherhood and masculinity, and for a bit of weekend fun, we leave you with some celebrity gossip.
Enjoy.
1. Inside Trump’s new immigration dragnet
At the peak of Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown, armoured vehicles occupied neighbourhoods, while masked agents violently pulled people from the streets. After officers killed two US citizens during the raids in Minneapolis, public backlash prompted Trump to try a new approach. Now, ICE arrests have hit record levels. In this series, ICE 2.0, Guardian reporters track how, despite the administration’s change of tactics, ICE is everywhere.
Notable quote: “Before, they were storming around, making a lot of noise Now, they are moving more quietly.”
The violence continues: People are arrested while pumping gas, leaving behind their empty cars. They are arrested on their way to work, or on their way home. Recently, an ICE agent shot Wilber Rafael Garcés Pérez in Texas. That same day, in Grand Rapids, Michigan, a Guatemalan man died in a fiery crash while fleeing federal immigration agents. ICE is now detaining more immigrants than ever before, despite the new secretary of homeland security, Markwayne Mullin, promising to avoid negative headlines by cutting the flash and fanfare.
How long will it take to read: Under four minutes.
Further reading: All the stories from the series ICE 2.0: inside Trump’s new immigration dragnet.
2. Why does millennial motherhood feel so impossible?
Women today are more educated, more employed and more engaged in childcare arrangements than ever before. But research shows that the expectations facing modern mothers continue to grow. In Australia, the statistics illuminate a global phenomenon. New research shows that the cost for Australian families of raising two or more children has risen to at least $36,500 a year. The cost of keeping a family afloat has increased by 134% in two decades, while household income has grown by only 102% in the same period.
Between juggling rising costs and managing careers, is there any way out of the total overwhelm?
A problem with no solution: In this personal piece, Kate Lyons writes that millennial women no longer feel trapped in their homes like generations before, but rather, by the impossible juggle of managing their career, relationships and children. Lyons recounts a friend reaching out for advice late one night after their five-year-old had a meltdown before bed. Another woman Lyons spoke to got so desperate she turned towards ChatGPT, asking the AI chatbot how to make her life work. But solutions are not easy to come by. After Lyons assessed the state of her living room, which, “looks as though someone has taken the contents of a laundry basket, a toy box and a nappy bag and Jackson Pollocked the floor with them”, all she could offer was solidarity.
Notable quote: “It’s not that I want to be at home five days a week. I don’t want to be exactly like my mum was. But I want to pick them up from school and take them home and calmly wind down the day with them. There’s absolutely no way I can do that.”
How long will it take to read: Just under six minutes.
Further reading: Why birthrates are plummeting, and why workplaces were built for men.
3. Trump’s testosterone culture war
Polls show that Donald Trump is losing support with the bros that got him elected. As the midterms approach, the cost of living and the war on Iran have left male voters increasingly disillusioned. So how does one win them back? The health secretary, Robert F Kennedy Jr, and the defence secretary, Pete Hegseth, seem to think the hormone testosterone, often known simply as “T”, is the answer. Or as Sam Wolfson explains, Trump is hoping that “the male populace will vote not with their heads or their hearts, but with their hogs”.
The testosterone dog-whistle: Testosterone is found in the bodies of men and women, with a low amount all that is needed for normal function. But the hormone has emerged on the frontlines of the Trump administration’s many culture wars. While the war in Iran causes problems for Trump back home, Hegseth has shifted the military message to one of machismo. On the campaign trail, he said, “We’re reminding our warriors that their sole purpose is to be the most lethal fighting force on the planet. Full stop. We’re not here to do social engineering, or social justice, or gender-bending, or DEI, or dudes and dresses.” But Wolfson writes that Hegseth’s testosterone push is a “sciencey” way to dog-whistle his sexist message.
Notable quote: “Everything has been politicized in the United States. Vaccines are liberal and TRT is Maga. The needle is apolitical but the content of the syringe is decided by who you vote for.”
How long will it take to read: eight minutes.
Further reading: The Pentagon and “incel” slang, plus RFK Jr’s “peptide wild west”.
4. Exposing the world’s biggest porn bosses
Patricia Nilsson was determined to bring porn industry leaders out of the shadows. For five years, she subjected the adult industry to forensic analysis in an effort to reveal who was getting rich through porn and how they were doing it. For decades, the owners of these companies have escaped scrutiny, and they have often enjoyed relative anonymity. But porn is everywhere, and for many young men and women, adult content can be their default sex education. Nilsson argues the owners of businesses that are recalibrating our sexual culture deserve further investigation.
Notable quote: “My argument is not that we should be neutral towards porn, but that we need to accept and understand it as a real industry, and ask what its growth and popularity says about the state of our economy and the world of work.”
The story of porn is the story of the internet: Nilsson argues that even if you do not consume explicit content online, the industry has shaped the way you interact with the digital world. We have porn to thank, she says, for high-quality video streaming and the way influencers sell their online personas. “Staring at content that is algorithmically engineered to arouse you is a perfect metaphor for our relationship with our devices and the internet and social media,” Nilsson says.
How long will it take to read: About five minutes.
Further reading: The malignant rise of OnlyFans managers and the rise of deepfake pornography in schools.
5. Christine Baranski and Richard E Grant on sex scenes, parties and theatre
Christine Baranski and Richard E Grant have stories to tell. The actors have joined forces for the first time in a London production of Noël Coward’s comedic play Hay Fever. The Guardian sat down with the actors to get a glimpse of the tall tales told backstage.
Notable quote: When asked if she has ever worked with Grant before, Baranski wryly says: “Regrettably not. We could have had some good fun a few decades ago. A girl could have got into some real trouble. But here we are, and now we’re the veterans.”
Skinny dipping in the dark: Recalling her “marvellous house” on a lake in Connecticut, Baranski recounts an evening spent with Mark Rylance when the pair went skinny-dipping and ended up howling at the moon till four in the morning. Pressed on whether taking your clothes off is a prerequisite for visiting, Baranski says: “I encourage people only if they’re comfortable and if it’s pitch dark.”
How long will it take to read: five minutes of gossipy joy.

US-Ukraine fund signs first critical minerals deal worth US$30 million
Conor Coleman, Chief of Staff at the US International Development Finance Corporation (DFC), has said that the joint Ukraine Reconstruction Investment Fund (URIF) has signed its first critical minerals deal and approved four other projects.
Source: Reuters
Details: Coleman said the fund's current portfolio of projects is worth around US$70 million in total.
"It's absolutely imperative for the Ukrainian people that we're investing now," he said.
The first minerals deal involves an investment of around US$30 million in a "joint investment platform" with BGV Group, a company founded by Hennadii Butkevych, co-owner of Ukraine's ATB supermarket chain.
Coleman said the platform will initially focus on early-stage mining projects across Ukraine, targeting deposits of rare earth elements, uranium, beryllium and zirconium.
"They are all on the US critical minerals list, so it ties in very well with what we're looking to do from a [US] administration priority [standpoint]," he noted.
Two other new projects are aimed at strengthening Ukraine's electricity and heating networks ahead of winter.
Coleman said one of them will complement an almost US$100 million loan to Ukraine's largest private energy company DTEK for a new battery storage system capable of providing backup power to around 600,000 households for two hours. The new deal will ensure the company has access to capital if its equipment is damaged by Russian strikes.
In addition, the investment fund will acquire a stake in a cogeneration platform that will develop a network of decentralised energy hubs. These are intended to help restore the supply of essential services to Ukrainian homes.
Coleman said that URIF is currently seeking additional capital to expand its investment capacity.
Background:
- Ukraine and the US signed a strategic minerals agreement on the initiative of US President Donald Trump in April 2025.
- Under the agreement, the governments of the two countries established the joint Ukraine Reconstruction Investment Fund (URIF). Its main purpose is to attract US and international capital into five key sectors of the Ukrainian economy: mineral extraction, the defence industry, energy, infrastructure and telecommunications.

Curious people tend to have more of the experiences linked to cognitive reserve, study finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
22:00:02 UTC
07:00:02 KST

A small study in the Netherlands found that people with a more curious personality tended to score higher on indicators of cognitive reserve, such as education and mentally stimulating leisure activities. However, neither curiosity nor these indicators of cognitive reserve were associated with performance on cognitive tests. The paper was published in Personality and Individual Differences.
As people age, many experience gradual cognitive decline. However, not everyone experiences this decline at the same pace or at the same age. While some individuals show marked cognitive decline relatively early, others maintain normal cognitive abilities into very advanced age. To help explain these differences, scientists developed the concept of cognitive reserve.
Cognitive reserve is the brain’s ability to maintain cognitive functioning despite aging, brain injury, or disease-related changes. It is thought to develop gradually across life through experiences that repeatedly engage the brain, such as education, intellectually demanding work, reading, learning new skills, and other mentally stimulating activities. In later life, greater cognitive reserve may help delay or reduce the cognitive effects of brain atrophy and other age-related changes, even though it does not necessarily prevent those physical changes from occurring.
One factor that may be of particular importance for building cognitive reserve is curiosity. Curious people are more likely to seek new information, explore unfamiliar experiences, and continue learning throughout adulthood. Activities encouraged by curiosity, such as reading books, learning languages, or exploring new places and ideas, may provide repeated cognitive stimulation over many years. Research has already linked the personality trait of openness to experience (a trait that also predisposes people to curious behaviors) to slower cognitive decline, suggesting that it may support resilience against it.
Study author Carolien Torenvliet and colleagues at Radboud University’s Donders Institute for Brain, Cognition and Behaviour explored the association between curiosity and various indicators of cognitive reserve. They also examined whether a curious personality (i.e., openness to experience and interest-based curiosity) was associated with cognitive abilities, and whether cognitive reserve might explain any such link.
Study participants were 106 adults recruited mainly from around Nijmegen in the Netherlands. They were between 40 and 85 years of age, with an average age of about 62, and 57% were women. People with current or past psychiatric or neurological disorders were excluded. Participants’ average estimated IQ was 118, well above the population average of 100.
Participants completed three questionnaires assessing curious personality: two measuring interest-based curiosity and one measuring openness to experience. They also completed the Dutch version of the Cognitive Reserve Index questionnaire, which estimates cognitive reserve from a person’s education, the complexity of their work, and their leisure activities. Finally, they completed three brief neuropsychological tests measuring memory, executive function, and processing speed.
Results showed that more curious individuals tended to score higher on indicators of cognitive reserve, specifically education and leisure activities, but not the complexity of their work. This association held after accounting for participants’ age. However, neither curiosity nor the cognitive reserve indicators were associated with performance on the cognitive tests.
“Although this study is limited by its cross-sectional design and relatively healthy sample, the results suggest that a curious personality may drive individual differences in cognitively stimulating experiences, but not cognitive abilities themselves,” the study authors concluded.
The study contributes to the scientific understanding of cognitive reserve. However, it should be noted that the design of the study does not allow any causal inferences to be drawn from the results. Curiosity may lead people to pursue more education and stimulating activities, but those experiences could also foster curiosity.
In addition, cognitive reserve was estimated from participants’ own reports of their past education, work, and activities rather than measured directly. Finally, participants were healthy and had higher-than-average estimated intelligence, and the sample was relatively small for a study of this type, which may have made it harder to detect links with cognitive performance.
The paper, “Curious people, resilient minds? The role of a curious personality in cognitive reserve and cognitive abilities,” was authored by Carolien Torenvliet, Dirk Bertens, Joukje M. Oosterman, and Iris Wiegand.

Israel could’ve ended Gaza war, freed captives sooner: Israel ex-negotiator
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
21:53:17 UTC
06:53:17 KST

Israel could’ve ended Gaza war, freed captives sooner: Israel ex-negotiator
Retired General Nitzan Alon says more captives could have been returned alive and a deal was possible ‘maybe a year earlier’.
A former Israeli general who was the army’s point person for hostage negotiations at the beginning of the Gaza war says that a deal to return all Israeli captives could have been achieved “much earlier” than October 2025 but it was prolonged unnecessarily.
“I think that we could [have gotten to] this point much earlier, maybe a year earlier or so, without any major implication on the other strategic goals of the war,” Major General Nitzan Alon said on Friday. “We missed it, actually. The war was too long.”
He was speaking during a Washington Institute for Near East Policy webcast marking three years since the October 7, 2023 Hamas attack on Israel preceding the genocidal war that has killed over 74,000 Palestinians.
Alon referred to Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s claim that Israel must achieve “total victory” before signing a deal as “false”.
He called the October 2025 “ceasefire” a “strategic achievement” that has since curbed Hamas’s military power. But he said it could have been secured much sooner with “maybe some hostages that got killed or murdered during their captivity [coming] back home alive.”
Hamas and Israel carried out a prisoner exchange deal in October 2025 under a ceasefire agreement that saw the release of nearly 2,000 Palestinians imprisoned in Israeli jails and 20 Israeli captives held in the Gaza Strip.
“We could have – and we should have – shortened the war, brought all the hostages back, maybe a year earlier, and moved forward and maybe, you know, saved thousands of lives on both sides,” Alon told the panel discussion organised by the United States think-tank.
Alon had made similar comments in July, when he also criticised Israeli Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, saying Smotrich had opposed some of the agreements put forward at various stages and therefore could not take credit for the return of all the captives.
‘Not just a missed opportunity, it’s tragic’
Speaking to Al Jazeera on Friday, former Israeli diplomat Alan Pinkas said Netanyahu had stalled the end of the war.
“A deal was possible very soon after the Hamas attack in October 2023,” he said.
“It took almost two years before the hostages were returned, so it’s not just a missed opportunity, it’s tragic.”
Earlier this week, Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman bin Jassim Al Thani said Israeli officials “rejected to entertain the idea” of a Hamas proposal to release all captives in exchange for a limited ceasefire soon after the attacks.
Al-Thani said Doha reached out to Israeli officials “on day one … Our message was very clear. They [Hamas leaders] are asking for a window of ceasefire to get the civilians out,” Sheikh Mohammed said in an interview with Piers Morgan. “And basically, they [the Israelis] were not interested to engage in the idea.”
Alon’s latest comments come less than a month before Israel’s October 27 legislative election, with polls showing the political battle remains at knife-edge.
Pinkas said Alon’s comments were unlikely to influence the outcome of the vote as polls already “reflect public anger” over the Netanyahu government’s failure to prevent the Hamas attacks.
A report by Israeli newspaper Haaretz claiming that United Arab Emirates President Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan had warned Netanyahu about a possible attack also sparked outrage across Israel last month.
Netanyahu said he would sue the outlet over its report, which he described as “fabricated” and “false”.

Roosters met with Rabbi Eli Schlanger days before Bondi attack
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
21:51:34 UTC
06:51:34 KST

Sydney Roosters met with Bondi victim Rabbi Eli Schlanger days before terrorist attack
On December 9, 2025, a group of Sydney Roosters players met with Rabbi Eli Schlanger and other leaders in the Eastern Suburbs Jewish community.
It was a Tuesday in the off-season for the rugby league club, months away from a ball being kicked or a tackle made.
They are a club on occasion tagged as well-oiled, representing the richest postcodes in Australia and lacking deep community ties.
But here were the Roosters, including Hugo Savala, Cody Ramsay and Billy Smith, eating kosher food, learning of Jewish customs at the Chabad of Bondi and walking along the beachfront and Bondi Pavilion.
Days later, metres away from that pavilion, the most devastating terror attack in Australian history occurred.
One of the 15 people killed in the mass shooting at Bondi Beach was Eli Schlanger.
Ten months on, and the Roosters are on the eve of a grand final against a Newcastle side almost universally cast as Sunday evening's community-minded underdog — but Easts' involvement and then support of their community during its darkest hour offers a glimpse into a story far more complex.
Rabbi Yehoram Ulman, Rabbi Shchlanger's father-in-law, was also on hand to meet with the players at the Chabad of Bondi Synagogue.
"They came to the synagogue, and they had a run-down of the different meanings and symbolisms," Rabbi Ulman told ABC Sport.
"And I remember they were very curious and very interested to understand everything that was going on."
Roosters CEO Joe Kelly, also present on the day, said the players took an immediate liking to Rabbi Schlanger — something that came as no surprise to Rabbi Ulman.
"Eli was a person who could connect with anybody," Rabbi Ulman said.
It was a "very happy occasion", according to co-CEO of the Executive Council of Australian Jewry, Alex Ryvchin, who was also present.
"The Roosters came, they were incredibly charming, engaged, very articulate, very knowledgeable already about the Jewish community in this area," Mr Ryvchin told ABC Sport.
"And just really thirsting for more knowledge and understanding of Jewish customs and traditions … really left a very positive impression on everybody they met."
But the players also ended the day with a greater understanding of some of the darkness experienced by the community in the 12 months prior.
While walking down the promenade at Bondi Beach, Ryvchin explained to them how the uptick in antisemitic incidents had impacted the local community.
"They had a very high level of awareness already in terms of the fire bombings that were happening here routinely," Mr Ryvchin said.
"They were concerned about it, but at that point it was still probably abstract for them."
The events of December 14 were deeply impactful for the Roosters, as they were for the entire country.
And for those players who had broken bread with Rabbi Schlanger earlier that week, Joe Kelly said he could feel the enormity of their grief and shock.
"[It had] a real impact on those players, and on the wider club," Mr Kelly said.
"The fact that it was only five days, it was really close to home for us, and I know that that was felt more broadly across the community as well as across the country."
Rabbi Ulman, who spoke at Rabbi Schlanger's funeral at the very synagogue that had hosted the Roosters barely a week earlier, could understand their grief.
"When we see something that happens in the world that is wrong, we are affected by it, and we automatically feel how wrong this is," Rabbi Ulman said.
"But when it happens to somebody that we know, it affects us so much more because it's close to home.
"They saw Eli, they connected with him, and five days later, you know, what happened, happened."
Away on a training trip on the day of the attack, the Roosters players gathered to pay their respects on Bondi Beach as soon as they could, before hosting an open training session on the sand in January.
The Tricolours also had Summer, sister of the youngest victim, Matilda, toss the coin and deliver the ball ahead of the Roosters' first home game of the new year.
Mr Kelly said the organisation "got around the community as much as we possibly could" — while Rabbi Ulman said the reaction of the club, especially from those players he met at the synagogue just days before the attack, said a lot.
"That just shows you that they are good people. Because any good person would be deeply affected by what happened," he said.

====================================================================================================

America’s only major etrog grower is in survival mode amid global competition
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
21:47:18 UTC
06:47:18 KST

On a small ranch in California’s Central Valley, below the foothills of the Sierra Nevada, an orchard grows an ancient and sacred fruit: the etrog, or citron.
At just 7 acres, the etrog grove at Lindcove Ranch in Exeter is a speck in Tulare County, where about 40% of California’s citrus crops are grown. But by another measure, the grove is giant: Lindcove Ranch is the only major commercial grower of kosher etrogs in the United States.
“This is my life — I really feel a calling to do this,” said Greg Kirkpatrick, 65, whose family has owned and operated Lindcove Ranch for more than 60 years.
The fruit looks like a strange lemon, with a knobby exterior, thick rind, and oblong shape. It exudes a sweet, fresh, lemony fragrance. It’s not a fruit you find in grocery stores. But for Jews, the etrog is crucial for fulfilling the commandments of Sukkot. During the holiday ritual, which includes a blessing, an etrog is held in the left hand while a bundle of palm, myrtle, and willow, called a lulav, is held in the right. Brought together, they are shaken in the four directions as well as upward and downward.
The Kirkpatrick family, who are not Jewish, began growing etrogs 46 years ago, when an Orthodox distributor from the East Coast reached out looking for a domestic grower. He wanted to avoid the costly import process of bringing in etrogs from any of the three major growing regions around the world: Israel, Italy, and Morocco.
Greg’s father, John, who was already a successful citrus farmer, decided to give the specialty crop a chance, and soon citrons became an important part of the ranch’s annual income. Its citron orchard is part of a larger specialty-citrus operation, which includes yuzu, finger limes, makrut limes and sour oranges on about 30 acres. The citron, however, has been the ranch’s top-earning crop.
The citron business is a difficult one that Kirkpatrick likens to the diamond industry, with single pieces of fruit selling for hundreds and sometimes thousands of dollars.
“It’s not so much how many we can grow. It’s the quality of the fruit,” he said.
An etrog must meet stringent requirements to be considered kosher for ritual use. It must be largely unblemished, retain its natural stem, called a pitom, and come from a documented lineage of trees that have never been grafted or crossed with another variety.
The requirements make growing them different from growing ordinary citrus, according to David Karp, a pomologist, citron expert and citrus researcher at UC Riverside.
“Many people have tried to grow citron in California,” Karp said, noting the financial allure of an etrog’s price tag. “But just because you can grow a lemon well doesn’t mean you can grow an etrog that’s right for Jewish ritual use. You can grow them, but you’ll end up selling them for $5 each, or feeding them to the cows.”
Karp said little in horticulture can compare to the scrutiny that etrogs undergo for physical appearance, all for the sake of religious ritual.
'Nothing remotely like this,' Karp says
“There’s nothing remotely like this,” Karp said. “In Japan and perhaps other countries in Asia … there’s a cultural predilection for perfect, extremely expensive fruit that would be given as a gift. But there’s nothing quite like the citron for Jewish ritual use.”
A typical crop may begin with 10,000 to 15,000 pieces of fruit, but perhaps only half will be suitable to bring to market, according to Kirkpatrick. His harvesters are trained to pick citrons carefully after inspecting them on the tree.
“Being able to judge on the tree if the fruit’s good enough to bring into the packing house or not is important, so we don’t have to spend hours wading through and washing and dealing with fruit that’s not going to make it to the market,” Kirkpatrick said.
Once picked, each fruit is placed in its own spot in a foam tray. The citrons do not touch one another through the picking or packing process because even minor bruising or scratches can reduce their value.
There are multiple grades of etrog, ranging from cheaper, wholesale stock sold in mail-order sets to exceptionally large and blemish-free fruit sought by elite buyers.
For decades, Kirkpatrick mostly sold his etrogs through a specialized marketing network to Orthodox Jewish customers on the East Coast, who seek citrons that are not only kosher but exceptional in size, shape and color.
“My partner sells to a very select group of Orthodox Jews in Lakewood, New Jersey, by appointment only,” Kirkpatrick said. “And if you don’t have appointment-grade fruit, they won’t come to buy your fruit.”
In 2023, the ranch received about 22 inches of rain and failed to get much of a crop. That same year, John died, leaving the grieving Kirkpatrick family to navigate the business without him. Then, in 2025, the ranch produced what Kirkpatrick thought was a successful crop, but his marketing partner was unable to sell enough of the fruit to recoup the $250,000 it cost to produce. Those years were the two worst for etrogs in the ranch’s history.
Distributors simply want more top-grade etrogs than the Kirkpatrick operation is able to supply.
Rabbi Menachem Sirota, a longtime etrog distributor based in Lakewood, New Jersey, who has purchased Lindcove Ranch citrons in the past, said he has opted to buy from larger growers who can supply more of the highest grade of the fruit.
“Personally, as a wholesaler, I need a very large quantity of nice ones,” Sirota said. “For a while I was getting them from California, but in recent years I was not so satisfied with the quality.”
As a result of the huge financial loss from this shift, one of the family’s homes on the ranch ended up in foreclosure earlier this year, Kirkpatrick said. With labor being one of the ranch’s biggest expenses, Kirkpatrick has had to cut back from eight full-time employees to five part-time workers.
One of the Lindcove Ranch etrogs that was delivered to Chochmat HaLev. (Aaron Levy-Wolins/J. Staff/Report For America)
The family is even thinking of selling the ranch.
But for now, Kirkpatrick is trying to save his business by becoming more of his own wholesaler.
“We’re reinventing ourselves,” he said.
The ranch is focused on selling bulk orders directly to congregations. Just before Sukkot began on Sept. 25, for example, Kirkpatrick delivered a shipment to Congregation Beth Emek in Pleasanton and Chochmat HaLev in Berkeley, California.
Etrogs grown without pesticides, chemicals
Kirkpatrick is also courting a new customer base with a pitch built on a genuine difference between his etrogs and those grown abroad. His etrogs are grown without pesticides or other chemical treatments, so after Sukkot they can be eaten or made into jam, candied peel or liqueur.
That sets them apart from etrogs grown overseas, according to Karp.
“Because a citron is of little worth unless it’s cosmetically perfect, they spray the heck out of these trees and fruit,” he said, adding that he wouldn’t advise eating etrogs grown outside the United States. “It wouldn’t be my first choice for a marmalade, let’s put it that way.”
Whatever Kirkpatrick’s hopes, the fate of Lindcove Ranch, and of California-grown etrogs, will depend on several factors, including the weather and how the next growing season plays out.
“I’m a farmer, I’m always optimistic,” he said. “You have to be in the farming business.”
This story was first reported by J. The Jewish News of Northern California and is reprinted with permission.

====================================================================================================

Israeli television marks three years since October 7 massacre
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
21:47:14 UTC
06:47:14 KST

Three years after the Hamas attack on October 7, Israeli television is returning to the events of that day with an unusually wide range of documentaries, special broadcasts, interviews, and memorial projects.
What is most striking about much of the new programming is how different it feels from the documentaries made in the first months after the attack. Those early films, understandably, were compiled at breakneck speed using cellphone footage, security-camera recordings, interviews, news videos, and even clips filmed by the terrorists themselves, to establish what happened and preserve evidence.
Now, three years later, filmmakers have had time to follow survivors, bereaved families, soldiers, released hostages, and displaced communities as they try to rebuild their lives, heal, and honor those they lost. They have developed certain narratives carefully; many of the new documentaries are not simply about surviving October 7, but they examine what it has meant to keep living afterward.
KAN’s anniversary programming includes several major new productions, and one of the most distinctive returns to the first hours of October 7 from an unexpected vantage point: Soroka Medical Center in Beersheba.
On October 5, the program Zman Emet will air The Shift (HaMishmeret), a documentary by Chen Liberman and Roni Singer about what happened inside the Beersheba hospital as hundreds of casualties began arriving on the day. Soroka found itself at the center of what turned out to be an unprecedented medical emergency, treating hundreds of wounded patients in a single day while the attack was still taking place.
Lineup of TV programs detailing life after Oct. 7
The program includes previously unseen security-camera footage from inside the hospital documenting the corridors, entrance plaza, and emergency-room gates in the hours after the massacre began.
KAN News will also broadcast After They Returned from October 5-7, a three-part series by anchor Tali Moreno.
Rather than focusing on the campaign to free the hostages, Moreno visits families after their relatives have come home. They speak about physical and psychological pain, the need to get to know returning family members again, and the growing realization that release from captivity did not mean a return to the life that existed before October 7.
On October 6, Hanoch Daum’s Taboo brings together four former hostages – Aviva Siegel, Doron Katz-Asher, Eitan Mor, and Guy Gilboa-Dalal – for a kind of retreat on a moshav. The four speak openly about how they survived, recalling the constant fear and how they maintained hope, and they open up about the long and complicated process of rebuilding life after their release. In keeping with Daum’s irreverent style, there is some black humor along the way.
A new documentary, His Footprints Remained, airing on October 5, tells the story of Ibrahim Kharouba, a veteran Bedouin IDF tracker who was killed fighting at the Nahal Oz base. Kharouba, who came from a family of trackers and had devoted his life to military service, joined the effort to defend soldiers trapped at the base during the attack.
KAN will also revisit October 7 through its digital memorial project, “7.10.360,” an interactive reconstruction of events in communities, towns, and roads throughout the Gaza border area. Drawing on thousands of hours of footage, testimony, WhatsApp messages, documents, recordings, interviews, and news reports, the project allows users to follow events beginning at 6:29 a.m. and currently includes around 250 individual stories.
HOT 8 is also featuring innovative programming that spotlights new angles, such as Saved by the Ball (Segel Haser), a film by Aviad Livny, about the Kfar Aza Foxes soccer team. The movie was screened at Docaviv 2026 and will air on October 5 at 9:15 p.m. on HOT 8 and will also be available on HOT VOD and NEXT TV.
Just days after October 7, the surviving players, who had been evacuated with other residents of Kfar Aza to Shefayim, began playing soccer again. They did so without the shoes they had left behind in homes they had fled, and without many friends and relatives who had been murdered or kidnapped.
They soon realized that soccer provided something almost nothing else could: 90 minutes during which they could feel, at least a little, like the people they had been before the attack. Roughly every two weeks, the Foxes began playing anyone willing to face them, including teams from other kibbutzim, hi-tech companies, Maccabi Tel Aviv veterans, Supernova music festival survivors, and Ashdod Port employees.
But when organizers tried to revive the tournament among Gaza-border kibbutzim in the summer of 2024, the Kfar Aza players refused. Their position was simple: They would not return “until everyone comes back.”
Displacement, bereavement, uncertainty: how 'Whose Are You?' explores life after Oct. 7
Another new HOT 8 film, Whose Are You? (Shel Mi At?), directed by Dotan Naveh, approaches Kfar Aza from a very different perspective. Ten women who married men from the kibbutz had formed a WhatsApp group called “Whose Are You?” as a way of helping each other find their place in the tight-knit community. On October 7, that ordinary question suddenly took on an entirely different, and often tragic, meaning.
The documentary focuses on three of the women who all experienced October 7 in different ways, despite living so close to one another. It follows them for over two years through displacement, bereavement, new motherhood, uncertainty, and the attempt to decide whether – and where – they can make a home again. It will air October 5 at 7:30 p.m. on HOT 8 and will also be available on HOT VOD and NEXT TV.
Another HOT 8 premiere, You Don’t Bury a Soul (Neshama Lo Kovrim), directed by Adi Feineru, focuses on 13 parents who lost children on October 7 as they travel for two weeks through southern India, accompanied by a team from Adama Tova, a therapeutic community that works with bereaved families. As they find themselves growing interested in the sights and sounds of India, they grapple with a painful question: If they allow themselves to move away from their grief and focus on other things, are they somehow abandoning their children? The film will air October 7 at 9:15 p.m. on HOT8.
HOT8 will also present Imprints of the Soul (Rishumei Nefesh), a collection of five short docu-poetic films by young filmmakers from the western Negev. The collection, which screened at Docaviv 2026, will be available beginning October 5.
HOT will also make a large number of previously released October 7-related documentaries and programs available again.
Among the most prominent is Yariv Mozer’s Emmy-winning We Will Dance Again, in which survivors speak about the attack on Nova. It’s a harrowing film and not easy to watch, but memorable and beautifully made.
Tom Shoval’s A Letter to David, winner of the Ophir Award for Best Documentary, is a cinematic letter to David Cunio, who was kidnapped on October 7 from Kibbutz Nir Oz, along with his wife, children, and his brother Ariel. David and another brother, Eitan, starred years earlier in Shoval’s first feature film, Youth. The movie is an intimate look at a community that was torn apart by grief and loss, and Shoval re-edited it when David and Ariel were released in October 2025.
Other returning programming includes October 7: Emergency Call, which tells the story of Magen David Adom personnel through testimony and calls from residents of Gaza-border communities; Waiting for Him, about two young women whose partners were killed together during military service; and Omri Assenheim and Gilad Tokatly’s documentary series What Happened to the IDF?, which looks beyond October 7 itself to examine developments within the military over preceding decades.
HOT 8 will also broadcast the documentary, The Campaign: Disinformation in a Time of War, airing October 4 at 9:15 p.m., which examines propaganda and digital influence during the Israel-Hamas war. Journalist Warren Kinsella looks at bot networks, fake accounts, algorithms, coordinated campaigns, and Hamas’s international messaging strategy.
Two new Israeli documentaries on Yes Docu look at another group still living with the consequences of the war: reservists.
Good Morning Gaza, which premieres October 4 at 9 p.m. on Yes Docu and Yes VOD, focuses on how Or Brandes, a psychology student and reserve-duty soldier who served in Gaza as a tank driver, began broadcasting what amounted to an improvised podcast to other soldiers over the military radio network. The soldiers express emotions ranging from denial and thoughts of revenge to humor, and they even play pranks on each other. Through recordings from the radio network, combined with intimate footage from combat, the film offers a window into the emotional world of soldiers in the period after October 7. The film competed at the 2026 Jerusalem Film Festival and was directed and written by Hanan Brandes and Matan Sacofsky.
After the film airs, Yes VOD will also make available a companion podcast in which Brandes and Sacofsky discuss the making of their first film, reserve duty, war, trauma, and loss.
Immediately afterward, at 10 p.m., Yes Docu will premiere One Eye Open, directed by Tom Giat and produced by Ohad Milstein, which won the First Film Award at Docaviv 2026 and the 2026 Weil-Bloch Film Award. Over more than 400 days of reserve duty in Operation Iron Swords, Giat closely documented the growing crisis he and his fellow soldiers faced. The film traces the quiet voices of a group of reservists who answered the call to serve and found themselves staggering under the burden. It draws you into their world and makes you understand their stress and coping strategies.
These films will deepen people’s understanding of the tragedy itself, what led up to it, and, perhaps most importantly, will be helpful in grappling with the question of what to do next.
Cellcom TV and Keshet had not announced their special programming to mark the outbreak of the Israel-Hamas War by press time.

Britain has seen a significant rise in antisemitism since Hamas's October 7 massacre that triggered the subsequent war in Gaza, including a series of attacks on Jewish sites in London earlier this year.
"It is no secret that this country faces a range of serious threats from the Iranian regime," Home Secretary (interior minister) Shabana Mahmood said in a statement. Iran has denied the accusations.
Counterterrorism police said Salehi and Ahmadyan had allegedly tried to acquire components and equipment to make an improvised explosive device and conducted reconnaissance on potential targets for attack.
Police also said the two men had allegedly been in contact with an overseas third party who might be in Iran.
Both men travelled to UK to seek asylum
The pair, who Mahmood said had arrived in Britain on a small boat from Europe several years ago, will appear at London's Westminster Magistrates' Court on Saturday. One of the men had been granted asylum, and the other had a live asylum claim, the interior ministry said.
The charges were announced a year after a fatal attack on a Manchester synagogue by a British citizen of Syrian descent. Earlier this week, Britain said Tehran had been involved in an alleged plot targeting an airbase used by the US to launch attacks against Iran.
"I'm aware that the news of this alleged plot coming during the High Holy day period has caused a great deal of concern to the Jewish community, as well as with the wider public," Vicki Evans, Senior National Coordinator for Counter Terrorism Policing, said in a statement.
"It also coincides with the anniversary of the devastating terrorist attack last year at Heaton Park synagogue and comes in a wider context of increasing antisemitic incidents across the UK."
No connection with RAF Fairford terror plot
Detectives said there was no connection between Friday's charges and the suspected plot involving the RAF Fairford air base, over which a dual UK-Iranian national was arrested on Thursday.
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said there were "strong indications" Iran was involved in relation to RAF Fairford, though Iran denied any involvement and said speculation would "fuel Iranophobia propaganda."

More than 48 hours after an apparent attempt to crash a flydubai flight bound for Tel Aviv, the incident is raising fresh security concerns for Israelis and Jewish communities abroad, while leaving hundreds of Israeli travelers stranded in the United Arab Emirates.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu warned in an interview with CNN that Iranian proxies “are planning attacks against Israel and Israeli civilians abroad.” In a separate statement, Netanyahu said he had instructed Israel’s security establishment “to prepare for additional potential threats.”
Doron Spielman, a spokesman for the Prime Minister’s Office, told the Jewish Telegraphic Agency on Friday that Netanyahu’s statement applied to “intelligence about threats against Israelis and against Jews in Israel and around the world,” and that Israel was “employing additional procedures” as a result. He did not disclose the details of the extra precautions.
Spielman added that “all of the Jewish communities around the world know that they’ve been on heightened alert since the seventh of October, but especially right now.”
The incident has also left Israelis stranded in the United Arab Emirates, after flydubai suspended its flights to and from Israel while the investigation into the incident continues.
Netanyahu had told international media on Wednesday that Israel was preparing “rescue flights” to bring Israelis in the UAE home and had ordered increased security. The measures apply to both Israeli and foreign airlines operating flights to Israel.
Dorin Turgeman, an Israeli citizen currently in Dubai, told the Jewish Telegraphic Agency that she had been scheduled to return to Israel Wednesday on a flydubai flight that was canceled. She managed to book a flight with the Israeli airline Arkia but said she remained concerned that it would also be canceled.
Turgeman said Israelis waiting at the Dubai airport were moved to an isolated area and that the area was cordoned off.
“The situation is stressful,” she said, describing the uncertainty as “very frustrating.”
Ophir Shir, an Israeli who lives in Dubai, told Israel’s Kan public broadcaster that the incident had “shaken the sense of security” he’d had. As someone who frequently travels the route of the flydubai flight, he noted that, “In the short term, I will definitely be afraid to take such a flight.”
Dubai an increasingly popular destination for Israelis
Dubai has become an increasingly popular destination for Israelis in the wake of the signing of the Abraham Accords establishing diplomatic relations between Israel and the UAE. It also now serves as a major transit point for Israelis traveling onward to destinations in Asia. Israeli travel groups on social media have been filled with posts expressing concern about the security situation and uncertainty over how travelers will return home.
The security concerns come as investigators continue to explore the motive behind the incident and whether the pilot was acting alone.
“As time goes by, the picture becomes clearer,” Netanyahu said in an official statement on Friday. “The perpetrator underwent Islamist radicalization. He came to crash the plane. We are now investigating whether he was sent, and whoever sent him will pay a very heavy price.”
Netanyahu separately told CNN that Israel believes it should participate in the investigation. He said UAE President Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed had agreed that Israel would “join the interrogation.”
Netanyahu also told Fox News that “It looks very likely that he was going to down the plane.” He pointed to what he described as “the Islamist tendencies, that radicalization that are found in his background,” saying they were “a pretty good clue,” while stressing that he was not yet drawing a final conclusion.
“I don’t make final conclusions yet. But that’s the indication we have now,” Netanyahu said.
The UAE on Friday publicly described the incident for the first time as a terrorist attack. Anwar Gargash, a senior Emirati official, called it “a dangerous terrorist act and a potential disaster.”
The Omani pilot, whose identity has not been publicly released, was transferred from Saudi Arabia to the UAE, according to Israeli and international media reports.
Captain Smit Machchhar praised as hero
The other pilot, Indian national Captain Smit Machchhar, has received widespread praise for his actions during the flight. According to passenger accounts and leaders who spoke with him, Machchhar was injured by the Omani pilot but managed to open the cockpit door, allowing passengers and crew members to overpower the attacker and safely land the plane.
“When I was on the ground, I realized the aircraft was falling down. And I knew in that moment, one last push, Smit! Just do it. The door is right there,” Machchhar told Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi in a conversation while still wearing a bandage on his head.
“And even at that time, he was beating me up. And then I just opened it … and then everybody came,” Machchhar said. “I was doing this for my life, but at the same time, I knew that I couldn’t let everybody else die.”
Leaders around the world have praised Machchhar for his actions. Modi told the pilot that his “courage, patience and quick thinking saved the lives of so many people.”
US President Donald Trump called Machchhar a “hero” and described his actions as “amazing.” Netanyahu said Machchhar had “prevented a 9/11 disaster.”

"What they promise Ukraine is a lie": Albania's prime minister comments on EU accession
Kyiv • UNN
Edi Rama believes that Ukraine will not join the EU through the standard procedure. He called for creating a different path to membership for it.
Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama stated that, in his opinion, Ukraine will not be able to become a member of the European Union under the current standard accession procedure, despite the promises being made to it. Instead, he called on the EU to find another path for Ukraine to achieve full membership. Rama said this in an interview with Germany's WELT AM SONNTAG, UNN reports.
Details
Speaking about the enlargement of the European Union, Rama urged European leaders to act more boldly and cited Ukraine as an example of a country for which the traditional accession process would not work, in his opinion.
Look at Ukraine. What they promise it is a lie. Under the ordinary accession procedure, with all the criteria, it will never be admitted. Everyone knows this
Rama proposed another path for Ukraine
At the same time, the Albanian prime minister did not oppose Ukraine's membership in the EU. On the contrary, he proposed involving Ukraine in the work within the European Union already now, and granting it full membership through a process that would depend on the country's specific results.
Rama also advocated abolishing the veto power within the EU. According to him, further enlargement creates the risk of new states emerging that would be capable of blocking decisions by the entire Union.
Albania itself is a candidate for EU accession. Rama stated that his country seeks to join the bloc as soon as possible, but considers the current decision-making model in the European Union insufficiently effective.

Roundup: Lebanon's wineries strive to stay afloat as war, weak demand bite
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
05:42:31 CST
06:42:31 KST

BEIRUT, Oct. 2 (Xinhua) -- Lebanon's wine producers have largely kept production alive despite the country's prolonged conflict, but falling domestic demand and mounting export pressures are weighing on wineries, according to exhibitors at Vinifest, a wine exhibition running from Thursday to Saturday in Sin El Fil, east of Beirut.
"Since the war started, there has been a major decline in the domestic market," said Eva Naim, co-owner of a family-owned winery Chateau Qanafar in West Bekaa.
Naim estimated that her chateau's domestic sales had dropped by more than 40 percent, blaming weaker purchasing power, the departure of people from Lebanon, and a shrunken hospitality sector.
"Wine is not an essential product," echoed Natalie Saade Touma, owner of Chateau Saint Thomas, noting that consumers under economic strain prioritize food and other necessities.
Chateau Saint Thomas saw a decline of about 20 percent in domestic sales in the first nine months of 2026 compared with the same period in 2025, while Chateau Ksara, a renowned local winery, reported a 30 percent fall, according to its deputy general manager, Kamil Chawi.
Production had largely endured amid the conflict.
Chawi said Ksara harvested all its vineyards in 2024, with no significant damage in 2026. Naim said her chateau maintained output because its vineyards in Kherbet Qanafar stayed accessible.
However, not all escaped harm: Saade Touma said Chateau Saint Thomas could not harvest one vineyard in the Bekaa in 2023 because security conditions blocked access.
An Agriculture Ministry assessment updated through August 2026 found that 26.76 hectares of vineyards in assessed conflict-affected districts in Lebanon required replanting or rehabilitation, with direct damage estimated at about 668,880 U.S. dollars.
The assessment covers selected districts rather than all Lebanese vineyards and distinguishes physical damage from production losses caused by restricted access and interrupted agricultural operations. Updated production-loss estimates for perennial crops remain pending.
Agriculture Minister Nizar Hani said the wine sector was affected particularly in parts of the Bekaa Valley, where Israeli airstrikes and difficulties reaching vineyards delayed harvesting and caused partial crop loss.
While domestic sales remain weak, exports have offered little relief.
Naim estimated that Chateau Qanafar's exports had fallen by around 50 percent, while Chateau Saint Thomas reported a 20-percent decline.
"There are many global factors that have affected the wine market," Naim said, citing inflation and shipping costs up some 50 percent.
Chawi said Ksara's exports outperformed its domestic business, though higher shipping, fuel, and raw-material costs still weighed on the winery.
Competition from lower-priced European wine amid global oversupply has compounded the squeeze, both abroad and at home, Hani said.
In response, wineries in Lebanon are pivoting outward, with some courting clients in Europe, the Gulf, and the United States.
Ksara has strengthened its export sales team, while Hani called for stronger promotion of Lebanese wine in restaurants, hotels, and foreign markets, alongside efforts to cut costs and boost competitiveness.
On Sept. 23, Lebanon's National Institute of Vine and Wine and the Syndicate of Owners of Restaurants, Cafes, Nightclubs, and Pastry Shops signed a cooperation memorandum, aimed at promoting Lebanese wine locally and abroad.
Member of parliament Razi El Hajj estimated Lebanon's annual wine production at around 12 to 13 million bottles and said that a parliament's economy committee stands ready to support the wine sector, which he called a value-added industry capable of sustaining farmers, jobs and investment. ■

SANAA/RIYADH, Oct. 2 (Xinhua) -- More than 70 people have been killed in fierce fighting between Yemen's Houthi group and government forces in southwestern Taiz province over the past 24 hours, military and medical sources said Friday, as the Houthis reported 94 Saudi air and missile strikes while Riyadh claimed interception of three Houthi ballistic missiles.
A Yemeni government military official, speaking on condition of anonymity, said more than 20 government soldiers and nearly 10 allied local fighters had been killed and dozens of others wounded in fighting in Taiz over the past 24 hours.
The official described fierce battles across several fronts, with opposing forces engaging in close-range combat for key positions in the province.
The most intense confrontations were concentrated in rural areas stretching toward Yemen's Red Sea coast, where government forces were seeking to halt Houthi advances and prevent the group from consolidating its recent gains near the Bab al-Mandab Strait, according to the official.
In the southern port city of Aden, government forces' air defenses intercepted several Houthi drones as they approached vital facilities and public service sites in the city, according to a statement posted on social media platform X.
Majid al-Nuzaili, spokesperson for the government forces, said on X that government forces had carried out 474 strikes and targeting operations against the Houthis using fighter jets, drones, and other weapons. He claimed the strikes had killed or wounded 1,540 Houthi fighters, most of them in Taiz, and destroyed or disabled 216 pieces of military equipment.
On the other hand, a medical source affiliated with the Houthis, also speaking on condition of anonymity, told Xinhua that more than 40 Houthi fighters had been killed and dozens of others wounded over the past 24 hours.
"Many of the deaths resulted from airstrikes on vehicles transporting reinforcements to active combat areas in rural Taiz," the source said.
In a separate statement posted on X, Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Sarea said 94 Saudi air and missile strikes had hit areas across the provinces of Sanaa, Saada, Taiz, Hajjah, Amran and Ibb over the previous 24 hours. He claimed civilian sites were among the targets and that the attacks had caused casualties, without providing a detailed toll.
He said the latest attacks brought the total number of air and missile strikes recorded by the group since the current escalation began to 1,350.
Meanwhile, the Saudi-led coalition's spokesperson Turki Al-Maliki said on X that three ballistic missiles launched by the Houthi group toward Khamis Mushait were intercepted and destroyed.
The latest fighting is part of a broader escalation around the Bab al-Mandab Strait, the strategic waterway linking the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden and a major route for international shipping.
Clashes have intensified in Taiz and neighboring Lahj since the Houthis captured the Red Sea port city of Mocha on Sept. 10 and Mayyun Island, also known as Perim, on Sept. 11, expanding their presence around the strait and pushing some of the heaviest ground fighting into nearby mountainous areas.
The escalation has also been accompanied by renewed Houthi attacks against Saudi Arabia and what the group says are Saudi air and missile strikes on Houthi-held areas in Yemen, reviving cross-border hostilities that had largely subsided after a UN-brokered truce in 2022.
Yemen's conflict began in late 2014 when the Houthis seized the capital Sanaa and much of northern Yemen, prompting a Saudi-led coalition to intervene in March 2015 in support of the internationally recognized government. ■

OSLO, Oct. 2 (Xinhua) -- The Norwegian government and eight labor and employer organizations reached an agreement Friday to promote the safe and responsible use of artificial intelligence (AI) in the workplace while protecting employees' rights, according to a press release by the government.

JOHANNESBURG, Oct. 2 (Xinhua) -- South Africa is stepping up efforts to root out corruption and fraud at its borders and ports of entry, with officials implicated in misconduct facing disciplinary action, dismissal and criminal charges, an official said Friday.
The Border Management Authority (BMA) handled 57 labor and disciplinary cases involving breaches of internal controls, fraud, corruption and other misconduct in the last quarter, while 33 cases remain under disciplinary proceedings, BMA Commissioner Michael Masiapato said during a quarterly anti-corruption campaign at O.R. Tambo International Airport in Johannesburg.
The campaign brought together government and law-enforcement bodies including the Special Investigating Unit (SIU), the Department of Home Affairs and the National Prosecuting Authority.
Masiapato said corruption at ports of entry could involve border guards, immigration and customs officials, port operators and others exercising discretionary powers.
Such misconduct includes colluding with travelers or third parties to evade duties and taxes, facilitating the movement of illicit goods, soliciting bribes for routine services and fraudulently issuing travel or immigration documents, he said.
In February, the SIU said South Africa's immigration system had been treated as "a marketplace," where permits and visas were sold to the highest bidder through corrupt networks involving officials and external actors.
The Department of Home Affairs said at the time that it had identified more than 2,000 study visas fraudulently issued through such syndicates and that administrative processes were underway to cancel them.
Rooting out corruption in the immigration system is also part of the government's comprehensive approach to migration management adopted in June. President Cyril Ramaphosa said when announcing the measures that the government would strengthen border security, crack down on violations of immigration laws and continue efforts to eliminate corruption in the immigration system. ■
