Kiev trying to spark war on Korean peninsula – Seoul
South Korea has accused Ukraine of trying to spark war on the Korean Peninsula, with President Lee Jae-myung threatening a response unless Kiev apologizes for breaching a confidentiality agreement.
Vladimir Zelensky announced publicly last week that Ukraine had transferred two North Korean prisoners to South Korea. Seoul says the arrangement was supposed to remain secret, but Kiev has denied that claim.
Writing on X on Friday, Lee said Ukraine had initially requested secrecy, then disclosed the transfer unilaterally and made him look like “a liar” by denying the agreement.
He further accused Kiev of responding to demands for an apology by trying to shift the conversation to an imminent military clash between North and South Korea, describing its conduct as “attempting to provoke a war on the Korean Peninsula.”
“If the refusal to acknowledge the facts and issue a public apology continues, we will take additional measures,” Lee warned, stressing that South Korea’s national dignity is at stake.
The dispute began with Zelensky’s September 23 address to the UN General Assembly, when he announced the transfer of the North Korean soldiers and said it was “not easy to capture them alive.” The servicemen were reportedly taken prisoner in January 2025 in Russia’s Kursk Region, where North Korean troops helped repel a Ukrainian incursion.
According to Seoul, Kiev initially sought secrecy to avoid domestic criticism for giving up prisoners who could have been exchanged for captured Ukrainians. South Korea also cited the safety of the soldiers and their families, alongside sensitive diplomatic and security concerns.
Zelensky adviser Dmitry Litvin responded to Seoul’s apology demands by denying any secrecy agreement existed, prompting South Korea to summon Ukraine’s acting ambassador on September 28.
Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrey Sibiga subsequently tried to downplay the falling out, calling it a “diplomatic misunderstanding” and said he was working to resolve it.
South Korea has provided the country with humanitarian and financial assistance since 2022 and pledged another $100 million in July, but has drawn the line at weapons deliveries. Lee did not specified what measures he would take, but analyst Cho Han-bum told Reuters they would most likely involve assistance programs.
The Zelensky government has repeatedly clashed with countries providing substantial support throughout the conflict. In Poland, Ukraine’s continued glorification of nationalist forces responsible for massacring Poles has provoked outrage and demands from politicians to halt free weapons deliveries despite Warsaw’s extensive assistance.
Public enthusiasm for aid has also shown signs of weakening in recent years, including in Germany, where polling this year found declining support for increased military assistance. Earlier surveys in France and Italy also revealed divisions over continued support for Kiev.

How Syria’s Signal Company 134 tracked down Israeli spy Eli Cohen
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
18:55:31 UTC
03:55:31 KST

A radio frequency, encrypted messages and an unidentified transmitter were the only clues available when a Syrian military signals unit began tracking what would eventually lead it to Israeli spy Eli Cohen.
More than six decades later, retired Syrian officer Said Jawish has provided a detailed account of the operation, describing how Signal Company 134 followed the transmissions for three years before locating Cohen’s apartment in Damascus.
Jawish presented his account in a multipart interview with Saudi Arabia-based Al Majalla magazine. The first installments were published on Sept. 30 and Oct. 1.
Cohen lived in Syria under the identity Kamel Amin Thabet between 1962 and 1965. Posing as a wealthy Syrian businessman who had returned from abroad, he developed relationships with senior political and military figures and transmitted information to Israel.
Idea born from wartime radio signal
Jawish said the operation had its origins in 1956, when he was teaching students at the Military Academy in Homs how to operate a Canadian radio set dating from World War II.
During one lesson, he intercepted military call signs that he identified as Israeli.
The discovery prompted him to ask why the Syrian army was not systematically monitoring Israeli military communications.
His initial proposal was dismissed by senior commanders, but Jawish continued seeking support.
An officer who had previously served in the Signal Corps eventually backed the plan, leading to Jawish’s formal assignment on Sept. 30, 1957.
Jawish established an initial listening position at Na’ran in the Golan Heights, operating under a cover story intended to conceal the post’s real purpose.
After spending about a year monitoring and recording communications, he trained 44 noncommissioned officers in Israeli radio procedures.
Listening stations were subsequently established at Skoufia, Na’ran and Zaoura in the Golan Heights, as well as in Damascus.
Together, they formed Signal Company 134, which operated under the army’s Signal Corps rather than its intelligence services.
The company monitored Israeli military communications, radio broadcasts and news agencies. It also intercepted anonymous Morse-code transmissions composed of five-letter or five-number groups.
Although the unit could record the signals, Jawish said it could not break the Israeli encryption system.
Following unknown transmitter for 3 years
The unit intercepted the first message later connected to Cohen in 1962, but investigators did not know the sender’s identity, location, or the contents of the transmission.
Each unknown transmitter was assigned a code, while its frequency and transmission dates were recorded.
Copies of intercepted messages were sent to one team attempting to decipher them and another using Soviet direction-finding equipment to locate their source.
Over three years, the search area was gradually narrowed from Damascus to a section of the Abu Rummaneh district and then to a single residential building.
Investigators initially suspected a Syrian Airlines pilot of Greek origin who lived there.
His travel records appeared to correspond with interruptions in the transmissions: The signal was generally absent when he traveled and returned when he was in Damascus.
Using a drug investigation as cover, Jawish and his team searched the pilot’s apartment.
They also searched the homes of a foreign officer attached to an international monitoring mission and a Turkish Embassy diplomat in the same building but found no radio equipment.
The searches generated complaints and prompted Jawish’s commander to close the investigation.
Rooftop antenna provides breakthrough
Jawish nevertheless continued working on the case.
He returned to the building and inspected its roof, where he found an antenna that appeared to have been professionally installed and differed from the improvised aerials used by other residents.
A black coaxial cable led from the antenna to a fourth-floor apartment registered under the name Kamel Amin Thabet.
The following morning, Jawish’s team returned at around 7 am, when the unknown operator was expected to transmit.
When the signal began, Jawish cut the electricity to the apartment three times using an exterior circuit breaker.
The three interruptions appeared in the unit’s recording, confirming that the transmission originated inside the apartment.
Fearing the interruption might alert the signal’s recipients and allow the operator to escape, Jawish and two colleagues forced their way inside.
They found Cohen in a sparsely furnished room.
An initial search produced nothing, but Jawish noticed a dark object inside a wooden curtain pelmet above a window.
A Kodak film container concealed there held a small Morse key and a radio device.
According to Jawish, Cohen then disclosed that the equipment was a backup transmitter. The main transmitter was hidden inside a green leather-covered document case on a table.
Investigators also found frequency crystals, an emergency frequency, a notebook containing daily cipher information and objects resembling colored soap bars that contained explosive detonators.
Jawish said Cohen cooperated after the equipment was discovered and told investigators that he had initially encrypted messages using a French edition of The Three Musketeers as a codebook.
Cohen was subsequently prosecuted in Syria and executed in Damascus on May 18, 1965.
Al Majalla’s interview series is expected to provide further details about the interrogation, intercepted messages and wider counterintelligence operation in its remaining installments.

Yemeni army says 1,540 Houthis killed or wounded over past 24 hours
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
18:54:39 UTC
03:54:39 KST

Sahin Demir
02 October 2026•Update: 02 October 2026
The Yemeni army on Friday said that it carried out 474 operations against Houthi targets across several fronts over the past 24 hours, killing or wounding 1,540 members of the group.
Military spokesman Majed Abdullah al-Nazili said the operations used warplanes, drones, artillery, missiles and rocket launchers to target Houthi positions, movements, reinforcements and military capabilities.
The operations covered fronts from southern Haradh and the coast to Kitaf, Al-Jawf, Marib, Al-Bayda, Lahj, Sanaa and Saada, with a particular focus on Taiz, Nazili said.
He said the operations targeted what the army described as sources of threats, Houthi gatherings, reinforcements, command-and-control centers and other military capabilities.
Nazili claimed 1,540 Houthi fighters were killed or wounded, most of them on the Taiz fronts. He also claimed 216 military vehicles and other assets were destroyed or damaged.
The spokesman claimed the operations halted Houthi advances in Taiz and prevented the group from achieving a breakthrough on the ground.
The announcement came amid intensified fighting across Yemen. Earlier Friday, the army said its warplanes carried out 20 strikes against Houthi movements and reinforcements in Taiz.
Government forces also reported strikes against what they described as high-value targets in Sanaa and Saada.
On Wednesday, the army said it carried out 468 operations against Houthi fighters and military equipment on three fronts, claiming hundreds of Houthi casualties.
The latest fighting is part of a military escalation that began in July, the broadest since the relative calm that followed a 2022 truce.
Yemen has been engulfed in conflict since the Houthis seized Sanaa and several provinces in 2014, prompting a Saudi-led coalition to intervene in 2015 in support of the internationally recognized government.

US-Ukraine investment fund seals first critical minerals deal

US-Ukraine investment fund seals first critical minerals deal
- The US-Ukrainian reconstruction investment fund secured its first critical minerals deal investing about US$30 million in early-stage mining projects targeting rare earths, uranium, beryllium, and zirconium.
- The fund supports Ukraine’s recovery by focusing on five sectors, including minerals, defence, energy, and infrastructure, with total project investments around US$70 million.
- New projects aim to strengthen Ukraine’s power and heating networks, including a US$100 million battery system for backup power to 600,000 homes and an equity stake in heat and power co-generation platforms.
AI generated
LONDON - The joint US-Ukrainian reconstruction investment fund has sealed its first critical minerals deal alongside four other new projects, one of its top US officials told Reuters.
The fund, established as part of the minerals pact the two countries signed in April 2025 following a push by US President Donald Trump, is focused on five strategic sectors from minerals and defence to energy and infrastructure.
Conor Coleman, head of investments at the US International Development Finance Corporation (DFC), said the fund’s projects now total around US$70 million (S$89 million) and showed Washington’s support for Kyiv in the long-running war with Russia.
“It’s absolutely imperative for the Ukrainian people that we’re investing now,” Coleman said in an interview, referring to the ongoing damage to Ukraine as it faces another winter.
The long-anticipated first minerals deal will inject roughly US$30 million into a “joint investment platform” with BGV Group, a firm founded by Hennadii Butkevych, the billionaire co-owner of Ukraine’s largest supermarket chain ATB.
Coleman said it would initially focus on early-stage mining projects across Ukraine and target rare earths, uranium, beryllium and zirconium deposits.
“They are all on the US critical minerals list, so it ties in very well with what we’re looking to do from a (US) administration priority (standpoint),” Coleman said.
Power projects
Two of the other new projects announced on Oct 2 aim to shore up Ukraine’s power and heating networks after a rise in Russian attacks on key infrastructure ahead of winter.
Coleman said one would add to the near US$100 million the DFC has just agreed to lend Ukraine’s largest private energy company DTEK for a new battery system that will provide backup power to approximately 600,000 Ukrainian homes for up to two hours.
The project will also have “access to capital if damages arise”.
The fund will also take an equity stake in a combined heat and power co-generation platform designed to help build and run off a number of “energy hubs” aimed at restoring damaged electricity and heat supplies to households.
Coleman also said the fund was looking for more capital to increase its capacity. REUTERS

Sudan’s army says it captured RSF stronghold in North Kordofan
Sudanese Armed Forces reportedly retake al-Mazroub, advancing the army’s goal of cutting the RSF’s supply lines.
The Sudanese Armed Forces say they have taken control of al-Mazroub in North Kordofan state following fierce battles with the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), marking a significant gain in one of the war’s main battlegrounds.
In a statement on Friday, the military said fierce battles resulted in casualties among the paramilitary RSF forces, as well as heavy combat vehicle losses.
“The Armed Forces urge citizens in the liberated areas to rest assured and return to their normal lives,” the statement added.
A Sudanese army source told Al Jazeera that al-Mazroub was the RSF’s largest stronghold in North Kordofan.
Army Special Forces spokesman Mohammed Deidan told the Anadolu news agency that the city links the states of North Kordofan and West Kordofan and that, by seizing it, the army was advancing its goal of cutting the RSF’s supply lines.
Fighting in Sudan’s Kordofan region has intensified since late 2025, turning it into one of the main battlegrounds in the war between the army and the RSF, now in its fourth year.
The vast region – which comprises North, West and South Kordofan states – lies where the two sides’ areas of control meet, between the army-held central region and the RSF-controlled Darfur in the West.
Since the war began in April 2023, one in five recorded attacks in Sudan has taken place in Kordofan.
The army has the upper hand in the north, the RSF in the west, and South Kordofan remains contested.
Adding another layer of ethnic friction to the country’s wider civil war, last month the Sudan Doctors Network accused the RSF-allied Sudan People’s Liberation Movement-North (SPLM-N) of carrying out the artillery attack in the town of Dilling, in the South Kordofan province.
The SPLM-N is a breakaway faction of the SPLM, the governing party of neighbouring South Sudan. Its leader, Abdel Aziz al-Hilu, has aligned his fighters with the RSF and joined ranks with the RSF-led parallel government in Sudan.

Washington should pay attention to Ukraine's new robotic counteroffensive
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
18:47:12 UTC
03:47:12 KST

Washington should pay attention to Ukraine's new robotic counteroffensive
Preparation of an unmanned ground vehicle (UGV) for deployment. (NC13 Strike UGV Unit of the 3rd Separate Assault Brigade, 3rd Army Corps)
Kateryna Lisunova
Ukrainian journalist
Imagine heavy drones flying 15 to 20 kilometers (approximately 9.3 to 12.4 miles) deep into enemy rear positions and then deploying unmanned ground vehicles, or UGVs (unmanned ground vehicles), essentially robots, that drive even deeper into the rear.
There, in areas the enemy considers relatively safe and calm, these robots can destroy Russian logistics, strike dugouts, eliminate military personnel, and sometimes even take prisoners of war. Russian soldiers can surrender directly to the robots, which then escort them toward Ukrainian positions under the watch of a small robotic weapons system.
And all of it happens live, with both video and audio. The video comes from the robots and drones. The audio comes from intercepted Russian communications, as soldiers panic and try to understand who or what is attacking them.
In one such intercepted conversation, Russian soldiers were even arguing that it was impossible for Ukrainian UGVs to have reached so far into the rear. They suspected that what they were seeing might actually be friendly fire from their own side.
And now imagine that you do not actually have to imagine any of this. This is a new military tactic being used in Ukraine today. The first successful operation took place in January 2026. By now, the unit has more than 100 successful operations under its belt.
This tactic is called Gryphon, in honor of a servicemember from the unit who went missing during a combat mission near the village of Andriivka in Donetsk Oblast, not far from Bakhmut. It is the same place from the Oscar-winning Ukrainian filmmaker Mstyslav Chernov's documentary "2000 Meters to Andriivka," which chronicles the Ukrainian counteroffensive in this area.
It sounds like science fiction: flying robots delivering ground robots that can perform tasks traditionally carried out by infantry, participate in assault operations, and help liberate Ukrainian territory while reducing the risks to Ukrainian soldiers.
These operations are being carried out by NC13, essentially the world's first strike UGV unit, which operates within Ukraine's Third Army Corps.
Today, the tactic is also part of Operation Vivaldi, a major Ukrainian counteroffensive that has restored Ukrainian control over 176 square kilometers (nearly 68 square miles) of territory.
According to President Volodymyr Zelensky's office, Russian forces suffered more than 5,000 killed and wounded during the first three phases of the operation, while Ukrainian forces captured another 250 Russian troops. The Third Army Corps separately reported 2,000 Russian personnel losses during the most recent phase alone.
Ground robotic systems carried out 80% of logistics and 90% of casualty evacuations during stages of Operation Vivaldi, according to NC13 Commander Mykola Zinkevych and reporting by UNITED24 Media.
Ukraine has spent more than four years fighting a technologically adaptive conventional war against Russia.
Its troops have accumulated experience in drones, electronic warfare, robotic systems, battlefield artificial intelligence, communications, and rapid-cycle weapons development under conditions no NATO military has experienced at a comparable scale, and this story matters beyond the front line — it is the expertise Ukrainian allies should finally recognize as invaluable to them as well.
This is the latest example of Ukraine's battlefield innovation that Western partners, unfortunately, cannot keep up with.
U.S. President Donald Trump, meanwhile, has been very explicit that his approach to diplomacy and support is transactional. He is more likely to provide aid to partners when he sees clear value in the investment and a benefit to the United States.
The missing piece in this equation is how to explain to the administration that Ukrainian military innovation is not only helping Ukraine survive, but it is also an investment in future global security and in America's own defense capabilities.
The challenge is that this is becoming harder to explain as the technology evolves faster and becomes more sophisticated almost every week.
At some point, descriptions of the modern Ukrainian battlefield begin to sound more like Sci-Fi movies than conventional warfare.
And this lack of understanding is not only an American problem. It is increasingly a challenge for the broader Western world.
"There is some understanding of what we're talking about when we describe what we're deploying, what we're using, and how it works. But they don't seem to fully grasp its importance and value on the battlefield, or the extent to which the battlefield itself has changed," says NC13 Commander Mykola "Makar" Zinkevycn, referring to the Western allies.
At the same time, Ukraine urgently needs additional air-defense capabilities, particularly Patriot interceptors, as Russia continues its missile attacks. Kyiv and Washington are currently working on plans related to Patriot interceptor production in Ukraine and additional air-defense support ahead of winter.
In a relationship where Washington increasingly asks what strategic value the United States receives in return, explaining the revolutionary nature of Ukraine's military innovation could become part of the argument for continued support.
The question, in other words, is whether the United States sees Ukraine primarily as a recipient of Western military technology, or also as a source of battlefield expertise that Western forces may increasingly need themselves.
The answer may determine not only how Washington understands this war, but how prepared it is for the next one. Failing to grasp the significance of the transformation unfolding on Ukraine's battlefields risks losing sight of an ally that is the first in modern warfare to deploy robots at such scale and speed in the largest war Europe has seen since the last century.
Editor's note: The opinions expressed in the op-ed section are those of the authors and do not purport to reflect the views of the Kyiv Independent.

On October 13, the EU may potentially open two negotiating clusters each for Ukraine and Moldova. Montenegro may close three chapters, while Albania may close one.
The European Union may take a new step in the enlargement process on October 13 and open two more negotiating clusters for Ukraine. On October 2, Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty Europe editor Rikard Jozwiak wrote about this on his page on the social network X, reports UNN.
Details
According to Jozwiak, October 13 could potentially become another "Super Tuesday" in the EU enlargement process.
"Potentially, this looks like another EU enlargement 'Super Tuesday' on October 13, if everything goes smoothly," the journalist wrote.
He noted that two negotiating clusters are planned to be opened for Ukraine on that day. Similarly, two clusters may be opened for Moldova. At the same time, according to his information, Montenegro may close three negotiating chapters, while Albania may close one.
Context
Under the EU accession methodology, the negotiating chapters are grouped into six thematic clusters: "Fundamentals of the accession process," "Internal market," "Competitiveness and inclusive growth," "Green agenda and sustainable connectivity," "Resources, agriculture and cohesion," and "External relations." In June 2026, the EU and Ukraine opened the first negotiating cluster, and in July they began negotiations on the "External relations" cluster.
Earlier, the EU also announced a significant acceleration of the enlargement process. On October 2, European Commissioner for Enlargement Marta Kos called 2026 a record year for the EU's enlargement policy and emphasized that the accession process remains based on candidate countries' fulfillment of the necessary criteria.
We remind you
The European Commission plans clear reform and negotiation schedules for Ukraine, Montenegro, Moldova, and Albania. They will not yet be offered to the other candidates.

Lawmakers Push for Bipartisan Solution to Golden Dome’s Funding Crunch
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
18:43:57 UTC
03:43:57 KST

Some lawmakers in the Senate are advocating for a more bipartisan approach to paying for the Pentagon’s $185 billion Golden Dome missile defense project, arguing that the effort’s goal of bolstering homeland defenses has support across ideological lines but the process for funding it has been politically charged—leaving the program’s near- and long-term future uncertain.
During a Sept. 29 hearing of the Senate Armed Services Committee’s strategic forces subcommittee, lawmakers bemoaned the Pentagon’s decision to use a controversial funding tool called reconciliation—which allows Congress to appropriate funds with a simple majority vote—to kickstart President Donald Trump’s Golden Dome initiative in 2025. That decision, they argued, took a program whose mission has broad support in Congress and enveloped it in politics.
“Should it have been necessary to go to reconciliation to get this started? I would say no. This should have been on a bipartisan basis,” Sen. Mike Rounds (R-S.D.) said during the hearing. “I won’t lay fault for why that’s happening, I’m just simply saying we need to get back to a bipartisan approach to this as soon as possible.”
Sen. Angus King (I-Maine) said the effort is one of the “most expensive and important initiatives of this government” that has strong support in Congress, making it “very bothersome” that the Pentagon and the White House opted to circumvent the traditional appropriations process to resource it.
And Sen. Deb Fischer (R-Neb.) pointed out that while Golden Dome as a program materialized under President Donald Trump’s administration, its roots are bipartisan. The Senate Armed Services Committee inserted language into the Fiscal 2024 National Defense Authorization Act codifying the need for a layered missile defense architecture.
“So, it came from us,” she said.
Yet it was Trump’s announcement in January 2025 that the Pentagon would build an expansive homeland missile defense architecture that brought major attention and funding to idea. First called “Iron Dome For America” and later changed to “Golden Dome,” the vision is for a layered architecture comprised of sensors, ground and space-based interceptors, and interconnected command-and-control systems designed to defeat a range of threats, from drones and more traditional weapons to advanced hypersonic and cruise missiles.
To date, the Pentagon’s strategy for funding the program has been to bypass the annual budget process and rely instead on reconciliation. As part of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which Congress passed in July 2025, Golden Dome received $25 billion—90 percent of which it had obligated as of mid-August, according to Golden Dome Director Gen. Michael Guetlein.
This year, the Pentagon requested $17 billion for the effort as part of a proposed $350 billion reconciliation package, and just $400 million in the normal “base” budget for fiscal 2027. For now, though, there appears to be little political will to pass another spending bill via reconciliation, leaving Golden Dome without a clear path for near-term funding.
That challenge is exacerbated by the fact that the federal government is now operating under a continuing resolution, a stopgap funding measure aimed at avoiding a wholesale shutdown that holds spending at prior year levels. The CR took effect Oct. 1, the first day of the new fiscal year, and because Golden Dome does not have a fiscal 2026 appropriation to serve as its baseline, the program has nothing to fall back on.
Guetlein warned in August that a CR presents a real challenge for the program, and a failure to provide any funding in fiscal ‘27 would be disastrous.
“A CR doesn’t help me under Golden Dome because I don’t have a topline to fall back to to get that percentage of the continuing resolution,” he said during the Space and Missile Defense Symposium, adding that if Congress and the Pentagon can’t find a way to pay for the effort in fiscal ‘27, “there is no Golden Dome because there is no funding.”
During this week’s hearing, Rounds urged his colleagues in Congress to find a solution.
“Let’s get back to a bipartisan [approach], and let’s include it in the underlying appropriations bill,” he said.
Meanwhile, experts testifying in front of the Senate panel agreed that it’s important for Congress to address the funding quagmire, but added that there’s a broader risk that the politicization of the program could make it a target in the future.
Tom Karako, director of the Missile Defense Project at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, noted that even Golden Dome’s name is polarizing and argued that Congress should consider potentially renaming the effort in future policy legislation. He also suggested making steps to institutionalize the project and Guetlein’s acquisition authorities within the broader missile defense enterprise.
In his written statement, Karako noted that Guetlein’s status as a direct reporting portfolio manager, or DRPM—which means he reports directly to Deputy Secretary of Defense Steven Feinberg—is meant to be temporary, and said now may be the time to start thinking about the program’s long-term management and where it should sit within the enterprise after that moniker and its associated authorities fade.
Karako offered that while the Pentagon and Congress could opt to create a permanent entity to oversee Golden Dome, that approach may lead to duplication with other organizations like the Missile Defense Agency and the military services and would take time to establish. But merging Golden Dome with MDA could be a viable solution, he said.
“Whatever the scope of mission for the future air and missile defense of the homeland, its realization and governance will benefit from unity of effort with clear authority, high level access, control of resources, and appropriate acquisition authorities,” Karako said in his statement.

A7 ‘categorically’ rejects US claims of Iran and terrorism links
Unknown

A7 ‘categorically’ rejects US claims of Iran and terrorism links
Russian fintech company A7 has “categorically” rejected US accusations linking it to Iran and terrorist groups, calling the claim a “blatant lie and slander.”
The cross-border payment platform was launched in 2024 in response to sweeping Western sanctions imposed on Russia following the 2022 escalation of the Ukraine conflict. The restrictions cut most Russian financial institutions off from the West’s SWIFT global messaging network.
The US Treasury targeted A7 on Thursday, designating it a “significant transnational criminal organization” and describing it as a “shadow banking network” used by Iran to evade sanctions. Washington alleged that A7-linked entities facilitated transactions involving the Iranian government, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), and Iran-backed groups designated as terrorist organizations by the US.
“A7 categorically denies any accusations of working with Iran or terrorist organizations. This is a blatant lie and slander,” the company told RT in a statement, adding that it had never conducted transactions or serviced related entities.
The new US measures “do not affect” A7’s operations, the company added.
Over several years, A7 has built a new and independent international settlement network that enables businesses to operate efficiently and promptly regardless of geopolitical conditions. Sanctions against us are precisely recognition of this efficiency.
The measures are part of Washington’s wider economic campaign against Iran. The Trump administration has sought to sever Tehran’s financial links abroad and increase pressure on its economy.
The effort has coincided with a US blockade of Iranian ports as the ongoing conflict continues to disrupt energy markets. Traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, which carried around a quarter of the world’s seaborne oil before the February 28 US-Israeli attack on Iran, remains disrupted. Global fuel prices have also faced pressure from Russia’s extended diesel export ban amid the Ukraine conflict.
The action against A7 comes just weeks after US President Donald Trump signed the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act into law. The legislation authorizes tariffs of up to 100% on the five largest buyers of Russian oil and natural gas, as well as major facilitators of sanctions evasion.
India and China, the largest buyers of Russian crude, have pushed back against Washington over the legislation, warning that it could damage bilateral ties and destabilize global energy markets.

Awe in the Age of AI
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
18:35:04 UTC
03:35:04 KST

Another day, another jaw-dropping feat by AI. Just last month, OpenAI announced that it had solved one of the seven Millennium Prize Problems, a set of complex unanswered questions proposed by the Clay Mathematics Institute in 2000. Then there was Google DeepMind’s new AlphaGenome Atlas, which predicted the biological effects of all 9 billion possible single-letter changes in the human genome.
These feats are awe-inspiring. As are the countless number of milestones and accomplishments each successive AI frontier model has racked up since ChatGPT was launched in 2022. But as we marvel at the machines, what gets crowded out are the humans. While acknowledging the amazing capacity of AI, we shouldn’t lose sight of the irreplaceable value of human-generated awe.
Dacher Keltner, professor of psychology at Berkeley, studies the impact that experiences of awe have on our physical and mental health. He describes awe as “the feeling of being in the presence of something vast that transcends your current understanding of the world.”
The triumphs of AI certainly qualify. But one of Keltner’s studies, which looked at 2,600 stories of awe across 26 countries, had a very revealing finding. “What most commonly led people around the world to feel awe?” he writes. “Nature? Spiritual practice? Listening to music? In fact, it was other people’s courage, kindness, strength, or overcoming.”
The finding, Keltner says, caught his team off guard—they were expecting nature and spirituality to come out on top. Keltner called it “moral beauty,” which he defined as “witnessing the kindness, courage, strength, or selflessness of other people.” Of the moral beauty that inspired awe in the study, 95% came from witnessing actions that people took on behalf of others.
Keltner listed moral beauty as the first of his “eight wonders of life” that are everyday sources of awe. The others are collective movement, nature, music, visual design, spirituality and religion, big ideas, and life and death. Technology can play a part in many of those, but they’re mostly deeply shaped by humans and human connection.
Many of the benefits of awe have a deeply human element. Keltner cites research showing that awe quiets the regions of the brain associated with excessive ego, self-criticism and anxiety. And this can have an expansive and collective impact. “In moments of awe,” Keltner writes in Awe: The New Science of Everyday Wonder and How It Can Transform Your Life, “we shift from the sense that we are solely in charge of our own fate and striving against others to feeling we are part of a community, sharing essential qualities, interdependent and collaborating.”
But what happens when a new technology, like AI, disrupts our sense of authentic community? To be sure, the ease with which our heads can be turned by machines long predates AI and has been with us as long as machines have. The term "technological sublime" was coined by the Harvard historian Perry Miller, who found that by the early nineteenth century "technological majesty" had joined "the starry heavens above and the moral law within to form a peculiarly American trinity of the Sublime.” In 1994, historian David Nye’s American Technological Sublime explored the impact that awe inspired by achievements like automated factories, the first canal systems, and the moon landing had on national identity. Nye notes how tech-inspired awe crowded out the human element. Writing about the awe-inspiring view from the new skyscrapers, he observed that it "divorced the observer from the sense of connection with others." From that height, the people below became "mere insects whose humanity had disappeared.”
And of course, all of us know how the awe of being connected to the entire world through our phones can simultaneously disconnect us from those around us.
Nearly a century ago, Albert Einstein was addressing the students of Caltech—many of whom would no doubt go on to create awe-inspiring technology themselves—and gave them this charge: “Concern for man himself and his fate must always form the chief interest of all technical endeavors... in order that the creations of our mind shall be a blessing and not a curse to mankind. Never forget this in the midst of your diagrams and equations.”
So sure, we will be awed by what the machines can do. But there is also so much awe to be had in our everyday lives, both in nature and in the moral beauty of humans. As Keltner notes, experiencing awe “doesn’t require money or the burning of fossil fuels.” Or tokens!
“Because we have a basic need for awe wired into our brains and bodies,” he writes, “finding awe is easy if we just take a moment and wonder. All of us, no matter what our background, can find our own meaningful path to awe.

She said the parliament’s decision reflected the Iraqi people’s “aspiration to restore and consolidate state sovereignty after the prolonged presence of foreign forces.”
“That presence had effectively continued since 2003 – from the moment of the American invasion under a completely contrived pretext, which triggered decades of instability across the wider region,” Zakharova said in a ministry statement.

“They are capable, among other things, of countering the terrorist threat emanating from ISIS (Daesh) and other such organizations,” she added.

She also reaffirmed Russia’s proposed “Collective Security Concept for the Gulf Region.”
Zakharova said the concept is based on the understanding that states in the region, including Iraq, play the leading role in maintaining stability through close interaction.
On Wednesday, the US Defense Department said the US and its coalition partners “formally concluded Operation Inherent Resolve in Iraq.”
It said the “orderly departure” of coalition forces and equipment from Erbil Air Base marked the conclusion of the military mission.
Baghdad and Washington agreed in September 2024 to end the coalition’s military mission in Iraq under a timetable extending through the end of September 2026, with a transition to bilateral security relations between Iraq and member states.
The coalition was formed under US leadership in 2014 after ISIS seized large areas of Iraq and Syria, providing Iraqi forces with air, intelligence and training support during operations against the terrorist group.
Iraq announced in December 2017 that it had regained full control of territory seized by ISIS.
US forces first invaded Iraq in 2003 to remove Saddam Hussein and withdrew at the end of 2011.

41 Ukrainians made the long journey from occupation to Ukrainian-controlled territory after enduring Russian pressure, detention and control
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
18:31:33 UTC
03:31:33 KST

Ukraine helped 41 citizens escape from Russian-occupied territories into Ukrainian-controlled territory in August and September, including four children and five teenagers, Ukrainian Ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets said.
For many, the crossing marked the end of months or years under Russian occupation and the beginning of their return to life in government-controlled Ukraine.
They returned to Ukraine via Belarus through the Mokrany-Domanove crossing in Ukraine's Volyn Oblast.
From occupation to safety
Lubinets described several cases among those who returned.
One family was able to leave after the father was released from Russian captivity. Their older son remains in captivity, while the woman and her younger son had been under the control of occupation authorities and, according to their account, were previously taken to a detention facility under the pretext of providing medical care and subjected to forced treatment.
A young medical worker was evacuated shortly before she could have been mobilized into Russia’s armed formations, according to Lubinets.
Another returned man had been detained several times in occupied territory and held in basements. His Ukrainian passport had also been confiscated.
Help continues after the crossing
For those returning, reaching Ukrainian-controlled territory is only the first step. The Ombudsman’s Office and partner organizations provide assistance with restoring documents, financial support, temporary accommodation, psychological and social services, and onward travel.
The office said that, in August and September, its joint project with Caritas Ukraine provided assistance to 1,140 people, including people evacuated from occupied territory.
Ukraine’s efforts to facilitate returns are taking place against a broader problem of displacement from occupied territory. A 2026 UN report documented forcible transfers and deportations from areas occupied by Russia, as well as barriers that make it difficult for displaced Ukrainians to return.
The Mokrany-Domanove crossing is one of the routes through which Ukrainians can return to government-controlled territory, making it a key part of Ukraine’s effort to bring civilians home from occupation.
Others are still waiting to leave
Lubinets said his office continues receiving requests from people seeking to leave occupied territory and works with Ukrainian, international and third-country partners to find routes out.
Lubinets noted that the situation remains particularly difficult in Oleshky and surrounding settlements in Kherson Oblast, where Ukrainian authorities say elderly people, people with disabilities, sick residents and families remain without reliable access to food, water, medicine, healthcare and communications. Recent reporting has put the number of civilians still in Oleshky at around 2,000, including about 50 children.

SEFE is a key company in Germany’s energy supply sector, the country’s economic ministry noted.

Why keeping Tom Cruise's secret made Sophie Wilde 'so stressed'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
18:30:00 UTC
03:30:00 KST

Why keeping Tom Cruise's secret made Sophie Wilde 'so stressed'
There have been few movie secrets in 2026 as fiercely guarded as "Who is Digger Rockwell?".
A cryptic teaser landed all the way back in December 2025, showing Tom Cruise's superstar silhouette transformed into something softer and pudgier. In the long months between the teaser and the trailer, rumours whipped around the Alejandro G Iñárritu (Birdman, The Revenant) satirical black comedy.
It was a musical, it was set in purgatory, Digger was based on Dallas Cowboys owner Jerry Jones, it was a bomb, it was a masterpiece.
The narrative remained a mystery right up until a few months ago when audiences learned that Digger Rockwell is an oil magnate with a direct ear to the US president (John Goodman), an uncanny valley cat companion, and a catastrophe on the horizon.
However, secrets and whispers still shrouded the movie with theories on what the "twist" embedded in the film could be.
Digger's enigma was so important to Iñárritu that right up until a few days before release, it hadn't even been announced which character Australian actor Sophie Wilde would be playing.
"I literally feel like Tom Holland right now!" Wilde tells ABC News, referring to the Marvel star's infamous habit of accidentally breaking embargos on his own projects.
"I haven't been able to say anything. It's stressful keeping the secret of the film but I think that the kind of mystery around it is really exciting. I'm very curious how audiences will be receptive to it."
Standing up to Tom Cruise
Digger exists on two different planes: an overt, sneering satire which sees Cruise's business tycoon breathlessly deal with the fallout from his oil drilling causing a Greenland ice shelf to collapse and make its way to mainland Europe.
But lurking beneath the bombastic bluster is something more slippery, a B-plot which re-contextualises Digger's story while forcing the audience to contemplate the very nature of their lives.
"We are trapped in our own narratives, telling our story and we are so distracted that we don't see the story that actually we are living, meaning reality," Iñárritu tells The Screen Show's Jason Di Rosso.
"[Digger] is about storytelling exactly and the power of it and sometimes how useless it is."
It's in this meta B-plot that Wilde's Hannah exists, but to unveil the character any more would go against what Cruise, Iñárritu and a bevy of critics have firmly reiterated — keep Digger's secret.
What can be revealed is Wilde is one of the only actors in the whole production to stand up to Cruise's character. It's a prospect that delighted the young Australian actor.
"Reading that in the script, it's like what an incredible opportunity to get to butt heads with such an amazing actor like Tom. I was nervous, but excited to kind of delve into that," Wilde says.
"I think what's incredible about Alejandro is that we have such an extensive rehearsal period. Then we'd shoot a scene over multiple days. So it was kind of amazing because you had so much time to explore with each other, find new things and really lean into the kind of energy of the scene.
"It felt like a theatre company with the rehearsal process and it felt like a real family."
From NIDA to Digger
Standing alongside industry titans like Cruise and Iñárritu on an immensely high-profile project is an achievement Wilde's not taking lightly.
Involved in acting since she was a child, Wilde graduated from the prestigious Australian National Institute of Dramatic Arts just seven years ago. Not long afterwards, her starring role in Danny and Michael Philippou's breakthrough horror Talk To Me catapulted her into international consciousness.
Since then, she's featured alongside Nicole Kidman in Babygirl and ventured further into TV with Boy Swallows Universe, but Digger was on a whole new level.
"I had so many moments on this film that were pinch-me moments where I was like, 'This is what I imagined making a film like when I was like five years old and I wanted to be an actor,'" Wilde says.
"You're sitting there on these huge sets in Pinewood [studios London] and you're like, 'Wow, like, I'm making a movie.'"
Wilde doesn't take her career for granted, having stuck through the slow shuffle towards stardom that is almost a rite of passage for local actors.
"It's a hard industry and it can be disheartening when things aren't coming your way," she says.
"But I think that everything happens for a reason and it happens at the right time. If you just stick to your guns and continue pursuing what you love, something will come out of it."
Digger in in cinemas now.

Trump's 'excursion into hell' commentary may come back to bite
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
18:30:00 UTC
03:30:00 KST

analysis
Iraq 'excursion into hell' may be over, but there's no end in sight for today's worsening conflicts
There has been a tendency to give a low mark for veracity to many of the utterances of US President Donald Trump in recent times.
But many might find themselves agreeing with his observation this week that the American ventures into Iraq this century have been a "very expensive excursion into hell".
His comments came as the US military announced it had completed its withdrawal of all American troops from Iraq.
"It's been a long time with very bad decision making that got us involved in this quagmire in the first place," Trump said. "It was a quagmire. For many, many years it lasted. But soon that part of history will be over."
Given the war against Iran — which he claimed would only take a couple of weeks — is now in its eighth month, with no end in sight (and possibly even a resurgence), there seemed to be some characteristic chutzpah in Trump's remarks.
He compared the sad US story in Iraq to his administration's actions in Venezuela, and even to the Iran war in terms of the number of US casualties.
But what so many of the current major global conflicts have in common with the debacle in Iraq is their undefined, or sometimes not truthfully defined, missions.
The lack of definition so often explains why there is no end in sight to them and why they seem to only be spreading and escalating by the day.
What happens next is unclear
What happens next in Iraq is not clear. It is already embroiled in the Iranian war, due to the involvement of Iranian-backed militias in Iraq. There are concerns that the United States' withdrawal will also leave a broader vacuum in a still fragile and unstable state.
Trump continues to prevaricate over his next moves against Iran: deploying thousands more troops and a third aircraft carrier strike group to the Middle East, but still flip-flopping about both his bargaining position and the goal of the whole exercise.
The US is talking more again about foiling Iran's nuclear capabilities, rather than regime change or opening the Strait of Hormuz.
US Ambassador to the United Nations Mike Waltz claimed this week that Iran is enriching uranium to 60 per cent with "no credible civilian purpose".
But with the US mid-term elections only a month away and current indications that the Republicans face a drubbing, most analysts believe Trump will be reluctant to escalate action against Iran before November 3.
A poll this week found 71 per cent of Americans disapprove of the president's handling of Iran and the war.
Trump's ally in that war — Benjamin Netanyahu — faces his own election even sooner, with Israel going to the polls on October 27.
Netanyahu under pressure
There was an extraordinary escalation this week in what it is hard not to see as external interventions in the Israeli election campaign.
Over the course of September, there has been revelation after revelation about Netanyahu's knowledge of, and therefore culpability for, the greatest lapse in Israeli intelligence in its history, which in turn led to the horrors of October 7.
There have been revelations piling up from the Israeli newspaper Haaretz, the New York Times, the Wall Street Journal and The Atlantic magazine.
All document claims that Netanyahu was directly warned before October 7 that Hamas was planning a major attack, and that those warnings came from no less than the president of the United Arab Emirates and the head of the Egyptian Intelligence Service.
Netanyahu branded the stories as "lies". But tellingly, other governments have not denied them.
The former head of Israel's domestic counter-intelligence agency Shin Bet, Ronen Bar, also announced he will sue Netanyahu for defamation over the PM's claims he was not told of any threats by his officials, saying he had warned the PM "of an impending disaster, and he ignored me".
And then came the Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani who, as part of a broad attack on Netanyahu as a "war criminal", told British broadcaster Piers Morgan that Qatar had been involved in negotiations with Hamas immediately after the October 7 attacks, approaching Israel with a proposal to release civilian hostages in exchange for a temporary ceasefire window.
According to Al Thani, Israeli officials declined to engage with the proposal, responding that Hamas should release the captives without receiving anything in return.
His statements appeared to confirm earlier reporting that there had been a window in which the Israeli government could have got at least the young and old hostages back from Gaza, but refused to act.
It was hard to escape the impression that even some of those Gulf states closer to Israel had formed the view that there was little chance of stability being gained with Netanyahu in office and were emerging to confront Israeli voters with what they believed was the Israeli PM's record.
All these claims were starting to put intense pressure on Netanyahu in a political environment of a knife-edge election campaign.
There seemed the slightest whiff of panic when Netanyahu emerged on Tuesday to claim there were new "indications that … our enemies will try to attack us" ahead of the October 27 vote.
He did not elaborate on the nature of the threat or give any details — prompting Opposition scepticism and reported denials from officials and the Israeli Defence Force.
The Jerusalem Post reported officials saying there was "currently no specific intelligence warning on the table".
Opposition parties demanded a briefing. Afterward, opposition leader and founder of the centrist Yesh Atid party, Yair Lapid, criticised Netanyahu, saying there was no reason to panic the public, and that if the PM was so worried about security, he should draft the ultra-orthodox Jews who currently had an exemption from military service.
Loading
The flydubai shock turns into a brawl
Then came the extraordinary story of the flydubai plane and the apparent attempt by the co-pilot to crash it, imperilling 174 people flying from Dubai to Tel Aviv.
Such is the political mood in Israel now that, once the shock and relief of the near-miss had eased, the political brawl has all been about Netanyahu.
His opponents have accused him of trying to exploit the incident. His supporters have argued it shows he had been right to issue the unspecified alarm (even though he conceded later there had been no reference to an attack on a commercial airliner).
Israel's election is being fought in an environment where its own war aims — in Gaza, in the West Bank, in Lebanon, and Syria — seem likely to create as much of a mire as Iraq once did.
Another war that was supposed to only take its aggressors a few weeks until victory drags on, with the rhetoric only escalating by the day between Russian President Vladamir Putin and NATO, as Putin finds himself bogged down in the frontline battle in Ukraine.
Alarmingly, Russia now paints NATO as the aggressor, sending the Western military alliance a letter this week threatening to use its nuclear weapons if NATO hinders its access to the Baltic Sea exclave of Kaliningrad.
Germany's Chancellor Friedrich Merz warned this week that Europe is preparing for "severe" Russian hybrid attacks, after Putin threatened that his conflict with the West could reach a "fatal point of no return".
The world now seems to be facing a much broader, multi-fronted and expensive incursion into hell, than it did in Iraq.
Laura Tingle is the ABC's Global Affairs Editor.

Far right shifts from organized groups to digital networks in 2026
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
18:22:00 UTC
03:22:00 KST

Far-right extremism has increasingly shifted from traditional groups with identifiable leaders to decentralized online networks, creating a more fragmented environment that makes radicalization and potential threats harder to track, according to an assessment provided by sources covering the first half of 2026.
The assessment said the transformation has accelerated over the past decade as extremist activity moved further into digital spaces, where narratives previously associated with fringe neo-Nazi and white supremacist circles can reach broader audiences.
It recorded 255 far-right incidents across 30 countries in the first six months of 2026, ranging from propaganda and demonstrations to threats, assaults and serious violence.
The U.S. accounted for 82 cases, followed by the U.K. with 33, Italy with 20 and Spain with 16.
Serious violence or attempted violence, including shootings, bombings, arson and killings, accounted for 37 cases, or 14.5% of the total.
Most of the recorded activity instead involved propaganda, public mobilization or intimidation. Rallies, demonstrations, concerts and public statements accounted for 81 cases, while 77 involved graffiti, leaflets or other written material. Another 60 cases involved assaults, insults or threats.
Racial or ethnic hostility was the most frequently identified motive, accounting for 76 cases. Anti-immigrant and anti-foreigner sentiment followed with 62 cases.
The assessment recorded 41 anti-Muslim incidents and 28 antisemitic cases, while 31 involved anti-government or anti-system ideologies, including accelerationism.
Accelerationism advocates intensifying political violence and social instability to hasten the collapse of the existing political order, with some far-right adherents seeking to replace it with a white ethno-nationalist system.
The assessment said ideological motives often overlap, with white supremacism, anti-immigrant rhetoric, Islamophobia, antisemitism, conspiracy theories and hostility toward state institutions appearing within the same extremist environments.
Security agencies have also focused increasingly on the role of digital platforms in spreading extremist material and connecting individuals across national borders.
Europol has warned that online platforms remain central to extremist propaganda and radicalization, while lone actors and small networks pose particular challenges because they may operate with few direct links to established organizations.
The Terrorgram Collective has emerged as one example of the changing structure of far-right extremism. Individuals influenced by Terrorgram material have been linked by authorities to attacks and plots in several countries, highlighting the ability of extremist propaganda to cross borders without the infrastructure of a conventional organization.
The U.S. designated the transnational white supremacist network and three of its leaders as Specially Designated Global Terrorists in January 2025. U.S. authorities said the predominantly online network promoted violence, circulated material offering guidance for attacks and encouraged supporters to target government officials and minority communities.
The growing role of online communities has also complicated efforts to distinguish between extremist rhetoric and individuals moving toward violence. Much of the material may not cross the threshold for criminal prosecution, leaving authorities to identify the smaller number of users progressing toward threats, attack planning or violent acts.
The figures in the assessment do not represent a comprehensive global count of far-right activity. Its definition covers a wide range of incidents, from propaganda and demonstrations to killings, and no publicly accessible incident-by-incident database was provided to independently verify all 255 cases.
The findings, however, come amid similar warnings from European and U.S. security researchers about the increasingly decentralized nature of far-right extremism and the role of digital communities in radicalization.
Security agencies are increasingly dealing with individuals who may consume extremist propaganda, interact with like-minded users and radicalize online without ever becoming members of a formal extremist organization.

A popular national footwear brand recently published a collaborative Instagram post with a fraternity, despite two former members being recently accused of disseminating nonconsensual intimate images of a fellow college student.
On September 25, HeyDude, a viral shoe brand that was acquired by Crocs in 2022, posted a photo on its Instagram account promoting shoes that appeared to be UF versions of the brand’s popular “Wally” loafer, a lightweight slip-on sneaker with a foam insert.
“@heydude called, @thetachiflorida answered,” the caption read, alongside photos of Theta Chi members clowning around and wearing orange-and-blue sneakers. The brand also posted a video on its TikTok account outside of the Florida fraternity house with the caption “wtf is any shoe besides a HEYDUDE?”
The post led to backlash in the comments section, with many questioning why the brand would choose to work with the fraternity. “#CancelHeyDude,” one person wrote. Another chimed in: “I would boycott if I wore fucking ugly shoes but I don’t so I can’t.”
As WIRED previously reported, two former members of the UF chapter of Theta Chi, Kamran Ahmed and Brendan Pitfield, allegedly used anonymous burner accounts with the handles "Steve 'SC’ Cumfull" and "Arnie_Grape16" to disseminate a nonconsensual intimate video of Maddie Kowalski, then a 19-year-old UF student. One of the "Steve 'SC' Cumfull" posts on X identified Kowalski by her full name and sorority affiliation.
According to affidavits from the Gainesville Police Department, the posts accumulated thousands of views. Kowalski’s name went viral on X, causing her “widespread public humiliation and significant emotional distress,” according to the affidavit. Ahmed and Pitfield are currently being charged with sexual cyberharassment, a first-degree misdemeanor punishable by up to a year in jail and a $1,000 fine. Kowalski is also suing both men for financial damages in Florida Northern District Court. Through their attorneys, Pitfield (who has entered a plea of not guilty) and Ahmed did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Though no other Theta Chi members have been charged, a screengrab of Instagram comments from an account linked to Ahmed appears to show fellow members referencing his alleged burner name. Some comments also appear to reference a cryptocurrency in Kowalski’s name, that the police affidavit alleges Ahmed promoted on X. When reached for comment, Theta Chi CEO Michael Mayer previously told WIRED that the alleged behavior described in the affidavit is “reprehensible” and “completely contrary to Theta Chi’s ideals.”
The charges against Pitfield and Ahmed, as well as WIRED’s reporting on the case, sparked an outcry on the UF campus. On September 15, a group of students advertised a protest outside the Theta Chi fraternity house, circulating a flier demanding that the chapter be removed from the UF campus. “They need to be held accountable,” the flier reads.
On YikYak, the anonymous campus forum, there have also been calls to “boycott” or “nuke” Theta Chi, according to screengrabs reviewed by WIRED. Some anonymous YikYak posts appeared to suggest that the September 15 protest was broken up by campus police outside of Theta Chi: “Cops nuked the theta chi protest good job UF,” one reads. “Typical.” Blake Trauschke, the assistant director of public affairs for UF, tells WIRED that while “there were calls and social media posts for a protest,” she was on site and “none emerged.” She clarified that, as standard UF practice, university police were present “to ensure the safety and security of all.”
Founded in 1856, Theta Chi has established more than 246 chapters at colleges and universities across the country, and it has more than 250,000 initiated members nationwide, according to the organization’s website. At UF specifically, Theta Chi has 190 active members, according to the UF Interfraternity Council.
When asked about the post with HeyDude, a representative for Theta Chi tells WIRED Ahmed and Pitfield are no longer members of Theta Chi Fraternity. “If it is determined through the legal process that the defendants are guilty of the alleged behavior described in the complaints, Theta Chi will support the maximum allowable penalty under the law and the permanent expulsion of the student offenders from the University of Florida,” the spokesperson says.
In mid-September, the Cornell Sun published the names of seven Cornell University students who a former student alleged gang-raped her in 2024 at a Chi Phi frat house; In September, the Jane Doe filed civil cases against them. The revelation has sparked widespread criticism of frat culture on social media. The content creator and activist @bluraybeyond, who has also posted about the Kowalski case, made a Reel calling out HeyDude for posting with UF Theta Chi, writing in a caption “@heydude what the actual heck is your problem #maddiekowalski.” “HeyDude is sending the same message we're seeing out of Cornell and the DA's office: Survivor experiences [are] unimportant to us,” she tells WIRED. She believes the company “has chosen to reward sexual [exploitation] with a lack of accountability and free PR swag.”
After seeing the collab post with HeyDude, Kowalski tells WIRED she and her mother emailed the company to ask why they had decided to work with the UF chapter. She says they did not hear back.
In a statement to WIRED, a HeyDude spokesperson says the company “has no affiliation, sponsorship, or ongoing partnership” with UF Theta Chi and that the post was part of a larger “HeyDude Tailgate Tour” visiting various locations, including frat and sorority houses, across the country.
“We were unaware of the allegations made against” members of the UF Theta Chi chapter “when the tour was planned,” the spokesperson says. “Our company does not support this alleged behavior and takes allegations such as these very seriously. We will reevaluate future stops for the remainder of the tour.”
As of Friday morning, the post was still up.

Residents of Ras al-Ahmar say Israeli restrictions have cut access to water, animal feed, healthcare, as military barrier reshapes Jordan Valley.
Saeed Ayed* watches over his livestock herd. The animals are starving and parched due to a two-week-long Israeli siege on the Ras al-Ahmar Bedouin community in the occupied West Bank’s Jordan Valley.
Access to the community has been blocked since mid-September, as Israeli forces continue building a barrier through Palestinian land in the area, including a road for military patrols, trenches and embankments.
Since the road closures began, movement for Palestinians has been severely restricted. They are forced to move around at night, transporting water, fodder and milk via donkeys under the cover of darkness to avoid detection by Israeli soldiers and settlers.
Ayed told Al Jazeera that no water had entered the community over the past three days after Israeli forces sealed the access points residents had been using to bring in supplies.
“The situation is dire. We are completely besieged, and the livestock cannot survive without water and food for this long,” Ayed said. “We own 15,000 head of livestock, and we fear they will perish because of the siege.”
Ras al-Ahmar is a 300-person village home to around 50 families who have lived off livestock and herding since the 1970s. Ayed said that Israeli settler attacks – part of a wider pogrom against Palestinians across the West Bank – had intensified since February, accusing settlers of trying to force residents out to seize their land.
“We have faced livestock theft, attacks on our dwellings, beatings of residents and vandalism of our homes. This was happening almost daily, yet we refused to leave. Now, they are completely besieging us to force us out,” he added.
The greatest challenge facing residents is restricted access to medical care as a result of the siege, a particular concern for the elderly.
Disease is also rampant among livestock, particularly newborn animals. And with veterinary teams unable to reach the area and treat the animals, deaths have been reported.
The military barrier – which Israel calls Crimson Thread and says it is needed for security – runs for roughly 20km (12 miles) through the northern Jordan Valley, with a width of up to 50 metres (165 feet).
Construction expanded early this year, including the digging of trenches and the bulldozing of agricultural land that damaged wells, water networks and greenhouses. The Israeli military seized nearly 115 hectares, 85 percent of which is privately owned Palestinian land, according to Kerem Navot, which monitors Israeli land policies in the West Bank.
Abdullah Bisharat, head of the village council of Ras al-Ahmar and Atuf, a nearby rural area also facing the military blockade, told Al Jazeera that the Israeli blockade has stopped 51 schoolchildren from attending classes for two weeks because vehicles can no longer reach them.
Israeli forces confiscated a tractor belonging to the village council on Sunday, detaining its driver as he was delivering animal fodder and water to Ras al-Ahmar, Bisharat said.
“We reached out to human rights organisations, but unfortunately no one was able to break the siege. Hundreds of people there are suffering, the majority of whom are women and children,” Bisharat added.
Broader context
The targeting of Bedouin and herding communities in the Jordan Valley is part of a mounting pressure campaign on residents to abandon their properties by restricting access to land and pastures. The tactics include settler violence, the demolition of structures and the closure of roads and access points.
The United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) has described Bedouin and herding communities as among the groups most vulnerable to displacement in the West Bank. Dozens of Palestinian communities across the West Bank have been entirely or partially displaced since 2023, when Israel began its genocide in Gaza and ramped up its attacks on the West Bank after the October 7 Hamas attack.
OCHA has reported that at least 130 Palestinian communities have experienced full or partial displacement since January 2023, with 48 communities completely displaced, including 12 from January to August.
According to OCHA, more than 2,500 Palestinians were displaced in 2026 due to settler attacks and related access restrictions, out of a total of more than 6,400 displaced since 2023.
As the Israeli elections – scheduled for October 27 – approach, Palestinian analysts and rights advocates argue that the measures being implemented on the ground are entrenching a new reality that may persist regardless of the next government.
Hassan Mleihat, chairman of the al-Baydar Organization for Defense of Bedouin Rights, told Al Jazeera that settlers appear to be rapidly intensifying measures aimed at displacing Bedouin communities in the lead-up to the elections.
Mleihat said that Israel’s objective was to expel as many Palestinians as possible and seize control of their land.
“The road being constructed near Ras al-Ahmar aims to dominate the area’s land under security pretexts and to isolate Palestinian communities into tiny geographical pockets, effectively confining their presence there,” he said.
A new reality
Observers believe the significance of these Israeli measures against Palestinian communities extends beyond their immediate impact on the population, creating demographic, geographic and security-related changes that may prove irreversible even if the Israeli political landscape shifts after the elections.
Adel Shadid, an expert on Israeli affairs, told Al Jazeera that Israel currently exercises an unprecedented degree of control over Palestinian territory in the West Bank. Palestinians, he said, live in small, fragmented and scattered enclaves with Israeli control over security, military and economic matters, as well as the minutiae of daily life.
He said the change was not only limited to geography but also entails normalising the presence of illegal Israeli settlements in the West Bank so that they are viewed as an integral part of the region’s fabric, rather than a temporary presence or a reality subject to change.
“This shift is accompanied by the entrenchment of the perception that the West Bank is no longer viewed as a Palestinian area – or even a disputed one – but rather as a territory where Jews have the right to live in safety and security,” he said.
Shadid argued that this perspective also shapes how Israeli and Palestinian communities in the West Bank are perceived by the Israeli state. Israeli settlers are presented as a population requiring protection, while Palestinians are increasingly framed primarily as a security threat.
“This logic extends to how the land and the very elements of life are treated. A tree, for instance, might be viewed as a potential resource for acts targeting the Jewish community; consequently, cutting it down is seen, within this framework, as a security measure that warrants no intervention,” he said.
Shadid said this was also changing perceptions of the role of the Israeli army and police in the West Bank. He argued that the security forces’ role was increasingly seen as protecting settlers against a so-called “Palestinian threat”, rather than restraining settler aggression against Palestinians.
“This new reality is not tied to the current Israeli government. Rather, it creates a dynamic that will persist beyond the elections, regardless of the outcome,” Shadid said.
*Saeed Ayed is a pseudonym used at the individual’s request for security reasons.

The New York Times obtains a purported Russian plan to cripple Ukraine’s power grid, including by cutting electricity and heat supplies to three major cities by 90%

The New York Times obtains a purported Russian plan to cripple Ukraine’s power grid, including by cutting electricity and heat supplies to three major cities by 90%
Russia plans to disable Ukraine’s entire energy system. Ukrainian authorities have obtained a Russian Defense Ministry document outlining the plan, The New York Times reported. Ukrainian Energy Minister Denys Shmyhal showed it to two European politicians in late September, sources told the newspaper. The Times also obtained a copy of the Russian-language document but said its authenticity could not be verified.
The plan calls for a large-scale campaign using various types of missiles, guided aerial bombs, and drones, including jet-powered models. According to the document, Russia plans to carry out the campaign in three stages:
- First stage: Strikes on substations along Ukraine’s western border to prevent the country from importing electricity from Europe.
- Second stage: Strikes on hydroelectric power plants.
- Third stage: Strikes on substations that supply electricity to the three nuclear power plants still under Ukrainian control. Russian troops occupy Ukraine’s fourth nuclear power plant, the Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant.
The campaign’s ultimate goal is to cut off electricity, heat, and water to major Ukrainian cities to provoke a humanitarian crisis.
The plan identifies Kyiv, Kharkiv, and Odesa as the main targets. It calls for reducing electricity and heat supplies to these cities by 90% and disabling a substantial portion of their sewage systems.
The document indicates that Russia plans to eliminate nearly 15 gigawatts of generating capacity — almost as much as Ukraine had at the end of summer 2026, the Times reported.
In August, Shmyhal told Ukraine’s parliament, the Verkhovna Rada, that the country would have 21 gigawatts of generating capacity by the end of the year. That would be enough to meet peak demand, which reached 18 gigawatts last winter. But Russia continues to strike Ukraine’s energy facilities, which could undo the country’s efforts to increase capacity ahead of winter, experts told the Times.
The war in photographs
On October 1, Russian forces deliberately struck a bridge across the Dnipro River in Kyiv for the first time since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Russian drones attacked the bridge three times that day. On the morning of October 2, the Southern Bridge was closed to traffic, and traffic was restricted on the Paton Bridge and the Metro Bridge. Kyiv saw massive traffic jams.
