DR Congo Ebola outbreak killed more than 4,000: official figures
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
16:40:42 UTC
01:40:42 KST

The worst ever Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo has now killed more than 4,000 people out of more than 8,000 confirmed cases, Congolese officials said on Friday.
The Ebola outbreak, officially detected in mid-May, has hit unstable regions in the vast central African country where armed clashes and violence, alongside a critical lack of resources, have hindered the health response to the deadly virus in recent days.
According to the latest official data, there have been 4,018 fatalities from 8,300 cases, with 2,162 people recovering, giving a fatality rate to date of 48.4 percent.
Also recorded have been four deaths among six cases in North Kivu province in the northeast in areas controlled by the anti-government group M23, the Kigali-backed group stated Friday.
After starting in Ituri, also in the northeast, the current outbreak has spread to seven provinces in the north and east.
The response has been hindered by conflict but also mistrust of authority which runs deep among inhabitants of several provinces.
Violent clashes disturbing health aid
Recent days have seen violent clashes between local militias that have hampered the response in Ituri, with more than 5,000 people displaced, the UN said on Thursday.
A transit centre for Ebola patients burned down Tuesday in the same province after soldiers entered a site for displaced people who promptly fled, according to the UN.
A contractor responsible for detecting cases was also killed in an attack on a health facility in North Kivu province, Congolese authorities said Wednesday.
French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot was due in Ituri capital Bunia on Friday to show Paris' support for local authorities and humanitarian workers.
There is no indication France is offering fresh humanitarian aid, but the country did allocate €13.4M to the fight against Ebola between January and July.
The United States has meanwhile announced it is releasing a further €237M to combat the spread of the disease.
Healthcare workers are notably at risk of contracting the virus in poor and remote regions where healthcare infrastructure is poor.
Several vaccines and treatments are currently being studied to combat the Bundibugyo strain of the Ebola virus, which is behind the current outbreak.
The first doses of the Ervebo vaccine — which has been proven effective against the Zaire strain, the most common variant, in the past — have been administered in recent weeks to volunteers among frontline staff as part of a clinical trial.

Burnham to pass law scrapping pension triple lock before next election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
16:39:11 UTC
01:39:11 KST

Andy Burnham will pass legislation to scrap the state pension triple lock in this parliament, even though the guarantee will remain until 2030, the government has said.
The prime minister used his conference speech to announce a change to the policy, which guarantees that the state pension rises by the highest of 2.5%, inflation or earnings growth.
In future, the earnings element will be adjusted to avoid much larger pension increases in years when wages spike.
In his speech, Burnham said the triple lock would remain in place until 2030 – after the next election – keeping Labour’s manifesto promise to retain the guarantee.
However, guidance published alongside the speech shows that the government intends to legislate before then, requiring MPs to vote on the changes.
It means parties will go into the next election setting out in their manifestos whether to retain Labour’s changes or repeal them if they win power.
The guidance also shows that the government estimates that the adjustment to the triple lock would reduce state pension spending by £15bn a year by the end of the 2030s and by £50bn a year by 2050.
However, the Resolution Foundation said on Friday that it was extremely difficult to estimate the savings, with figures ranging from nothing to about £24bn a year depending on which recent decade was used as a model.
Ruth Curtice, the thinktank’s chief executive, wrote on Friday: “The adjusted triple lock saves most in a volatile world, and so saves nothing in the 90s or 00s, and £24bn in the 10s.
“Over the longer term, which will most likely deliver some mixture of all of these economic realities, the new mechanism should trend closer to earnings.
“If real earnings growth permanently disappoints then even the protections in the new mechanism could prove expensive. A new, if not the main, reason to fight to avoid stagnant wages.”
Since it was announced, the policy has been criticised by the Conservatives, Reform UK and the Liberal Democrats – although some Tory and Lib Dem MPs are unhappy with their leaders for campaigning to retain a policy they believe is too costly.
Sharon Graham, the Unite general secretary, said earlier this week that getting rid of the pension triple lock to help fund social care changes would be “electoral suicide”.
However, YouGov has published polling suggesting voters support Burnham’s plan by 48% to 28%.
In his conference speech, Burnham confirmed he would end the pension triple lock and use the savings to fund a national care service in England that would be free at the point of use.
He said his changes would still leave millions of pensioners better off and that they would benefit from the new care system, which is expected to follow the Scottish system by covering care costs but not accommodation.
Burnham also promised to exempt lower-income pensioners from income tax during this parliament.

A Chinese financing company owned by several local government entities has funded the purchase of restricted Nvidia Corp chips, according to documents filed with Beijing regulators, suggesting state support for an illicit trade that Washington worries is fueling China’s artificial intelligence (AI) progress.
Over the past year, Semi-Tech Leasing Group Co (半導體科技租賃) has provided capital to another company called Glory View Technology Co (宏景科技) for the purchase of more than 700 servers, the documents show. One contract identifies funding for 32 units of Asustek Computer Inc (華碩) servers equipped with Nvidia’s B300 chips, bought from a separate Chinese company about which little public information is available.
The regulatory filings give a glimpse into a trade that US President Donald Trump has made clear he does not want to see happen and years of Washington restrictions have sought to prevent. The B300 is part of Nvidia’s powerful Blackwell family of products, and US regulations forbid their sale to China absent an explicit license.
Photo: AFP
However, the rules have failed to entirely stop the movement of those prized semiconductors. Government authorities have alleged that black-market brokers have smuggled into China billions of US dollars worth of Nvidia hardware, including Blackwell chips — exploiting what some US officials see as glaring gaps in corporate due diligence and weak government enforcement.
An order of 32 servers — model name XA NB3I-E12 — is small. While hundreds of other servers that Semi-Tech Leasing purchased match the specifications for Nvidia Blackwell chips, the documents do not explicitly identify the hardware in question. Still, the records point to a key dynamic of the illicit trade: the Chinese government, at least in this instance, has helped make it happen.
Nvidia said it is “looking into this report and will work with our OEM customer to investigate,” a reference to so-called original equipment manufacturers like Asustek that buy Nvidia chips and assemble them into servers. Asustek said in a statement that the company “is committed to strict compliance with all applicable laws and regulations, including export controls.”
Semi-Tech Leasing, which in June changed its name from Sino IC Leasing Co (芯鑫融資租賃), was set up in 2015 by the China Integrated Circuit Industry Investment Fund — colloquially known as the Big Fund — to provide financial support to the semiconductor industry. After the Big Fund sold most of its shares in 2020, local governments in Shenzhen, Beijing and other provinces have jointly controlled most of Semi-Tech Leasing’s shares, according to Chinese company registry information.
In recent years, Semi-Tech Leasing has expanded its remit to data center infrastructure and deployed more than 11 billion yuan (US$1.6 billion) to “create an ecosystem encompassing model training, chips and other aspects of the AI industry,” the company’s chairman said at an April financial conference in Shanghai, according to local reports. Semi-Tech Leasing, he added, “spares no effort in serving and supporting national strategy.”

The Coast Guard Administration (CGA) yesterday said it expelled two Chinese fishing boats that had entered Taiwan’s prohibited waters near Pratas Islands (Dongsha Islands, 東沙群島).
At about 11am on Thursday, an unidentified boat was detected about 15.5 nautical miles northeast of Pratas Island, or 5.5 nautical miles inside Taiwan’s prohibited waters, it said.
The Yunlin patrol vessel was dispatched to the area, and at about 3pm, it found two Chinese fishing boats — the Yue Hui Dong Yu 75066 (粵惠東漁75066) and the Jin Sha (金鯊) — about 27 nautical miles east of Pratas Island, or 8 nautical miles inside restricted waters, the CGA said.
Photo courtesy of the CGA
The Yunlin repeatedly issued warnings to the boats and asked them to leave, it said.
The Yue Hui Dong Yu sailed away, but the Jin Sha refused to leave, the CGA said.
After three unsuccessful attempts to get the Jin Sha to leave, the coast guard used its water cannon for 30 seconds about 200m away from the Chinese vessel — in line with the law — but that, too, proved ineffective, it said.
The Yunlin then gradually approached the Jin Sha and sprayed water at it for 90 seconds, the agency added.
The decision to use low-lethality weaponry to drive the boats away from Taiwan-controlled waters was in line with CGA standard operating procedures, it said.
The Yunlin later provided 35 hot meals to the Jin Sha’s crew members at the Chinese boat’s request, towed it out of restricted waters and handed it over to a Chinese work vessel early yesterday morning, the CGA said.
The agency said it is committed to lawfully driving away vessels that have crossed into its borders, and that its mission to safeguard national maritime borders and carry out humanitarian assistance remains unchanged.
The CGA also urged China to prevent further illegal fishing activities in the area and to protect marine resources.
Dongsha, which is about 450km southwest of Kaohsiung and where about 300 CGA personnel are stationed, is one of two island groups controlled by Taiwan in the South China Sea.
The other is Itu Aba (Taiping Island, 太平島) which is about 1,600km southwest of Kaohsiung. About 200 coast guard personnel are stationed there.
The CGA defines “prohibited waters” as territorial waters, which extend 12 nautical miles around Taiwan proper and varying distances around Taiwan’s outlying islands.
“Restricted waters” refer to a contiguous zone, which states use to bolster their law enforcement capacity in areas just outside their territorial seas.
That contiguous zone extends 24 nautical miles around Taiwan proper, and varying distances around the nation’s outlying islands.

Egypt arrests independent publication’s entire team
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
16:38:56 UTC
01:38:56 KST

Egyptian authorities swept up the entire editorial team of one of the country’s few independent media, accusing them on Thursday of belonging to the outlawed Muslim Brotherhood.
The arrest this week of the six journalists of Matsadaash (Arabic for “Don’t Believe”) sparked an outcry from international and regional rights groups, which called it an “alarming escalation on independent media and freedom of expression.”
Authorities accused the six of being members of the Muslim Brotherhood, alleging they produced fabricated news for an online outlet in exchange for foreign funding.
Photo: AP
Matsadaash cofounder Abdelrahman Mansour denied the allegations and said he and their families have no idea where they are.
“Everyone on this team knew the risks when they went to work every day, but it’s unacceptable for the government to make false accusations and forcibly disappear journalists just because they’re afraid of a free press,” he said, speaking from outside Egypt.
“Their families are worried, we’re worried, we just want them released unharmed,” he said.
Founded eight years ago as a fact-checking platform, Matsadaash has since expanded into investigative reporting in Egypt and other Arab countries.
Mansour said two of the outlet’s editors were arrested in 2023, but were released without charge after State Security investigators found no affiliation with the Muslim Brotherhood.
“It’s very difficult for us to understand why this is happening,” he said.
Egypt is among the world’s worst jailers of journalists, the US-based Committee to Protect Journalists said. The Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights says 26 journalists are behind bars in Egypt.
The Egyptian Ministry of the Interior on Thursday described Matsadaash as an unlicensed page managed from abroad by a “fugitive Brotherhood member” it identified as Mansour.
It said the six people detained were part of a Brotherhood “media committee” that prepared false and fabricated news for Mansour to publish. Only one of the six is a member of the Journalists’ Syndicate, the national press union, the statement said. It said legal measures have been taken, but did not specify charges.
The first arrest occurred on Monday night when authorities went to the home of Abdallah Qadry, Mansour said.
The other five members of staff were arrested on Tuesday, starting with Mohamed Abu Emaira, who was taken from his home in the early hours.
Omar Helal was arrested in Port Said and Islam Barakat in Gharbia Governorate. Two other members of Matsadaash’s newsroom staff — Mohamed Mahmoud and Mohamed Adel — were arrested in Cairo.
All had their cellphones and computers confiscated.
The Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights said the whereabouts of all six remain unknown.
“They have not been allowed to contact their families or legal team,” the advocacy group said.
It was the first time an entire newsroom had been arrested in Egypt.
Matsadaash, founded in 2018 as an online platform, has gained credibility and a large following in Egypt, where independent media are stifled and government censorship and oversight over newspapers and TV networks are the norm. The Matsadaash Web site is blocked in Egypt, but its Facebook page has more than 1 million followers.
More than 80 international and regional rights groups, civil society organizations and independent media called on the Egyptian authorities to release the journalists, condemning what they called an escalating crackdown on independent media.
“Matsadaash has operated openly for years and has built a reputation for credible and accurate reporting on a range of public interest issues across Egypt,” said the petition, signed by groups including Human Rights Watch and Reporters Without Borders. “Egyptian authorities’ failure to allow free expression to thrive flies in the face of a purported commitment to dialogue, transparency, anti-corruption, and regional leadership.”

US to put anti-ship missiles on island near Taiwan for drill
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
16:38:55 UTC
01:38:55 KST

The US military is planning to deploy an advanced anti-ship missile system to a Japanese island close to Taiwan for the first time during a major training exercise later this month.
The Navy-Marine Expeditionary Ship Interdiction System is slated to be moved to the island of Yonaguni during the bilateral exercise known as Keen Sword, according to a person familiar with the matter. An outline of the exercise plans, published on the island’s website yesterday, shows the Japanese military may deploy its own anti-ship missile and surface-to-air missile systems for the drills.
Yonaguni is just 110 kilometers east of Taiwan, the closest point in Japan to the democratically governed island that is also claimed by China. The potential deployment of the missile systems and other hardware such as electronic warfare vehicles to Yonaguni for training would represent a step up from previous military exercises on the island.
Photo: US Marine Corps via Bloomberg
Last year, the US military held a training exercise to bring supplies to Yonaguni to simulate the creation of a forward-operating base that might be needed in any regional crisis. The striking range of the NMESIS system is around 115 miles, which means it could reach ships around Taiwan.
A Chinese foreign ministry spokeswoman said last year that Japan’s plans to permanently station surface-to-air missiles on Yonaguni from 2030 would “create regional tension and provoke military confrontation.” Meanwhile, Chinese state media criticized a move last year by the US to send the NMESIS system to the Philippines for exercises.
Keen Sword takes place once every two years and is one of the largest joint military exercises by the US with Japan. It will take place from Oct. 19 to 29 this year across Japan’s southern island chain as both nations work on making training more realistic for a possible crisis, such as an attempt by China to seize Taiwan.
US military hardware in the Asia-Pacific region has been depleted by deployments to the Middle East for the war against Iran, including the aircraft carrier USS George Washington, which is usually based in Japan.
Still, after a recent summit meeting in New York with US President Donald Trump, Japan’s Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi played up the strength of the alliance between the two countries.
At the same time, Takaichi has come under pressure from China to retract remarks she made last year that suggested Japan might mobilize its military in any collective effort to defend Taiwan from an invasion.

Vice President Hsiao Bi-khim (蕭美琴) yesterday praised a Taiwan-made robotic dog and emphasized the importance of integrating traditional and emerging industries to drive defense and dual-use innovation.
Hsiao made the remarks while touring the Taichung Smart and Artificial Intelligence Manufacturing Show’s defense industry pavilion, which showcased uncrewed aerial vehicles, small arms and Taiwan’s first domestically made robotic dog named “Taiwan Tu Gou” (台灣土狗), a reference to the Taiwanese mountain dog, also known as the “Formosan dog.”
The government places a premium on Taiwan’s precision manufacturing, machine tooling, artificial intelligence (AI), and other innovative sectors based in Taichung, Hsiao said.
Photo: Tsai Shu-yuan, Taipei Times
Integrating innovation into traditional manufacturing, national defense industrial base, dual-use technology and civilian applications are major priorities for Taiwan’s economic policy, she added.
Hsiao praised the research and development team, saying that they made a laudable contribution to Taiwan’s AI and manufacturing industries.
Parkson Wu Industrial Co chairman Wu Ming-hsi (吳銘禧) said they collaborated with Jia Chen Electronic Co in developing Taiwan Tu Gou.
The robot dog’s research and development, component sourcing, manufacturing and assembly process are fully Taiwanese, he said, adding that the system can be utilized for security patrols, transportation and other tasks requiring precise movement.
Jia Chen Electronic Co vice president Liu Jen-jui (廖仁瑞) said Taiwan Tu Gou used a planetary speed reducer, and an integrated engine and motor driver board module that made the system extremely compact.
The most powerful of the robot’s joints has an instant torque of 250 Newton-meters, he added.
The Tu Gou can leap, has a 30kg load-bearing capacity and can navigate complex terrain that would allow it to perform military roles, including autonomous patrols and operations in special environments, he said.
Taiwan Tu Gou is a practical design capable of carrying meaningful cargo and performing real-world tasks at a competitive price point, compared with “for show only” pieces produced by the Chinese industry, he added.

Taiwan receives first 2 F-16V Block 70s
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
16:38:53 UTC
01:38:53 KST

Taiwan yesterday took delivery of the first two of 66 F-16V Block 70 jets purchased from the US after years of delays, helping to strengthen an air force that has to scramble almost daily to shadow China’s military.
The aircraft, bearing tail numbers 6727 and 6728, landed at Chihhang Air Base in Taitung County at about noon after departing from Hawaii and making a stop in Guam.
The two fighter jets had been expected to arrive in Taiwan by the end of August, but remained in Hawaii without explanation as US President Donald Trump prepared to meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping (習近平) late last month.
Photo: Yu Tai-lang, Taipei Times
The delivery comes amid growing concern in Taiwan about the Trump administration’s commitment to arming Taipei, despite Washington saying there has been no change in policy.
President William Lai (賴清德) welcomed the arrival of the two aircraft.
“This is an important milestone in strengthening Taiwan’s air defense capabilities. It also demonstrates our resolve to bolster self-defense and ensure peace through strength,” Lai wrote in a social media post.
Lai said it was his administration’s “unwavering” goal to preserve peace in the Taiwan Strait, and that investing in national defense, which increases the cost of invading Taiwan and lowers the risk of miscalculation, helps further that aim.
Air Force Command said in a statement that it would carry out a planned transition training and gradually complete preparations for the new aircraft to ensure that their operational capabilities are brought online in phases.
The F-16V Block 70s would be operated by the 7th Tactical Fighter Wing, which was established on Dec. 1, 2023, it said.
The wing is being organized into operational squadrons in three phases, with air and maintenance personnel being sent to the US in batches for transition training, it said.
Some of the remaining F-16V Block 70s have reached the stage of being ready for delivery, it said, adding that it would continue coordinating with the US program office and managing the delivery and return of the aircraft to Taiwan according to the planned schedule.
Earlier in the day, Minister of National Defense Wellington Koo (顧立雄) told reporters at the Legislative Yuan that “there will be more than two jets delivered this year.”
The delivery dates of subsequent F-16V Block 70s would be determined in coordination with the US, he said.
Asked where the new F-16Vs would be stationed, Koo said that, in line with the military’s strategy, eastern Taiwan would be an important stronghold for preserving combat power. He did not elaborate.
The US approved the sale of 66 F-16Vs and related equipment to Taiwan in 2019 for about US$8 billion. Delivery was expected to begin in 2023 and be completed this year, but delays due to technical issues have pushed the timetable back.
The arrival of the first two aircraft yesterday also came almost exactly a week after Trump met Xi in Washington.
Trump said after meeting Xi in Beijing in May that he was holding a new US$14 billion package for Taiwan in abeyance, although he did approve one worth US$11 billion in December last year.
The F-16Vs have advanced avionics, weapons and radar systems to better counter the Chinese air force, including its stealthy J-20 fighters, though Washington has been unwilling to provide Taiwan its most advanced fighters such as the F-22 or F-35.
An upgrade program for Taiwan’s existing F-16s was completed in 2023.
The US is bound by law to provide Taiwan with the means to defend itself, but the two have no formal diplomatic relations.
“We continue to stand with friends and allies across the Indo-Pacific to advance our shared prosperity, security and values — that includes Taiwan,” a US Department of State spokesperson said when asked about the new F-16s.
Dozens of locals, some carrying binoculars and telephoto lenses, gathered near the air base’s perimeter fence to watch the highly anticipated arrival of the jets.
Kimi Chi, a salesman from Taichung, had traveled through the night to be able to photograph the aircraft landing in Taitung.
He was philosophical about the delays, saying “good things take time.”
“In terms of hardware capabilities, there will definitely be an improvement,” the 37-year-old told reporters.
“But what we are actually lacking the most right now is pilots. Of course, I hope the government can provide better additional allowances for these military pilots,” he said.
Former air force serviceman Eric Chan, 57, marveled at the improvements made to the F-16 over the past 30 years and said the fighter jets based in Taitung would “play a very important defensive role” against China.
“The threat from the Chinese Communist Party has always been there, so we definitely need to strengthen our defense capabilities,” Chan said.

Citi’s token service lets Taiwan firms shift cash any time
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
16:38:52 UTC
01:38:52 KST

Taiwanese companies with overseas operations can use Citigroup Inc’s digital payment service to move funds between eligible Citi accounts around the clock, helping them manage cash across different time zones without being constrained by conventional banking hours, Citi Taiwan executives said yesterday.
Citi Token Services is already operating in seven markets — the US, UK, Hong Kong, Singapore, Ireland, Japan and the United Arab Emirates — and supports US dollar and euro transactions.
Taiwan is not among the markets where the service operates, but local clients with Citi accounts in those markets can use it for liquidity and other operational needs, Citi country officer for Taiwan Christie Chang (張聖心) said at a media briefing in Taipei.
Photo courtesy of Citi Taiwan
The service allows companies to transfer funds between eligible Citi accounts almost instantly, including on weekends and public holidays. Hundreds of clients are using the system, with about US$1 billion in tokenized deposits moving through it each day, Citi Taiwan head of treasury and trade solutions Vivien Cheng (程雯) said.
For Taiwanese companies with factories, suppliers or customers in different markets, the service can reduce the need to wait for banks to reopen when moving funds between regional operations, Cheng said.
Citi Token Services uses blockchain technology to represent bank deposits digitally and transfer them between eligible accounts. The funds remain within Citi’s banking network and are deposits held with the bank, rather than cryptocurrency, Cheng said.
Unlike some other foreign banks, Citi does not require customers to set up a separate digital account to use its blockchain-based payment service, allowing them to use their existing Citi accounts, Cheng said, adding that the service is increasingly used by Asian e-commerce providers doing business in the US.
Citi is also working with cryptocurrency exchange Coinbase Global Inc to connect traditional banking services with stablecoins, digital tokens designed to maintain a stable value against currencies such as the US dollar.
Coinbase has selected Citi’s Virtual Account Wallet to support its Coinbase Virtual Accounts, which provide bank-account-like functions for receiving, holding and making payments, Cheng said. Traditional currency received through the service can be automatically converted into stablecoins.
The service, still emerging in Taiwan, is particularly useful for companies operating in markets with volatile currencies, where sudden exchange-rate swings can quickly erode profit margins, Cheng said.
Citi Taiwan said it has seen double-digit growth across all of its businesses so far this year and expects to remain profitable for the rest of the year and beyond.

A US lawmaker has called on Starbucks to close its first stores in Xinjiang, China, calling it a “morally bankrupt decision” to do business in a region where Uighurs face repression.
China denies widespread accusations about abuses of the Uighurs, a mainly Muslim people, saying its policies there were aimed at combating terrorism, separatism and religious extremism.
Starbucks opened its first two stores this week in Xinjiang’s capital, Urumqi, including one at the city centre’s grand bazaar and a second at its international airport.
Photo: Reuters
John Moolenaar, chairman of the Select Committee on China of the House of Representatives, called on Starbucks to “immediately reverse course and close its stores.”
“This is a shocking and morally bankrupt decision by a company that prides itself on social responsibility,” he said in a statement published on Thursday.
“There is no justifiable reason for an American company to do business in a region where the CCP [Chinese Communist Party] has detained more than a million Uyghurs and is stripping them of their faith, language, and culture,” he said.
Neither Starbucks nor the Chinese Ministry of Foreign Affairs immediately responded to requests for comment. China is in the middle of its week-long national day holiday.
Starbucks said on its official WeChat platform this week that they were not just new coffee outlets in Xinjiang, but a new experience that blended local culture and customer needs.
The company would continue investing in Xinjiang, Starbucks China CEO Liu Wenjuan (劉文娟) said in the WeChat post.
Pictures of the stores posted on the platform showed Starbucks’ logo in English and Chinese. There were no obvious images of any Uighur-language signs. Uighur is written in an Arabic-based script and is meant to enjoy official parity in Xinjiang.
In April 2026 Starbucks finalised its China joint venture by bringing in a strategic investor, Boyu Capital, as its 60 percent stakeholder. The joint venture operates about 8,000 outlets in China.

Ten wishes for Teachers’ Day
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
16:38:51 UTC
01:38:51 KST

A teacher who is truly happy and supported in their work does not need extra fanfare and check ins — “are you happy?” — on Teachers’ Day. If they already enjoyed respect and trust in the day-to-day, they also would not need the minister of education to send a letter of thanks on the eve of the holiday. In fact, the grander the ceremony, the starker the contrast is with their everyday reality.
Every Sept. 28, schools hold events in teachers’ honor; parent associations deliver gift boxes and education authorities send elegant greeting cards, but once the hoopla dies down and teachers return to the classroom, many are left with a sense of exhaustion and bitter irony. Teachers’ happiness should not be reserved for the holidays alone.
To that end, here are 10 things — addressed to schools, parents and the education system — teachers would truly like to receive.
First, to schools. We must return to the original purpose of education and reject internal conflict and division.
One: Stop holding teaching hostage to performance data. Test scores can never fully capture growth; we must let go of the obsession with performance metrics and allow teachers and students to return to the simple process of learning and growing together.
Two: Do not let “campus incident resolution councils” become tools for disciplinary crackdowns. The purpose of the system is to safeguard education, not to expand administrative power or suppress dissent. Schools should be protected spaces, not arenas for power struggles.
Three: Stop driving wedges between teachers. Administrators and educators are partners, not opposing camps to be divided through unequal treatment. Only by ending internal conflict can teachers fully exercise their expertise.
Next, to parents. Teachers must be seen as professionals, not service workers. When parents think of themselves as paying consumers, teachers are expected to become around-the-clock service providers. Complaints are lodged at the slightest issue, while teachers must be paragons of virtue and withstand whatever is thrown their way.
Four: Allow teachers to clock out. Drawing boundaries between work and personal life is not a sign of laziness.
Five: Respect teachers’ professional discretion. Try trusting teachers’ judgement before complaining about classroom management.
Six: Remember that the teacher-parent relationship is a partnership, not a client-server dynamic. What teachers truly want is not a gift box, but for someone say: “Let’s figure this out together.”
Finally, education authorities must serve as a real backstop, not a public-relations front. If conflict resolution is simply to appease public criticism and always demand that teachers apologize, even the most beautiful greeting cards offer little comfort.
Seven: Guarantee fair pay and working hours. Education should not become a “sweatshop” in which teachers work without overtime pay and must be constantly available.
Eight: Establish the facts before taking a position. Each unreasonable demand given in to is another blow to teachers’ dignity.
Nine: Protect the teaching environment. Those outside the profession should not dictate teaching decisions, and education must not be consumed by political theatrics.
Ten: Make it unnecessary to ask teachers “are you happy?” on Sept. 28 by empowering them in their work on the other 364 days of the year.
When the day arrives that these 10 wishes are realized, teachers would at last be able to feel that the system has their back — and that the phrase “Happy Teachers’ Day” would truly carry weight.
Chin Ching is an educator.
Translated by Gilda Knox Streader

Bureau dismisses early HSR deployment suggestion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
16:38:50 UTC
01:38:50 KST

The Railway Bureau has dismissed a suggestion that the new high-speed trains could be put into service ahead of schedule to ease capacity constraints, saying that the trains must pass all required tests before they can enter service.
The first of 12 newly acquired high-speed trains arrived in Taiwan in mid-August and has been assembled, but still needs to undergo static and dynamic testing, said Railway Bureau director-General Yang Cheng-chun (楊正君) told reporters in Tainan on Thursday.
“Testing is a mandatory part of the approval process,” Yang said, adding that the Ministry of Transportation and Communications would not authorize Taiwan High Speed Rail Corp (THSRC) to put the new trains into service unless all required tests have been completed.
Photo courtesy of the THSRC
Yang made the remarks in response to a suggestion that new high-speed trains be deployed to ease capacity constraints after many passengers with reserved seats were unable to board their trains on the day before last week’s Mid-Autumn Festival and Teachers’ Day long weekend, as aisles in reserved-seat cars and passageways between carriages were blocked by passengers spilling over from non-reserved cars.
Aside from the one that arrived in mid-August, two other new trains are scheduled to be delivered to Taiwan next month and in January next year, respectively.
Under the THSRC’s plan, the three new trains are scheduled to be in operation by July next year. The remaining nine trains would be gradually added to the fleet by 2028.
The main dynamic and static testing is scheduled to be completed around April next year, with further document reviews and related procedures expected to take place in May and June, Yang said.

ANALYTICAL ENGLISH 解析英語(常春藤)
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
16:38:49 UTC
01:38:49 KST

Toxic chemicals from discarded electronic devices may be threatening endangered dolphins and porpoises in the South China Sea, according to a recent scientific study. Liquid crystal monomers (LCMs), chemicals widely used in smartphones, televisions and computer screens, were detected in several marine mammals. Scientists warned that these substances could pose risks to humans as well through contaminated seafood and water sources. The findings have raised concerns about the growing environmental harm caused by electronic waste worldwide.
The chemicals were found in different parts of the animals’ bodies, including blubber, the liver, the kidneys, muscles and even brain tissue. After examining tissue samples collected from Indo-Pacific humpback dolphins and finless porpoises between 2007 and 2021, researchers discovered how widely the pollutants had spread. What worried them most was that the chemicals had already crossed the blood-brain barrier and could damage important biological functions in marine animals.
Scientists believe the pollutants likely reached the marine mammals through the ocean food chain. Earlier studies had already identified similar chemicals in fish and other sea creatures commonly eaten by dolphins and porpoises. Some laboratory experiments have also shown that contact with LCMs may disrupt normal cell growth and DNA repair. Scientists also think the chemicals may accumulate in animals higher up the food chain.
Photo: AdobeStock 照片： AdobeStock
As electronic waste continues to increase around the world, the problem may become even more serious in the future. Scientists urge consumers to extend the life of their electronic devices through repairs and to dispose of old electronics properly. They also call for stricter regulations for harmful chemicals used in electronic products as well as further research into how LCM pollution affects wildlife.
根據近期一項科學研究，廢棄電子裝置中的有毒化學物質可能正對南海瀕危的海豚與鼠海豚造成威脅。液晶單體（LCMs）是廣泛用於智慧型手機、電視與電腦螢幕的化學物質，已在數種海洋哺乳動物體內被檢出。科學家警告，這些物質也可能經由受汙染的海鮮與水源而對人類造成風險。這些發現使外界對全球電子廢棄物日益加劇的環境危害感到憂心。
這些化學物質在動物身體的不同部位中被發現，包括脂肪層、肝臟、腎臟、肌肉，甚至是腦組織。研究人員在檢驗 2007 年至 2021 年間採集的中華白海豚與江豚組織樣本後，發現這些汙染物已廣泛擴散。最令他們擔憂的是，這些化學物質已經穿越血腦屏障，可能會損害海洋動物的重要生理功能。
科學家認為，這些汙染物很可能是透過海洋食物鏈進入海洋哺乳動物體內。先前的研究已在魚類及其他海豚與鼠海豚常食用的海洋生物中發現類似化學物質。一些實驗室研究也顯示，接觸液晶單體可能會干擾正常的細胞生長與 DNA 修復。科學家也認為，這些化學物質可能會在食物鏈較高層的動物體內逐漸累積。
隨著全球電子廢棄物持續增加，這個問題未來可能變得更加嚴重。科學家呼籲消費者透過維修來延長電子裝置的使用壽命，並妥善處理廢棄電子產品。他們也呼籲政府對電子產品中使用的有害化學物質實施更嚴格的規範，並進一步研究液晶單體汙染對野生動物造成的影響。
What Did You Learn?
1. What devices mentioned in the passage contain LCMs?
2. How do LCMs most likely enter the bodies of dolphins and porpoises?
參考答案:
1. Smartphones, televisions and computer screens.
2. Through the ocean food chain.
Words in Use
1. toxic a. 有毒的
The factory dumped toxic chemicals into the river near the village. 這家工廠將有毒化學物質丟棄在村莊附近的河流裡。
2. discard vt. 丟棄（本文為過去分詞作形容詞用）
Hospitals must follow strict rules to discard medical waste safely. 醫院必須依照嚴格規範，安全丟棄醫療廢棄物。
3. mammal n. 哺乳動物
The blue whale is the largest mammal living on Earth today.
藍鯨是現今地球上最大的哺乳動物。
4. contaminated a. 受汙染的
Residents were warned not to drink the contaminated water.
居民被警告不要飲用受汙染的水。
5. tissue n.（動植物細胞的）組織
Doctors examined tissue samples collected from several sick marine animals.
醫生檢查了從數種患病海洋動物身上採集的組織樣本。
Practical Phrases
1. raise concerns about. . . 引發對……的擔憂
concern n. 擔心（的事）
The rise in food prices has raised concerns about inflation. 食品價格上漲已引發對通貨膨脹的擔憂。
2. urge. . . to V 敦促∕力勸……（做）……
urge vt. 力勸
Environmental groups urged companies to reduce the use of plastic packaging.
環保團體敦促企業減少使用塑膠包裝。
3. dispose of. . . 處理∕處置……
dispose vi. 處置
Hospitals must dispose of sheets and gowns carefully. 醫院必須小心地處理床單和病袍。
4. call for. . . 呼籲∕要求……
Many citizens called for better public transportation in the city.
許多市民呼籲改善該市的大眾運輸。

Botanically, it belongs to the same family as spinach and beets. It is not a true grain at all, but a seed humans have relied on for thousands of years. Quinoa originated in the Andes Mountains of South America—particularly in Peru, Bolivia and Chile—where it has been cultivated for over 5,000 years. National Day to showcase Taiwanese vitality: official
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
16:38:49 UTC
01:38:49 KST

Legislative Speaker Han Kuo-yu (韓國瑜) yesterday said this year’s Double Ten National Day celebrations would feature a wide range of programs showcasing the diversity, vitality and unity of Taiwanese society.
Han, chairman of the National Day Preparatory Committee, made the remarks at a news conference held at the Legislative Yuan. It was attended by officials, including Taitung County Commissioner Yao Ching-ling (饒慶鈴) and Deputy Minister of the Interior Wu Tang-an (吳堂安).
The National Day ceremony on Saturday next week would feature performances by the military honor guard and parades by civic and student groups, among others, he said, adding that they intend to showcase Taiwanese society’s diversity, vitality and dignity.
Photo: CNA
The ceremony would pay tribute to the land and all those who have contributed to the country, while reflecting on the nation’s development and the achievements of Taiwanese around the world, Han said.
There will also be celebrations outside Taipei, such as an evening celebration at New Taipei City’s Banciao Stadium titled “A Stage for the World — Together in Taiwan,” he said.
That would feature a concert with performances by local and foreign artists including singer Enno Cheng (鄭宜農) and Indonesian pop band Grrrl Gang.
On Oct. 10, a fireworks display will be held at Taitung’s Haibin Park, he added.
At a separate event held yesterday, Presidential Office Secretary-General Pan Men-an (潘孟安) said this year’s light projection show on the Presidential Office building would spotlight the 30th anniversary of Taiwan’s first direct presidential election by looking back at the country’s democratic development over the past three decades.
It would tell Taiwan’s story while looking ahead to the next 30 years and the future of its democracy, Pan added.
National Cultural Association of Taiwan Secretary-General Lee Hou-ching (李厚慶) said previous light shows highlighted important periods in Taiwan’s history and culture.
This year, the show aims to remind spectators that “Taiwan’s democracy is not simply a subject in history books, but a part of everyday life,” while highlighting the role Taiwanese have played in shaping the nation’s democratic development, Lee said.
The National Day light show starts next week, from Wednesday to Sunday, with projections shown every 30 minutes from 7pm to 9:30pm.

Manchester City are expected to press ahead with an appeal against findings that they breached Premier League financial rules by yesterday’s deadline, opening a fresh chapter in a case that has already become one of the most significant in English soccer.
The club has consistently denied wrongdoing, and indicated they would challenge an independent commission’s findings that they used “sham” commercial contracts as part of schemes to inflate revenue and understate costs by more than ￡900 million (US$1.19 billion) over nearly a decade.

Photo: AP
The Premier League’s new fast-track rules state that an appeal hearing must be held within 12 weeks of an appeal being lodged, with a decision due within 30 days of the hearing concluding.
However, City is expected to argue the rules were not in place when they were originally charged in February 2023.
The breadth of the fallout facing Manchester City extends well beyond soccer sanctions.
On Thursday, the chair of the Treasury Committee asked Britain’s tax authority HMRC what action it was taking in response to the Premier League’s findings.

S Korea’s Lee strips prosecutors of power
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
16:38:46 UTC
01:38:46 KST

South Korean President Lee Jae-myung has pushed through a sweeping overhaul of the criminal justice system, stripping investigative powers from prosecutors he accuses of abusing their authority, including criminal cases against him before he took office.
A revised law that came into force yesterday focuses on shifting power to police from prosecutors, leaving the latter primarily to decide whether cases should go to trial.
“The purpose of prosecution reform is to ensure that the powers and responsibilities entrusted to investigative and prosecutorial authorities to protect victims, human rights and the social order are not abused for politically motivated investigations and prosecutions,” Lee said last month, vowing to make the reform irreversible.
Photo: EPA
South Korea’s prosecutors have long been accused of exercising excessive power, but the move has raised concerns that it might create gaps that leave crime victims worse off. The optics of the reform, led by a president who faces pending cases launched by prosecutors, are also feeding into a drop in Lee’s public support.
Supporters of the move claim it would help break up an institution that has contributed to political instability over the years. Of the eight presidents who served before Lee since the country embraced direct democratic elections in 1987, four have been imprisoned, ousted or both after investigations by prosecutors. Another, Roh Moo-hyun, died by suicide while facing an investigation into allegations of bribery involving his family a year after his term ended.
Lee’s own ascent to the country’s top job last year followed a martial law fiasco triggered by his predecessor and top prosecutor-turned-president, Yoon Suk-yeol.
The overhaul scraps the Supreme Prosecutors’ Office and launches two new agencies to take on some of the office’s functions. A new Prosecution Service is to make decisions on whether to indict suspects and handle prosecutions in court.
The newly formed Serious Crimes Investigation Agency will take responsibility for launching and carrying out probes into seven categories of crimes, including corruption and national security transgressions. The police and the Corruption Investigation Office for High-Ranking Officials are to take the lead on other investigations, though there still might be scope for disagreements over which agency has jurisdiction.
The revision comes as Lee’s own trials have been suspended while he serves as president. Those trials surround accusations over aiding private land developers, misusing public funds and infringing election law. Lee has denied any wrongdoing and called the indictments politically motivated.
“I have been, still am, and will continue to be one of those who have suffered the most from the prosecutors’ abuses,” Lee has said.
The overhaul is seen as one of the factors weighing on Lee’s approval rating, now hovering below 40 percent with nearly four years still remaining in his single, five-year term. A Gallup Korea poll in August showed half of respondents were against the reform, while 27 percent supported the plan.

OpenAI fires three over sensitive information
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
16:38:42 UTC
01:38:42 KST

ChatGPT maker OpenAI said on Thursday that it has fired three researchers for allegedly mishandling “sensitive information” and violating company policies, including work that involved an external organization that evaluates artificial intelligence models.
The San Francisco-based AI lab did not confirm their identities, but at least two of the employees worked on safety and alignment, according to the Wall Street Journal and Bloomberg.
“We have parted ways with three individuals,” OpenAI told AFP in a statement. “Our investigation confirmed that these individuals mishandled sensitive information outside established company procedures, violating our policies and breaking the trust essential to our work.” The firings come amid a tense debate about AI safety and whether the technology presents an existential risk to humanity.
Photo: Reuters
Last month, a 27-year-old researcher named Jacob Coxon resigned from Anthropic with a stark warning that the leading AI labs, including OpenAI, where he previously worked, were “gambling with our lives” by racing toward developing ever more powerful models.
The three researchers fired by OpenAI are Jasmine Wang, Tomek Korbak and Mikita Balesni, according to the WSJ. The researchers did not immediately respond to AFP’s request for comment.
All three have regularly posted about AI safety-related issues on X in recent weeks.
“i am at OpenAI and i think AI is >10% likely to kill all humans,” Balesni posted on Sept. 10, echoing statements made by other AI employees in recent weeks.
As speculation swirled about why employees at OpenAI and Anthropic were speaking so freely about their personal beliefs, Korbak jumped into the public discourse.
“I’m quite unhappy with much of what OpenAI does. I am very happy that Im allowed to say ‘I’m quite unhappy with much of what OpenAI does,’” Korbak wrote on Sept. 11. “It’s hard to overstate how dangerous speeding towards RSI is,” Wang posted in response to Coxon’s resignation, referring to recursive self-improvement, which is a technique where software is designed to continuously teach itself.
Leading US tech companies signed a voluntary pledge this week to regulate themselves on safety after meeting with US President Donald Trump at the White House.
Trump called it a “morally binding” commitment to build adequate safeguards on the fast-moving technology.
Executives from Nvidia, Google, Meta, xAI, OpenAI and Anthropic signed the agreement.
Concerns about the safety of advanced AI models have escalated in recent months. OpenAI canceled the release of a new model, Astra 6.1, because it deemed the model unreliable and found that it frequently ignored instructions.
Instead, the company launched GPT-6.1 Sol, an updated version of a different model, during its annual DevDay conference on Tuesday from San Francisco. OpenAI said Sol would cost one-fifth the price of Astra.
In July, AI agents developed by OpenAI attacked Hugging Face, an AI model and application library, during an incident where the autonomous software escaped its confined testing environment.
Since then, additional security incidents have been reported that involved models developed by OpenAI, Anthropic and Google. On Thursday, cybersecurity firm Asymmetric Security said in a report that agents developed by OpenAI covered up their own tracks after gaining unauthorized access to government Web sites.

Sweden gives hope to real conservatives everywhere
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
16:38:40 UTC
01:38:40 KST

Ulf Kristersson’s Moderates, who have spent four years leading Sweden’s governing coalition, did what voters wanted. The center-right party got growth going: It is expected to be 2.5 percent for this year and next year, remarkable for a European nation. Inflation is 0.3 percent, and — of greater importance to plenty of Swedes — asylum applications this year will be the lowest since 1985. They have even started building nuclear power plants again.
And, in gratitude, voters at last week’s national election handed a 176-173 lead to his opponent: a left-wing bloc led by by Magdalena Andersson’s Social Democrats. Still, that is not the real story here. The Swedish center-right might well have secured its long-term future in this vote. That should comfort them, as well as their beleaguered counterparts elsewhere in Europe.
The last government was an unwieldy coalition between the Moderates, who won just 19.1 percent of the vote in 2022, and two smaller center-right parties. It stayed in power thanks to outside support from the far-right Sweden Democrats. Kristersson kept the extremists out of his cabinet, yet they were able to impose many of their priorities on him.
Illustration: Kevin Sheu
Happily, as is often the case when a hard-right program is actually implemented, the wavering voter has been repelled. The Sweden Democrats pushed for hardline changes to immigration, including retrospective alterations to citizenship law and the deportations of non-citizens who had been in Sweden for decades. These excesses turned off Swedes, many of whom blamed the far-right and not Kristersson’s government.
And so the Moderates’ vote increased to nearer 20 percent, pushing them back in front of the Sweden Democrats. The latter’s share fell by three percentage points — the first time its election support has fallen since the party was founded.
Even the headline “loss” to the left-wing bloc is deceptive. I spent time recently in Hammarby Sjostad in southern Stockholm, an ex-industrial area so beautifully redeveloped over the past couple of decades that it could be a World Heritage Site. Many of its comfortably-off, far-right-hating voters defected to Andersson’s Social Democrats in the most recent election. This time they came back.
The Moderates would have done even better if many supporters had not lent their votes to a small center-right party to keep it above the 4 percent threshold needed to stay in parliament. Sweden’s electoral landscape is complicated.
Andersson has little to celebrate. The left won more seats, but the Social Democrats had a poor campaign and suffered their worst result in more than a century, also losing three percentage points of the vote. She knew the Greens would work with her, but she also needs support from a centrist and a far-left party. On Monday, she declared “there is currently no possibility” that she could get those two to work together.
Her troubles began because many Swedes voted strategically, both for and against parties in her center-left coalition. Backing for the Greens and the Left Party (the far-left outfit) surged in this election, but a cohort of voters also shifted to the Centre Party, because it will only support Andersson if the far-left is kept out of government in the same the way as the Moderates excluded the Sweden Democrats. Obviously that is unacceptable to an ascendant Left Party, which snagged 30 parliamentary seats and reckons it should pick up a few ministerial jobs.
This is a familiar dilemma for social-democratic politicians all over Europe, who have struggled with how to cope with the rising popularity of hard-left parties without having to sign up to their policy programs. Andersson does not seem to have any answers for the center-left. But there is another Nordic model that attracts many of them: Denmark’s Social Democrats, who were re-elected in March. Instead of worrying about their left flank, they neutralized the far-right by turning hawkish on migration years ago.
Sweden’s Moderates might provide an equivalent blueprint for Europe’s mainstream right. And a necessary one, because if Europe’s center-left has faltered, the center-right has failed outright. The Conservatives in Britain, the Republicans in France and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s flailing Christian Democrats should check out how Kristersson has kept his party afloat. He has governed sensibly, delivering substance where the far-right has offered noise, and he has let extremists shoulder the political costs of their own excesses.
The most telling part of all this was how the political conversations I had in Sweden felt strangely normal, even timeless. People argued about private profits in schools or modest differences in tax rates — the stuff of decade-ago elections in the rest of Europe, before migration ate our politics whole.
Sadly, Andersson’s failure to unite left and center might allow the Sweden Democrats a way back into the governing picture. It was foolish of Kristersson to promise, when he was trailing in the polls, to give the far-right ministerial posts this time around. But this election shows mainstream conservatives can take the heat out of migration politics in a modern European democracy. They just need to be disciplined — and then deliver.
Mihir Sharma is a Bloomberg Opinion columnist. A senior fellow at the Observer Research Foundation in New Delhi, he is author of Restart: The Last Chance for the Indian Economy. This column reflects the personal views of the author and does not necessarily reflect the opinion of the editorial board or Bloomberg LP and its owners.

He is an exceptional storyteller, with an ability to present a vision

Manufacturing sector flashes ‘green’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
16:38:39 UTC
01:38:39 KST

Taiwan’s manufacturing sector flashed a “green” light, indicating stable growth, in August, retreating from “yellow-red” in July, as old-economy industries faced weaker end-user demand, the Taiwan Institute of Economic Research (TIER, 台經院) said on Friday.
The August TIER composite index, which gauges the manufacturing sector’s overall health, fell 1.36 points from July’s revised 17.32 to 15.96, within the green-light range of 13-16, after a yellow-red light in July.
TIER uses a five-color system to assess activity: “red” for booming or overheating, “yellow-red” for fast growth, “green” for stable growth, “yellow-blue” for sluggish growth and “blue” for contraction.
Photo: CNA
TIER, one of Taiwan’s leading think tanks, said the local tech sector continued to benefit from the global AI boom and preparations by international brands ahead of new product launches, which pushed up the country’s exports.
However, TIER said old-economy industries largely became cautious due to weaker demand and clients’ reluctance to build up inventories.
Of the five factors in the August index, only the cost subindex rose by 0.03 from a month earlier.
In contrast, the subindices for the general business climate, purchases of raw materials, demand and pricing fell by 0.74, 0.28, 0.19 and 0.18 points, respectively, from July.
Despite the TAIEX, the Taiwan Stock Exchange’s benchmark index, rebounding in August, more manufacturers became cautious about their operational outlook, TIER added.
TIER said industries flashing a blue light accounted for 1.76 percent of manufacturing output value in August, up from 0.28 percent in July, while those flashing a yellow-blue light accounted for 20.06 percent, up from 10.10 percent.
By industry, TIER said the textile industry flashed a green light in August, retreating from a yellow-red light in July as end-user demand stayed weak, sending production lower, while the transportation industry continued to flash a yellow-blue light due to falling car sales and production adjustments.
The computer and optoelectronics index flashed another red light in August as AI demand stayed robust, with clients keen to build up inventories, boosting the industry’s exports and production, TIER said.
Although business opportunities created by AI are expected to drive Taiwan’s economic growth, TIER also identified several uncertainties in the global economy. These include military conflict in the Middle East, higher crude oil prices, which are raising production costs for businesses, and inflationary pressure that could prompt major central banks to raise rates, TIER said.

“It’s not something that happens very often, so it was a first for me,” she told reporters.

“I was in a little pain, but once I got on the mat, the adrenaline kicked in and I didn’t really notice it, so it was fine,” she added.

World Cup will not placate Morocco’s disillusioned generation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
16:38:36 UTC
01:38:36 KST

The spectacle of young migrants swimming en masse from Moroccan waters to the Spanish exclave of Ceuta exposed the frustration felt by a generation. One-third of the population of Morocco is aged between 15 and 30, and more than one third of that cohort is unemployed. A dearth of opportunity at home incentivizes young men in particular to take huge risks to reach the EU. More than 100 people died in that attempted exodus, most of them by drowning.
Worryingly, an adequate domestic response to a huge generational challenge is a long way off, if Morocco’s latest parliamentary election serves as any guide. In the wake of the Arab spring, democratizing reforms were introduced to Morocco’s monarchical system. But a decade and a half after that supposedly transformative moment, last week’s poll laid bare an alarming collapse of trust in politics among the young.
Overall turnout among those who had registered to vote was a miserable 38 percent — the lowest in two decades. But among those under 35, the election was in effect ignored, with only 19 percent bothering to register. In total, less than one in four Moroccans of voting age cast a ballot, as a center-right coalition led by the Authenticity and Modernity party held on to power. In what is essentially a hybrid democracy, where King Mohammed VI retains a dominant role, such numbers suggest grave problems might be being stored up for the future.
The lack of youthful participation should not be mistaken for apathy and indifference. Exactly a year ago, a gen Z protest movement organized the largest demonstrations since 2011, focused on demands for investment in public goods such as health and education. The demonstrators also gave voice to widespread anger at the vast sums of government money being diverted to preparations for the 2030 FIFA World Cup, which Morocco is to host alongside Spain and Portugal. One popular chant in the streets was “Healthcare first — we don’t want the World Cup.” Rattled authorities subsequently made thousands of arrests, amid allegations of brutal beatings. Hundreds remain in prison.
As the young have more or less opted out of mainstream politics, lip service is paid to the need to encourage their greater participation. However, there is little chance that the king and his incoming administration will act on demands to shift resources from a World Cup primarily set to benefit big cities and an insider elite. The IMF has calculated that expenditure on the tournament could amount to almost 12 percent of Morocco’s 2024 GDP, and preparations are set to dominate the country’s politics throughout the next parliament. Royal Moroccan Football Federation president Fouzi Lekjaa is widely tipped to be the next prime minister, having joined the Authenticity and Modernity party a few weeks before the election.
In Ceuta, a humanitarian emergency continues to unfold as thousands languish in a tented camp in the port area of the territory. In four years’ time, Morocco will be the focus of global attention and the Grand Stade Hassan II, projected to be the world’s biggest soccer stadium with a capacity of 115,000, could conceivably be hosting the World Cup final. However, among the country’s disillusioned young, the frustrated desire is for less circus, more bread and far better prospects.

Throughout the past decades of local elections, I have not seen anyone seriously discuss a long-term vision for urban planning, let alone with the kind of clarity and insight that Shen possesses that compels people to keep listening. He is an exceptional storyteller, with an ability to present a vision
If Taiwan falls, the true battle moves from the beaches into the concrete streets. Western analysts fixate on the invasion phase. China’s Wang Xiyu, fresh from conquering top seed Alexandra Eala, toppled Zhang Shuai to win Asian Games women’s tennis singles gold yesterday — and a ticket to the Los Angeles Olympics.
The 25-year-old Wang breezed past her compatriot 6-2, 6-1 in 66 minutes at the Higashiyama Park Tennis Center in Nagoya.
Tennis is one of seven sports at the Games where the winners receive an Olympic qualification place.
Photo: AP
Wang paid tribute to the 37-year-old Zhang, who has won multiple Grand Slam doubles titles and has now added a second Asian Games singles silver medal to the one she won in 2018 in Jakarta.
The veteran Zhang also bagged a team tennis gold in Guangzhou in 2010, when Wang would have been just nine years old.
“She is someone I really respect. Everything that she’s been through is also a form of encouragement to me,” Wang said.
“Still, on the court, the biggest form of respect I can show is by bringing my best to play her.”
The one-sided match was a contrast to the battle Wang had with Philippines star Eala 24 hours earlier, when the Chinese world number 85 came through 3-6, 6-3, 6-2 after two hours and 34 minutes of intense action.
“This is what sport, what elite competition, is like. Your actions speak for you,” added Wang.
“It’s when you experience success through the trials that you know what it was all for. Keep trying,” she said.
She then revealed her tennis skills were way ahead of her culinary efforts, but said it was important never to give up.
“I tried to make a dish of stir-fried cauliflower and it all became burnt,” Wang said. “There’s some difficulty in that dish, it’s so easy to get it wrong. I’ll keep trying.”
The men’s singles gold medal match tomorrow would see Hong Kong’s world No. 100 Coleman Wong take on China’s 111th-ranked Wu Yibing.

Ministry recognizes heat management as priority
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
16:38:33 UTC
01:38:33 KST

Heat management is the priority in climate adaptation globally, Deputy Minister of Environment Hsieh Yein-rui (謝燕儒) said yesterday, adding that the Ministry of Environment would assist other central agencies in identifying heat adaptation issues.
Hsieh made the remarks at a public hearing on the draft of the fourth-phase National Climate Change Adaptation Action Plan.
Hsieh said that the nation’s hottest 11 years occurred from 2015 to last year.
Photo: CNA
Taiwan has been preparing for heat-related compound disaster risks since 2024, with a focus on medical care, social safety nets, power supply and transportation, he said.
The nation’s current heat adaptation plans were made according to 1.5°C and 2°C global warming scenarios, he said, adding that the ministry expects to plan toward the 40°C scenario.
Heat management has become the priority issue for climate adaptation in many countries, including Singapore, Japan, South Korea and European countries, Hsieh said.
The ministry has focused on examining existing heat management efforts by ministries under the action plan’s previous phases, he said.
International heat adaptation experiences were introduced to help the ministries identify their heat-related issues and countermeasures, Hsieh said.
National Science and Technology Center for Disaster Reduction official Chen Yung-ming (陳永明) said that the action plan was formulated based on the projected warming scenarios proposed in the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change’s sixth assessment report.
The report said that a 1.5°C or 2°C rise in global warming is inevitable from 2020 to 2060, whether global carbon reduction efforts are successful or not, he said.
Taiwan’s national heat adaptation scenarios were defined according to the temperature rise, Chen said.
However, the World Meteorological Organization updated the projections months ago, announcing that the likelihood of global warming by 1.5°C over the next five years has reached 75 percent, he said.
The National Science and Technology Council would plan for 3°C and 4°C warming scenarios, while the ministries would still focus on preparing for a 1.5°C rise by 2040 and a 2°C rise by 2060, Chen said.
Although the warming scenarios were not changed for the ministries, latest scientific data and more variables would be incorporated into the fourth-phase action plan, he said.
In accordance with Article 18 of the Climate Change Adaptation Act (氣候變遷因應法), the environment ministry last year promulgated the Regulations for Climate Change Risk Assessment (氣候變遷風險評估作業準則) to establish a consistent methodology for developing adaptation plans, Chen said.
According to the fourth-phase action plan, eight fields were identified as vulnerable to the impact of climate change: essential infrastructure, water resources, land use, marine and coastal areas, energy supply and industries, agricultural production, ecosystems, and public health.
The environment ministry has adopted a four-tier grading approach to assisting ministries in planning toward heat adaptation across the eight fields.
The four tiers include: Update existing risk assessment results or adaptation strategies; complete ongoing risk assessments and identify adaptation gaps; define the scope and identify the link between ministerial work and climate risk; and other tasks unrelated to risk assessments.
Chen said that 104 adaptation measures have been established and more than half of them involve risk assessments.

India’s “Cockroach” youth movement yesterday called for new protests in Mumbai to demand the resignation of the chief election commissioner over a contentious revision of voter lists.
The movement, which began as an online campaign and now calls itself the Cockroach Janata Party, forced India’s education minister to resign in July with its street protests. The Mumbai rally is meant to start a new series of demonstrations nationwide.
Separately, police prevented student and civil society groups from gathering yesterday at Jantar Mantar, a designated protest site in New Delhi, to also demand the commissioner’s resignation. Police detained some opposition leaders heading to the site, which had been barricaded off.
Photo: AP
The protests add to mounting pressure on India’s Election Commission, which oversees polls across the country. Critics and opposition parties accuse it of altering voter registrations to give an advantage to the ruling Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party, led by Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi. The commission and the government deny any wrongdoing.
The Indian Express newspaper last month reported that two of the three election commissioners had formally objected to several decisions involving voter list revisions, registration procedures and the commission’s digital systems.
The two commissioners questioned the legality of some of the decisions, but Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar disregarded their objections, the report said.
Indian law requires the three-member Election Commission to make decisions by majority vote.
The commission disputed the report, saying it was based on “differing views and deliberations” among the commissioners rather than formal written objections.
India’s voter list revisions began last year in the eastern state of Bihar ahead of state elections, and have since expanded to most of the country’s states and federally administered territories.
Known as Special Intensive Revision, the revisions have drawn criticism over the documents required to establish voters’ eligibility. Critics say the requirements have been confusing and difficult for many voters to meet, potentially leaving millions off the registration lists and unable to vote.
Election Commission data show voter lists in some regions could shrink by as much as 30 percent.
The commission says the objective is to remove duplicate and ineligible entries while ensuring eligible voters remain on the lists. Opposition parties and activists say it risks excluding legitimate voters. They also accuse Kumar of political bias and allege the revisions benefit Modi’s party.
The Election Commission and Modi’s party have rejected the allegations.
The youth movement, which emerged earlier this year out of anger over high unemployment among young people and leaked examination papers, has grown into a political force.
Led by Abhijeet Dipke, it rose to national prominence after organizing mass protests over examination paper leaks. The demonstrations culminated in the resignation of the education minister.
The movement has since sought to take up other issues beyond education, such as government accountability and democratic institutions.

Two indicted over camellia oil fraud case
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
16:38:28 UTC
01:38:28 KST

Taipei prosecutors yesterday indicted two people on charges of fraud, alleging that they used Chinese tea seeds to produce camellia oil that was falsely labeled as being entirely made from Taiwanese tea seeds.
The two were Chen Chung Hsiu-hui (陳鐘秀惠), a business manager at Taipei-based Dynas International Corp, who was in charge of producing the company’s camellia oil products, and independent tea seed supplier Chen Yuan-nong (陳沅農), the Taipei District Prosecutors’ Office said.
Dynas shareholder Tu Chieh-sheng (?傑生), registered representative Chin Tien-li (金天麗) and product manager Tsai Meng-chieh (蔡孟潔) were not indicted due to insufficient evidence.
Photo: Wu Sheng-ju, Taipei Times
Prosecutors said that from 2023 through the end of 2024, Chen Chung either directly purchased China-made camellia oil from Yuan Chuen Oil Mill, based in Chiayi County, for Dynas or commissioned the mill to produce camellia oil using Chinese tea seeds.
Under her alleged instructions, the oil was then bottled and sold to the public under the “Gaoyangsan” brand with labels falsely stating that it was made from “100 percent Taiwanese native tea seeds” and bearing an “Origin: Taiwan” designation, they said.
Prosecutors said that Chen sometimes worked with Chen Chung and also independently supplied Chinese tea seeds to Dynas at different times while falsely claiming that they were from Taiwan, for personal profit.
Chen Chung allegedly knew that all of the camellia oil Yuan Chuen produced for Dynas from 2023 onward was made using Chinese tea seeds, but deliberately concealed this from Tingmao Agricultural Biotechnology Co and Yuen Foong Yu Biotech Co, who placed orders with Dynas, prosecutors said.
Prosecutors estimated that Dynas made NT$17.79 million (US$556,829) in profits from selling camellia oil made using Chinese tea seeds, while Chen made NT$2.07 million from selling them to Dynas.
Prosecutors yesterday indicted Chen Chung and Chen on charges of committing fraud for profit and false labeling under the Criminal Code, and requested that the court seize their criminal proceeds.
In the indictment, prosecutors said the two suspects put consumers at risk by concealing the true origin and quality of the oil for personal profit, and asked the court to hand down heavy sentences.
The case emerged amid food safety concerns over excessive levels of the carcinogen benzopyrene found in cooking oil in the past few months. Several batches of camellia oil sold by Dynas were subsequently found to contain excessive levels of benzopyrene.

Drones cannot replace jets in warfare, expert says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
16:38:28 UTC
01:38:28 KST

F-16C/D Block 70 jets remain relevant in modern warfare even as drones are playing an increasingly prominent role, an expert said, citing their ability to conduct combat air patrols (CAPs) and threaten conventional surface warships, including Chinese aircraft carriers deployed in waters off Taiwan’s east coast, an expert said.
Taiwan yesterday received two of the 66 F-16C/D Block 70 (or F-16V Block 70) jets it ordered from the US in 2019. The full order was due to be delivered by the end of the year, but supply chain disruptions and other issues have pushed back the schedule.
During wartime, Chinese forces would try to damage airbases’ runways to prevent fighter jets from taking off, Institute for National Defense and Security Research associate research fellow Shu Hsiao-huang (舒孝煌) said.
Photo: Ann Wang, Reuters
While airbases in eastern Taiwan would less likely be targeted by Chinese ballistic missiles or long-range rockets, they would still be vulnerable to ship-to-surface and air-to-surface weapons, Shu said.
China could also deploy its aircraft carriers and other large surface vessels far away from Taiwan’s east coast to evade coastal missiles, and threaten shipping routes used to transport weapons, gas and fuel, Shu said.
Those threats are why drones cannot replace fighter jets, he said.
Drones cannot be deployed as effectively against large surface vessels, such as aircraft carriers, due to their limited payload capacity, Shu said, adding that the ability of drones to detect and track airborne targets is not as extensive as those of fighter jets, which provide more effective deterrence against airborne threats.
“The ability of fighter jets to conduct CAPs, generally speaking, cannot yet be replaced,” he said.
Research Institute for Democracy, Society and Emerging Technology policy analyst Cathy Fang (方怡然) said drones are meant to complement conventional fighter jets, not replace them.
“The value [of drones] is not that they replace conventional systems. It is that they add larger numbers of dispersed, lower-cost, and more replaceable sensors and shooters, increasing the density and resilience of Taiwan’s existing defense architecture,” he said.
Despite the F-16V Block 70’s larger fuel capacity, which allows the jets to remain airborne for longer periods, and their ability to carry more missiles, they would be at a disadvantage against China’s fifth-generation stealth fighter jets, such as the J-20, Shu said.
“They are not easily spotted, but they can see us,” Shu added.
The threat becomes more serious if enemy stealth fighters are equipped with beyond-visual-range missiles such as the PL-15 or PL-17, he said.
One system that could help overcome this capability gap is Lockheed Martin’s Legion-ES IRST21, also known as the Legion Pod, which can be integrated with F-16s, Shu said.
The pod uses infrared search and track technology to trace the thermal signatures of stealth fighter jets without activating a radar, and can support targeting for weapons such as AIM-120 Advanced Medium-Range Air-to-Air Missiles, he added.
“The enemy would not easily detect that we are monitoring it or firing at it,” Shu said. “This way, we could ambush the adversary and pose a substantial threat to enemy warplanes.”
While Lockheed Martin does not publicly disclose the Legion Pod’s detection range, the system is designed to detect and track airborne targets at extended ranges, with its effective range depending on factors such as the target’s thermal signature and environmental conditions.
Taiwan has agreed to purchase 55 Legion Pods for its F-16 fleet. The US Department of State approved the sale in August 2023, and the systems are scheduled to be delivered in full by June 2031.
