Spanish Congress rejects both of government's housing decrees
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
14:36:31 UTC
23:36:31 KST

Beyza Binnur Donmez
02 October 2026•Update: 02 October 2026
Spain's Congress of Deputies on Friday rejected two housing decrees approved by the government earlier this week, dealing a double defeat to its efforts to introduce new tenant protections and address housing affordability.
The first decree was defeated by 178 votes to 172, with the conservative People's Party, far-right Vox and Catalan separatist Junts voting against it.
The measure included protections against certain evictions, regulation of seasonal and room rentals, measures aimed at expanding affordable housing and restrictions on certain property purchases by investment funds.
A second decree was rejected by a wider margin, with 184 lawmakers voting against it and 166 in favor.
That measure included the automatic renewal of primary-residence rental contracts in cases where landlords could not provide legally recognized grounds for ending them.
Junts opposed both decrees and had called on the government to withdraw the measures before the votes and negotiate new legislation instead.
The two decrees had been approved by the Council of Ministers on Tuesday as part of the government's response to concerns over housing affordability and protections for tenants.
The votes came amid protests over Spain's housing crisis, with demonstrators who had been camping in Madrid's Puerta del Sol marching toward Congress on Friday to demand approval of the measures.
The protests followed the Sept. 23 eviction of 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal from the Madrid apartment where she had lived for more than 70 years.
She was removed on a stretcher and taken to a hospital, with the case becoming a symbol of the country's housing crisis.
Abascal has since reached an agreement with the company that owns the apartment, allowing her to return to her home after leaving the hospital with a similar rent under a new contract, averting a significant price hike.

The case involving the embezzlement of millions at the Ministry of Justice has been sent to court — who is among the accused
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
17:35:58 EEST
23:35:58 KST

The case involving the embezzlement of millions at the Ministry of Justice has been sent to court — who is among the accused
Kyiv • UNN
The case concerning the Ministry of Justice’s procurements at inflated prices has been referred to court. Six officials and company executives are among the accused.
The indictment in the case involving the misappropriation of funds belonging to the Ministry of Justice during the procurement of services for upgrading a hardware-and-software complex and 1,285 multifunctional devices has been sent to court. This was reported by the press service of the SAPO, according to UNN.
The defendants include:
-  the former State Secretary of the Ministry of Justice; 
-  the head and deputy head of departments of the Ministry of Justice; 
-  the beneficial owner and two executives of a private company. 
As part of the pre-trial investigation conducted by NABU detectives, it was established that the company's beneficial owner devised a criminal scheme involving officials of the Ministry of Justice in order to misappropriate public funds during procurement procedures.
"First episode: officials of the Ministry of Justice amended the estimate for 2021, while executives of the private company organized the preparation of technical specifications for upgrading the hardware-and-software complex, including specific requirements for the equipment's characteristics that ensured this particular company would win the tenders. In addition, it was found that the cost of the services indicated in the company's commercial proposals had been significantly inflated," the SAPO stated.
To create the appearance that the tender process was lawful, the individuals involved another private company; however, its tender proposal was deemed less commercially attractive. Implementation of this scheme caused losses of more than UAH 10 million to the Ministry of Justice.
"Second episode: in order to procure multifunctional devices, officials of the Ministry of Justice arranged for the relevant amendments to be made to the estimate for 2021. Subsequently, to establish an inflated expected procurement value, requests for commercial proposals were sent to the private company and other companies identified in advance, and the necessary responses were obtained. To create the appearance of competition, the participants in the scheme ensured the formal participation in the tender of another enterprise, whose tender proposal was deemed less commercially attractive than that of the controlled company. As a result, the Ministry of Justice purchased multifunctional devices at an inflated price, and the state lost more than UAH 8.9 million," the SAPO added.
The perpetrators transferred the money obtained in this way to the accounts of business entities showing signs of being fictitious.
The individuals' actions were classified under Part 5 of Article 191 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine. One of the private company's executives was additionally charged under Part 2 of Article 209 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine, while the head of a department of the Ministry of Justice was charged under Part 1 of Article 263 of the Criminal Code of Ukraine.
It will be recalled
NABU and the SAPO completed the pre-trial investigation in the case concerning the alleged misappropriation of public funds during procurements by the Ministry of Justice of Ukraine.

Woman in alleged Cornell gang-rape case was ‘failed’ by system, New York governor says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02

Kathy Hochul, New York’s governor, said on Friday that she would “ensure” that all the facts of the alleged gang-rape at a fraternity house at Cornell University “are brought into the light”, while harshly criticizing the elite institution for how it handled the 2024 case.
Hochul, a Democrat, said the woman in the case, was “failed” by people obligated to protect her, including the police and the county prosecutor.
“I’m deeply disturbed at Cornell University’s police and how they handled this,” Hochul said of the Ivy League university in Ithaca in upstate New York.
In a rare legal development, Hochul late on Thursday announced that the state attorney general, Letitia James, was taking over the entire case as a special prosecutor.
“I will not allow anyone to sweep this case under the rug,” Hochul said in a press conference on Friday morning alongside James.
“Every New Yorker deserves to know that when they report a crime, they will be investigated fully and fairly. That they will be seen and heard. I stand ready to lead a process guided by the facts and the law,” James said.
James will oversee the investigation and, if warranted, present evidence to a grand jury in a process that could lead to criminal charges.
Hochul sharply criticized the investigation that began in 2024 after the woman in the case went to the police.
“In what world would the police learn from a victim that she’d been literally gang-raped while intoxicated by five men in a fraternity house, and not elevate those allegations to the district attorney?” Hochul said, of the alleged assaults.
The governor also criticized what she called “a gap in state law” that makes it very difficult to bring charges relating to accusations of sexual crimes when the alleged victim was voluntarily intoxicated.
She said: “If someone is too intoxicated to consent, it should not matter whether they chose to use drugs or alcohol. Voluntary intoxication is not a license for sexual assault or gang-rape. Period.”
Hochul said on Thursday she was appointing James after she “lost faith” in the ability of the local Tompkins county district attorney, Matthew Van Houten, to oversee the case after he decided not to prosecute the case in 2024, among other reasons. Prior to James’s appointment this week, Van Houten had reopened the investigation.
A former Cornell University student, who identifies by the pseudonym Jane Doe, filed a civil lawsuit in September alleging she was gang-raped at a fraternity in 2024, when she was 20. She said she was drugged and repeatedly raped over the course of seven hours. The case has sparked national outrage, roiled the campus and raised questions about why no criminal case was brought.
Thomas Giuffra, a lawyer for Jane Doe, told CNN on Friday morning that his client was “not doing well” amid the uproar and that they feel as though “a cover-up was going on” in order to protect the university and its reputation. He added that he had “a real issue” with the district attorney and accused him of trying to “throw” his client “under the bus”.
On Friday, Cornell University said it supported Hochul, including her effort to pass legislation to update the relevant law.
“We fully support the appointment of a special prosecutor and efforts to change New York State’s rape law and are committed to an independent external review of all aspects of how Cornell has handled this case,” a spokesperson said.
Two members of the Chi Phi fraternity at Cornell were expelled, but none of the seven were arrested nor faced any legal consequences. Some were made to write essays, attend workshops or serve short suspensions. Now, Doe is suing the seven men whom she said perpetrated the assault, and also the university itself, the fraternity and others. Some in the group argue that sexual contact was consensual, others deny such participation.
On Monday, Van Houten said the allegations presented in the lawsuit were “dramatically different” from the statement the alleged victim gave the police two years ago. He said the woman’s first testimony did not include allegations that she was drugged, incapacitated beyond the ability to consent or forced into sex. However, he later told CBS News he had never seen her detailed account, but relied on a statement written by a campus police officer.
Hochul further said on Friday that Van Houten had said that Doe’s statement “did not establish that a crime had occurred” – but that new reporting raises serious questions about the information his office relied upon when it made that decision.
Now, she demanded that James conduct a “fresh and thorough review of all the facts” and “go wherever it leads”.
Hochul said: “Every parent who sends their child off to college expects them to be safe, and if something terrible happens, the student deserves to know that the people they turn to will listen to them, protect them, and fight for them. That is the bare minimum.”
James said her first priority was the criminal investigation into the alleged rape. “At this time we will not be focusing on the actions of the district attorney,” she said.
Cornell, which is a private sector elite university, has suspended the Chi Phi fraternity indefinitely. A fraternity is a selective, traditionally all-male club at a university in which some male undergraduate members may live together in residential fraternity houses on or near campus.
Cornell agreed on Wednesday to bring in outside lawyers to independently investigate how it handled the woman’s allegations.

Rebel-held eastern Congo records six new Ebola cases

• The Rwanda-backed AFC/M23 rebels control large parts of North and South Kivu provinces after staging a lightning offensive last year
• The rebels declared areas under their control Ebola-free in late June, having previously recorded only four cases, but a new case was confirmed in Kayna health zone in North Kivu in early September. That patient was discharged on Tuesday after spending 26 days at the Ebola treatment centre there
• Two new cases were detected in Kayna health zone and four in neighbouring Alimbongo health zone on Friday, the rebels said in a statement
• The two health zones are near Lubero, close to the front line with government forces

• Four of the cases were identified through post-mortem testing of people who died in the community, while the other two patients are receiving treatment, the rebels said
• Efforts are underway to identify and trace contacts, the statement added
• The Ebola outbreak in eastern Congo was declared on May 15 and has now caused more than 4,000 deaths among 8,300 confirmed cases, according to government data released on Friday REUTERS

Iran-EAEU trade on an upward trend: TPO head
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
14:32:53 UTC
23:32:53 KST

Iran-EAEU trade on an upward trend: TPO head
TEHRAN- The Head of Iran’s Trade Promotion Organization (TPO), in a meeting with the Trade Minister of the Eurasian Economic Union, referring to the upward trend of trade between Iran and the member states of the union, emphasized the Islamic Republic of Iran’s determination to expand and deepen trade relations and strengthen ties between the private sectors of the two sides.
According to a report by the Public Relations of Iran’s Trade Promotion Organization, Mohammad Ali Dehghan Dehnavi, in a meeting with Slepnev, referring to the course of trade between the Islamic Republic of Iran and the member states of the Eurasian Economic Union, said: “Despite all challenges and problems, trade statistics between Iran and the Eurasian Economic Union have taken an upward trend, and this promises bright prospects for the development of trade relations in the future.”
The Deputy Minister of Industry, Mining and Trade, emphasizing the will and determination of the Islamic Republic of Iran to expand trade relations with the member states of the Eurasian Economic Union, added: “Iran has regular cooperation and trade relations with Russia and other member states of the union, and we are striving to make these ties deeper than before.”
Dehghan Dehnavi also expressed hope that the second meeting of the joint committee of Iran and the Eurasian Economic Union will be held in Tehran soon, and continued: “Holding this meeting in Tehran can be a suitable opportunity to strengthen communication between the private sectors of Iran and the member states of the union and to form new economic and trade cooperation.”
The Head of Iran’s Trade Promotion Organization also stressed the continuation of consultations and the use of existing capacities to develop economic and trade cooperation between Iran and the member states of the Eurasian Economic Union.
It is worth noting that Dehghan Dehnavi traveled to Minsk to participate in the 19th meeting of the Joint Economic Cooperation Commission of the Islamic Republic of Iran and the Republic of Belarus.
Also, in mid-September, Iran’s Minister of Economic Affairs and Finance, offering a positive assessment of the results of his Tuesday meetings with officials of the Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU), announced the proposal of initiatives such as setting a base currency to accelerate transactions and appointing special representatives to resolve obstacles facing bilateral trade.
According to IRNA, Seyyed Ali Madanizadeh, speaking to reporters after separate meetings and talks with the Chairman of the Executive Board and the Minister of Trade of the Eurasian Economic Commission at the union's headquarters in Moscow, added: "We held very good sessions."
He stated: "On Iran's behalf, we expressed our interest and readiness to expand relations and fully implement the free trade agreement with the Eurasian Economic Union, and that we are prepared to cooperate with this union in various fields; the union's officials, in turn, expressed their willingness and interest in expanding ties with our country."
The Minister of Economic Affairs and Finance, referring to the efforts of the enemies of the Iranian nation to fuel economic warfare and block trade and financial channels, said: "What is evident is that, thanks to God, these countries support Iran and our economy, and that Iran has managed to maintain production and trade relations with countries under the toughest conditions." He added: "The member states of the Eurasian Economic Union are equally committed and eager to develop these relations."
Continuing his Moscow visit agenda for multilateral consultations, the Minister of Economic Affairs and Finance attended the Eurasian Economic Union's headquarters and met with the Chairman of the Executive Board and the Minister of Trade to discuss accelerating bilateral trade.
Seyyed Ali Madanizadeh, and Bakytzhan Sagintayev, Chairman of the Board of the Eurasian Economic Commission, emphasized their shared determination to expand cooperation during this meeting.
Prior to this meeting, the Minister of Economic Affairs and Finance held a separate session with Andrey Slepnev, Minister in charge of Trade of the Eurasian Economic Commission, and a group of union officials to review the progress of cooperation following the implementation of the free trade agreement. Slepnev, noting that the second meeting of the Iran-EAEU working group would be hosted by Tehran in the coming months, expressed hope that the upward trend in bilateral trade would continue.
Iran's Ambassador to Russia, Kazem Jalali, and Mehdi Heydari, Deputy Minister of Economy and head of Iran's Organization for Investment, Economic and Technical Assistance, accompanied Madanizadeh during these meetings.
The free trade agreement between Iran and the Eurasian Economic Union came into force in May 2025 after completing legal procedures in the signatory countries, subsequently eliminating customs duties on 87% of goods in bilateral trade.
Within this cooperation framework, the path has been smoothed for Iranian goods to enter the market of over 180 million people in the union's member states, and reciprocally, this opportunity is available for traders from the five signatory countries in commerce with Iran.
Russia, Belarus, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, and Armenia are members of the Eurasian Economic Union, and Iran holds observer status in the union.
The Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU) is a regional economic integration bloc in the post-Soviet space, established by a treaty signed in 2014 and launched on January 1, 2015. Its five member states are Russia, Belarus, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, and Armenia, with Iran, Cuba, Moldova, and Uzbekistan holding observer status.
Modelled in part on the European Union, the EAEU aims to create a single internal market with the free movement of goods, services, capital, and labour. Its core objectives include improving living standards, ensuring sustainable economic development, and boosting the global competitiveness of member economies.
The bloc is driven by institutions such as the Supreme Eurasian Economic Council and the Eurasian Economic Commission. While the EAEU has expanded external ties—notably through a free trade agreement with Iran—internal integration remains uneven, with Russia dominating trade flows in a "hub and spoke" model. The bloc has set a long-term vision to become a self-sufficient and attractive macro-region by 2045.

Mirage 2000 Makes History—Russian Banderol Cruise Missile Shot Down With Guns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-02
14:31:30 UTC
23:31:30 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Mirage 2000 Makes History—Russian Banderol Cruise Missile Shot Down With Guns
A Ukrainian Mirage 2000-5F has reportedly scored a first, shooting down a Russian S8000 Banderol cruise missile not with an air-to-air missile, but with bursts from its built-in 30mm cannons.
“Late-night information: the Mirage 2000-5F was the first Western fighter aircraft to destroy a Russian S8000 Banderol cruise missile with the cannon,” according to Militarnyi, citing OSINT analyst French Aid to Europe on October 2.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The claim has not yet been publicly confirmed by the Ukrainian or French defense ministries.
France transferred Mirage 2000-5F fighters from its own Air and Space Force inventory to Ukraine beginning in 2025, giving Kyiv another Western fighter type for air-defense and strike missions.
The aircraft is particularly well suited to interception work. France describes the 2000-5F as an air-defense-focused variant equipped with an RDY multimode radar, MICA air-to-air missiles and two internal 30mm cannons.
Those guns are DEFA 554 revolver cannons mounted inside the fuselage. Each carries roughly 125 rounds and can fire at rates reaching about 1,800 rounds per minute, giving the pilot an extremely short but intense window of fire during a close-range interception.
If confirmed, the engagement would be particularly notable because the target was not a slow propeller-driven Shahed.
The S8000 Banderol is a small Russian jet-powered cruise missile developed by Kronstadt JSC. Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence lists its top speed at roughly 620–650 kilometers per hour, with a cruising speed of 520–560 km/h and a range of around 500 kilometers.
The weapon is primarily launched from Russia’s Orion UAV and is also being adapted for use from Mi-28N attack helicopters. It combines relatively low production cost with the speed and flight characteristics of a small cruise missile, making it a more difficult interception target than conventional Shahed-type drones.
The Banderol carries a large high-explosive fragmentation warhead and has increasingly appeared in Russian attacks against Ukraine since its first documented combat use in spring 2025. Ukrainian intelligence says the weapon relies on numerous foreign-made components, including its propulsion and electronics.
Earlier, two Mirage 2000 fighter jets crewed by French and Ukrainian pilots participated in France’s Bastille Day military parade on July 14, with one aircraft expected to appear in the colors of the Ukrainian flag.

Israeli officials to question co-pilot of flydubai flight, source says

Israeli officials to question co-pilot of flydubai flight, source says
TEL AVIV, Oct 2 - Israeli officials are expected to question the co-pilot who allegedly attempted to crash a commercial passenger flight from Dubai bound for Tel Aviv, according to a source briefed on the investigation.
Disaster was averted on flydubai flight FZ1073 on Wednesday after passengers and crew subdued the co-pilot, who had stabbed the captain in what Israeli officials have said was an apparent attempt to crash the plane carrying over 170 passengers and crew.
A reserve flydubai pilot crew travelling on the flight landed the plane at Tabuk airport in northwestern Saudi Arabia, where the co-pilot was detained by Saudi Arabian authorities.
The co-pilot was transferred on Thursday to the UAE, where the source said Israeli officials were expected to question him.
The source declined to say which Israeli agency or authority would take part in the questioning.
Asked whether Israeli officials would question the co-pilot, an Israeli government official told Reuters that Israeli investigators would take part in the UAE-led investigation alongside Emirati authorities, seeking to determine what happened and examine the suspect's motives and background.
The UAE foreign ministry did not immediately respond to a request for comment on whether Israeli officials would question the co-pilot.
In his first public comments on the incident, flydubai Chief Executive Ghaith Al Ghaith said on Friday that authorities were conducting an official investigation, supported by the airline, after what he described as a "safety incident" in the cockpit.
"It is important that we allow this process to establish the facts," he said in a written statement, acknowledging that there were "many questions" about what happened on flight FZ1073.
The UAE state news agency reported on Thursday that Emirati authorities had opened an investigation seeking to establish the circumstances and motives and determine "whether the incident was linked to any terrorist activity or purpose, or involved prior planning or direction".
MOTIVE NOT YET ESTABLISHED
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said on Friday that Israel was looking into whether the co-pilot had acted under anyone's direction, warning in a video statement released by his office that whoever was involved would pay a "heavy price".
Most of the passengers on board were Israeli nationals.
Netanyahu on Thursday said that the co-pilot, whom he has identified as an Omani national, had undergone radical Islamist indoctrination and was clearly suicidal, but that so far a motive for his actions had not been established.
Israel does not have official diplomatic relations with Oman, and Netanyahu has said pilots from such countries were not permitted to operate flights to Israel. It was not clear how the co-pilot came to be assigned to the flight to Tel Aviv.
The aircraft plunged some 16,625 feet in just over 30 seconds as it flew over Saudi Arabia on the journey from the United Arab Emirates to Israel, according to data from flight tracker Flightradar24. The route is popular among Israelis.
CAPTAIN HAILED AS HERO
The co-pilot's identity has not been publicly disclosed beyond his nationality. The captain who was stabbed has been identified as Indian national Smit Machchhar, who has been hailed as a hero by Netanyahu and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi.
Omani authorities have not commented on the incident.
The incident heightened security fears in Israel weeks before Israelis vote on October 27, in the first general election since the Hamas-led attacks on October 7, 2023, with Israel's security featuring prominently in the campaigning.
The US and Israel launched strikes against Iran in February, in a war that quickly spread to the Gulf and Lebanon, where Israel has been fighting Iran-backed militant group Hezbollah.
Since coming under attack by Iran this year, the UAE has strengthened its relationships with Israel, with which it opened ties as a result of the 2020 Abraham Accords. REUTERS

‘This can’t go on’: tens of thousands protest against housing crisis in Spain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
14:19:46 UTC
23:19:46 KST

Tens of thousands of people have taken to the streets of Madrid and other Spanish cities as they step up demands for action to tackle a mounting housing crisis after government measures were struck down by the opposition.
Demonstrators on Saturday waved posters calling for a general strike after the measures drawn up to address mass anger over the eviction of an 87-year-old woman in Madrid, and other housing issues, were rejected in parliament on Friday.
Authorities said 70,000 people were protesting. Organisers put the figure at 500,000.
“It’s a shame,” Nando de Anguulo, 26, who joined the protest in Madrid, told Reuters. “It only proves that it is us the people who have to adapt to the political parties, and not the politicians to what the people want, and this can’t go on like that.”
Spain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, may call a snap election for November after the legislation failed to pass, Spanish media reported on Friday, and would be watching the strength of Saturday’s protests before making a decision.
The demonstrations have dominated the national conversation, breathing new life into Sánchez’s beleaguered government and shifting attention away from the lingering impact of recent events in Ceuta.
Protests on Saturday were peaceful in 50 Spanish cities. In the south-eastern city of Valencia, demonstrators clashed with police who fired rubber bullets and teargas to break up the protests.
About 30 people managed to get inside the City of Arts and Sciences, a landmark cultural building in the city, before they were ousted by police.
One protester in Madrid, Marcos Sainz, a librarian aged 26, said he used to rent a two-bedroom apartment with friends for a monthly rent of 900 euros ($1,000) but that a one-bedroom flat often now cost 1,000 euros – or half the median monthly salary in the capital.
He told AFP he would protest rental spikes “until someone dares to regulate it all as (otherwise) we’ll all have to leave Madrid and that would be a shame as I am from Madrid”.
Javier, 31, a solar panel installer, said: “We are demanding a fundamental right: decent housing, stability and conditions allowing us to construct a decent life project.” He added: “I spend half of my salary on a tiny room”.
“What we are feeling in the streets is a new energy that we haven’t seen in a long time, an energy that is showing that eight days of people power can achieve more than eight years of progressive government,” Valeria Racu, one of the spokespeople of the Tenants’ Union organising the protest, said in a statement.
“Now begins real politics – politics which has always belonged to the people and which will return once and for all to the streets,” she said.
On Friday, Sánchez’s Socialist-led coalition put forward two decrees that included a range of measures aimed at improving access to housing, from a ban on evictions until 2030 to the regulation of temporary lettings and lettings by room.
Despite the anger of the protesters outside parliament, the conservative People’s party, the far-right Vox and the Catalan pro-independence party Junts voted against both decrees.
The People’s party said it had voted in line with its belief that building, rather than regulating, was the best way to address the crisis. “Housing doesn’t become more affordable through decrees; it becomes more affordable by building more homes,” said the lawmaker Juan Bravo.
News of the package’s rejection was met with boos and cries of “shame” outside. “Your profits, our misery,” the protesters chanted.
The long-simmering anger at soaring housing costs boiled over late last month, when 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal, who uses a wheelchair, was evicted from the home she had lived in for 70 years. The octogenarian said she was unable to afford the 230% rent hike demanded by the investment fund that bought her apartment.
Reuters and AFP contributed to this report.

Teaching is just the start: The crushing burden on India's college teachers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
14:18:24 UTC
23:18:24 KST

According to a survey on higher education, while recommended student-teacher ratio (STR) targets in higher education range between 15:1 and 20:1, the national average hovers between 24:1 and 27:1.
In a brightly lit classroom at an engineering college in Bengaluru, a fourth-year Computer Science lecture is underway. At the front, a professor moves through a technical lesson while also keeping track of attendance sheets and administrative requirements.In the middle rows, a student sits quietly, mentally calculating train schedules between Bengaluru and Pune. He is trying to work out how to explain to a corporate employer that a career-launching Pre-Placement Offer (PPO) could be at risk because of a mandatory offline attendance requirement for a single elective subject.The scene captures a growing tension inside India’s higher education system.For final-year students, college is no longer only about completing a degree. With competition for jobs intensifying, students are increasingly focused on internships, practical skills, early employment and mental health support. But the institutional framework around them remains tied to attendance thresholds, credit requirements, standardised evaluation and administrative compliance.Caught at the centre of these competing pressures is the college teacher.According to data from the All India Survey on Higher Education (AISHE), while recommended Student-Teacher Ratio (STR) targets in higher education range between 15:1 and 20:1, the national average hovers between 24:1 and 27:1.
In public and state institutions, that figure can rise to 35:1 or 50:1, with individual undergraduate lectures accommodating 80 to 120 or more students per section.The pressure is compounded by faculty shortages. Central universities report faculty vacancy rates between 29% and 34%, while senior professor vacancies frequently exceed 50%. Across technical institutions such as the IITs, NITs and IIITs, unfilled positions range from 30% to over 50%.This leaves teachers performing several roles at once: academic instructors, institutional policy enforcers, career advisers and, often, informal listeners when students are struggling.At the same time, they have to manage UGC Academic Performance Indicators, NAAC and NIRF documentation and heavy teaching loads.
Modern classroom: More than academics
For today's students, particularly those in their final year, the classroom is closely linked to the question of what happens after graduation.“A student may come because he is confused about an internship, worried about placements or simply doesn't know how to deal with something happening at home. We try to listen, but there is a limit to what a subject teacher can realistically handle,” Prakash, a college faculty member at an engineering college says.From the student's perspective, the final year can feel like a race against time, with academic requirements running alongside internships, placements and preparations for entering the workforce.Pranav Vats, a final-year Computer Science and Engineering student in Bengaluru, describes what students prioritise:“Whenever a guy comes to a college, he eventually wants to get placed. He doesn't want to get a 9 plus CGP every semester. He just wants to get placed in a good company and do well in his career financially and also growth-wise... I have been doing internships from the first year itself. And whatever interviews I have been going through, nobody asked me about what my CGPA is. Everybody just asked, okay, how much do you know, how much practical skills you have, and how well you understand the market and how well do you understand your business in which you are going to work now.”That shift creates a difficult balance for teachers. Students may see practical experience as more directly connected to employment, while faculty members remain responsible for ensuring that students complete prescribed courses, credits and attendance requirements.
When attendance collide with career
The tension becomes particularly visible during placement and internship season.Pranav describes a situation in which he had secured an internship opportunity in Pune after clearing an interview:“Two, three months back, I got an interview. I've cleared it. I went to Pune. And at that time, I got permission from college. They gave me this letter of acknowledgement that you can go and pursue your six months internship, and all. But all of a sudden, after two months, they are saying that no, you have to fulfil your academic requirements and all... This company is very good. I'm doing very well there. And they are giving me the PPO for it. I could have got placed. But right now, this company is not giving away. College is saying that you have to attend weekly once class. As a student, it is not possible for me to come from Pune to Bangalore every week to attend some stupid class that is not even relevant to my coursework, which is not even relevant to my computer science degree... It is just an open elective subject.”He says discussions with his mentor, department head and other authorities did not resolve the problem.“What they said to me is, ‘No, do you want your graduate certificate or you want your internship certificate? So fulfill your graduation thing first, then you go and do whatever you want to do.’ They just want, basically, to fulfill what the college needs. And apart from that, you can do whatever you want to do. We don't care.”Pranav says similar situations have affected other students, including those with jobs or internships in Bengaluru itself.He says, “There is this one guy who got placed in Nokia in Bangalore itself. And he said, ‘Sir, I can't attend this class this week because I've got placed here at Nokia.’ They said, ‘You have to do it. I don't care. You have to fulfill this academic thing’.”For teachers, however, understanding the student's situation does not necessarily mean being able to change the rule.“The final year is particularly difficult because everything seems to happen at once. Students are completing projects, dealing with attendance and examinations, and at the same time worrying about placements and what they are going to do after graduation. You can see that pressure building up, especially when a student's plans don't work out,” the faculty said.The faculty member explains the dilemma:“There are situations where a student gets an internship or an opportunity outside the college and genuinely needs flexibility. As a teacher, you may understand why that opportunity matters to him. But you are also responsible for implementing the academic requirements. That can put the teacher in an uncomfortable position because you may sympathise with the student without having the authority to change the rule.”
Teacher becomes institutional buffer
The teacher is therefore often caught between three sets of expectations.The administration expects attendance, syllabus completion and documentation for institutional requirements. Students expect empathy, career guidance and flexibility. Parents expect academic performance, safety and career outcomes.The teacher may have to explain an institutional decision to a student without having any authority over that decision.“Sometimes the student is upset with the institution, the parents are worried about the student's performance and the department is concerned about academic requirements,” the teacher explains. “The teacher ends up sitting in the middle. We are expected to explain one side to the other, even though we may not have control over the decision ourselves.”For students, this can reinforce the perception that teachers are primarily there to enforce attendance and award marks.Pranav puts it bluntly, “They don't care, they just want these things to attend classes, they want attendance, they want marks, that's it... If you go to an off-campus thing, where majorly everybody is applying right now, nobody asks you about your CGPA. They just want you to have your practical skills. But this CGPA thing or whatever coursework they are teaching us in college, it is not even relevant to what we will work in our offices.”
When personal problems enter classroom
The pressure is not limited to academics and placements.Teachers are also increasingly expected to recognise when students are struggling emotionally, even though they may not be trained to provide professional mental health support.“You spend enough time with a class to notice changes,” the faculty member observes. “If a student who is normally interactive suddenly stops speaking, misses classes or stops submitting work, you notice it. The difficult part is deciding whether to ask, ‘Is everything okay?’ because you don't know whether the student wants you to enter that part of his life,” Prakash say.The teacher describes the boundary involved, “There is a very fine line between being concerned about a student and becoming intrusive. If I ask too many questions, it may seem intrusive. If I don't ask anything, I may miss something important. Teachers are constantly trying to judge where that line is.”At the same time, faculty members recognise their own limitations.“I want my students to know that they can approach me, but I also have to be honest about my limitations. I can listen, I can help them think through a problem and I can direct them towards the right person. But I am not trained to provide therapy, and pretending otherwise can be harmful,” Prakash says.
Counselling gap, a stigma problem
Many institutions have counselling cells or mentor-mentee systems, but having a service does not necessarily mean students will use it.Pranav says his mentor-mentee system is largely focused on academic issues:“For every 20 or 30 sets of people there is assigned one mentor. So whatever the issues you have regarding the college, you can talk with them and they can get a resolution about it... [But] there is nothing like that through which we can discuss our career... They are strictly for the subject.”He says students also face peer pressure around seeking counselling.“We have one basically like they have hired a person... if you have any emotional issues or something like that, then you can go schedule a session,” Pranav says. “[But] if you suppose you go to a counsellor there is this peer pressure. If you go to a counselor, or maybe you're discussing things with the teacher, you would seem like a weak person.”“This thing is very very disturbing to the students and nobody talks about it because everybody feels that okay, if I talk about it I can feel weak about it and people will think that okay he's not mature enough to deal with his own problem on his own... I talk to some of my friends about it who are eventually on the same path... but majorly I work with my pressure on my own,” Pranav adds.When behaviour changes significantly, teachers also have to balance intervention with confidentiality.“If I feel that a student's behaviour has changed significantly, I cannot just say, ‘That's his personal matter.’ There are situations where you have to involve the appropriate support system. But you also have to be careful about confidentiality and about not turning a student's difficulty into a public issue,” Prakash says.
Emotional burden on teachers
While student stress receives increasing attention, the pressure on faculty can remain largely invisible.A teacher managing a class of 80 to 120 students may also have to deal with staff shortages, administrative work, evaluations, meetings and institutional documentation. A difficult conversation with a student does not necessarily end when the class does.The faculty member says teachers need institutional support if they are expected to take on these additional responsibilities.Prakash says, “I don't think teachers are unwilling to take on a larger role. Most teachers care about what happens to their students. But if the expectation is that we should identify emotional distress, provide career guidance, handle academic problems and support students through personal crises, then the institution also has to give teachers training and a proper support structure.”
The experiences of both students and teachers point to a larger structural problem.When colleges rely on individual teachers to enforce academic rules, handle administrative requirements, guide students through careers and respond to emotional distress, the teacher becomes the point where multiple pressures meet.The solution therefore cannot rest entirely on individual faculty members.As colleges respond to changing job markets and rising student pressures, the system would require clearer boundaries for faculty responsibilities, greater flexibility for final-year students navigating legitimate career opportunities, and stronger professional support systems.For the teacher standing at the front of the classroom, the challenge is no longer simply teaching the subject. It is managing everything that happens around it, often without the authority, time or institutional support required to do so.

Her stories explore how policy, technology, economic shifts and social change influence people's everyday lives. Her work also focuses on bringing depth, context and a human perspective to complex issues.
Her reports primarily cover society, healthcare, safety, public policy and emerging trends, alongside other political developments.

Houthis blame Saudi air strikes as loud blasts rock Yemen's capital Sanaa
Houthi-linked media reported "Saudi aggession" on Saturday after loud explosions rocked the Yemeni capital Sanaa, which is controlled by the Iran-backed rebel group. Earlier this week, the Houthis accused Saudi Arabia of bombing Sanaa for the first time since renewed fighting broke out between the two sides in July.
Loud explosions were heard in the Yemeni capital of Sanaa on Saturday, as the Houthis reported air strikes in the area by Saudi forces.
One correspondent heard at least five blasts in different areas, while another saw two warplanes firing missiles on the city.
Al-Masirah TV, a Houthi-affiliated media outlet, reported "Saudi aggression" against the capital, without providing details on the targets or casualties.
The channel had also earlier on Saturday reported missile strikes on the telecommunications network in the northwestern governorate of Saada, a Houthi stronghold.
Saudi Arabia bombed the Yemeni capital on Thursday night for the first time since renewed fighting broke out between the two sides in July, the Houthis claimed.
After several years of calm, Yemen was plunged back into civil war in July, pitting the Iran-backed Houthis, who control most of northwest Yemen including Sanaa, against Yemen's internationally recognised government, which is backed by neighbouring Saudi Arabia.
The government, based in the city of Aden, controls much of the country's south and east – a region that is larger but less populated.
Hostilities were reignited after fours years of a fragile truce when Iran sent a plane to Sanaa carrying a Houthi delegation.
The flight did not seek authorisation from Saudi Arabia, contravening a practice in place for a decade.
Riyadh retaliated with strikes on Sanaa airport, and in response the Houthis attacked Saudi territory for the first time since 2022.
Read moreSaudi-led coalition accuses Houthis of striking Medina power station
Since then, fighting has intensified with the Houthis launching a lightning offensive which saw them seize control of coastal regions along the strategic Bab al-Mandab strait.
They have also struck multiple Saudi targets including oil infrastructure and the capital Riyadh while also announcing a naval blockade on Saudi ships in the Red Sea.
Flames and smoke were seen rising from a facility belonging to Saudi oil giant Aramco south of the kingdom's capital Riyadh on Saturday, an AFP journalist said.
The circumstances remained unclear but in recent weeks Aramco, majority-owned by the Saudi state, has come under attack from the Houthis.
Both the Houthis and Saudi authorities had yet to comment on the incident.
Battle for Taiz
Fighting in recent days has centred on Taiz, where 80 combatants in the conflict were reported dead on Friday by sources on both sides.
The Houthis reported 55 of their fighters had been killed while government sources told AFP that 26 troops had died.
The battle for Taiz is taking place on several fronts, including highlands overlooking coastal areas recently seized by the Houthis.
While the Houthis have conquered swaths of territory, they have yet to wrest control of Taiz city, which is Yemen's third-largest after Sanaa and Aden.
The Houthis also on Friday said Saudi Arabia had launched 94 strikes against areas under their control in the past 24 hours.
Saudi authorities meanwhile reported a Houthi projectile had damaged a school in the city of Najran near the Yemen border.
Riyadh has reportedly requested help from the United States, a call so far rebuffed by US President Donald Trump.
On Saturday US media outlet Axios reported that top cabinet members in the Trump administration met the day before to discuss Yemen as well as the Iran conflict, citing three US officials.
The meeting was not officially announced.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

Israeli forces attempt assassination of senior Hamas leader in Gaza

Uganda’s UN-supported wildlife forensics lab turns ivory seizures into convictions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-03
12:00:00 UTC
21:00:00 KST

Uganda’s UN-supported wildlife forensics lab turns ivory seizures into convictions
The package originated in Entebbe, Uganda, bound for Cairo, containing 10 kilograms of thumb-sized pieces that could have been either bone or elephant ivory.
When detectives from the Uganda Police Force and investigators from the Uganda Wildlife Authority intercepted the package in January 2025, they needed more than suspicion to investigate the person who sent the package.
The police sent a sample to the Uganda Wildlife Forensics and Timber Laboratory in Entebbe, a facility that has been supported since 2019 by the UN Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC).
Scientists found a distinctive cross-hatched pattern associated with elephant ivory. DNA testing later confirmed that the material came from an elephant, lab manager Patrick Chiyo told UN News.
Two months later, police arrested the man who sent the package. At his residence, investigators found additional elephant ivory, along with warthog ivory. He was charged with attempted trafficking and illegal possession and sentenced to 15 years in prison or a fine equivalent to 140 million Ugandan shillings – or more than $35,000 USD.
For Mr. Chiyo, the case illustrates why forensic evidence matters in the fight against wildlife crime: it can establish what an animal product is when traffickers have cut it into small pieces or removed the physical characteristics that would make it easy to identify.
“Poachers are removing identification features from wildlife carcasses to evade detection,” Mr. Chiyo said.
He added that DNA reports are increasingly being required by Uganda’s wildlife court and that suspects are pleading guilty more often thanks to the lab.
From seizure to science
Evidence from the UN’s 2024 World Wildlife Report shows that Uganda is as a significant hub of organised wildlife trafficking networks – especially of elephant ivory but also pangolin, a scaly anteater.
In April, the Uganda Wildlife Forensics and Timber Laboratory opened with support from Denmark, the European Union and UNODC to help address the ivory issue.
It builds on a national training and technical support centre established in 2019 as a pilot wildlife forensics facility through a partnership involving UNODC, the TRACE Wildlife Forensics Network and the Ugandan Government. The earlier facility has assisted hundreds of investigations and prosecutions connected to illegal wildlife trade.
The lab’s work often begins far from Entebbe. Officers may seize sacks containing ivory pieces, pangolin scales or smoked bushmeat. Because these seizures can be bulky, scientists collect samples at police stations, documenting each step along the way.
Evidence is photographed before it is opened, and again after sampling. The original exhibit is returned to police custody, while sealed samples are transported to the lab for analysis.
The process can take a significant amount of time, Mr. Chiyo said, but it can be decisive, especially when animal remains are incomplete, altered or difficult to identify.
In one case in 2023, Mr. Chiyo travelled about four hours north of Kampala after a suspect was arrested with six skins, six heads, two sacks of meat, 24 hoofed legs and a fetus believed to be from wildlife. The skins appeared to come from antelope, but their exact identity could not be confirmed from appearance alone.
Mr. Chiyo and his team collected samples from the skins and fetus, then used DNA analysis to determine that they came from bushbucks. Mr. Chiyo later testified in court, and the suspect was sentenced to three years in prison.
Targeting wildlife crime
The lab most commonly receives evidence involving elephant ivory, bushmeat and pangolin scales, Mr. Chiyo said.
Bashir Hangi, from the Uganda Wildlife Authority, told UN News that elephants, pangolins, primates and some bird species are among the animals most threatened by illegal poaching and trade in Uganda.
Some people hunt animals for household consumption, while others kill wildlife for commercial gain, Mr. Chiyo said. Commercial trade is the larger threat for wildlife conservation, he added.
Although Mr. Chiyo said Uganda does not have a domestic market for ivory and pangolin scales, there is a thriving market for poached bushmeat. Authorities have encountered cases involving nearly a tonne of meat, he said.
Mr. Hangi said wildlife crime is driven both by organised criminal networks and by local communities facing economic hardship.
The impacts can also fall heavily on communities living near protected areas, where wildlife-related conflict and crop raiding have caused significant problems.
Mr. Chiyo said enforcement must reach the person who kills or captures an animal and those higher up in criminal networks who also profit. Prosecuting higher-ups requires more investment in interagency networks, he added.
At the same time, he said, criminal justice is not enough. Alternative livelihoods are important, although they may not eliminate poaching linked to cultural values. He suggested a combined approach of livelihood support, preventive patrols and legal deterrence.
“A living wildlife is worth more benefits for many more people than a dead one,” Mr. Chiyo said.
New focus on timber
The Entebbe lab expanded into timber forensics in April, adding a new capability as Uganda confronts the environmental consequences of illegal logging and timber trafficking.
According to Ugandan authorities, Uganda’s forest cover has fallen from 24 per cent in 1990 to roughly 13 per cent in 2025, in large part due to timber trafficking. The new forensic capacity is intended to strengthen efforts to investigate illegal logging.
Timber cases are more complicated than wildlife cases, Mr. Chiyo said, because harvesting is also permitted and regulated in many circumstances. Determining whether a piece of wood was obtained illegally can require additional steps and presents different challenges from identifying animal products.
The lab is only beginning to handle timber cases and has not yet seen evidence that illegal timber is moving through the same networks or routes as wildlife products, he said.
Critical for conservation
Still, the lab’s expansion reflects an increased recognition of the role of cracking down on wildlife and timber trafficking on protecting the environment.
Gladys Kamasanyu, the chief magistrate of the Uganda Wildlife Court, told UNODC in April that criminal justice and law enforcement can play a key role in these efforts.
“The forensic laboratory is critical to the criminal justice system, significantly enhancing the court’s ability to hold offenders accountable by providing objective, scientifically validated evidence to protect Uganda’s natural heritage for future generations,” Ms. Kamasanyu said.
Recognising the same relationship between law enforcement and conservation, Mr. Chiyo said his benchmark for success in the next few years would be “a sustainable and fully government supported wildlife and timber forensic laboratory in Uganda.”
At the current lab, however, each confirmed DNA sequence and seizure can help close the gap between a suspicion of trafficking and a prosecutable crime.
“Enhancing criminal justice through wildlife and timber forensics is an important pillar in environment protection,” Mr. Chiyo said. “Environmental justice will usually benefit the very vulnerable in society.”
